title: gcp-cloud-run: a remote asset download can hang a render forever on Bun 1.3.9 (Readable.fromWeb stalls; the download timeout never fires)
body:
### Describe the bug

On the Google Cloud Run image, a render request sometimes hangs until the platform request timeout, with no error and no timeout log. The cause is a remote asset download that never settles.

The image (`packages/gcp-cloud-run/Dockerfile`) installs Bun 1.3.9 and runs `bun dist/server.js`. Every remote asset goes through `downloadToTemp` in `packages/engine/src/utils/urlDownloader.ts`. `fetchToPartial` streams the body with:

```ts
await pipeline(Readable.fromWeb(response.body), inspector, createWriteStream(partialPath, { flags: "wx" }));
```

On Bun 1.3.9, under a burst of parallel downloads, the `Readable.fromWeb` bridge occasionally stops reading in the middle of a body. The attempt's `AbortController` deadline (300s by default) then aborts the fetch, but the abort never reaches the pipeline. The `pipeline` promise never resolves or rejects, so `runDownloadAttempt` never gets to its timeout or retry path. This is Bun's `Readable.fromWeb` error and cancel propagation bug, oven-sh/bun#34559, fixed in Bun 1.4.0 (oven-sh/bun#32863, #33300, #34025).

In a Cloud Run deployment of the producer, about 6% of `plan` requests hung for the full 60-minute Cloud Run request timeout. Each plan downloads about 25 remote assets in parallel, and the hangs start within seconds of `handler_start`, during that burst. Nothing was logged between `handler_start` and the platform's 504. A retry of the same render on another instance finished in about 20s. About 0.3% of `renderChunk` requests also hung. That path downloads from GCS rather than through `downloadToTemp`, so I have not tied those hangs to this bug, though the Bun bump may cover them too.

There is a second, smaller problem on Bun 1.4.2. If a body stalls mid-stream and the fetch is aborted, Bun 1.4.2 ends the web stream as if it were complete, so the same `pipeline` **resolves** with a truncated file. Node and Bun 1.3.9 reject with `AbortError`. The downloader's `Content-Length` check catches that when the server sends a length. A chunked or content-encoded response has no length to check, so the truncated file would be published.

### Link to reproduction

https://github.com/ArcadeHQ/hyperframes-repros/tree/patch/bun-fromweb-download-stall

### Steps to reproduce

The repro has no HyperFrames code. `repro/download-stall.ts` uses the same body-consumption shape as `fetchToPartial`, against a local HTTPS server. Each round starts 11 parallel downloads and aborts every fetch at 3s. A download still pending at 8s never settled after its abort.

1. `git checkout patch/bun-fromweb-download-stall`
2. `./repro/setup-cert.sh` (a throwaway self-signed cert for 127.0.0.1)
3. `node repro/server.mjs &`
4. `export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`
5. `bunx bun@1.3.9 repro/download-stall.ts fromweb` (exits 1 when any download hangs)
6. `bunx bun@1.4.2 repro/download-stall.ts fromweb` and `node repro/download-stall.ts fromweb` (exit 0)
7. `bunx bun@1.3.9 repro/download-stall.ts signal`: the same code with `pipeline(..., { signal })`
8. For the second problem: `bunx bun@1.4.2 repro/abort-resolves.mjs` against `node repro/abort-resolves.mjs`

### Expected behavior

Every download either completes or rejects soon after its fetch is aborted. In HyperFrames terms, a stalled download becomes a `timeout` attempt failure and a retry, never a request that waits forever.

### Actual behavior

Measured on macOS arm64. Each run is 200 rounds, which is 2,200 downloads. Hung downloads out of the total:

| Runtime | `fromweb` (the downloader's shape) | `signal` (`fromweb` plus `pipeline(..., { signal })`) | `reader` (`getReader()` loop, control) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bun 1.3.9 | **16 / 6,600** (3 runs: 6, 2, 8) | 0 / 4,400 (10 rejected with `AbortError`) | 0 / 2,200 |
| Bun 1.4.2 | 0 / 4,400 | — | — |
| Node 24.21 | 0 / 2,200 | — | — |

A hung round prints:

```
  round 38: 1 download(s) still pending 8000ms after start (fetch aborted at 3000ms): sizes 385068
bun 1.3.9 mode=fromweb downloads=2200: ok=2194 rejected=0 hung=6
```

Second problem (`repro/abort-resolves.mjs`: 10 KB, then the body stalls; abort at 1s):

```
bun 1.3.9 chunked: rejected: AbortError
node v24.21.0 chunked: rejected: AbortError
bun 1.4.2 chunked: RESOLVED after abort, 10000 bytes on disk (expected a rejection)
```

### Environment

```shell
hyperframes doctor

  ✓ Version          0.8.65 (latest)
  ✓ Node.js          v24.21.0 (darwin arm64)
  ✓ CPU              10 cores · Apple M1 Pro @ 2400MHz
  ✓ Memory           16.0 GB total · 2.4 GB available
  ✓ Disk             229.3 GB free
  ✓ Frames cache     $TMPDIR/hyperframes-extract-cache-501 · 229.3 GB free · default
  ✓ Archive extractor unzip
  ✓ Environment      non-TTY
  ✓ whisper-cpp      /opt/homebrew/bin/whisper-cli
  ✗ TTS (Kokoro)     Not installed (optional — local voice fallback)
  ✗ BGM (MusicGen)   Not installed (optional — local music fallback)
  ✓ onnxruntime-node Not installed (installs on first use)
  ✓ @google/genai    Not installed (installs on first use)
  ✓ FFmpeg           ffmpeg 9.0.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin/ffmpeg
  ✓ FFprobe          ffprobe 9.0.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin/ffprobe
  ✓ Chrome           cache: ~/.cache/puppeteer/chrome-headless-shell/mac_arm-152.0.7977.54/…
  ✗ Docker           Not found
  ✗ Docker running   Not running
```

Runtimes under test: Bun 1.3.9 (the Cloud Run image's pin) and Bun 1.4.2 via `bunx bun@<version>`, and Node v24.21.0. The production hangs were on the Linux Cloud Run image. The measured repro is on macOS; I did not run it inside the Linux image (no Docker on this machine).

### Additional context

Proposed fix, in two independent parts:

1. **Bump the Cloud Run image to Bun 1.4.2**, the one `bun-v1.3.9` line in `packages/gcp-cloud-run/Dockerfile`. This removes the stall. The server bundle builds and `bun dist/server.js` starts and answers under 1.4.2, and `packages/gcp-cloud-run` tests pass (101). The AWS Lambda adapter runs on the `nodejs22.x` runtime, and CI's `setup-bun` already uses the latest Bun, so neither is affected. `Dockerfile.test` pins Bun 1.3.13 for the regression image only.
2. **Make the attempt deadline authoritative:** `pipeline(readableStream, inspector, fileStream, { signal: controller.signal })` in `fetchToPartial`. The abort then rejects the pipeline on every runtime, whatever the web-to-Node bridge does. On Bun 1.3.9 a stall becomes a logged timeout and a retry instead of a hang. On Bun 1.4.2 an aborted chunked body is no longer published truncated.

`downloadToTemp` is the only `Readable.fromWeb` user in `packages/*/src`. `fetchPublicHttpsText` reads with `getReader()` and is not affected.

PR to follow.

title: fix: a stalled remote asset download no longer hangs a Cloud Run render
body:
## What

A stalled remote asset download can no longer hang a Cloud Run render. The PR has two commits that are independent of each other:

1. `fix(gcp-cloud-run)`: the Cloud Run image installs Bun **1.4.2** instead of 1.3.9. This is the one `bun-v1.3.9` line in `packages/gcp-cloud-run/Dockerfile`.
2. `fix(engine)`: `fetchToPartial` in `packages/engine/src/utils/urlDownloader.ts` passes the attempt's abort signal to the body pipeline, so the attempt deadline always ends the attempt:

```diff
-  await pipeline(readableStream, inspector, fileStream);
+  await pipeline(readableStream, inspector, fileStream, { signal: controller.signal });
```

## Why

The downloader streams every remote asset with `pipeline(Readable.fromWeb(response.body), inspector, fileStream)`. Its deadline only aborted the fetch. It then relied on the web-to-Node bridge to pass the abort on to the pipeline.

- **Bun 1.3.9** (the image's pin): under a burst of parallel downloads, `Readable.fromWeb` sometimes stops reading mid-body and never passes the abort on (oven-sh/bun#34559, fixed in Bun 1.4.0). The pipeline never settles, so the attempt never reaches its timeout or retry path. In a Cloud Run deployment of the producer, about 6% of `plan` requests hung this way until the 60-minute request timeout, with nothing logged. A retry of the same render finished in about 20s.
- **Bun 1.4.2**: the stall is gone. But when a body stalls and the fetch is aborted, Bun 1.4.2 ends the stream as if it were complete, so the pipeline *resolves* with a truncated file. Node rejects with `AbortError`. A `Content-Length` response is still rejected by the length check. A chunked or content-encoded response has no length to check, so the truncated file was published.

The first commit removes the cause. The second makes the deadline hold whatever the runtime's bridge does: on 1.3.9 a stall becomes a logged `timeout` and a retry, and on 1.4.2 an aborted chunked body is never published. Each commit helps on its own. Together they cover both runtimes.

Repro (no HyperFrames code): https://github.com/ArcadeHQ/hyperframes-repros/tree/patch/bun-fromweb-download-stall

## How

- `packages/gcp-cloud-run/Dockerfile`: `bun-v1.3.9` → `bun-v1.4.2`. The comment above it still applies: the pin stays deliberate. The other Bun pins stay as they are. CI's `setup-bun` has no version, so CI already runs the latest Bun. The AWS Lambda adapter runs on `nodejs22.x`. `Dockerfile.test` (Bun 1.3.13) builds the regression-test image and does not serve renders.
- `urlDownloader.ts`: `{ signal: controller.signal }` on the `pipeline` call, with a comment on why.
- `urlDownloader.test.ts`, next to the existing "keeps the deadline active through a stalled response body" test:
  - "keeps the deadline active when a stalled body never observes the abort": the first body enqueues a chunk and then neither ends nor errors, even on abort, which is what the 1.3.9 bridge does. The download must time out, retry, and publish the second response.
  - "does not publish a chunked body that ended because the deadline aborted it": the first body closes cleanly when the fetch is aborted and has no `Content-Length`, which is what 1.4.2 does. It must not be published, and the retry's bytes must be.

## Verification

- Repro loop, 11 parallel HTTPS downloads per round, every fetch aborted at 3s. Hung downloads out of the total:
  - The downloader's shape: Bun 1.3.9 hung **16 / 6,600** over three runs. Bun 1.4.2 hung 0 / 4,400, and Node 24.21 0 / 2,200.
  - The same with `pipeline(..., { signal })` on Bun 1.3.9: 0 / 4,400 (10 stalls rejected with `AbortError` instead).
- `bunx vitest run src/utils/urlDownloader.test.ts` in `packages/engine`: 82 pass. With the `urlDownloader.ts` change reverted, both new tests fail. The stalled one hits the 5s test timeout, and the chunked one publishes `partial` after one fetch. The existing tests pass either way. The file also passes under Bun (`bun --bun x vitest run`, 1.4.2).
- `bun run --cwd packages/engine typecheck`: clean. `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on the touched files: clean. `bun run check:gcp-cloud-run-dockerfile`: passes.
- Bun 1.4.2 image path, without Docker: `bun install --frozen-lockfile` and every build step of the Dockerfile's runtime stage passed under 1.4.2. Then `PORT=18080 bun dist/server.js` started and logged `server_listening`, and `GET /healthz` returned `{"status":"ok"}`. A `POST /` reached the action dispatcher. The built `@hyperframes/producer/dist/distributed.js` also imports under 1.4.2 with `plan`, `renderChunk` and `assemble` present. `bun test` in `packages/gcp-cloud-run`: 101 pass.
- About 220 repeated runs of this test file or of its three stalled-body tests (the existing one and the two new ones), some with 8 in parallel: one run had one failure that I could not reproduce or attribute. The new tests use a real 20ms deadline for each attempt, like the existing test, so a very slow retry could trip it.
- Not run: `docker build` of the image, and a real render on Cloud Run with 1.4.2. The repro was measured on macOS, not in the Linux image.

Compatible with #4190: that PR holds the 1s attempt deadline in this test file, and the new tests use 20ms like the existing stalled-body test, so their timers stay real.

Closes #4342

title: fix(cli): keep live reload working after an atomic save on Linux
body:
## What this fixes

On Linux, Studio's live reload goes deaf for a file once that file has been replaced by rename. After that, no edit to it, in place or by another rename, reaches the preview until the server restarts.

Renames are common:
- editors save atomically (write a temp file, rename it over the original)
- Studio's first open stamps ids into every file the same way
- coding agents often write by rename

A minimal Node repro on Linux (Node 22.22.1):

```
1 in-place write:        change index.html, change index.html
2 replace by rename:     change index.html (x3)
3 in-place write:        NO EVENT
4 in-place write:        NO EVENT
```

## Root cause

`fs.watch(dir, { recursive: true })` on Linux is emulated in JavaScript by Node (`lib/internal/fs/recursive_watch.js`):
- It opens an inotify watch on each file (`#watchFile` calls `watch(file)`).
- inotify follows the inode, not the path. After a rename-replace, the watch stays on the old, unlinked inode.
- The callback's `statSync` still finds a file at that path, so Node never re-arms the watch.
- Its directory rescan (`#watchFolder`) skips paths it has already seen, so the new inode is never watched.

## What changed

`packages/cli/src/server/fileWatcher.ts` now watches the project tree itself instead of asking Node for `recursive`, on Linux only:
- **One non-recursive watch per directory.** A directory's inotify watch reports its children by name, so rename-replace and in-place writes are both seen. It also needs far fewer inotify watches than one per file.
- **Scope.** It descends into every directory the watcher already cares about (`shouldWatchProjectFile`), plus `.hyperframes/` itself for Studio's two manifest files, not below it.
- **Changing tree.** New directories are watched as they appear, and removed ones are dropped with their subtree.
- **Failures.** A subdirectory that cannot be watched (EACCES, inotify limit) is skipped; it no longer costs the rest of the tree.
- **Other platforms.** macOS and Windows keep Node's native recursive watch, whose OS APIs track paths and don't have this problem.
- **Unchanged:** the filtering, the debounce and what reaches Studio.

I chose per-directory watching rather than a periodic rescan, because it fixes the cause (the watch follows the directory, not the replaced inode) and has no polling delay or cost.

## Tests

- **New `fileWatcher.fs.test.ts`**, on real files with no fs mock:
  - a root file and a nested scene each go through rename-replace, then an in-place write, then rename-replace again
  - a directory created after start
  - a write to `.hyperframes/studio-motion.json`
  - a sibling whose name starts with a removed directory's
  On Linux it fails on main with `expected [] to include 'index.html'`, and passes with this change, 10/10 on repeat.
- **New mocked test:** one subdirectory whose `watch()` throws ENOSPC still leaves the rest of the tree watched and closable.
- **Proven non-vacuous.**
  - Removing the `.hyperframes` case fails the manifest test.
  - Changing the subtree prefix match to drop the separator fails the sibling test.
  - Removing the subdirectory guard fails the ENOSPC test.
- **Checks.** `tsc`, oxfmt and oxlint are clean for cli. Each test file was run alone on Linux.

## Not exercised

- **The project root itself replaced by rename** (for example, the whole folder swapped by a tool). On Linux the watcher is still blind to that, exactly as Node's own emulation was on main; macOS survives it. Nothing here makes it worse.
- **Files created in a brand-new directory before its watch is armed.** The directory itself is reported, so the preview reloads anyway.
- **macOS and Windows.** Unchanged code path. The fs tests pass there without exercising the Linux branch.

title: perf(cli): tell the preview about a file edit 30 ms after it lands, not 300
body:
## What this fixes

Every on-disk edit waited for 300 ms of quiet before the preview server told Studio about it. On a one-scene edit that is 300 ms of pure waiting, before any rebuild or reload starts; about a third of what was left of edit-to-screen on a fast build.

## What changed

`packages/cli/src/server/fileWatcher.ts`:
- **A save** now reaches Studio 30 ms after the writes go quiet. webpack's default aggregate timeout is 20 ms.
- **At most one flush every 300 ms.** A checkout or a tool writing many files still coalesces instead of starting a preview rebuild per file. A save that lands late in that window waits only for what's left of it.

Nothing else changes: the same filter and the same events.

## Measured

Same run, interleaved, 4 rounds, on a quiet 32-core Linux box (measured at the previous commit of this branch; the throttle only changes saves within 300 ms of an earlier flush, and every edit here comes after a longer quiet). One on-disk edit to one scene of a 12-scene, 60 s fixture project (text, colour and timing edits); headless Chrome. Median of 12 edits per build:

| Edit to new pixels on screen | without this PR | with this PR |
|---|---|---|
| main | 2.08 s | **1.90 s** |
| main + the pending preview-assets change | 1.09 s | **0.85 s** |

In a hop-by-hop profile, the `file-change` event now reaches the browser 33-57 ms after the write, against 303-307 ms before.

## Tests

`fileWatcher.test.ts`, run alone: 5/5.
- The burst test now pins delivery time: nothing at 29 ms, delivered at 30 ms. It fails on main.
- New: "flushes at most once per 300 ms while writes keep coming". It fails with no throttle (3 flushes instead of 1), and fails if a save late in the window has to wait a full 300 ms.
- `tsc`, oxfmt and oxlint are clean for cli.

## Not exercised

- **A file written in chunks more than 30 ms apart** (a slow copy of a large asset) can be read once before it is complete. The next event reloads it, and the throttle limits this to one early read per 300 ms. 300 ms never guaranteed a complete write either.
- **A save right after another flush** waits up to 300 ms minus the time since that flush; never more than before.
- **macOS and Windows** event shapes, not measured here.

title: feat(registry): cocoa powder dissolving in milk, with an optional maths view
body:
## What this adds

A new catalog block, `powder-dissolve`: a spoonful of cocoa lands on milk seen from above, floats dry and pale, wets through from its edges and along cracks in the crust, then its colour reaches out in dark fingers and blooms into marbled clouds until the milk is one even chocolate tint. The motion slows to near stillness, so it works as a calm background.

What you can change:

- **Powder colour** and **milk colour** (matcha on oat milk works too). The powder tints the milk by absorbing light, so pick a powder darker than the milk; a pale powder barely shows once dissolved, as in real life.
- **Dissolve duration**, 3 to 30 s. A longer dissolve plays out in full when the clip is longer than the default 10 s.
- **Show the maths** (off by default). A panel with the equations that drive each phase: landing, heap and noise field, wetting front, diffusion, crust cracks, fingers, tint mix. The phase happening now is in full ink, finished phases are dimmed, later ones stay hidden, and each shows its live value (landing progress, wet %, front radius in px, finger strength, tint %). Every line is something the code computes.

## Why every frame renders on its own

Every frame is a pure function of time: the clump layout comes from a fixed seed, grain and noise from position hashes, and the spreading colour from the closed-form solution of diffusion (a Gaussian convolved with a Gaussian stays a Gaussian), so frame N never reads frame N-1.

Checked on a Linux box with the repo CLI (`--format png-sequence`, 1 worker vs 4 workers, byte for byte):

- Default look: 100 of 100 frames identical, and 30 of 30 again after the review fixes.
- Maths on: 30 of 30 identical in each of three runs.
- The same check on a copy with `Math.random()` injected: 20 of 20 frames differ, so the check can fail.
- Rendered frames against a Studio-style preview (the same font injection and the renderer's Chrome text flags): the effect is identical pixel for pixel; panel text matches in layout, with small antialiasing differences at glyph edges that an existing text-only catalog block shows too.
- `lint-registry-items`: 0 errors. `hyperframes lint`: 0 errors, 1 warning (file length). `oxfmt --check`: clean.

The maths panel uses only fonts the renderer supplies itself (EB Garamond and Inter), with no web-font link: a link declared after the renderer's own font faces can override them whenever it loads in time, which made early frames differ between workers. Every character in the panel was checked against the font files the renderer actually embeds.

## Source files only

This PR adds only `registry/blocks/powder-dissolve/{powder-dissolve.html, registry-item.json}`. The generated catalog files (registry index, search vectors, payload, docs page) are left to the catalog automation in #4337. The preview video and poster use the standard CDN paths and still need uploading; the preview should be the maths version.

Pattern: raw WebGL1 full-screen fragment shader like `registry/blocks/domain-warp-dissolve`, with the repaint on a GSAP-tweened property setter like `registry/blocks/spiral-galaxy`, so seeking repaints too.

## Before

Searching the catalog for "powder dissolve" finds only unrelated dissolve transitions:

![Before: catalog search for powder dissolve](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/11fb74c2-c518-4d97-9188-0ad3482d2a78)

## After

Default look (0.3 s landing, 1.2 s floating, 2.5 s wetting and cracks, 3.5 s fingers, 4.5 s bloom, 9 s even tint):

![After: default look over time](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/739eb873-708d-438a-8cd1-964b6fe68515)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5780d83a-d306-4b6a-a653-4c598c4ed777

Maths on:

![After: maths on over time](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1b5598b4-29fb-4f91-8cba-8d84114d40d1)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b6eff2eb-61d4-4fa8-b491-f1dc7c1d3c8a

## Review

An independent adversarial review ran against this branch. Findings and their fixes:

- **Blocker, fixed:** with the maths panel on, 1-worker and 4-worker renders could differ in the first frames' text, because the Google Fonts link overrode the renderer's own font faces when it loaded in time. The link is gone and the panel uses fonts the renderer supplies.
- **Major, fixed:** the panel left out terms the code computes (the extra wetting paths and the marbling step). It now shows them.
- **Major, fixed:** an empty dissolve value (`null`) was read as 0 and clamped to 3 s instead of the default 8 s.
- **Major, documented:** a pale powder barely tints the milk; the powder colour's description says to pick one darker than the milk.
- **Major, out of scope here:** wrong-typed values given to `hyperframes add --vars` are not checked for boolean, colour or string variables. Follow-up in its own PR.
- **Minors, fixed:** 3-digit hex colours, defaults kept in one place in the file, missing constants in the panel text.

| Audited | Trusting | Not exercised |
|---|---|---|
| Shader edge cases (pow, log, division, loop bounds), variable parsing, schema and consumers of every variable, 1 vs 4 workers with maths on and off, forward vs reverse seeking, NaN and infinite seeks, lint and format | That the font copies the renderer downloads stay the same between days (the fetch happens once per render, before the work is split across workers) | Real GPUs (all rendering here used software GL) |

title: fix(producer): contain render output paths and restrict previewUrl to loopback
body:
## What

The producer's HTTP render API took two unvalidated inputs from the request body: `outputPath`, the file the finished render gets written to, and `previewUrl`, a URL whose response body becomes the render source. Nothing checked where `outputPath` landed, so a caller could name any path on disk the server can write, and `previewUrl` was fetched verbatim, whatever host it pointed at. This change rejects explicit output paths that resolve outside the producer's renders directory, anchors bare filenames to the renders directory instead of the process working directory, and restricts `previewUrl` to loopback hosts unless an environment variable extends it. Studio and CLI renders are untouched; they run in-process and never go through this HTTP surface.

## Why

The render handlers are unauthenticated by design, and `startServer()` binds every interface by default because `@hono/node-server` is called without a hostname. That combination turned the two inputs into direct primitives. For `outputPath`, the flow is: the handlers write the encoded video to the caller-supplied path, register it in the artifact store, and `GET /outputs/:token` streams the file back to whoever presents the token. A request naming a path outside the renders directory gets the server to create directories and write attacker-chosen content anywhere the process can write, and the response confirms the write by returning the absolute path.

`previewUrl` is a read primitive. The server fetches the URL and embeds the response into the render project, and the render output (or the error text) comes back to the same caller, so a request pointing at an internal service returns a readable rendering of that service's response. There was no scheme or host check at all; the only thing stopping `file://` was undici's own refusal, which is incidental rather than a boundary the server states.

While testing I found a smaller bug in the same spot: a bare filename like `out.mp4` was resolved against the process working directory, so `outputPath: "out.mp4"` landed wherever the server happened to be started from, outside the renders directory that the default path (no `outputPath`) always uses. That behavior is fixed here too.

On the legitimate side: Studio renders and CLI renders both call `createRenderJob`/`executeRenderJob` directly in-process and build their output paths server-side, so neither goes through this API. The parity harness passes `previewUrl` to a browser for screenshot capture; it never posts it to the render endpoint. I found no in-repo consumer that posts either field, and the loopback rule matches the endpoint's actual purpose, which is rendering the co-located preview server's output. For deployments that do want other hosts, `PRODUCER_PREVIEW_HOST_ALLOWLIST` (comma-separated hostnames) extends the rule explicitly.

## How

Output path containment lives in `resolvePreparedRenderOutput`, which both the sync and the SSE handler already share. A new `validateRenderOutputPath` runs before resolution: a candidate with no path separators and no absolute form is treated as a bare filename and allowed, since it now joins the renders directory; anything else must resolve inside the renders directory, checked with the same `path.relative` plus `isAbsolute` containment pattern the repo uses elsewhere (`isWithinProjectRoot` in the parsers package, the `resolveWithinProject` chokepoint from #1477). On violation the sync handler answers 400 and the SSE handler emits a validation error event, matching how `prepareRenderBody` errors already surface. The existing fallback in `resolveOutputPath`, a safe `producer-fallback-*.mp4` when resolution fails for other reasons, is unchanged.

The bare filename fix sits in `resolveRenderPaths` in `packages/producer/src/utils/paths.ts`, since that is the single place that owns the relationship between `outputPath`, the renders directory, and the default `<projectName>.mp4` name. Bare filenames now join the renders directory; relative paths with separators and absolute paths behave as before, except that they must land inside the renders directory.

The `previewUrl` guard is a small exported function, `validatePreviewUrl`, called by `resolveInlineRenderHtml` before the fetch. It requires http or https, requires the hostname to be `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `::1`, and otherwise accepts a hostname listed in `PRODUCER_PREVIEW_HOST_ALLOWLIST`:

```bash
PRODUCER_PREVIEW_HOST_ALLOWLIST="staging.example.com,render.internal" producer-server
```

One test-facing subtlety worth documenting: `resolveInlineRenderHtml` checks `body.html` before it ever looks at `body.previewUrl`, so a request carrying both silently renders the inline HTML. The guard tests post `previewUrl` on its own for that reason. I left that precedence alone since it is existing behavior with its own tests.

## Test plan

title: fix(skills): keep script imports inside installed skill directories
body:
Installed video skills failed to assemble because their imports reached into sibling skills and the repository's CLI source tree. The scripts now ship local copies generated from their existing owners. Assemblers import only the small music-volume policy, rather than the download providers.

A parser checks every published skill's literal relative imports. Copy parity and isolated-install tests guard the shipped modules, and skills failures now fail the required Test check. Packet tests verify module imports only; packet generation still uses its documented sibling resource files.

Restoring main's imports made five isolated-install tests fail, plus the boundary and parity checks. Formatting, lint, manifest and test reachability checks passed.

title: perf(studio): show a film's first frame sooner by loading preview assets by URL
body:
## Summary

On a cold open of a real 58 s film with about 25 MB of assets, Studio's Play button now enables and the film
starts playing about twice as fast. The preview document no longer inlines every image, video and font as
base64. It keeps the asset URLs and loads them from the preview asset route, like any web page.

## What changed

- A new `PREVIEW_BUNDLE_OPTIONS` (`inlineAssets: false`) is used by both Studio hosts: the CLI server
  and the vite dev adapter. Renders, export, validate and every other `bundleToSingleHtml` caller keep
  inlining, unchanged.
- A test covers the asset forms that must resolve through the preview's `<base>`: a video poster,
  `srcset`, a CSS `url()` in `@font-face`, and a nested sub-composition's asset.
- The asset route now serves every image and video of the preview, so its revalidation tag matters
  more. It used mtime and size. Two same-size writes inside one filesystem tick share an mtime, and
  copy tools (`cp -p`, rsync) set mtime back, so a browser could keep stale bytes after an edit.
- The route now tags a file by inode, change time and size, and only once its last change is at least
  3 s old. A younger file is served without a tag and refetched.
- On Windows, Node reads change time from NTFS `ChangeTime` (libuv `fs__stat_handle`), which
  `SetFileTime`, and so robocopy or PowerShell `LastWriteTime`, do not set back. The new real-file
  test (old mtime restored with `utimes`, no tag) runs on the Windows test lane too.

## Measured

Cold first open in Studio of a 58 s HyperFrames film (1.2 MB `index.html`, 25 PNGs of which 17 are over 0.5 MB, one 5 MB mp4).
Each open used a fresh `hyperframes preview` server, an empty browser profile, and deleted `.hyperframes`
and `.thumbnails`. This branch and its base (fb0d33c49) were interleaved, with the order flipped each
round, 3 opens each, in headless Chrome on a shared 8-core Linux box (load 8 to 10). Seconds from
navigation, median (range):

| | base fb0d33c49 | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| preview settled on the correct frame 0 | 23.3 (21.8-25.1) | 9.4 (8.2-10.6) |
| player reports its assets ready | 24.1 (22.2-25.8) | 9.8 (8.4-11.1) |
| server listening, from launch | 5.7 | 5.2 (not what this PR targets) |

This film's frame 0 is black (a render of it outside Studio is black too), so the first row is the moment
the preview settles on the right black frame, checked against the settled picture. The recordings below
measure what a person sees: the preview's pixels.

The earlier stress fixture (8 PNGs totalling about 12 MB, one 5 MB mp4, 60 s timeline) is a worst case for inlining.
On it, main didn't paint 3 of 5 cold opens within 60 s; this PR painted all 5, median 26.6 s.

Current main is slower than this PR's base for another reason. Since #4353, lint's source-location
mapping is quadratic, and `hyperframes preview` lints before it listens. On this film, main takes 43 to
53 s to listen and never paints within 60 s. That regression has its own fix in #4373; this PR doesn't
touch it.

### Where this sits in the load-time stack

The target is a cold first frame of about 0.3 s. This PR alone doesn't get there. Same film, same
method:

| Build | correct frame 0 | assets ready |
|---|---|---|
| base fb0d33c49 | 23.3 s | 24.1 s |
| this PR | 9.4 s | 9.8 s |
| this PR plus the rest of the load-time stack (follow-up PRs, one cause each) | 1.7 s (1.4-2.0) | 1.7 s |

The stack row comes from a separate run of 3 cold opens on the same box. Past 1.7 s, the remaining time is
Studio's own boot (about 0.5 s) plus parsing and running the whole film before frame 0 (about 1.1 s).
Reaching 0.3 s needs frame 0 to start without the whole film, and that isn't in any open PR.

## Tests

- The asset URL test: poster, srcset, `@font-face`, and a sub-composition.
- A file changed in the last moments gets no tag, including one whose mtime a copy tool set back
  (real file, `utimes`; fails if the tag goes back to mtime).
- The tag helper's settle window, and a file replaced at the same size and change time gets a new tag.
- The existing proxy revalidation tests run past the settle window.

## Before

Cold open of the film on this PR's base (fb0d33c49), recorded from the moment a fresh server listens, with
empty caches. Studio's Play button is clicked the moment it enables. The browser reaches the server through
an ssh tunnel, so both recordings run slower than the headless numbers above. Measured on the preview's
pixels: black until 18 s, then from 18 to 25 s a mid-film scene drawn at the wrong size with an empty
timeline (not frame 0). Play enables at 26.4 s and the film plays from about 27 s.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/24ff2212-d045-448d-94d6-8f5509efac14

## After

The same open on this branch, recorded right after the Before on the same machine. There is no
wrong-content flash. Play enables at 13.2 s and the film plays from 13 s; it reads 00:03 at 16 s and 00:09 at
22 s. Both recordings play the same pictures at the same pace once started.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ee8d5112-638a-485c-a3ce-1bb7fdc0ef14

## Not covered

- Pressing Space in the seconds before Play enables starts the film, and Studio's preview-load step then
  pauses it at 0. This is older than this PR and also happens on the base (about 1.4 s window there, about
  3.5 s here, because the frame's load event now waits for assets loaded by URL). It gets its own fix.

## Review notes

An independent adversarial review found no blocking or major issues. Three minor notes, none introduced
here:

- The asset route stats a file for its tag and again for its size. A rewrite between the two can pair
  new bytes with the older tag; the next request's tag then differs, so the browser refetches. It can't
  serve stale bytes.
- More assets now go through the asset route's in-project path check (lexical, like the renderer's
  file server, so an in-project symlink to a shared folder still works). Video already did; the route
  itself is unchanged.
- An edit that lands mid-load can show one asset a version behind until the next reload signal.

title: fix(producer): deterministic font faces win over later font stylesheets
body:
## What was wrong

When a composition also loads a font stylesheet (a Google Fonts `<link>`, or an `@import` that the compiler turns into one), that stylesheet could replace the deterministic fonts the renderer embeds. The deterministic `@font-face` rules were inserted as the first element of `<head>`. For the same family, the rule declared later wins, so whenever the network stylesheet had loaded in time, its faces drew the text instead. Which faces drew the early frames depended on network timing, so renders with different worker counts could differ in their text.

It is rare. A catalog item's review caught 8 of 30 frames differing between 1 and 4 workers; four reruns of the same item showed no difference.

## The fix

The deterministic font faces now go directly after the last stylesheet in the document (any `<style>` or `link[rel~=stylesheet]`, in the head or the body), and at the end of `<head>` when there is none. The same function prepares Studio's preview, so preview and render change together.

## Proof

- New test `deterministicFonts-order.test.ts`: the faces must follow a font link in the head and one in the body. Fails on main (0 of 2), passes with the fix (2 of 2). The other deterministic-font test files and `htmlCompiler.fontEmbed.test.ts` pass unchanged.
- Render check with the repo CLI on Linux. The fixture's `data:` stylesheet link redefines "Inter" as a local monospace font; it loads instantly, so on main it always wins:

![Before and after: a later stylesheet no longer replaces the deterministic Inter face](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5a702d04-fa88-49c8-96bd-a742dd865eab)

- Fixture with a real `fonts.googleapis.com` link, PNG sequence, 1 vs 4 workers, byte for byte: 20 of 20 frames identical both on main and with the fix. The race is too rare to show up in a short run, which is why the test above pins the ordering itself.

## Review

An independent adversarial review found no blockers and no majors. It reproduced the test results with two mutations: appending only to `<head>` fails the body-link case, and the original first-child placement fails both. Two minors, left as is:

- `link[rel~=stylesheet]` also matches inert links (`alternate stylesheet`, `media="print"`). Placing the faces after one of those is harmless, because they still come after every stylesheet that applies.
- Some checked-in `packages/producer/tests/*/output/compiled.html` baselines now differ from a fresh compile in where this style sits. Their comparator (`validateCompilation`) checks timing and structure, not head markup, so no test changes; the baselines can be regenerated separately.

Not covered: a stylesheet a script adds at runtime still lands after these faces in the cascade. A compile-time fix cannot reach that, and none of the fixtures do it.

title: fix(lint): report exact JS, CSS and GSAP source positions
body:
## What

Lint reports the offending JS token, CSS declaration/error, and supported GSAP call in the original source file instead of the beginning of a script snippet. Browser consumers use Acorn without `new Function` or server-side compilation.

## Why

Follow-up to #4353: a JS error on line 9 could report line 6, and CSS parser positions were discarded. HTML comment deletion and template unwrapping also made rule offsets differ from original-file offsets.

## How

Retain UTF-16 source mappings through the existing preprocessing, then attach rule-owned positions. PostCSS offsets retain external stylesheet identity. Acorn call evidence is cached per script; ambiguous aggregate font findings and unsupported call locations remain unlocated rather than guessed. Browser-safe parser imports avoid the existing Recast → Node `os` dependency.

The syntax check preserves the prior top-level-return handling and module skip. Two tested Acorn grammar differences are intentional: top-level `new.target` is rejected; a leading hashbang is accepted. This does not add runtime JS execution.

## Test plan

- [x] 698 lint tests and 17 CLI formatter tests pass; lint typecheck and oxlint pass.
- [x] Full workspace build passed; rebuilt parser/lint/CLI packages again after review corrections.
- [x] Full `hyperframes-launches` corpus pinned at `23f225fc550e94e907981b091fb4d3307602303d`: all 185 HTML files exercised. 683 applicable JS syntax / Math.random / GSAP / CSS injected-error position assertions pass; 57 cases have no eligible inline classic script/style block.
- [x] Actual rebuilt CLI from all 26 parent projects: 159 scanned HTML files (26 roots + 133 subcompositions), 633 exact file/line/column checks in both JSON and terminal output, including 529 subcomposition checks. All 26 projects restore identical baseline findings after mutation removal.
- [x] All 6 external CSS sources retain their own file identity and exact injected-error location. Unmodified diagnostic signatures on all 185 HTML files match published 0.8.67.
- [x] Separate font mutations on three complex fixtures: unique declaration located exactly; two aggregate multi-font diagnostics correctly omit a single location.
- [x] Fully bundled browser engine passes JS/CSS/GSAP diagnostics under CSP prohibiting eval and connections.
- [x] Original composition diagnostic signatures match published 0.8.67. Five-run median lint times before/after: connector 124/127 ms, inspector 1092/1082 ms, texture 100/106 ms (local measurements, not performance guarantees).
- [x] Independent review: no remaining actionable findings after correcting mixed-CR/LF CSS mapping and repeated Acorn parsing.
- [ ] Documentation updated (not applicable; existing line/column output contract retained).

The launch fixtures were copied for static linting; their scripts were not executed. Missing downloaded media and pre-existing composition findings are not claimed clean. Module GSAP call locations, multi-declaration aggregate locations and rules without exact evidence can remain file-level.

## Post-Deploy Monitoring & Validation

After release, rerun the pinned mutation fixtures with the published CLI and compare JSON and terminal positions. Wrong file/line, changed baseline findings or a browser CSP failure should block rollout of these coordinates. Home owns the first-release verification; no production service or DB change is involved.

title: fix(scripts): retry a fresh GitHub attachment's transient 404 in the captures gate
body:
## Why

Found while shipping #4325 this week: the captures gate 404'd on an asset I had just attached, on multiple consecutive reruns of the same identical payload, with the failing asset always being whichever one was uploaded most recently. Reran the exact same run without touching the PR — same asset, then a different asset, then it passed clean.

The gate already retries 429/5xx with backoff (`downloadAsset`), but treats every other status as final. A freshly uploaded `github.com/user-attachments/assets/*` URL can 404 for up to a few minutes before GitHub's read-path catches up with the write. That's a `NonRetryable` today, so it fails the check on the first attempt and forces a body edit → re-attach → wait cycle that itself risks losing the attachments (`--body-file` detaches them — a separate footgun, not this PR's problem).

## What changed

- `isRetryableStatus` now also retries a `404` when the URL is a GitHub attachment host (`isAttachmentUrl`, already used elsewhere in this file for the same host check). Any other host still fails a 404 on attempt 1 — a typo'd link or a deleted gist should not spend three minutes retrying.
- `403` stays non-retryable everywhere, attachment host included — it means something else (auth, an asset another workflow can't see), not propagation lag.
- Widened the retry window to match observed lag (up to ~3 min): 3 attempts → 5, delays `[1s, 3s]` → `[5s, 15s, 30s, 60s]`, deadline 45s → 180s.

## No visible change

`scripts/` only — this is the CI gate itself, not `packages/studio` or `packages/player`.

## Test plan

- Split the old combined "does not retry a 404 or 403" test: 403 stays its own test (still non-retryable); added a case where a 404 on the attachment host retries and succeeds on the third attempt with the new backoff delays; added a case where a 404 on a non-attachment host stays final on attempt 1.
- Updated the existing 5xx-backoff test's attempt count / delay assertions for the new constants.
- 73/73 tests green (`node --test scripts/check-pr-captures.test.mjs`), oxlint/oxfmt clean.

title: fix(studio-server): stop mislabeling two more read-route failure shapes
body:
## Why

Follow-up to #4325's stale-tree investigation, from probing the read route with every way a listing (`walkDir`) can show a path this route can't serve. Two of the shapes I generated to rule things out turned out to be genuine, separate mislabels.

**A path replaced by a directory answers a bare server error.** `existsSync` passes, `readFileSync` throws `EISDIR`, and Hono answers plain-text `Internal Server Error` — not JSON, not a reason, and (per #4325) the exact shape that used to escape `readProjectFileOptional` and get blamed on the composition before that PR guarded `res.json()`. This is the same failure class one layer earlier: an unhandled response shape masquerading as something else.

**A dangling symlink answers `403 forbidden`.** `isSafePath`'s `realpathSync` throws on a link whose target does not exist, and — by design, per its own comment — that fails closed as unsafe, indistinguishable from a real path-traversal attempt. Correct for containment. Wrong for the response: a broken link is broken plumbing, not an attack, and the `why: "outside_project"` label the client already surfaces asserts something that isn't true.

## What changed

- `statSync(...).isFile()` after the existing `existsSync` check → `404 { why: "not_a_file" }` for the directory-in-place case, same shape as any other missing-file 404 the client already handles.
- `isDanglingSymlink`, checked **only after** `resolveWithinProject` has already refused the path — nothing about what is *permitted* changes, only which `why` a refusal carries. A symlink resolving to something real outside the project is still `outside_project` / 403, unchanged and pinned by test, so this can't regress into loosening containment.

Deliberately did not touch `isSafePath` / `resolveWithinProject` themselves — they're the shared containment primitive for every write route too (rename, upload, patch), and failing closed on a dangling symlink there is correct: the target could be created later and point outside the project between the check and the write. The classification lives one layer up, at the read route's response, where only the label is at stake.

## No visible change

`packages/studio-server` only — no `packages/studio` or `packages/player` files touched.

## Test plan

- Dir-in-place → `404 { why: "not_a_file" }` instead of a plain-text 500.
- Dangling symlink → `404 { why: "dangling_symlink" }` instead of `403`.
- Symlink resolving outside the project → still `403 { why: "outside_project" }` — the guard the new branch must not weaken.
- 102/102 in `files.pathSafety.test.ts` + `files.test.ts`; 247 green across `packages/studio-server/src/routes` overall (one pre-existing cwd-dependent test fails when run from the repo root instead of its own package dir — unrelated, passes either way). oxlint, oxfmt, `tsc --noEmit` clean.

title: hyperframes_version mp4 tag is always 0.0.0-dev: readEngineVersion() resolves ../../package.json and overshoots the package root
body:
## Summary

`readEngineVersion()` resolves `../../package.json`, which overshoots the package root in the published layout. The lookup throws `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, a bare `catch` swallows it, and every rendered mp4 is stamped `hyperframes_version = 0.0.0-dev` instead of the real version.

`hyperframes_renderer` is stamped correctly, so the tag block looks healthy at a glance.

## Affected

`hyperframes@0.8.68` (current). Present in both `dist/cli.js` and `dist/fontLocalizeCli.js`.

## The code

`dist/cli.js:74652`

```js
function readEngineVersion() {
  try {
    const version2 = createRequire(import.meta.url)("../../package.json").version;
    return typeof version2 === "string" && version2.length > 0 ? version2 : UNKNOWN_VERSION;
  } catch {
    return UNKNOWN_VERSION;   // UNKNOWN_VERSION = "0.0.0-dev"
  }
}
```

## Reproduce

```
mkdir /tmp/hf && cd /tmp/hf && npm pack hyperframes@0.8.68 && tar xzf hyperframes-0.8.68.tgz
node -e '
const p = require("path");
const cli = p.resolve("package/dist/cli.js");
for (const rel of ["../../package.json", "../package.json"]) {
  const r = p.normalize(p.join(p.dirname(cli), rel));
  console.log(rel, "->", r, require("fs").existsSync(r) ? "EXISTS" : "MISSING");
}'
```

Output:

```
../../package.json -> /tmp/hf/package.json          MISSING
../package.json    -> /tmp/hf/package/package.json  EXISTS
```

End to end: render any composition to mp4 and read the tags back.

```
ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 out.mp4 | grep hyperframes
```

Expected `hyperframes_version=0.8.68`, actual `hyperframes_version=0.0.0-dev`.

## Suggested fix

`../../package.json` → `../package.json` at both sites.

Separately worth considering: the bare `catch` is why this went unnoticed. A `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` here means the build layout moved, which is not the same as "version unavailable" — logging it, or distinguishing it from a genuinely absent version, would surface the next occurrence rather than silently degrading to a sentinel that reads like real data.

## Why it matters

The tag is the only in-band record of which engine produced a file. When it is a constant, a rendered mp4 carries no evidence of its own provenance, and a pinned version cannot be verified after the fact from the artifact — only from whatever external notes happened to be kept.

<!-- hyperframes-triage-followup:2026-09-23 -->
## Triage follow-up — September 23, 2026

Existing implementation: #3695 (`fix(engine): resolve provenance version from the owning package`), which predates this report. It is open and awaiting review; please reconcile this report with that PR before starting another implementation.

Current main `fa4261bee` still contains the depth-specific lookup in `packages/engine/src/utils/renderProvenance.ts`. The reporter's correction is important: changing `../../` to `../` fixes the flat bundle but breaks the source layout.

Review scope: source, standalone engine, bundled CLI, foreign-package fallback, and actual output-version tagging. The proposed PR's tests were not rerun in this triage pass. `difficulty/medium` reflects the packaging/test matrix; the issue stays in triage until current-head verification and scope reconciliation are complete.

title: Clip with z-index: -1 silently does not render (snapshot and render); z-index 0 and 1 siblings are fine
body:
## Summary A clip with `z-index: -1` does not render. Sibling clips with `z-index: 0` and `z-index: 1`, identical in every other respect, render correctly. The element is silently absent — no warning from `lint`, `validate` or `render`, and the render exits 0. This affects **both** `snapshot` and `render`, so it is not capture-specific. ## Affected `hyperframes@0.8.68`. ## Reproduce `index.html` — three absolutely-positioned full-width bands, identical `class="clip"` attributes, differing only in `z-index`: ```html
``` ``` hyperframes snapshot . --at 0.5 --no-end -o snap --describe false hyperframes render . -o out.mp4 ``` ## Measured Mean RGB sampled inside each band: | element | authored | snapshot | render | |---|---|---|---| | `z-index: -1` | `(245,230,200)` | **`(10,10,10)`** | **`(7,9,9)`** | | `z-index: 0` | `(32,160,240)` | `(32,160,240)` | `(29,157,238)` | | `z-index: 1` | `(208,32,32)` | `(208,32,32)` | `(206,30,27)` | `(10,10,10)` is the bare `body` background — the band is not drawn at all, rather than drawn and covered. The `z-index: 0` and `z-index: 1` bands land on their authored values in both paths (the small render deltas are encode rounding). ## Expected Either the band renders, or something says why it does not. Per CSS painting order a negative-`z-index` child paints above the canvas background and below its parent's content, so on a transparent `#root` over a dark `body` the band should be visible. If clips are composited such that negative `z-index` is deliberately out of range, that is a reasonable design choice — but it is currently undocumented and silent, and the failure is invisible at every gate: `lint` passes, `validate` passes, the render exits 0, and the output is a plausible-looking file with an element missing. ## Suggested Whichever way it is resolved, the valuable half is a diagnostic: flag a negative `z-index` on a clip at `lint` time, or warn at render when a declared element contributes zero pixels. Silent omission is the expensive failure mode — an absent element is indistinguishable from one that was authored wrong, so debugging effort goes to the composition rather than to the pipeline. Workaround for anyone hitting this: express paint order with DOM order (`insertBefore`) rather than negative `z-index`. Positive values behave correctly. ## Triage follow-up — September 23, 2026 A plain-browser control reproduces the essential symptom without HyperFrames. In Chrome 150.0.7871.24, the supplied negative-z-index band over the opaque body background yields RGB (10,10,10) at (200,80). Adding `isolation: isolate` to `#root` changes that pixel to the expected band RGB (245,230,200). This is evidence of CSS stacking behavior, not by itself evidence that HyperFrames drops an element. The isolated control has not yet been compared across HyperFrames snapshot/render, so this issue is not being closed. ### Decision needed The smallest contribution candidate is documenting negative-z-index stacking and a minimal before/after example beside the paint-order guidance in `docs/concepts/data-attributes.mdx` and `docs/reference/html-schema.mdx`. A diagnostic is a separate scope decision: blanket rejection of negative z-index would reject valid CSS. title: fix(engine): cross-check nb_frames when video stream duration is absent
body:
## Summary

- When ffprobe omits the video stream's `duration` field, `extractMediaMetadata` falls back to container duration (`format.duration`), which includes the longest stream — often a longer audio track in stock/looping clips
- This inflates `videoStreamDurationSeconds`, causing the coverage gate to expect 2x the frames FFmpeg produces — the "50% cluster" failure pattern (~100 of 497 coverage failures over 3 weeks)
- Cross-check with `nb_frames / fps` when stream duration is absent; if the frame-derived duration is >10% shorter than the container, use it instead
- `nb_frames` and `frames` were already parsed and exposed on `VideoMetadata` — this change just uses them to bound the fallback

## Test plan

- [x] New test: nb_frames bounds video duration when stream duration absent and audio is longer
- [x] New test: falls back to container duration when nb_frames is also absent
- [x] New test: keeps container duration when nb_frames-derived duration is within 10%
- [x] New test: prefers stream duration over nb_frames when both present
- [x] Existing coverage tests pass (the held-tail / looping credit tests at `videoFrameCoverage.test.ts:250-270` model the corrected metadata shape)

title: fix(cli): add --vars refuses a value of the wrong type instead of writing it
body:
## What was wrong

`hyperframes add <item> --vars '<json>'` checked only enum and number values. A wrong-typed boolean, colour or string was written into the project anyway. For a component, every non-number value was also stored as a string, so `true` became `"true"` and the component's own check read it as false. For a block, the values went into the mount snippet with no check at all. Either way the render later warns and falls back to the default, which looks exactly like `--vars` being ignored.

## The fix

- Values are checked by the runtime's own validator (`validateVariables` in core) for every declared type. Numbers keep the CLI's existing check (a numeric string is accepted, min and max are enforced).
- Values are stored with their own JSON type.
- `add` fetches and checks every item in the plan (the requested item and every dependency it pulls in) before writing any of them, and refuses when the item's declaration rejects a value. It exits with `--vars refused: <id>: <reason>`, and nothing is written: no files, no dependencies, no lock record entries. The same two-phase install also means a failed download partway through no longer leaves some files written.
- A file the project has edited is still never overwritten. That check now runs again right before each write, so an edit saved while `add` was still downloading the rest of the plan is kept too.
- `add <tag> --vars ...` now says why an item was skipped instead of only `(skipped)`.
- An id the item does not declare is still only a warning.

## Proof

- New tests in `variableDefaults.test.ts` (typed rejections, booleans stay booleans) and `installer.test.ts` (a block and a component refuse a wrong-typed value and write nothing). They fail on main (2 of 12 and 2 of 17) and pass with the fix (12 of 12, 17 of 17). A new `add.test.ts` case (a block with a dependency refuses a wrong-typed value) fails before the plan-wide fix because the dependency's files were already on disk, and passes after it. A new `installer.test.ts` case saves an edit between download and write and checks it survives; it fails when the write-time check is removed. All three files: 55 of 55. Typecheck, format, lint and the complexity audit are clean.
- Real run against the live registry with `halftone-field` (boolean `quantize`):
  - `--vars '{"quantize":1}'` prints `--vars refused: quantize: expected boolean, got number`, exits 1, writes no files.
  - `--vars '{"quantize":true}'` installs and prints the snippet with `data-variable-values='{"quantize":true}'`.

## Review
An independent adversarial review ran against the first version of this branch. Findings and what happened to them:

- **Blocker, fixed:** a refusal only held inside one item. Dependencies were written before the requested item's values were checked, so a refused `--vars` left them installed. The whole plan is now prepared before anything is written, with a test.
- **Major, fixed:** `add <tag> --vars` hid the reason an item was skipped. It now prints it.
- **Minor, not changed:** a colour value is checked to be a string, not a valid colour format. That matches what the runtime itself checks.
- **Minor, not changed:** a numeric string is accepted for a number at install time, as before.

A second review of the fix found:

- **Major, fixed:** checking the whole plan before writing lengthened the time between "is this file edited?" and the write, so an edit saved during a slow download could be overwritten. The check now also runs at write time, with a test.
- **Major, fixed:** nothing tested checking several items before writing any. The two new tests cover it.
- **Minor, not changed:** `FileOutcome` is exported for type declarations but not re-exported from the registry index; nothing imports it.

A third review of the final version found nothing at any severity. It also checked that two items in one install writing the same file still end with the later item's version, and that a file kept at write time is not reported as having its variables applied.

title: fix(studio): refresh the file tree on external change, and say when a composition is gone
body:
## Summary

Third and final PR in the stale-file-tree investigation (dashboard 2117955). Proven root cause: `refreshFileTree` is only ever called from Studio's own file operations (create/delete/rename/upload/block install), never on an external change (agent edits). An agent removing or replacing a composition leaves the file tree stale — the old path stays listed and clickable, opening it opens an SDK session that reads `reason: absent` forever, and every subsequent edit silently falls back to the (also failing) server path with no signal to the user.

Two refresh triggers, belt and braces:

- `useExternalFileChangeCoordinator` gains an optional `refreshFileTree` collaborator, invoked alongside `reloadPreview`/`reloadSdkSession` on every accepted external change. Wired through `useStudioExternalFileChanges` from `fileManager.refreshFileTree` (already in scope).
- `useSdkSession` gains `onAbsentRead`, fired once per `(projectId, path)` when a read reports `reason: "absent"` — the fallback for a change the SSE stream never delivered (server restart, missed watcher event). Guarded by a ref-tracked set so a genuinely-gone file can't loop; cleared on project change.

New: `sdkHandle.compositionMissing` and `CompositionMissingBanner` — sibling of `ProjectUnreachableBanner` (that one is "the whole project is unreachable"; this one is "the project is fine, this one file inside it is not"). The read failure alone was silent; this tells the user their edits stopped landing.

Deliberately not touched: `activeCompPath` is never auto-cleared when a path leaves the tree — a prior investigation already ruled that out (`useAutoOpenRootComposition` latches once; a null path never recovers), so the banner is additive, not a replacement for that decision.

## Before

Composition removed externally: tree keeps listing it, no signal to the user that edits are no longer landing.

![before](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/08c39b7a-b7c5-4591-9913-ca97838f92b9)

## After

Same scenario: file tree refreshes and drops the stale entry, and if the path is still open, a banner names exactly which composition is gone.

![after](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fe19e31c-d97e-4732-92fc-7f5c122d9650)

## Test plan

- [x] `useExternalFileChangeCoordinator.test.tsx` — refresh fires once per accepted external change, not for a self-write echo, no-ops without the collaborator
- [x] `useSdkSession.lifecycle.test.tsx` — `compositionMissing` set/cleared correctly, `onAbsentRead` fires once per path, fires again for a different path, guard resets on project change, no-ops without the collaborator
- [x] `CompositionMissingBanner.test.tsx` — names the missing path, does not claim the whole project is gone
- [x] Full `packages/studio/src/hooks packages/studio/src/components` suite: 2830/2831 passing (the one failure is pre-existing and unrelated — confirmed via `git stash`)
- [x] `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, `tsc --noEmit` clean

title: fix(core): the runtime never reports a film's length as Infinity
body:
The runtime's timeline message no longer reports a film's length as `Infinity`. A film whose animations end a little after its voiceover now reports its real length, and a genuinely looping timeline reports the finite length the runtime already chose for it.

## The bug

`collectRuntimeTimelinePayload` flagged the root GSAP timeline as loop-inflated whenever it ran more than 1 s past the media or sub-composition window. With no `data-duration` on the root, the message then said `durationSeconds: Infinity`, `durationInFrames: Infinity`. That happened even though the runtime had already resolved the root's length to the media window.

A real film hit this: animations ending at 156 s, voiceover at 154.8 s, no root `data-duration`. The runtime player plays 156 s. Studio in same-origin mode recovers by reading the root's `data-duration` from the document. A host that sees only this message, such as `@hyperframes/player` (its message handler ignores a non-finite duration) or a preview in an opaque sandbox, has nothing to fall back on, and its total reads 00:00 while the film plays.

## The fix, two commits

1. **Only endless-loop scale counts as loop-inflated:** `LOOP_INFLATED_TIMELINE_SECONDS = 7200`, the length Studio's `sanitizeDurationSeconds` already rejects. GSAP reports 1e10 s for `repeat: -1`. Below it, the message uses the timeline, which is what the player's clock plays (`max(timeline, media)`).
2. **No more `Infinity` in the message.** When a timeline is loop-inflated, the message carries the length the runtime resolved (the media window), instead of throwing it away.

## What I measured

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `timeline.test.ts` | 66 passed, exit 0 |
| 156 s timeline with a 154.8 s voiceover, on the old rule | fails: `expected Infinity to be 156` |
| Endless loop (1e10) on commit 1 alone | fails: `expected Infinity to be 154.8` |
| `tsc --noEmit` (packages/core, after build) / `oxlint` on the changed files | exit 0 / 0 errors |
| Three real affected films, this branch's built runtime swapped into a sandboxed preview | totals 02:36, 02:36, 01:42, all playing (were 00:00) |

## Review

Independent adversarial review, one round plus a delta on this head (delta: no BLOCKERs, no MAJORs):

| Severity | Finding | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| MAJOR | 7200 s and above still emitted `Infinity`, so the same 00:00 | Fixed at the source by commit 2 |
| MAJOR | A finite ambient loop (e.g. 300 s over 60 s of media) now reports 300 s, not `Infinity` | Withdrawn in the delta: the player's clock plays 300 s there |
| MINOR | 7200 duplicates Studio's literal | Linked by comment; sharing one constant touches Studio and is a follow-up |
| MINOR | Commit wording overstated agreement with the player for endless loops | Commit 2's message makes no such claim |

No reader of this message's duration was found outside the preview hosts (producer and thumbnails don't consume it).

## What I did NOT exercise

- A finite ambient-loop film walked in Studio (unit and probe level only).
- With no media at all, a 1e10 timeline still reports 1e10, as before this change.
- Studio's comment in `useTimelineSyncCallbacks.ts` saying the runtime can emit `Infinity` is now stale; its clamp stays correct for older runtimes. It's left for the Studio follow-up.


## Before / After

A look-alike film with the same shape (animations end at 2:36, narration at 2:34.8, no root `data-duration`), played by `<hyperframes-player controls sandbox-origin="opaque">`. The film carries the runtime built from `main` (Before) or from this branch (After). Both are captured 4 s after Play. Before, the runtime reports `Infinity` and the player reads 0:04 / 0:00; after, it reports 156 and reads 0:04 / 2:36.

![Before (main runtime): 0:04 / 0:00](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/13e52a9b-da5f-4a6a-a9a1-17b885c34368)

![After (this branch): 0:04 / 2:36](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8cc7a404-01a6-4c1a-8232-f84de6ab134e)

title: fix(lint): locate findings in linear time on large compositions
body:
## Summary

`hyperframes preview` and `hyperframes lint` are fast again on large compositions. Since #4353, mapping each lint
finding back to its source line built a whitespace-collapsed copy of the file one character at a time and checked
`endsWith(" ")` on every step. In Node, that check flattens the growing string each time, so the cost grew with the
square of the file size: about 31 s of CPU for a 1.2 MB `index.html`, spent before Studio even starts listening.

## What changed

- `normalized()` in `packages/lint/src/sourceLocations.ts` collects characters into an array and tracks whether the
  last one was a space, then joins once. Same output and same offsets, linear time.
- A test locates a snippet at the end of a 312 KB source and requires it to finish in under 1 s.

## Measured

A real 58 s HyperFrames film (1.2 MB `index.html`, 28 lint warnings), cold `hyperframes preview` with an
empty browser profile and no `.hyperframes` cache, on a shared 8-core Linux box (load 8 to 10), Node 22.

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `normalized()` CPU in one server start (`--cpu-prof`) | 30 860 ms | 97 ms |
| launch to server answering, profiled start | 43.6 s | 9.0 s |
| launch to server answering, 3 cold opens | 42.5, 47.8, 53.4 s | 5.3, 5.6, 7.9 s |
| Studio first frame on screen, same 3 opens | not painted within 60 s, 3 of 3 | 22.4 s median (21.2-30.2) |
| the new test's 312 KB input, in vitest | 5 131 ms | 85 ms |

Main is 922be55e5; this branch is one unrelated producer commit later. For the 3-open rows, the main and
PR columns come from separate runs, not interleaved. Under Bun (JavaScriptCore) the old code
was already linear; the quadratic cost is V8's.

## Tests

- `packages/lint/src/sourceLocations.test.ts` alone: exit 0, 22 passed. The new test fails on the old code
  (5 131 ms against the 1 000 ms bound) and passes in 85 ms with the fix.
- Whole lint package (`vitest run --maxWorkers=4`): exit 0, 19 files, 699 passed.

## Not covered

- Each located finding still slices and splits the source up to its offset (`at()`) and scans the
  normalized text twice for its snippet. That is linear per finding: 0.63 ms per call on average across
  the 1.2 MB film, so 28 findings cost about 18 ms and 1 000 would cost about 0.6 s. A line-start index
  would make it logarithmic; not done here.

## Review notes

An independent adversarial review found no blocking issue. It fuzzed the old and new `normalized()`
against 20 000 random inputs plus edge cases (BOM, NBSP, surrogate pairs, the `\0` comment fill, empty
and leading whitespace): 0 mismatches in text or offsets. Its one major note is the per-finding cost
above. It also noted the test's timing margin (about 12x) and that `packages/lint` runs only on Linux
runners in CI.

title: docs: define contributor and agent issue triage
body:
## What

Document how contributors and agents classify and claim issues. `TRIAGE.md` separates difficulty, readiness, and availability, and defines the preparation and mentoring commitment required for `good first issue`.

## Why

The existing difficulty labels had no definitions and were unused on the open backlog. Many apparently available issues already have implementation PRs. A repeatable triage process should prevent duplicate work and give newcomers clear scope and a testing path.

## Related work

This establishes the contribution process; it does not resolve the implementation issues used as rubric examples. Repository label descriptions and the four `triage/*` labels have been configured. Initial intake labels were applied and read back on 29 open issues (the dependency dashboard was excluded); four received source-supported difficulty labels. No newcomer invitations, assignments, issue closures, or PR dispositions were changed.

- Add `TRIAGE.md` with label definitions, ownership rules, agent procedure, discovery guidance, queue searches, and examples.
- Link the guide from `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

title: feat: add Gemini TTS models and service-account auth to media skills
body:
## Summary

The bundled audio workflows cannot currently select Gemini narration. This adds opt-in Gemini TTS through the Developer Interactions API, with API-key and service-account OAuth authentication. Generated audio is saved as local WAV, and the existing transcription pass supplies caption word timings.

Supported models:
- `gemini-3.8-flash-tts` (default)
- `gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts`
- `gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview`
- `gemini-2.5-pro-preview-tts`
- `gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts`

3.8 uses structured delivery metadata and native WAV output. Older models receive delivery prompts and return PCM, which is wrapped as WAV at the returned sample rate. Custom voice IDs are limited to 3.8. Product-launch, faceless-explainer, and PR-video adapters forward model/style options; automatic provider selection stays unchanged.

Service-account authentication uses Google's Python auth library (`google-auth requests`) and accepts a JSON file through `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` or injected JSON through `GCS_CREDS`. API keys take precedence. OAuth tokens use the `generative-language.retriever` scope and are refreshed per generation. This implements the Developer API, not Cloud TTS/Vertex or general ADC discovery.

## Validation

- 92 targeted provider, auth, engine, and workflow tests pass, covering auth precedence, credential redaction, legacy PCM conversion, invalid responses, and mocked caption metadata. This includes a Python credential-boundary suite (7 tests) and absent/expired HeyGen credential regressions.
- Live tests through the updated helper generated valid 24 kHz mono WAV files for all five models using service-account OAuth, repeated successfully with the narrower scope after review. All three older-model transcripts matched the supplied script; 2.5 Pro local transcription succeeded on retry.
- A real 3.8 shared-engine run generated narration and an exact 11-word transcript with ordered timestamps within the audio duration. A captioned fixture passed HyperFrames 0.8.33 browser/static checks with zero findings and rendered a 4.8-second 1280x720 H.264/AAC MP4. Inspected the exported frame and confirmed non-silent audio.
- JavaScript lint/format, skill lint, manifest synchronization, and Mintlify build/broken-link checks pass.

API-key authentication is unit-tested but was not live-tested. The live render covers 3.8 Flash; other models were verified through synthesis and WAV inspection, with additional transcription checks for older models. These are short integration tests, not multilingual or subjective voice-quality benchmarks. No credentials or trial media are committed.

Review follow-up: HeyGen headers are resolved only for selected retrieval work, so an expired unrelated HeyGen login no longer blocks Gemini-only narration. Main was merged without rewriting history. Per-line token refresh remains; in-memory caching is a deferred nonblocking optimization.

Validation limitation: merge-time workspace typecheck could not resolve existing package declarations in the borrowed dependency tree; fallow could not create its comparison worktree. Those two hooks were excluded for the merge commit after verifying package/script code matches main. The targeted tests, lint, manifest, copy-parity, and skill-import checks passed.

title: lint: text inside quoted attributes can suppress real muted diagnostics
body:
Adding a tooltip containing the word `muted` makes lint treat an unmuted video as muted. This suppresses both `video_missing_muted` and `video_audio_double_source`, although audio behavior has not changed. ## Reproduction From the repository root: ```sh cat > /tmp/hf-d1.ts <<'TS' const { lintHyperframeHtml } = await import(`${process.cwd()}/packages/lint/src/hyperframeLinter.ts`); const wrap = (body: string) => `
${body}
`; for (const title of ["", ' title="an unmuted muted clip"']) { const html = wrap(``); console.log(title || "without title", (await lintHyperframeHtml(html)).findings.map((f: {code: string}) => f.code)); } TS bun /tmp/hf-d1.ts ``` Observed: ```text without title [ "video_missing_muted", "video_audio_double_source" ] title="an unmuted muted clip" [] ``` Expected: both inputs produce the same two diagnostics. A word inside `title` is not a `muted` attribute. ## Scope and suggested approach [hasAttrName](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/86fa10ced4297bfd9f4fe67b6767afae7a07fd3c/packages/lint/src/rules/media.ts#L40) regex-searches the raw attribute text, including quoted values. Replace that check with existing parsed attributes or quote-aware attribute-name detection. Preserve HTML Boolean semantics: `muted`, `muted=""`, and even `muted="false"` are present attributes. Do not change runtime playback behavior or unrelated diagnostics. Add cases to [media.test.ts](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/86fa10ced4297bfd9f4fe67b6767afae7a07fd3c/packages/lint/src/rules/media.test.ts). ## Acceptance criteria - Text within a single- or double-quoted attribute value cannot impersonate `muted`, `crossorigin`, or other names checked by this helper. - Real bare/valued Boolean attributes and case-insensitive HTML attribute names retain their existing behavior. - The reproduction yields the two expected errors both with and without the tooltip. - Existing media-rule tests pass. Estimated difficulty: **easy**. Reviewer/mentor: pending. ## Related work No matching active implementation found in the checked inventory. Issue #2775 concerns missing narration ledger entries and speech seam placement, not quoted-attribute parsing. Keep the scope in this helper; do not take over that audio-pipeline issue. ## Validation From a dependency-installed repository checkout, run the reproduction above with Bun. title: Global asset view reports failures and unmatched searches as an empty cache
body:
Studio's global asset list reports **“No assets in the global cache yet”** for three different situations: an actual empty cache, a failed request, and a search that matches none of the existing assets. This tells users that their cache is empty when the data is unavailable or merely filtered out.

### Reproduction and evidence

Verified against `origin/main` **86fa10ced4297bfd9f4fe67b6767afae7a07fd3c** on September 23, 2026. Relevant source is unchanged from the browser probe.

In Studio's Assets panel, select the global asset view:

1. Return HTTP 500 from `/api/assets/global`, or reject that request. The view displays the empty-cache message.
2. Return `{ "assets": [{ "id": "logo", "type": "image", "description": "Brand logo" }] }` successfully and search for `zzz`. The view again displays the empty-cache message.
3. Clear the query. The existing `Brand logo` row reappears.

All these cases were executed in Chrome with the actual `GlobalAssetsView` component and mocked fetch responses. A successful response containing zero assets was also checked and currently displays the same message. This is an isolated component reproduction; the Assets panel caller was inspected in source rather than exercised through the complete application.

### Scope

Represent loading, request failure, empty successful result, and no matching search results separately. Offer a retry for request failures using the existing endpoint. Preserve the current asset rows and filtering behavior.

### Acceptance criteria

- A non-OK response or rejected request displays a failure message rather than an empty-cache explanation.
- Retrying a failed request can recover to a populated or genuinely empty result; there is no automatic retry loop.
- A successful empty response displays the existing empty-cache guidance.
- When the cache contains records but the query matches none, the view says there are no matching results.
- Clearing the query restores the existing records without requiring another request.
- Loading remains identifiable, and a response arriving after unmount does not update the disposed view.
- Component tests cover these states and recovery using controlled fetch responses.

### Code pointers and validation

- [GlobalAssetsView request and state handling](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/86fa10ced4297bfd9f4fe67b6767afae7a07fd3c/packages/studio/src/components/sidebar/GlobalAssetsView.tsx#L42)
