title: fix(studio): playback no longer re-renders the whole app every frame
body:
## What was broken

While the preview played, Studio's root `App` component re-rendered on every frame, 55-82 times a second in a real browser. With a heavy panel on screen, each of those renders is expensive. The Catalog tab, which is what shows after the Compositions tab is closed, took the median frame from 17 ms to 40 ms while playing, and the preview and playhead visibly stuttered. Paused, it was fine.

Cause: `useFrameCapture` is called from `App`. It passed a React state setter straight to `liveTime.subscribe`, and the playback loop notifies `liveTime` every frame. That goes against the design written in `useLivePlayheadTime`: the playback loop notifies `liveTime` instead of the store "so the playhead can move without re-rendering the app".

A second, smaller bug in the same hook: the Capture click and the link refresh read the store's `currentTime`. That value does not advance while playing, so a capture taken during playback used the frame from when Play was pressed.

## The fix

`useFrameCapture.ts`:

- **The live playback time goes into a ref, not state.** Nothing re-renders per frame.
- **One `playheadTime()` read:** the live time while playing, the store time while paused. That is the same rule `useLivePlayheadTime` uses.
- **The Capture link reads it** on focus and on pointer down (both already wired in `StudioHeader`), and at click.

Also found in review, and fixed here because the paused rule above depends on it:

- **`useTimelinePlayer.ts`:** hiding the tab during playback now calls `pause()` itself. Before, it ran a partial copy of `pause()`, which caused two bugs. It left the store at the time Play was pressed, so back on the tab Capture, Split and Delete used that old time while the preview showed another. And during a reverse shuttle (J) it did not stop the reverse loop: the film kept rewinding, and the next L resumed at double the last shuttle speed.
- **`useTimelineSyncCallbacks.ts`:** a comment that still named the capture link as a per-frame listener is corrected.

Known limits:
- **The link no longer rewrites itself every frame.** A keyboard-only "Copy link address" (Tab to Capture, playback runs on, then Shift+F10) copies the time from when the link got focus. Clicking, Enter, a screen reader, middle-click and right-click all read the live time.
- **The "live while playing, store while paused" rule now lives in two hooks** (`useFrameCapture` and `useLivePlayheadTime`). Giving `liveTime` a stored last value would leave one owner; that is a follow-up, not part of this fix.

## Measured in Studio (real browser)

Film `timeline-launch` from the public launch-video projects, headful Chrome. Same checkout, only this hook swapped.

| | App renders per second while playing | median frame, Catalog tab open, playing | paused |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | 82 | 40 ms | 17 ms |
| this branch | 0-0.3 | 18 ms | 17 ms |

Capture link while playing, checked in the browser: pointer down set the link to t=2.995 s with the runtime at 3.12 s. Before pointer down it keeps its last value instead of being rewritten every frame.

The recordings below run slower than those numbers because the screen recorder itself takes CPU. Measured from the page's own frame log during the 8 s of play: main 16 fps (42 ms median, 122 ms p90), this branch 43 fps (17 ms median, 31 ms p90).

## Tests

`useFrameCapture.test.tsx` (new):

- does not re-render on playback frames (30 `liveTime` notifies, render count unchanged);
- points the capture at the live playhead while playing;
- points the capture at the store time while paused.

The first two fail on main's hook and pass here.

`useTimelinePlayer.hiddenPause.test.ts` (new):

- hiding the tab while playing pauses on the adapter's time;
- hiding the tab stops a reverse shuttle for good;
- the shuttle speed does not carry past that pause.

All three fail on main. On this head, `src/player/hooks` plus `useFrameCapture` and `StudioHeader.dom`: 14 files, 136/136. oxfmt and oxlint are clean on the changed files, and the studio typecheck is clean.

## Before

Main: close the Compositions tab so the Catalog shows, then play 8 s. The playhead and preview stutter.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/aa9e4031-f0d3-4329-bceb-094d2b0f0f8b

## After

The same steps on this branch.

title: fix(core): a film stops at its declared length instead of playing its animation past it
body:
## What this fixes

A composition whose root declares a length (`data-duration="3"`) but whose animation runs longer (a 5 s timeline) misbehaved in preview:

- `<hyperframes-player>` fired `ended` again on every update after 3 s: 60 times in 7 s with loop off.
- Past 3 s the film went blank except for the animation still moving, because the root's own window had closed while the clock kept going.

The render already treats the declared length as the film's length: it captures `ceil(3 × fps)` frames and cuts the rest, and the docs say so ("The authored duration is the output window"). The runtime's `timeline` message agreed and reported 3 s. Only the runtime's playback clock disagreed. It counted the declared length as a minimum and took the timeline's 5 s, so the player saw a film that was past its 3 s end and still playing.

Now the runtime's one length function returns the root's declared `data-duration` when there is one, before any timeline or media reading. The clock, `__player.getDuration()` and the `timeline` message all say 3 s. The film stops there, resting on its last frame as the render ends.

This holds for any declared length the render accepts, including under a second and a single frame:

- **Under a second.** The `timeline` message used to round a film shorter than one second up to 1 s. It now reports the latest clip end or the root's length, and falls back to 1 s only when nothing gives a length. A root declaring 0.2 s stops at 0.2 s and the player's controls say 0.2 s. A root with no declared length and a 0.5 s timeline now also reports 0.5 s instead of 1 s.
- **One frame.** The runtime used to ignore a declared length of 1/60 s or less. It now takes any positive one, as the `timeline` message and the render do. A root declared as one 60 fps frame stops after that frame.

## Before

Main's runtime, a `sandbox-origin` player with loop off, a film that declares 3 s and animates for 5 s: `ended` fires 60 times, and the frame past 3 s has lost its background and title.

![Before: ended fires 60 times and the film goes blank past 3 s](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/690ac26f-ff92-4813-bf1a-dddeb926b821)

## After

This branch's runtime, same page: `ended` fires once at 3 s and the film rests on its 3 s frame.

![After: ended fires once and the film rests on its last frame](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2339e4ac-8a87-4428-824f-60f8146723b0)

## Behaviour change

Preview (the player and Studio) no longer plays an animation past the root's declared length. That tail was never in the rendered file. One existing test pinned the old preview behaviour ("keeps the timeline duration when it exceeds the root's declared data-duration") and now expects the declared length.

Other changed tests:

- Two render-seek tests changed only their expectations at times at or past the declared length. There, a clip that runs to the film's end now rests on the end frame, the rule `isClipVisibleAt` already states ("a finished film rests on its last frame instead of going blank"). Before, they passed only because their mock timeline ran a fraction of a frame past the declared length. The render never captures those times: its last frame is before the declared length.
- Two tests that check the idle loop notices a growing media or animation length now use a film without a declared length, since a declared one no longer grows.

## What I measured

- One runtime table test plays a 5 s timeline under a root declaring 3 s, 0.2 s and one 60 fps frame. Each stops with `ended: true` on the right frame, and the clock and the `timeline` message report the declared length. All three rows fail on main; the 0.2 s and one-frame rows also fail at this PR's first review head (the 1 s floor, and a clock that never stops).
- `timeline.test.ts` pins a 0.2 s root with and without timed clips. A player test takes a 0.2 s `timeline` message and ends at 0.2 s.
- Mutations each fail a test: removing the declared-length early return, restoring the one-frame threshold, and restoring the 1 s floor.
- Each run alone: `packages/core` `init.test.ts` (153), `transportPark.test.ts` (28), `timeline.test.ts` (70), `capturedMediaIdleRoute`, `domRealm`, `init.mediaClipIndex`, `init.timingResolver`, `pausedTransportInvariant`; `packages/player` `hyperframes-player.test.ts` (202) and `runtime-message-handler.test.ts` (21). An independent review also ran `runtime-in-srcdoc`, `composition-probe`, sdk `session.subcomp`, producer `coreRuntimeBrowser` and the Studio timeline, player and sync files: all green. Typecheck (core and player), lint, format, the comment ratchet and the fallow audit green.
- The render's frame count, by its own rule (`durationToFrameCount`, private to the producer): 3 s at 60 fps is 180 frames, 0.2 s is 12, one 60 fps frame is 1. All of them end before the declared length, so the end-frame rule above never touches a rendered frame.
- Captures: headless Chrome with the runtime bundle built from main and from this branch, the same player bundle, the same host page and composition (the 3 s case).

## What I did NOT exercise

- A real render of any of these films, and a capture of the sub-second case.
- Motion blur on the last frame of an overrunning film whose declared length falls between frames: its blur samples past the declared length now stop at it, as they already do for a film whose timeline ends on time.
- Studio by hand. Its transport ends at the runtime's length. Its readout builds the total from the `timeline` message's whole frame count at the 30 fps preview grid, so a length off that grid (4.97 s, or one 60 fps frame) reads rounded up, as on main.
- Studio's clip move and resize set the root's length from the furthest clip, not the animation, so such a film's preview now stops there too, as its render already did. Counting animation ends there is the next change.
- A root that declares its length only as `data-composition-duration` (the producer reads it after `data-duration`; this runtime does not). That, and the producer and the runtime choosing different root elements, go in a follow-up that gives both one owner for the root and its declared length.

title: fix(studio): an effect save resolves with whether it landed, was refused or failed
body:
## What changes

A host that awaits a timeline effect save can now tell whether it landed. `useTimelineEditing().setElementFxAttribute.setQuiet` (a clip's effect) and `setAudioGroupAttribute.setQuiet` (a group's audio effect) resolve with a `TimelineEditOutcome`:

- `{ status: "saved" }`: the write landed.
- `{ status: "refused", reason }`: nothing was written. The host's `canEdit` blocked a target, and `reason` is the host's own. Recording also refuses.
- `{ status: "failed", reason }`: the write was attempted and failed (the error message), or there was no project or nothing to address.

Studio's toasts are unchanged.

## Why it happened

Both saves resolved `undefined` in every case. The lock guard in `useTimelineEditing` toasted the host's reason and returned `Promise.resolve()`. The saves caught write errors, toasted and returned normally. So a host embedding Studio saw the same resolution for a landed save, a refused one and a failed one. The toast was the only signal.

## The fix

- Both saves are the path every timeline effect save goes through: clip fades, the track-header and group-row presets, and the group volume strip. They now return an outcome.
- The shared lock guard hands the host's refusal reason to the save's refusal handler and resolves with that handler's result. Handlers that pass no refusal handler (move, resize, delete, split, group edits) resolve as before.
- The recording and no-project checks the two saves shared are one helper, `projectForTimelineSave`. The refusal loop the gate runs is one function too.
- `TimelineEditOutcome` is exported from `@hyperframes/studio`. The callback and prop types for these saves widen to `Promise<TimelineEditOutcome | void>`, so a host that supplies its own save resolving nothing still type-checks.

I chose to resolve with a result rather than reject. Studio's own components fire these saves without awaiting them, so a rejection would surface as an unhandled rejection. A result only adds information for a caller that awaits.

## Tests

`useTimelineEditing.test.tsx`, "effect saves report what happened". All four fail on `main`:

- A clip effect that lands resolves `saved`.
- A clip effect on a locked clip resolves `refused` with the host's reason and writes nothing.
- A clip effect whose write fails resolves `failed` with the error.
- A group audio effect on a locked group resolves `refused` with the host's reason.

Breaking each of those four result paths on its own fails exactly its test. The typecheck passes, and so do 196 tests across the touched suites and the timeline components.

## Before

A minimal host page built on the package's public exports: `useTimelineEditing` with a `canEdit` that locks the music clip, a fixture film in the preview, and a button that applies an echo effect through `setElementFxAttribute.setQuiet`. The toast box shows what Studio passed to the host's `showToast`, and the log shows what the awaited save resolved with. Captured in headless Chrome with `main`'s hooks: the refusal toast shows, and the save resolves `undefined`, the same as a save that landed.

![Before (main): the refusal toast shows and the save resolves undefined](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d1e01152-9122-4850-a220-4e32ec12fa5b)

## After

The same page with this branch's hooks: the same toast, and the save resolves `{"status":"refused","reason":"The music clip is locked"}`.

![After: the same toast, and the save resolves refused with the reason](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b01c3952-075f-42ef-a304-c1e68449b18b)

Nothing else on screen changes: Studio shows the same toasts in the same cases.

## Not in this PR

- Automation-lane edits save through their own path: dragging a point (`useAutomationLanes.ts`), and Delete or paste on a lane selection (`useAutomationSelectionKeyboard.ts`). That path does not ask the host's `canEdit`, and a failed write there only toasts. The next PR routes those saves through the same gated, outcome-reporting path.
- A recording refusal does not undo the live preview of the value, as before, so the preview can show a value the outcome reports as refused. A lock refusal does undo it.
- The saves are untested for the recording refusal, the no-project case and a group write failure. The code paths are the shared helper and the same catch as the clip save.

title: fix(core): muting or unmuting an audio group while playing takes effect at once
body:
## What was broken

In Studio preview, muting an audio group while the film played did nothing: its tracks kept playing at full level until the next Pause and Play. Unmuting a group while playing had the opposite problem: tracks that the group had muted at Play time stayed silent until the next Pause and Play.

Studio mutes a group by setting `data-hidden` on the `<hf-audio-group>` element in the preview document. In the preview runtime (`init.ts`):

- **The mute never reached the bus.** The group sweep that calls `webAudio.setGroupMuted` ran only when a dirty flag was set. Only `[data-start]` nodes set that flag, and a group element has no `data-start`, so a group toggle never set it.
- **Unmuted members were never captured again.** A member of a muted group is left out of the Web Audio graph when playback is scheduled, the same way a hidden clip is. A per-clip `data-hidden` toggle while playing reschedules. A group toggle did not, so its members stayed out of the graph.

## The fix

`init.ts` only:

- **The group sweep runs on every visibility pass.** It still diffs each group against its last state, so `setGroupMuted` runs only when a group's mute changes. The dirty flag is gone. It saved very little, because the same pass already runs a whole-document `[data-start]` query every tick.
- **A mute is the bus gain's job alone.** The group's mute gain silences its members in the graph, and the per-tick media sync already zeroes a hidden group's members that play natively. So muting restarts nothing else in the mix.
- **An unmute reschedules only when it has to.** A member that was left out of the graph while its group was muted has to be captured again, whether it is playing now or starts later. So an unmute runs the reschedule a per-clip hide already uses, but only when the group has a member that has not finished yet, is not already routed through the graph, and is not muted on its own (the same check the scheduler uses to leave a clip out). A quick mute then unmute, where every member stayed in the graph, restarts nothing. Neither does unmuting a group whose members have all finished.

Known limits:
- **A group element replaced or renamed while playing** (a fresh, unhidden element instead of the muted one) is not seen as an unmute. I found no Studio path that does this: Studio edits the attribute in place, and file writes reload the preview.
- **Members the graph never takes** (a cross-origin member that stays native, a member with a non-numeric rate curve, a decoded member whose audio ended before its clip end) still make an unmute of their group reschedule once, which is an audible restart of the rest of the mix. Nothing is routed wrongly.
- **Members on the decode-to-buffer fallback** (cross-origin sources) go through the same group bus, but no test covers that route.

## Measured in Studio (real browser, audio recorded from the output)

Film `pr-to-video-launch` from the public launch-video projects, with its music track wrapped in an `<hf-audio-group>` and every other sound hidden, so only the group is heard. Play, then 2 s later mute the group the way Studio does, 2 s later unmute it, then Pause.

| | playing | group muted (from 0.3 s after the mute) | group unmuted |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | -22.5 dB | -23.6 dB (still playing) | -22.3 dB |
| this branch | -23.3 dB | digital silence | -23.7 dB |

With the other sounds left in, they keep playing through the group mute on this branch, as they should: they are not in the group.

## Tests

`capturedMediaIdleRoute.test.ts`, new cases "an audio group muted or unmuted while playing":

- silences its members at once;
- brings its members back through the group (heard, and not through the direct route);
- does not restart the rest of the mix to mute it (another track keeps playing, `stopAll` is never called);
- does not restart the mix to unmute it right after muting it;
- does not restart the mix to unmute a group whose members have all finished;
- does not restart the mix to unmute a group whose unfinished member is muted itself;
- brings a member that starts after the unmute in through the group.

Four of these fail on main. The first three "does not restart" cases fail on an earlier version of this fix that rescheduled on every group change. The "starts after the unmute" and "right after muting it" cases fail on a version that rescheduled only for members playing at the moment of the unmute. Dropping the muted-itself check fails its test. Run on this head: `capturedMediaIdleRoute` 10/10, `init` 153/153, `webAudioTransport` 80/80, `webAudioRoute` 29/29, `audioFx` 34/34, `media` 139/139. oxfmt, oxlint and the comment ratchet all exit 0.

The test's `heard()` helper follows the routing the runtime sets up. On the direct route a stopped element gets, the element's own volume applies. Inside a play, only the graph's gains apply.

## Before

Main: the group is muted 2 s into playback and the music keeps playing.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f539ffb9-17f8-4915-8fd0-41ec67e2b007

## After

The same steps on this branch: silent while muted, back on unmute.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4689fccd-39cf-4c3f-8757-1d787b5b4e5c

title: fix(studio): an automation lane edit is refused on a locked clip and reports how it saved
body:
## What changes

Automation-lane edits in the timeline now go through the same gated, outcome-reporting save as a clip's effect. This covers releasing a dragged point, Delete or paste on a lane selection, and the lane header's remove button.

- A host's `canEdit` now applies. An edit on a locked clip, or on a group with a locked member, is refused: nothing is written, the host's reason is toasted, and the preview and the lane go back to what is saved.
- `binding.onCommit` resolves the `TimelineEditOutcome` from the previous PR: `saved`, `refused` with the reason, or `failed` with the error.
- A timeline effect or automation save that does not land (a refusal while recording, a missing id, a failed write) now also puts back the live preview it was given. Every failure toasts.

## Why it happened

Lane edits saved through the property panel's quiet attribute commit, `handleDomAttributeQuietCommit`. That commit never asks the host's `canEdit`, and it resolves nothing. So a lane edit on a clip the host had locked was written to the file, and a failed write only showed a toast.

## The fix

- `useAutomationLanes` picks the timeline save that fits the element:
  - a clip's lanes use `onSetElementAttributeLive/Quiet`, the clip effect save gated on the clip;
  - a group's lanes use `onSetAudioGroupAttributeLive/Quiet`, the group save gated on its members.

  A group's synthetic lane element is recognised by `isGroupAutomationElement` in `groupAutomationElement.ts`.
- The panel commit did two things after a save that the timeline save did not. Both are kept:
  - The clip save now re-reads the lane store from the preview after a landed write. The group save already mirrors its automation.
  - The binder refreshes the property panel's current selection after a commit, so the panel's next edit starts from the new automation. `refreshDomEditSelectionFromPreview` is now on `DomEditActionsValue` for this.
- An attribute save joins its file's write queue before it reads the file, then patches and writes inside it (`persistElementAttribute`), so saves land in the order they start. Each lane (`createLiveLanes`) tracks its pending saves and, only while one is in flight, the last value it verified from the file: a save's own in-queue read, a save that landed, a read-back, or the value under a drag begun with no save pending. A save moves the store and preview only when no newer save is pending, and the preview only while no drag is live; that covers its success, its recovery, and its own optimistic patch and failure unwind. A save that does not land settles on what the file holds (`readSavedAttribute`, read behind any save already started), or on the last verified value when that read fails, never on an unsaved one. A drag refused while a save is pending puts its before-value back, and the pending save's result then lands. While a gesture is live the lane keeps its draft, so an older save landing mid-drag does not change what the release commits. Lane keys carry the open project, and each save captures its project when it starts: it reads back from that project and moves preview and store only while it is still open, so no value crosses between projects. `failedTimelineSave` owns the failure toast.
- A paste selects and marks its span only once its save lands, and only while it is still the latest paste, its clip is still selected and the selection is unchanged. A refused paste leaves no phantom span for the next Cmd+V to chain from, and pastes on two clips mark the latest one.
- `TimelineAutomationLane` drops the draft it drew for a commit once that commit comes back refused or failed. Otherwise the dragged point stayed on screen, and the next edit on the lane would save it.
- Removed because the change made them unnecessary:
  - `commitTargetKey` and the paste guard built on it. A save now addresses the clip the lane is bound to, not whatever the panel has selected, so pasting right after selecting another clip can no longer land on the previous one.
  - `automationGestureKeys`, and the panel commit's `coalesce` option that only the lanes passed. Live drag writes never recorded history, so the release is the one undo entry per gesture, as before. The undo label stays "Edit automation".
- The lane value reuses `automationAttrValue`.

- A failed save unwinds the preview to the value in the file, not to the live preview. Every live writer patches the preview before it commits: a fader drag writes every frame, and hovering a preset auditions the whole chain. So by the time the save runs, the preview already shows the new value. Unwinding to it did nothing, and the preview kept a value that was never saved and that a reload dropped.
- The group-info cache treats a DOM change as relevant only when a group element is added or removed, or a group attribute changes. Otherwise a composition that inserts nodes while it plays (split text, a typewriter) would expire the cache on every frame and fall back to scanning the whole tree on every read.

## Tests

`useAutomationLanes.save.test.tsx` mounts the real `useTimelineEditing` behind the lane binder:

- A clip lane edit saves, and the stored lane and the panel selection are refreshed.
- A clip lane edit on a locked clip resolves `refused` with the host's reason, and nothing is written.
- A dragged preview goes back when the lock refuses the release.
- A dragged preview goes back when recording refuses the release, and nothing is written.
- A clip lane edit whose write fails resolves `failed`, and the preview is unwound.
- A group lane edit with a locked member resolves `refused`.
- A group lane edit saves on the `<hf-audio-group>` and mirrors to its members.
- A group's dragged preview and store mirror go back when recording refuses the release.
- Two overlapping saves on one file, where the second fails: the preview ends at what the first saved.
- An older failure whose recovery read is pending while a newer save lands, and a newer live drag while an older recovery lands: file, preview and store agree.
- A drag refused between an older failure and a pending save, on the clip and group lanes, whether the pending save lands or fails: file, preview and store agree.
- An older save with a slow read, then a newer save that saves, fails or is refused by recording, on both lanes: saves land in the order they started.
- An older failed save whose read-back fails while a newer save lands: the newer value stays.
- A newer release keeps its preview while an older save fails under it.
- An older save that lands leaves the store to a newer pending save; a landed save survives a newer save that fails and cannot read the file back (clip and group).
- A refused save that cannot read the file back never brings back another save's unsaved value, even when that save's read-back fails too.
- A lane's first save that fails (offline, or its element gone from the file) and cannot read back puts the drag back (clip and group).
- A drag begun over a paste that then fails never records the paste's value (clip and group), and a refused drag in that state returns to the last saved value.
- After an undo, a later save that fails or is refused and cannot read the file back never brings back the removed value (clip and group).
- Across a project switch: another project's saved value never settles into a clip with the same key (clip and group); a save in flight across the switch leaves the new project alone; a save that fails after the switch reads back from its own project.

`TimelineAutomationLane.test.tsx` adds two tests: a drag whose save is refused draws the point back where it was, and a release after an older save lands mid-drag commits the dragged points.

All nine binder tests fail on `main`. Each of these breaks fails the test that covers it:

- dropping the store refresh, the panel refresh, the group routing, the outcome, the unsaved-exit revert, or the group mirror;
- keeping a refused draft;
- claiming the before-value after the write instead of before it;
- reading the file outside the write queue, letting a save's store or preview move while a newer save is pending or its preview under a live drag, not recording what an overtaken save landed, seeding the verified value from a before-value read with a save pending (or not seeding it at all), dropping the lane's draft under a live gesture or the group preview's store mirror, unscoped lane keys, the open-project check on settle or preview, reading back from the currently open project, keeping the verified value after the last save settles, not recording a save's in-queue read, and not marking a settled drag clean.

The typecheck passes, and so do 4749 tests across the player, hooks, contexts, editor components and utils.

## Before

A minimal host page with the lane binder, `useTimelineEditing` and a `canEdit` that locks the music clip. A button clears the music clip's volume lane through `binding.onCommit`. The panel commit is a stand-in that records a file write, because on `main` that is what the lane save reaches, with no `canEdit` check. On `main` there is no toast, the file is written, and the commit resolves `undefined`.

![Before: main, lane edit on a locked clip is written and resolves undefined](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6b61a6a8-8a55-4c6c-bb41-8d2681c49886)

## After

The same page on this branch shows the host's refusal toast. Nothing is written, and the commit resolves `{"status":"refused","reason":"The music clip is locked"}`.

![After: the same edit is refused with the host reason](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b633ef27-58e7-45e4-8f2f-76e473e6b29d)

## Not in this PR

- The FX rack's own automate and un-automate buttons still save through the panel commit, which does not ask `canEdit`.
- The timeline's effect-preset saves do not refresh the property panel's selection after they land. That was already the case before this PR.
- A second Cmd+V pressed before the first paste's save resolves anchors at the original selection instead of chaining.
- Cancelling an edge-stretch mid-drag re-previews the lane but leaves its drag marker, so a save that then fails can leave the preview off the file. That was already the case before this PR; a follow-up routes the cancel through the same revert.
- A drag cut off by a project switch leaves its starting value under the old project; it only matters after switching back, the file changing, and a double failure there.
- Next: exporting element delete.

title: perf(core): a paused preview stops running its audio output
body:
## What was wrong

The preview runtime creates its `AudioContext` when the preview loads and never suspends it. Once the context is
running (after the first Play, or at once where autoplay is allowed), a paused Studio keeps an audio output stream
rendering silence for the rest of the session. Chrome spends that CPU in its audio service thread and the page's
audio output thread. After 30 s of silence Chrome moves the context to a fake sink, which still renders on two renderer
thread-pool threads.

## The fix

`WebAudioTransport` owns the context, so it owns when the context runs:

- It suspends the context 10 s after the last Pause, seek or scrub stop, once no captured track is playing.
- It resumes for Play (both schedule paths) and when a captured track plays while paused (the scrub route from #4517).
- A decoded track reads its start time after the context wakes, so Play after an idle pause starts in step with the
  picture.
- It holds only the captured tracks that are playing, so a replaced track is released once it pauses. A track stopped
  by a reload (`load()`, a src swap) fires no "pause"; the idle check trusts `paused` and treats "emptied" like "pause".
- Why 10 s: a brief pause to scrub or check a frame keeps the output warm, so the next Play starts as it does today; a
  real idle lets it sleep. A stop-and-reschedule inside one play (a rate change, a hidden track, a seek while playing)
  never bounces the output either. The cost is up to 10 s of silent-stream CPU after each pause.
- A Play that lands while a suspend is still pending resumes anyway. A Pause that lands while Play waits on
  `resume()` lets the context go back to sleep once the resume lands.
- The idle timer is armed from the context's own `statechange` event, which Chrome fires after construction and on
  every resume, so a browser that starts the context a moment late still goes quiet. No timer is armed unless the
  context is running, so a paused seek on a sleeping context costs nothing.
- A context the browser suspends by itself (an OS or WebKit audio interruption) drops any armed idle timer, so a stale
  timer cannot put a later Play back to sleep while that Play waits on `resume()`.

Render is untouched: the producer mixes audio offline and never uses this context.

## Measured

Same film, same browser build (Chrome 152 headless), a 32-core Linux box, interleaved rounds. CPU is per thread over
the idle window, from the kernel's per-thread counters. The CPU runs used this branch's first two revisions; the review
fixes after them, apart from the delay, do not change when the context sleeps.

These runs used a 1 s delay, so the rows marked (asleep; 1 s delay) show the preview asleep for the whole window. At
10 s that holds from 10 s after the pause; the 35-55 s rows are unaffected.

After a user's Play then Pause (no autoplay flag), 3 interleaved rounds each, every round at 1-minute load under 10.
Figures are % of one core, medians of rounds:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Audio service + audio output threads, 5-25 s after the pause (asleep; 1 s delay) | 1.80 | 0.10 |
| Fake-sink threads, 35-55 s | 1.65 | 0 |
| Browser CPU total, 5-25 s after the pause (asleep; 1 s delay) | 10.0 (9.5 / 10.0 / 11.1) | 8.2 (7.7 / 9.2 / 8.2) |
| Browser CPU total, 35-55 s | 9.5 (9.5 / 11.4 / 9.4) | 7.8 (9.2 / 6.3 / 7.8) |
| Preview `AudioContext` state, 5-25 s after the pause, every round (1 s delay) | running | suspended |
| Preview `AudioContext` state, 35-55 s, every round | running | suspended |

The open-only case (no Play; the bench's autoplay flag lets the context start at load; 3 rounds, busier box, so only
per-thread figures): audio threads 1.65 -> 0.05 (asleep; 1 s delay), fake-sink threads 1.6 -> 0 at 35-55 s.

The windows are paused throughout. The Play-then-Pause case plays for 2 s before its window opens, so playback-time
rendering is not in these numbers.

Resume latency, the cost this adds to the first sound after a pause of 10 s or more: `resume()` on a suspended
context until its clock advances, same browser and box. The box was busy (1-minute load 14-21) for these runs, so read
them as upper bounds:

| Suspended for | Trials | Median | Max |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.15 s | 20 | 2.6 ms | 4.3 ms |
| 6 s | 10 | 3.1 ms | 6.1 ms |
| 20 s | 10 | 3.1 ms | 3.5 ms |

Headless Chrome renders to a fake output device. A real device, Bluetooth in particular, is not measured here. A Play
within 10 s of the last Pause, seek or scrub stop finds the context still running and pays nothing.

## Tests

- `webAudioTransportIdle.test.ts` (16 cases) over a fake context that applies `suspend()`/`resume()` in call order and
  fires `statechange` the way Chrome does. On main's transport the cases that describe new behaviour fail; the rest
  guard parts of the fix. Each guard was broken on purpose, and each break turns at least one test red: pending suspend
  on Play, no timer without a running context, a playing captured track, a captured track's play, a paused track
  released, a reloaded track (with and without "emptied"), the 10 s idle delay (both 0 ms and no timer), arming from
  `statechange` (including a context the browser starts late), the start time read after the wake, the pending
  flag cleared after a failed suspend and on `destroy()`, and the idle timer dropped when the browser suspends the context
  itself.
- `schedulePlayback` takes a time getter, so a decoded track reads the clock after the context wakes. `init.ts` passes
  `() => clock.now()`, and the 28 test call sites wrap their number the same way.
- Test doubles in `webAudioTransport.test.ts`, `init.test.ts` and `capturedMediaIdleRoute.test.ts` gain `suspend()`
  and `addEventListener`, which the real APIs have.
- Core suite: 152 files, 3200 passed.

Fallow notes two clone groups in `webAudioTransport.ts`: the two existing schedule methods share a prologue, and this
change edits one line in each.

title: fix(core): clips that meet within float rounding count as meeting in edits and playback
body:
## What this fixes

Two clips that meet should meet, not overlap, even when their times do not add up exactly in floating point. A clip at 19.8 lasting 6.4 ends at 26.200000000000003, so:

- `hyperframes timeline trim` refused to trim a clip starting at 26.2, as if the two overlapped, unless `--overwrite` was passed;
- the preview showed both clips at 26.2 (a real frame at 30 fps), because the runtime's half-open visibility test also runs on that float sum.

Now there is one rule, `sameInstant` in `@hyperframes/core/clip-facts`: two finite times a few floating-point rounding steps apart, scaled to their size (about 1e-14 s at 26 s), are the same instant. Nothing wider counts, so a real overlap of half a microsecond is still an overlap, and a clip with no known end (Infinity) is never mistaken for one ending now. The rule is used by:

- the CLI's edit-safety checks: move and trim conflicts need two clips to share time (`spansShareTime`), so a zero-length clip such as pending remote media never blocks a move, as before this change; `duplicate`'s insertion point must be strictly inside a clip to be refused (`isInsideSpan`); and a trim that would leave a clip one rounding step long is refused like a zero-length one;
- the runtime's `isInClipWindow`, so a clip ending on a float sum hands that instant to the next clip, and the preview and the saved file never disagree; a media clip starting on a float sum is seeked to its first frame, never a hair before it, and the live media index visits a clip whose start or end is the same instant as the seek, so a paused seek onto that start reaches the clip instead of skipping it; a video ending on a float sum at the composition's end still holds its last frame there;
- `duplicate`'s push-along step: clips at or after the insertion point move by the copy's length, and a clip that met the insertion point moves to exactly the copy's end; clips before it stay put;
- Studio's two private copies of the lane-overlap check, now one (`spansOverlap`); a zero-length clip inside another still gets a lane of its own, as before;
- the export engine and `hyperframes snapshot` now use the runtime's own clip window at both ends. A video starting on a float sum is drawn from its first frame at that instant, and a video is gone at the instant it ends, so at a shared boundary the export paints only the incoming clip, as the preview does. Before, the export's frame lookup kept a clip through its end instant (a rule copied from an older runtime), so at A = [0.1, 0.3] and B from 0.3 it painted both at frame 9. Every time the export draws is a frame start before the composition's end, so the runtime's terminal hold never comes up there. Snapshot can land exactly on the end, so it takes the composition's length and a video that runs to the end still holds its last frame there.

Times are written exactly as computed, as before (`20f` at 30 fps stays `0.6666666666666666`). A trim with `--end` picks the longest duration that, added to the start, does not end past the requested time: exact when a number lands exactly (26.2 to 29 writes `2.8000000000000007`, which adds to 29), otherwise the nearest number just before it (4.74 to 25.74).

## Visible change

In the preview, a clip that meets the next one on a float sum no longer shows for one instant together with it. In an export, a video that ends before the composition does is no longer drawn on a frame that lands exactly on its end; the frame before it is its last, as in the preview. Studio's lanes treat clips that overlap by more than a rounding step (previously more than 1 microsecond) as overlapping.

## Tests

- `clipFacts.test.ts`: 19.8 + 6.4 and 26.2, 0.1 + 1.1 and 1.2, and hour-scale sums are the same instant; 20/24 + 5e-7 and 20/24, 1.0000005 and 1 are not. Meeting clips do not overlap; clips sharing half a microsecond do.
- `clipFacts.test.ts` also: a zero-length span never shares time with another but still overlaps one for a timeline lane; a time on either edge of a span, within rounding, is not inside it.
- `clipWindow.test.ts`: at 26.2 only the clip starting there is in its window; a clip ending 5e-7 later is still in its window; a clip with no known end is in its window.
- `videoFrameExtractor.test.ts`: a copy starting at 0.1 + 0.2 is drawn from its first frame at 0.3, on a fresh sweep, a stepping sweep and a direct lookup. At a shared boundary, exact (0.3) and float sum (A ends at 0.1 + 0.2, frame 9 at 30 fps), only B is active on a fresh sweep and a stepping sweep, and a direct lookup of A returns nothing. A clip shows its last frame just before its end and nothing at it; a source shorter than its slot holds its last frame through the tail.
- `videoFrameBoundary.test.ts`: the real frame lookup, frame injector and page-side injection and visibility code, over a page with both videos: at frame 8 only A's frame is painted, at frame 9 only B's.
- `videoMetadata.test.ts` (distributed plan): a bounded open-ended clip ending with the composition at 8 s is drawn on the last rendered frame (8 - 1/30) and not at 8, which the export never draws.
- `snapshot.test.ts`: the float-sum start, and 19.8 + 6.4 at 26.2, sample frame time 0; a clip ending with the composition holds its last decodable frame at the end; a clip that ends before the composition does is gone at 15, at 15.001 and at 0.1 + 0.2.
- `media.test.ts`: a paused clip starting at 19.8 + 0.1 is seeked to exactly 0 at 19.9.
- `init.mediaClipIndex.test.ts`: after a paused seek to 19.8, a seek to 19.9 leaves a video starting at 19.8 + 0.1 (playback start 3) at source time 3, the same state as a pass that visits every clip.
- `media.test.ts`: a paused video from 19.8 lasting 6.4, in a 26.2-second composition, holds its last frame (source time 6.4) at 26.2.
- `timeline.e2e.test.ts`, each reading the saved file and deciding visibility with the runtime's own `isClipVisibleAt`:
  - the brief's trim succeeds and ends exactly at 29; a trim to 25.74 from 4.74 ends no later than 25.74 and only the next clip shows there; at 30 fps, `trim --end 20f` and `--start 20f` show only the second clip at frame 20;
  - a move to 20f at 24 fps and a `duplicate --at 1`, each landing half a microsecond inside another clip, are refused and leave the file unchanged;
  - a clip moves over pending remote media, whose unknown length counts as zero; a trim that would leave a clip one rounding step long is refused and leaves the file unchanged;
  - `duplicate` on three meeting layouts places the copy at the first clip's end and the next clip at the copy's end, with exactly one clip showing at each boundary; a clip wholly before the insertion point stays put, and a clip half a microsecond after it moves by exactly the copy's length.

Results: core `src/runtime` 1373 and `clipFacts` 7, studio-server `duplicateElement` 2, Studio `timelineZones` 23 and `timelineStackingSync` 30, CLI `src/timeline` 79 and `snapshot.test.ts` 42, engine `videoFrameExtractor`, `videoFrameInjector`, `videoFrameBoundary` and `screenshotService` 209 of 210 (one real-ffmpeg case also fails on the base commit on the test host), producer `src/services/distributed` 215; `tsc` clean in core, engine, producer, studio-server, studio and cli; Fallow, oxfmt and oxlint clean on the changed files. Single mutations each fail a test: a 1 microsecond tolerance (the half-microsecond move and duplicate are saved), exact comparison (the brief's trim is refused), the old runtime window (both clips show at 26.2), no before-check in the push-along step (a clip before the insertion point moves), a 1 microsecond snap (a clip half a microsecond after the insertion point lands on the copy's end), no finite-time guard (a clip with no end is never in its window), no clamp on the clip's local time (the float-sum clip is not seeked), no margin in the media index's endpoint search (the paused video stays at source time 0), an exact end in the terminal-frame check (the video at the composition's end is left at source time 0), the lane rule used for edit conflicts (the move over pending media is refused), a zero-length span used as the duplicate point (a duplicate inside a clip is allowed), an exact trim length check (a one-step clip is written), each of the engine's four start checks and snapshot's start check made exact again (the float-sum copy is not drawn), no clamp on snapshot's local time, the engine's inclusive end restored in the stepping sweep, the fresh sweep or the direct lookup (A is still active or drawn at the shared boundary; the injection test paints both), snapshot's inclusive end restored (a clip is shown at its interior end), and no terminal hold in snapshot (the end frame is not pulled inside the source).

## Before

Studio's preview on the base commit, seeked to 26.2 (frame 786 at 30 fps). Clip A starts at 19.8 and lasts 6.4, clip B starts at 26.2: both paint.

![before](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8fd30b34-cbe4-4dfe-9feb-4aeb66906a5b)

## After

The same project and seek on this branch (recorded at `e758bd2e`; later commits change edit checks, the export engine and snapshot, not this preview): only B paints. At 26.1 and 26.3 both commits show only A, then only B.

![after](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e10aea5e-371b-480f-a991-ab30c815abff)

title: fix(core): the picker offers what is drawn under the pointer, not see-through layers over it
fix(studio-server): history refuses once closed and reopens when a new project takes its folder
body:
## What this fixes

Two ways a project's history could reach the wrong project, both rooted in the history being tied to a folder path rather than the folder itself:

1. **A closed history kept working.** A handle taken before `close()` (an agent turn or edit window left open across a project rename) could still record and restore. If a new project had been created at the old path, its content could be recorded into the old project's history, or the old history restored into it.
2. **A renamed folder left the server's history stuck.** Rename a project folder, create a new project at the old path, press undo there: the preview server (and Studio's dev server) kept the old history open, and undo failed until restart.

Now:

- After `close()` every call refuses with `HistoryClosedError`, including windows begun before it. `close()` is safe to call twice: both calls settle together, and the ownership lock is released only after both.
- The history records the folder's identity (device and inode) when it opens. Where the engine touches project files (the sweep that reads them, and the one writer behind undo, step and restore), it checks that the folder at the path is still that folder:
  - a new folder at the path, or one carrying another project's history id, is **another project**: sweeps ignore it, writes refuse with `HistoryClosedError`, and `list`, `peek`, `next`, `pin` and `readBlob` refuse too;
  - a folder that is **gone** (moved away, nothing at the path) is no change for sweeps, and writes refuse instead of recreating the old path;
  - a folder whose `.hyperframes/history-id` is missing is another project too. A folder deleted and recreated at the same path can reuse the old inode number (ext4 does), so the id is what tells them apart. A project whose id file was removed (for example by `git clean`) gets a fresh history on reopen; its old history stays on disk.
- The history id's record now also keeps the folder's inode and creation time (not its device number, which changes when a drive is remounted), and only the folder whose inode and creation time both match the record keeps that history. An inode alone can be reused after a folder is deleted; the creation time tells a recreation apart. Anything that cannot prove it is that folder gets an id and an empty history of its own: a copy carrying the id (in either opening order; the moved original keeps its history), a project restored from a backup, a project moved to another disk, and a record written before this change, which has no inode. Before, a copy standing where the original was recorded took over the original's history. The old histories stay on disk; cleaning them up is a follow-up. A history root with no history under the id at all (another OS user's, or a different home folder) keeps the id instead of rewriting it, so a history already open elsewhere keeps recording. The record is written atomically, so a second process opening the project at the same moment never reads it half-written.
- A swap in the middle of an operation stops at the next file. Undo, step and restore check the folder synchronously right before each file they replace or delete, so none of the old project's bytes land in the new one and none of its files are removed. A sweep checks it again after copying each changed file and drops a file read from a replaced folder, so the old history never files the new project's content.
- Opening checks the folder's identity again after waiting for the history's ownership lock, so a copy that took the path during the wait is refused. The first baseline is dropped if the folder changes while it is read, and a file deleted meanwhile is skipped rather than failing the open.
- If the history's own record of its folder is deleted while it is open, the next write to its log puts it back, so the next open still finds its history.
- Opening refuses, with the same retryable error, when the folder is not there, moved away, or another project took its path while it waited for the history's ownership lock; both servers try that open again on the next request instead of leaving history off.
- A new `historyCache` in studio-server keeps a host's histories, one per project folder. When `replacedAtPath()` says another project now stands at the path, it closes the old history (committing what it had already seen) and opens the new project's own. The preview server and Studio's dev server both use it, instead of each caching an engine forever. A history closed at shutdown is not replaced, so a late request does not reopen it.
- `hyperframes history` commands release the history even when the folder changed during the command.

## What changes for a user

Each existing project starts with an empty history the first time it is opened after this change, because its record predates the inode. The same happens after a backup restore or a move to another disk. The old history is kept on disk, but it no longer shows in Undo.

Otherwise nothing changes unless a project folder is renamed or replaced while the preview or an agent turn is running. Then undo works on the new project at once, instead of failing until restart.

## Known limits

Each of these fails closed (a folder starts a fresh history) or leaves only empty folders; none attaches another project's history or writes its file contents:

- A folder renamed by another process in the microseconds between the final check and the one write or delete is not caught. Node has no file operations bound to a directory rather than its path.
- The steps before that check can create or remove empty folders inside a folder swapped in meanwhile, and a swap during a long copy can leave one temporary file in the moved original. A temporary copy of the old project's file can appear in a swapped-in folder while it is refused, and stays only if the process dies at that instant.
- Opening writes a new id into the folder a few microseconds after checking it; a folder swapped in during that gap has its id replaced and starts a fresh history.
- On file systems without a creation time, identity falls back to the inode alone. Where Node cannot read the creation time and reports the change time instead (WSL1, Linux before 4.11, containers that block statx), an open history closes at the first change to the project's top folder, such as a save, and starts fresh, so undo does not work there. On macOS, setting the folder's modified time earlier (for example restoring its contents in place with `rsync -a` or `tar`) moves its creation time back and closes an open history the same way.
- Ids are stored once in the folder but assigned per history root. If a copy is opened under a second root before the original, the original gets a new id there and, back under its own root, no longer finds its history (which stays on disk).

## Tests

- `projectHistory.test.ts`: every call refuses after close, through a window begun before it, and `readBlob` rejects rather than throwing; two concurrent closes both settle before the lock goes; a new project at the path is refused, the old turn still commits what it saw before the swap, and neither project's files change; a folder moved away refuses a restore and the old path is not recreated; a folder whose history id is gone is refused, with its files left alone; a copy put where the original was gets an empty history and the moved original keeps its own, in either opening order; an open that waited for the lock while the folder was moved away or replaced refuses, and so does an open of a folder that is not there; a changed device number keeps the history; a record without an inode gives the folder a history of its own; opening under a second, empty history root leaves the id alone and the open history keeps recording; a history whose folder record was deleted while open writes it back.
- `projectHistory.swap.test.ts`: the folder is swapped between two file writes of a restore, between a write's check and its rename, inside a restore's delete, between two copies of a sweep, and between two copies of the first baseline. Each is refused and neither project's files change; the moved original's baseline has only its own bytes. A file deleted during the first baseline is skipped.
- `projectHistory.test.ts` also: a record whose creation time differs gives the folder a history of its own; a copy carrying the id that took the path during the lock wait is refused.
- `studioServer.test.ts` and Studio's `vite.adapter.projects.test.ts`: after the folder is swapped, the next history request answers 200 from the new project's own history.
- `commands/history.test.ts`: a command during which the folder is swapped still releases the history.

Results: studio-server `src/history` 102 (2 skipped on Linux), `src/routes` 348; Studio `vite.adapter` 24; CLI `studioServer.test.ts` 28, `commands/history.test.ts` 32, `src/utils` 859; `tsc` clean in studio-server, studio and cli. Single mutations each fail their test: the closed check in the queue, the inode compare, accepting a record without an inode, rewriting the id for an empty history root, an inode-only compare, no identity check after the lock wait, no check in the first baseline, no check right before the rename, an unchecked asynchronous delete, failing on a file deleted during the first baseline, the missing-id refusal, each of the two write checks, the per-file write check, the sweep's check after each copy, the record write-back, the shared close, `readBlob` being async, the read-side refusal, the open-time id check, the missing-folder refusal at open, a copy keeping the id at the recorded path, the moved original losing its history, a device-number compare, the cache's reopen (both host tests answer 409), each server's retry after a refused open, and the command's close in `finally`.

## Before

Studio's dev server on `main`: project `demo` has one edit, its folder is renamed away and a new project is created at the same path. After a reload, Undo in the new project offers the old project's edit; clicking it writes the old project's file into the new one ("Old project, edited").

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4c946be2-870e-42ce-8e3f-8fdce773e9d1

## After

The same steps on this branch (recorded at `fe90b5e5`; later commits add the identity and write checks described above, which do not change these steps): the new project opens with Undo disabled and its own empty history, and its file stays "New project".

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dd26dbba-e128-4d3d-ba7b-66ae07738154

title: fix(core): pick mode keeps its highlight on the hovered element and offers it on click
body:
## What was broken

In the preview runtime's pick mode, the hover highlight flipped on every mouse move over the same spot, and a click never offered the element under the pointer.

`isPickableElement` rejected any element with the `__hf-pick-highlight` class, and `onPickMouseMove` puts that class on the element it highlights. So:

- the next move over the same spot skipped the highlighted element and highlighted the one under it, and the move after that flipped back;
- a click built its candidate list while the hovered element carried the class, so that element was left out.

The line dates from the first commit of the picker. Nothing but the hovered element ever carries the class.

## The fix

`picker.ts`: `isPickableElement` no longer rejects the highlight class. A repeated move over the same element now returns early, as the handler already intended, so it posts no repeated hover message.

## Measured in Studio

A fixture film at 00:06, pointer resting on the caption line. The rig sends the preview the mousemove events an unobstructed pointer would (Studio's own overlay sits above the preview), six times, then a click.

| | highlight after moves 1-6 | click offers first |
|---|---|---|
| main | `#cap2`, captions root, `#cap2`, captions root, `#cap2`, captions root | `#cap2`, without the highlighted captions root |
| this branch | `#cap2` six times | `#cap2`, then the captions root |

## Tests

`picker.test.ts`, "keeps the highlight on what the pointer is over, and offers it on click": two moves over a title keep the highlight on the title, and a click offers `#title`, `#bg`. On main it fails at the highlight check. With a single move, so that only the click check runs, it fails with `#bg` alone.

Two existing tests left pick mode on, so their document listeners stayed active for every later test in the file: "enabling twice is idempotent" and "ignores non-Escape keys". Both now turn it off at the end. The first one is what broke the new test's click, since a stale instance stopped the event; the second only protects tests after it.

`picker.test.ts` 22/22. oxfmt, oxlint and the comment ratchet exit 0.

This touches the same test file as #4536 (both add a `describe` block at the same spot). Whichever lands second needs a rebase that keeps both blocks. `picker.ts` merges cleanly.

## Before

Main: the highlight alternates on a resting pointer, and the click leaves out the highlighted element.

_Capture removed: it showed a private project; a fixture capture will replace it._

## After

The same steps on this branch: the highlight stays on the caption, and the click offers it first.

_Capture removed: it showed a private project; a fixture capture will replace it._

title: fix(core): an added sub-composition keeps its declared variable defaults when bundled
body:
## What changes

A sub-composition installed with `hyperframes add` keeps its declared variable defaults in two places: when the project is bundled with `bundleToSingleHtml`, and in Studio's standalone preview of that file. Inside the sub-composition, `getVariables()` returns those defaults again. The carousel blocks, for example, load their images from `assets/carousel-images/` instead of 404ing on bare file names and drawing white cards.

## Why it happened

`parseHTMLContent` decided whether its input was a full document or a fragment by checking whether it started with `<!doctype` or `<html`. `hyperframes add` writes a `<!-- hyperframes-registry-item: ... -->` marker comment above the doctype of every file it installs. Those files were therefore parsed as fragments and wrapped in a fresh `<html>`, which dropped their own `<html data-composition-variables>`.

The sub-composition inliner then read no declared defaults and emitted no `__hfVariablesByComp` entry for the instance, so the scoped `getVariables()` had nothing to return. The CSS custom properties for the same sub-composition were unaffected, because that path reads the defaults differently.

## The fix

- `isFullHtmlDocument` in core's `htmlDocument.ts` decides document versus fragment once. It skips leading whitespace and comments (an empty `<!-->` included), then looks for `<!doctype` or `<html` followed by whitespace or `>`. So a `<html-card>` element no longer counts.
- `parseHTMLContent` uses it. Every compiler path that parses a composition goes through `parseHTMLContent`, so the bundler, the sub-composition inliner and the template mount all see the file's real `<html>` element.
- Studio-server's preview had its own copy of the same check and hit the same bug. The preview of an installed block lost `data-composition-variables` from `<html>` and nested a second `<html>` inside `<body>`. That copy is deleted, and the preview imports the core predicate through `@hyperframes/core/compiler/html-document`.

## Tests

- `htmlDocument.test.ts`: a document that starts with a comment keeps its `<html>` attributes.
- `htmlDocument.test.ts`: document versus fragment past leading comments, an empty comment, and a `<html-card>` element.
- `htmlBundler.test.ts`: a sub-composition that starts with the install marker has its declared default in `__hfVariablesByComp` after bundling.
- `subComposition.test.ts` (studio-server): an installed block's preview keeps `data-composition-variables` on `<html>` and nests no `<html>` in `<body>`.

The first bundler and document tests fail on `main`, and the studio-server test fails on the previous studio-server code. The core suite passes (3199 tests), as do the studio-server helper tests (348) and both typechecks.

## Before

`carousel-orbit-1` added with `hyperframes add`, its snippet wrapped in a root `index.html`, bundled with `bundleToSingleHtml` (runtime inline) and loaded in Chromium on `main`. There are 48 failed image requests for bare names such as `/artist-bob-seger.jpg`, and every card is white.

![Before: bundled carousel-orbit-1 on main, 48 image 404s, white cards](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fc03e2cd-e308-40a8-bef5-5b8518742783)

## After

The same project bundled on this branch. The bundle carries the block's 24 image defaults, there are 0 failed requests, and the cards show their images.

![After: the same bundle on this branch, images load](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b871c162-8038-40fc-a5b7-b47aa520dcc2)

## Not in this PR

- The lint rule `root_composition_missing_html_wrapper` makes its own start-of-file check and would flag a root `index.html` that begins with a comment. Installed blocks are not root files, so they do not reach it.
- The carousel blocks fall back to a bare file name when `getVariables()` returns nothing for an image. It should keep the `assets/carousel-images/` folder. That affects 25 registry blocks and the generated catalog pages, so it is a separate PR.

title: fix(studio-server): background removal writes only where it checked, even through planted links
body:
## What this fixes

Background removal checks its output path when the request arrives, then hands it to a job that writes minutes later. Two ways a write could land outside the project while the job runs:

1. **A folder link on the path is retargeted.** If a link on the output path (say `cutouts/` pointing at an in-project folder) is pointed outside the project mid-job, the output followed it. Now the output and background-plate paths are pinned when checked: every link inside the project is resolved once, at validation, and the job writes to that folder. The input path is only read and keeps the plain check.
2. **A link is planted at the output file itself.** ffmpeg opened the output with create-and-truncate, which follows a link, so a link planted at `cutout.png` mid-job had its target overwritten. Now ffmpeg writes to an unguessable temporary name beside the output (same extension), and the finished file is renamed over the output, which replaces a link rather than following it. A failed job removes its temporary file. The proxy transcoder already writes this way.

3. **Two overlapping removals got the same name.** The route picks a free name by checking the disk, and the output now appears only when the job finishes, so a second removal of the same clip started while the first runs would have reused the name. Names held by running jobs are now reserved too, the cutout's own name is reserved before its plate's, and an explicit output path is normalized before it is compared.

What this does not close: if a real folder on the output path is renamed and replaced by a link while the job runs, the finished file still follows that new link. Closing it needs writes relative to an already-open folder, which Node does not offer; the file routes have the same limit.

## Visible change

Background removal writes where it did before. While a job runs, its output shows as a `.tmp-<id>-<name>` file beside the final name, and a link someone placed at a CLI `-o` target is replaced by the rendered file rather than written through. Two servers running on the same project folder can still give overlapping jobs one name, because each reserves only its own running jobs; reserving on disk would leave an empty file behind whenever a job fails.

## Tests

- `routes/media.test.ts`: the job retargets a folder link on the output path to an outside folder, then writes its output; the output lands in the in-project folder that was checked and nothing is written outside.
- `routes/media.test.ts`: two removals of the same clip while the first still runs get distinct names; so do an explicit output spelled another way and a plate asked for under the cutout's own name.
- `pipeline.windowsHide.test.ts`: a link to an outside file is planted at the output path while the encoder runs; the outside file keeps its content and the output is a regular file holding the render.

Link tests skip on Windows, where creating a symlink needs a privilege.

title: feat(core): the runtime reports where a composition's animations end, one cycle each
body:
## What this adds

The runtime now reports where a composition's animations end: `window.__hf.animationEnd()`, in seconds, or `null` when there is no animation. Studio uses it (in a follow-up change) so that moving or trimming a clip never saves a film shorter than its own animation, now that preview stops at the root's declared length as the render does.

The number is where each animation's first cycle ends, the latest one winning. It is not the film's length:

- **Not the runtime's own padding.** When the root timeline is shorter than the declared length, the runtime stretches it with a zero-length marker; when there is no usable root timeline, it builds a filler timeline. Both are tagged (`data: "hf-runtime-filler"`) and skipped, so a 4 s animation in a 10 s film reports 4 and an empty template reports `null`.
- **One cycle of a repeating animation.** GSAP's `timeline.duration()` counts every repeat of every child. The runtime walks the root timeline's children and counts one cycle each: a tween's `duration()`, a nested timeline's own one-cycle end, scaled by `|timeScale()|`. A tween with `repeat: 40` counts once. A stagger or keyframes tween counts one pass of its inner timeline, stretched to the tween's own duration as GSAP plays it, so keyframes given an overall `duration` end where they end and a stagger whose items repeat, even forever, counts its first pass. A child that still never ends is skipped rather than hiding the rest. Paused children count: skipping them made the answer depend on whether author code had played them yet.
- **The same answer whatever the playhead did.** CSS animations count from their computed `animation-duration` and `animation-delay`, read when the adapter discovers them, anchored at the clip's `data-start`; they are not read from the live animation list, which changes as animations finish or clips show and hide. Lottie counts one loop from its composition's start, as the runtime plays it, and an instance from a removed scene stops counting. Animations a script creates with `el.animate()` do not count: the runtime anchors them where it first sees them, so their end depends on seeks and scene swaps. Adapters answer only through the new optional `getAnimationCycleEndSeconds`; the WAAPI adapter does not implement it.
- **A scene only inside its clip.** A sub-composition timeline the runtime nests into the root counts up to the end of its host clip's window, read when asked, so a trimmed scene whose timeline is padded to full length counts only what shows.
- **Never media**, and a loop-inflated length reports `null`.

`getInferredDurationSeconds` and every length the runtime uses for playback and render are unchanged. One side fix in the CSS adapter: a rediscover first puts back the inline styles its own fallback seek wrote, so it does not read the seek position back as the authored delay.

## What I measured

- Real headless Chrome, the runtime built from this branch, `animationEnd()` read at load, after playing about 5 s and pausing, after `seek(9.9)` and after `seek(1)`:

  | Film (root 10 s) | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 s GSAP tween, 4 s CSS `slide 4s 1` on a clip at 0 | 4, 1, 1, 4 | 4, 4, 4, 4 |
  | 1 s GSAP tween, 4 s `el.animate()` on a clip at 0 | 4, 1, 1, 4 | 1, 1, 1, 1 (WAAPI not counted) |
  | CSS `pulse 1s 0.5s infinite` on a clip at 6 to 10 s | 7.5, 7.5, 11.4, 11.4 | 7.5, 7.5, 7.5, 7.5 |
  | Same with `1 both` | 7.5, 7.5, 11.4, 11.4 | 7.5, 7.5, 7.5, 7.5 |
  | 4 s tween plus an endless stagger | null (all four) | 4, 4, 4, 4 |

  Also constant across seeks, plays and scene swaps: a WAAPI animation created from a timeline callback or a swapped scene script (the GSAP part only); an author's paused timeline played later by a callback (7); a runtime-nested scene during play (3); a stagger repeating per item, finite (1.4) or endless (5).
- New `init.test.ts` tests with real GSAP 3.15 (added as a core dev dependency, one line in the lockfile): a 4 s tween under a declared 10 s root reports 4; an empty timeline the runtime fills reports nothing; a 1 s tween with `repeat: 40` reports one cycle; a nested timeline at `timeScale` 2 and a reversed tween count forwards; a sub-composition padded to 8 s in a 1 to 4 s clip reports 4; a per-item stagger repeat counts its first pass, finite (1.4) and endless (5); keyframes with `repeat: 3` count one cycle; array keyframes with an overall `duration: 4.4` at 1 s report 5.4; keyframes with a stagger and an overall duration, and a stagger given `.duration(4)` later, follow the stretch; a paused timeline played later reports the same before and after the play; a script-created WAAPI animation is not counted. Mock-timeline tests cover re-stretching to a longer declared length, loop-inflated timelines, an endless child next to a finite one and a Lottie animation past the root timeline.
- Lottie adapter tests: a 2 s Lottie in a composition starting at 5 s reports 7; an instance whose element was removed stops counting; a root instance reports its length.
- CSS adapter tests: one cycle per animation from the computed lists (milliseconds, a `none` entry, a shorter list repeating, the delayed animation the longest, an element with no live animation); a negative delay that ends before it starts is skipped; an element removed after discover is skipped; the authored delay survives a rediscover after a fallback seek.
- Mutations each fail a test: counting the runtime's filler, `totalDuration()` for `duration()`, dropping the absolute time scale, dropping the clip cap, ignoring a tween's inner timeline, dropping its stretch, dropping the stretch's finite check, dropping the Lottie composition start, counting a removed Lottie, adding the scene start or skipping removed Lotties in the length Lottie feeds to playback, keeping an endless child, skipping a paused child, falling back to an adapter's inferred duration, dropping Lottie's cycle getter, dropping the CSS delay, reading milliseconds as seconds, not repeating the shorter CSS list, keeping a non-positive CSS cycle, dropping the CSS connected check, not restoring inline styles before a rediscover.
- Each run alone: `init.test.ts` (178), `init.swapScenes.test.ts` (45), `adapters/css.test.ts` (19), `adapters/waapi.test.ts` (21, unchanged from main), `adapters/lottie.test.ts` (35), `transportPark.test.ts` (28), `timeline.test.ts` (70). Typecheck, lint, format, the comment ratchet and the fallow audit green.

## What I did NOT exercise

- Animations a script creates with `el.animate()` are not counted, so a film animated only that way reports `null` and Studio behaves as it does today.
- A scene the author nests into their own root timeline (rather than the runtime) is not capped at its clip.
- Padding an author wrote into their own timeline (for example `tl.to({}, { duration: 10 })`), a late `tl.call`, and a paused timeline the author never plays count as animation. That errs long, not short.
- A CSS animation added or changed by script after the adapter's discover (a class toggled by the timeline) is read as of the last discover. CSS naming missing `@keyframes` or with `animation-iteration-count: 0` still counts (errs long).
- A Lottie in a later clip of the root composition counts from the film's start, which is also where the runtime plays it today.
- A Lottie counts to its own end even when its scene's clip ends first, and one drawn into an element outside its scene keeps counting after a scene swap. Both err long.
- An eased keyframes tween whose last keyframe repeats reports its end early: the ease reshapes where that keyframe's first cycle lands, and the stretch is a straight ratio. Without an ease, or without a repeating keyframe, it is exact.
- On a render page the producer's early stub puts proxies in `window.__timelines`, so the clip cap would not match there. Nothing reads `animationEnd` on a render page.
- anime.js, Three, TypeGPU, D3 and the map adapters are not counted.

title: fix(runtime): make the preview's scene swap safe before Studio turns it on
body:
## Summary Five fixes to the preview's scene swap (`window.__hfSwapScenes`, #4502), needed before Studio turns it on for every edit (#4499). #4502 is merged; nothing calls the swap until #4499 lands, so this PR changes nothing a user sees on its own. 1. **A tween from outside the scene that moves the scene's elements no longer goes dead.** GSAP binds a tween to elements, so a root-timeline (or other-scene) tween on the scene's host or anything inside it kept animating the detached old copy, and the new scene never moved. The swap now refuses that scene before changing anything, and the caller's full reload handles it. The check runs after the swap's one wait (loading caption overrides), so a tween started during that wait is caught, and again after the old scenes' animations are stopped, since stopping one fires its `onInterrupt`. That second refusal comes after the swap has changed the page, which the caller's full reload replaces. The new scene scripts run only once every edited scene's host is replaced, so a new script cannot bind to the old copy of another scene the same swap replaces. 2. **A video that a scene script animates is kept, not reloaded, on a text edit.** The swap keeps a video or audio whose markup the edit left alone, comparing against the element as written. That record was taken at DOMContentLoaded, after the scene scripts ran, so a `tl.from()` on the video (which writes an inline style when the timeline is built) made every edit rebuild it and show an unready frame. The record is now taken as the page parses, before any scene script runs, and a media element the swap rebuilds is recorded from the new markup, before its new script runs. The swap keeps media only when the scene's scripts are unchanged: what an old script wrote to the element directly (`video.style.opacity = "0"`, `video.muted = true`) cannot be known, so when the edit changes a script the swap rebuilds the scene's media, which matches a fresh load. With an unchanged script, what it wrote to the element can still depend on the edited markup (it mutes the video, or sets a class, only while a heading reads a certain way). So an element is kept only if its live attributes (in any order) and content still match the new markup exactly, leaving out what the runtime itself writes: `style` (reset from the new markup), `preload` (set to auto, init.ts and media.ts), the parse-time opacity stamp, a moved element's original translate, the runtime's own `__hf-` classes (the picker's hover and the flash after an agent edit, which overlaps the swap that edit starts), and `src`, which is compared as written before any proxy rewrite and left to the variable binding when it has one. Anything else a script wrote, such as a class, `hidden`, `data-volume`, `data-playback-rate`, `poster`, `loop` or a child, rebuilds the element, which costs the same brief unready frame a script edit does. Properties show up in no attribute, so a kept element also gets back what the runtime gives a fresh one: `muted` (with the preview's own mute, as the runtime's mute handlers set it), `playbackRate` (the preview's rate), `defaultPlaybackRate` (1; the runtime reads it as a clip's rate when the markup gives none) and `preservesPitch` (true). Web Audio lets go of the element first, since its next stop puts back the mute and volume it saved under the old script. Volume needs nothing new: the swap already re-probes each kept element's volume envelope, which sets it from `data-volume` and the timeline. A video or audio a script gave a stream, an output device or a key session is rebuilt. Current time and play state stay with the timeline. The parse-time watch is installed only on a page that carries the scene-parts manifest, so renders and plain previews do not pay for it; on a manifest page it adds parse time (measured below). 3. **Three swap steps that no test pinned now have one each:** clearing the volume envelope cache for media kept through the swap, applying per-instance CSS variables to the scene host itself, and keeping asset-failure listeners out of the swap. 4. **Animations a scene script starts outside its registered timeline are stopped on a swap.** A scene script that builds a timeline it never registers, or calls GSAP under another name (`const g = gsap; g.to(...)`, `gsap["to"](...)`, `globalThis.gsap.to(...)`), left the old copy running beside the new one. The scene script wrapper now records everything the script adds to GSAP's global timeline while it runs, by composition id, and the swap reverts those along with the scene's timelines, nested compositions included, newest first by when each was created.
