A `gsap.set` completes as it is made, and GSAP drops a completed tween from its global timeline at once, so the wrapper turns that off while the script runs, records the set, then drops it from the timeline itself (a completed tween left there would keep GSAP's ticker awake). Reverting does not always put an element back as a fresh load has it: a `from()` writes as it is made while an earlier tween reads its start value later, so a revert can leave one animation's value behind. Animations on the scene's own elements need nothing more, since the swap replaces them. A video or audio the swap keeps is put back as written after the reverts and before the new script runs: GSAP's own `clearProps: "all"` empties its inline style and GSAP's cached values for it, then its authored `style` is restored and its Studio move is applied again as on a load, so the new script's tweens read what a fresh load's do. When any of the scene script's animations (its registered timelines, their tweens, or anything it started) writes to a page element outside the scene, the swap refuses and the caller reloads. A tween on a plain object, such as `tl.to({}, {duration: 2})` padding or a counter, is reverted with the scene's animations, and the new script makes its own object. It records only on a page that carries the scene-parts manifest, the only pages a swap can act on. The first scoped script checks for the manifest once, so renders and other previews record no animations and hold no extra references to them. 5. **A swap acts only on the page it planned against, and ends a shortened film where it stops.** A runtime-data handler or an animation's `onInterrupt` can run while a swap waits for caption overrides or stops the old animations. After the wait and again after the stops, the swap reads the timeline registry as it is then, stops whatever the stops themselves registered (up to eight rounds, then refuses), and refuses when any of a scene's parts was replaced, detached or moved to another parent, or when the film's scene layout changed. The layout is, for each element on a scene host's way up to the film root (its parent, that parent's parent, and so on, the film root included), the full order of its children, each parent recorded once. It is recorded before the wait and must be identical, element for element, after the wait and after the stops. So a scene is never dropped from the film, reordered, moved into another container or moved past other content in the film while the manifest advances, however the move was made (the host itself, a wrapper around it, a pair of scenes together, or a scene moved as a block with the elements on both sides of it). Elements the runtime inserts beside media and marks `data-hf-ignore`, such as colour grading's canvas, are left out of those orders, so grading a video beside a scene does not refuse its swap. Changes outside the scene hosts and their ancestors, such as something appended to the page during the wait, still swap: the swap removes the scene's old scripts and appends the new ones at the end of the page, so their place never matters. `__hfSwapScenes(html, signal)` takes an optional abort signal and refuses a cancelled swap after the caption wait, before it changes anything, so a caller that gave up (Studio at 5 s) cannot have the swap land later. When a playing film's new length is at or before the playhead, the swap stops it at the new end, as reaching the end does; it used to wrap to the start and keep playing. ## Decisions - **Item 1: refuse, rather than keep the old host and replace its contents.** Keeping the host element still needs a refusal for tweens on anything inside it, plus reconciling the host's attributes and script-written values. Refusing whenever a tween outside the scene's own timelines targets the host or a descendant is the smaller complete fix for both shapes. The check makes one pass over every tween in the film (`gsap.globalTimeline.getChildren`, paused and nested tweens included), keeps those whose targets are in the scene's subtree, and walks each up its parents; it is the scene's own when it reaches one of the scene's registered timelines, a nested composition's timeline, or an animation its script started (item 4). - **Item 4: record by diffing GSAP's global timeline around the script, not by intercepting methods on the scoped `gsap` proxy.** Anything a script creates, a tween, a timeline or a `delayedCall`, lands on the global timeline, whichever spelling reached GSAP. A diff taken around the script's run therefore also covers the unscoped global (`window.gsap`, `globalThis.gsap`, `self.gsap`, an alias of `window`), which a proxy cannot see. Those do not need their own refusal. - **Item 4: reset kept media to their authored state, and refuse animations outside the scene, rather than fix the revert order.** The right order is the order each tween first wrote, which the record does not have (GSAP's own `gsap.context` gets it from every tween at creation), and even one timeline does not revert exactly: with a `to()` before a `from()` on the same property, a kept video ended at opacity 0 against 0.375-0.5 on a fresh load. A kept video or audio is the swap's own element, so putting it back as written is correct whatever the script did with GSAP. An element outside the scene belongs to the rest of the film, which the swap does not rebuild. Real GSAP 3.15.0 in Chromium with the real runtime: the `to()` before `from()` video now matches a fresh load at every sampled time, and a nested timeline on an element outside the scene is refused. That edit takes a full reload rather than rebuilding just the scene: the case is rare and the reload is always correct. Studio logs the refusal's reason ("its animations write outside the scene") under `scene-swap-refused`, so a per-video rebuild follows only if that count shows it is common. - **Item 2: an edit to a scene's animation script rebuilds that scene's videos; text and markup edits keep them.** What an old script wrote straight onto a video (`muted`, an inline style) cannot be detected, so a kept video could show state a fresh load would not. A preview that differs from a fresh load is worse than one brief unready frame on a script edit. ## Cost Headless Chromium on a 32-core Linux box, medians. - **Parse time, 40,208-node page with 200 videos** (from just after the runtime script to the end of ``, two rounds of 6 loads): | | #4502 | this branch | |---|---|---| | without the manifest (renders, plain previews) | 676 / 670 ms | 668 / 669 ms | | with the manifest (Studio preview) | 666 / 688 ms | 814 / 803 ms | On a manifest page the watch costs 20-39% of parse time on this very large page across two measurements on a shared box (roughly 3-6 µs per node), paid only on the preview's first load. - **Swap of a 4,002-element scene in a film with 4,001 tweens:** the outside-tween check takes 1.5 ms (one pass over the film's tweens against a set of the scene's elements), where asking `gsap.getTweensOf` for all 4,002 elements took 46 ms; the whole swap went from 336 ms to 290 ms. The same film with one root tween on a scene element is refused in 37 ms. ## How many films this refuses A static scan of the films that have scene parts: every registry example and producer fixture with a top-level `data-composition-src` host. It resolves each root-script tween target, literal selectors and variables assigned from `document.querySelector` / `getElementById`, against the document with its sub-compositions inlined. **3 of 44 films hit the new refusal on a text edit in at least one scene (4 of 98 scenes):** `product-promo` (the root fades `#scene-2-4` out; #4503's static check already refuses that scene, so here this is a backstop), `sub-comp-t0` (the root animates both scene hosts) and `pip-video-late-host`. The 40 skill films with scene parts (motion primitives, remotion-to-hyperframes corpus) hit 0, and the CLI templates have no scene parts. Other-scene tweens were not scanned: scene scripts resolve selectors inside their own root, so they can reach another scene only through an element reference. The outside-the-scene refusal (item 4), by execution: every film with scene parts (83: registry examples, producer fixtures, skills) bundled for preview by the scene-parts compiler (#4503), loaded in headless Chromium with this branch's runtime and GSAP 3.15.0, and each of its 141 scenes swapped in with only its manifest hash changed, so every refusal comes from the film itself. 124 scenes swap. None is refused for animating outside the scene; counting a tween on a plain object as outside (the rule before this change) refused 12, among them `sub-composition-video`'s `tl.to({}, {duration: 2})` padding. The other 17 are refused by earlier checks: 3 by the outside-tween check of item 1 (all three scenes of `heygen-promo-preview-assets`, whose scripts take `document.currentScript.parentElement` as their root: in a bundled preview that is the body, so scenes 2 and 3 animate scene 1's elements), and 14 by the compiler's own marks (a script outside the scene selecting it, `THREE`, `getContext`, `repeat: -1`, `setTimeout`, an unknown library). ## Before / After in headless Chrome Headless Chromium with GSAP 3.15.0, on a 32-core Linux box. Base is #4502's runtime, after is this branch; each swapped page is compared with a fresh load of the same edited document. The playhead is paused at T and the edit changes only scene a's text unless noted. | Probe | Base | After | Fresh load | |---|---|---|---| | 1. Root tweens scene a's host opacity 1 to 0 over 2-3 s; opacity at 1 / 2.5 / 3.5 s | swapped; 1 / 1 / 1 | **refused** (full reload) | 1 / 0.5 / 0 | | 1. Control, no outside tween | swapped, matches fresh | swapped, matches fresh | | | 2. Scene script `tl.from("#v", {opacity: 0})` over 0-2 s | video rebuilt | **video kept**; 0 / 0.5 / 1 at 0 / 1 / 3 s | 0 / 0.5 / 1 | | 2. Edit 1 adds an attribute to the video, edit 2 is text only | rebuilt, then rebuilt again | rebuilt, then **kept**; matches fresh | | | 4. Unregistered `gsap.timeline()`: copies running after the swap | 2 | **1** | 1 | | 4. `const g = gsap; g.to(...)` | 2 | **1** | 1 | | 4. `gsap["to"](...)` | 2 | **1** | 1 | | 4. `globalThis.gsap.to("#out", ...)`, a target outside the scene | 2 (the two copies stack on `#out`) | 1 at the time of this probe; a later rule refuses it (full reload) | 1 | The item 4 witnesses are free-running tweens on GSAP's ticker, not on the paused film timeline, so their values follow wall-clock time in every run. The copy count is the comparison that matters there. ## Tests Each new test was run without its fix and failed: - Item 1: `refuses, changing nothing, when …` for the root timeline on the host, on an element inside it, and another scene's timeline on an element inside it. Without the refusal, each swap resolves. `swaps a scene whose elements only its own and its nested scenes' timelines tween` guards against over-refusal. - Item 2: `keeps a video a scene script wrote to while the page parsed` fails with the capture at init only. `keeps a rebuilt video through the next edit though its scene script writes to it` fails with the record taken after the script. `records a video's children that the parser adds after the video itself` fails without the refresh for children that arrive after the parser yields. - Item 3: dropping each step fails its test: `re-probes the volume of media kept through the swap`, `gives the swapped scene's host its per-instance CSS variables`, `adds no asset error listener to the swapped scene`. - Parse watch: `does not watch a page without a scene manifest as it parses` fails without the manifest check; `stops watching the page it parses once the runtime starts` fails without the disconnect at init. - Swap bookkeeping: `reverts a scene's timeline once though its script also recorded it` fails without the single-revert check (2 reverts); the item 4 tests also check the scene's animation record holds one entry after a swap, which fails when the record is not cleared. - Item 4: `stops what the old scene script started through …` for all four spellings runs the real scene-script wrapper. Without recording, the swap refuses (item 1 sees the untracked tweens on the scene's own `

`); with recording but no revert, 2 copies run. `records what a script starts on GSAP's global timeline, however it reaches GSAP` covers the wrapper on its own, and a second case checks that a page without the manifest records nothing (it failed before the manifest check). - Media an unchanged script wrote to over the old text: the tests run a script that writes only while the heading reads "A one" (`if (scene.querySelector('p').textContent === 'A one') video.muted = true;`) and edit the heading. `rebuilds a video as a fresh load has it when its unchanged script ran … only over the old text` covers a class, `hidden`, `data-volume`, `data-playback-rate`, `poster`, `loop` and an added child: all seven kept the video with the write on it before, and all fail without the comparison. The added child row also fails when content is left out of the comparison. `keeps a video through a text edit when its unchanged script writes nothing to it` pins the keep. `keeps a video on which the runtime wrote …` covers `preload`, a proxied `src`, a variable-bound `src` and the opacity stamp, and each fails when its exclusion is removed. The existing `keeps a moved video where it was moved …` fails when the position-edit marker is counted, and the tween-reset tests fail when `style` is counted. The GSAP row `a scene script with a counter on a local object on video` now expects the video rebuilt, since its callback writes `data-n` on it. `gives a kept video the %s a fresh load gives it …` covers muted, both rates, preservesPitch and volume. Removing each reset fails its row. title: fix(registry): carousel cards fall back to their sample image inside the assets folder
body:
## What changes

When a carousel block's image variable resolves to nothing, the card now falls back to the block's sample image inside `assets/carousel-images/`. Before, it fell back to a bare file name, which 404s beside the installed block and draws a white card.

This covers all 25 carousel blocks: circle, orbit, path, text-circle and vision, 1 to 5 each.

## Why it happened

Each carousel builds its cards from its image variables. For a variable with no value it used `DATA.cards[i].file`, the bare sample file name. It then marked the card as an absolute source and loaded it as-is. The block's own path for sample cards (`img.src = c.abs ? c.file : "assets/carousel-images/" + c.file`) and its `registry-item.json` both put those images in `assets/carousel-images/`, so the bare name never resolved.

#4539 fixes the bundler dropping the variables' declared defaults, which is what left them empty in bundled output. This PR makes the block itself resilient to an empty variable, from any cause.

## The fix

The fallback in each of the 25 blocks prepends `"assets/carousel-images/"`. The generated catalog pages and payloads are left to the catalog publish PR, as `check-catalog-source-pr` requires for item-source changes.

## Tests

`scripts/catalog/carousel-fallback.test.ts` picks every block in `registry/blocks` that reads an image variable (the 25 carousels) and fails if its fallback loads a bare file name or no longer matches the expected shape. It fails on `main`'s blocks.

## Before

`carousel-orbit-1` on `main`: added with `hyperframes add`, wrapped in a root `index.html`, bundled with `bundleToSingleHtml` (runtime inline) and loaded in Chromium. The bundler on `main` drops the variables' defaults, so every card takes the fallback. There are 48 failed requests for bare names such as `/artist-bob-seger.jpg`, and every card is white.

![carousel-orbit-1 on main: white cards](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/13b93f35-0121-490a-b806-c22472238238)

## After

The same project with this branch's block, still bundled by `main`'s core, so the variables are still empty. There are 0 failed requests, and every card loads its sample image from `assets/carousel-images/`.

![carousel-orbit-1 with this branch: every card loads](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/16fd33a4-2dfb-41f8-916a-264fbb39c192)

title: fix(core): a picked heading is named by its text, not just Heading
body:
## What was wrong

The preview picker names each element it offers or picks, in the `label` field of its messages and of `__HF_PICKER_API` results. Paragraphs, spans and divs are named by their short visible text, but every `h1`, `h2` and `h3` came back as "Heading". So a picker list with a title and a subtitle showed two identical "Heading" rows, and a pick reported "Heading" instead of what the heading says. `h4` to `h6` came back as "H4" to "H6".

## The fix

Headings, `h1` to `h6`, are named like text: their whitespace-collapsed text, trimmed to 56 characters. "Heading" is used only when the heading has no text.

The 56-character trim now counts characters, not UTF-16 units. Before, a label could end in half an emoji, which shows up as a broken glyph. This applied to paragraphs, spans and divs already.

Studio's own Layers panel and selection use a separate labeler, which already names a heading by its id, class or text. That labeler is unchanged, and nothing Studio displays changes, so this PR has no captures.

## Tests

- `picker.test.ts`: "labels a heading by its text, and by its role only when it has none".
  - An `h2` with text is named by its text, and an empty `h4` is named "Heading".
  - A long `h1` with an emoji at the cut point keeps the whole emoji.
  - Fails on main: the `h2` comes back as "Heading", and the emoji is cut in half.
- Picker tests 44/44. Typecheck, lint, format, comment ratchet and fallow audit are clean.

title: fix(player): a reloaded preview waits for its assets once, not twice
body:
## What was wrong

When Studio reloads the preview after a file change, the new, still-hidden player loaded its document and then ran the whole handshake a second time for that same document.

The runtime posts its timeline at DOMContentLoaded, so the player becomes ready, waits for assets and emits `ready` before the iframe's `load` event. On `load`, the player then dropped that handshake for any same-origin document: it cleared `ready`, probed again, emitted a second `ready` and started a second asset wait. Only opaque-origin documents were spared.

That second wait is extra work on every reload, and it holds back the swap to the new preview. While it runs, the player shows "Loading assets" for a document it had already reported `ready`.

## The fix

- **Player:** it remembers which document its handshake belongs to. On `load` it keeps the handshake if the loaded document is that same one, so there is one handshake per document. Every host-initiated navigation already clears `ready` first, so a new document still gets a fresh handshake.
- **Player, leaving a document:** stopping what the player ran for the old document used to happen in that `load` reset: its clocks, the loader, and parent-frame audio after an autoplay fallback. It now happens when the player navigates away (`src`, `srcdoc`, sandbox or shader-option reloads). A source change stops the previous film's audio at once instead of at the next document's `load`. The parent-frame copies of the old film's media are dropped as well, instead of only paused. Before, they stayed in the list, so when the next film also fell back to parent audio, the old track played again beside the new one, and a track with the same URL kept the old film's timing. An `audio-src` track is kept across the change. If it shares a URL with the old film's media, it gets its own proxy again, just as when `audio-src` is set before a film loads: it then covers the whole film rather than one clip's window. The `audioownershipchange` event with reason `iframe-reload` now fires when the player navigates away. That includes opaque-origin players, which never got it after a navigation before.
- **Player, first-frame media added before `load`:** the one asset wait scans pending first-frame media when the runtime reports ready, at DOMContentLoaded. A `<video data-start="0">` that a script adds after that, before `load`, is not in that scan. On main, the second handshake at `load` covered it. Now, at `load`, the player scans the same document once more. Only if a first-frame asset is still pending does it restart that one asset wait, with no second `ready` and no re-probe. Otherwise nothing happens, and first paint keeps main's timing.
- **Studio:** `Player.tsx` treated every iframe `load` as "not ready, not painted yet" and waited for the next `ready`/`painted` events. With one handshake per document those events can arrive before `load`, so Studio now reads the player's `ready` and `painted` getters at `load` instead of resetting them. Without this half, the reloaded preview would never be swapped in.

## Embedder impact

A same-origin composition now gets one `ready` and one `assetsready` event per document instead of two of each. An embedder that waits for `ready` after the iframe's `load` event should read `player.ready` at `load`, as Studio now does. The in-repo listeners (the slideshow, the docs gallery snippet, the perf server) take the first event only, so they are unaffected. Opaque-origin compositions are unchanged: they already had one handshake.

The player now registers its iframe `load` listener when it is constructed, so it always handles `load` before any host listener attached later, such as Studio's. It ignores loads until it is connected: the iframe's initial blank document can fire `load` while the player is being inserted, before its `src` is set. A host that reads `player.ready` or `player.painted` in its own `load` listener sees state for the document that just loaded. That includes a re-wait the player starts at `load`, and a page that navigated the iframe by itself.

## Tests

- `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: "keeps a same-origin handshake when that document's load event arrives after ready". Fails on main's guard (`_ready` goes false on `load`).
- `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: "hands audio back to the iframe and pauses the proxy as soon as the source changes". Fails if navigating away does not release the old document or leaves the parent clock running.
- `parent-media.test.ts`: "drops the previous document's proxies on reset and keeps the audio-src one". Fails on main.
- `parent-media.test.ts`: "keeps the audio-src track after a reset when the old document shared its URL". An `audio-src` pointing at a URL the film already uses gets its own proxy once the film's copies are dropped.
- `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: "stays unpainted for first-frame media a script adds before the document's load". Timeline at DOMContentLoaded, then a video with no data is added before `load`. Fails without the re-check at `load`.
- `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: "paints a document before its load when nothing first-frame is pending". Guards first-paint timing: fails if readiness waits for the page's `load`.
- `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: "handles its iframe's load before a host's load listener runs". Fails with the listener registered at connect.
- `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: "ignores its iframe's blank-document load that arrives before it is connected". Fails without that check, when a slow first film would get a false "timeline not found" error.
- `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: "keeps a same-origin handshake …" now also asserts that `load` with nothing pending sends no second `assetsready`. Fails if the player re-waits at every `load`.
- `Player.test.ts`: "can show a document whose player was ready and painted before its load event". Fails without the Studio half, and also fails if Studio ignores either getter.
- Player suite 442/442, Studio `src/player` 1613/1613. Typecheck, lint, format, comment ratchet and fallow audit are clean.

## Before

Studio dev server, a synthetic test film (a generated test pattern with tones), a file edit that triggers the preview reload. The overlay lists the new player's events. On main, one document gets two `ready` events and two asset waits, with the iframe `load` between them.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/155cacc0-5d29-4451-8a33-0ee858220d9f

## After

The same edit: one `ready` and one asset wait. Then `load`, `assetsready`, `painted`, and the new preview is swapped in.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fa833a3f-be92-4593-9474-da79d73dd794

Both clips were recorded against the same synthetic film, with the same edit, 30 seconds after it.

In these runs Studio kept the new player hidden until its last `painted`, so main's second wait never reached the screen. The captures show the cause, the duplicate handshake, rather than a loader on screen.

title: fix(cli): --yes in an unattended run no longer overrides a no saved by another process
body:
## What this fixes

An app that runs `hyperframes catalog --on-device` without a terminal asks first without `--yes`, and adds `--yes` only when the CLI says it never asked the person. If the person answers No in their own terminal between those two runs, the second run's `--yes` saved Yes over it and downloaded the on-device model they had just refused. `--yes` was treated as authorization, and the write did not look at what was saved meanwhile.

Now, in a run nobody watches, `--yes` only answers a question that was never asked. A run counts as watched only in an interactive terminal: stdin and stdout both terminals, no `--json`, and not CI (the same rule `hyperframes auth login --device` uses). A terminal with piped stdin, or a CI job with a terminal, is unwatched. The download offer the CLI makes after a thin word-match result follows the same rule, so an unwatched run is never asked and a piped answer can never save a Yes.

- The answer is decided from what is on disk at the moment of the write, under a lock on the CLI's settings file. Every writer of that file takes the same lock, from one helper: the CLI's own settings writes, the background auto-update step that records a finished update (it carries the helper's source, since it runs while the CLI's files are being replaced), and media-use's telemetry notice and id (media-use ships as standalone scripts, so it carries a copy the repo's parity check holds identical). Only the process that created a lock ever removes it: no process takes over another's lock, so two processes can never hold it at once. A lock older than any real hold (5 seconds) was left by a process that stopped mid-write; it is refused at once rather than waited on, with a message naming the file to delete, and `hyperframes doctor` reports it and how to remove it. The last two now also skip their write when the file exists but cannot be read, instead of replacing it, and media-use writes through a temporary file and a rename so a reader never sees half a file. A No saved by another process before the run installs anything stands: every path that installs the on-device runtime or model reads the saved answer right before it, including a later search that finishes an earlier yes, and a search never installs the runtime on its own (it uses what is installed, or falls back to word matching). The answer is read again between the runtime install and the model download. If a person's answer cannot be saved, the run says so and installs nothing.
- Every other settings write keeps the saved answer as it is on disk, so a copy of the settings read before another process saved a No can never put the question back to unasked.
- A settings file that exists but cannot be read or parsed, or holds an answer that is not a plain yes or no, counts as a No, never as a question not yet asked, so a damaged file can never lead to an unattended install. A person can still answer in an interactive terminal.
- A person who types `--yes` in their own interactive terminal can still reverse their own earlier No, as before. If a person's No cannot be saved, the CLI says so instead of reporting it as saved.

No new flag or option. The guarantee holds between CLIs at this version or later: an older CLI on the same machine still writes its settings without the lock.

Known limits:

- If a hyperframes process stops inside its millisecond hold (killed, crashed, Ctrl-C, power loss), its lock stays until a person deletes it. Until then settings writes fail closed: an unattended `--yes` never proceeds, best-effort writes skip without slowing commands, a background update is not relaunched on every run, each command run by a person in a terminal prints one line naming the file and `hyperframes doctor` (never with `--json`, piped input or output, or in CI), and `hyperframes doctor` reports it.
- A No saved while an install step is already running does not stop that step or the search it belongs to; the next run reads it.
- A lock is released without re-reading it, since no code removes another process's lock. If a person deletes the lock of a process that is alive but paused (the message says to delete it only when no hyperframes command is running), that process's later release can remove the next holder's lock.
- A settings file that cannot be read now reads as a No, and the message says the download was previously declined even if the person never answered.
- Consent is now saved before the on-device runtime is installed, so if that install fails, a Yes stays saved and later searches retry the runtime install. The two sentences an app can match ("previously declined", "pass --on-device --yes once they agree") keep their wording.

## Why this is one PR

It is about 15% over the usual size because each review round added a piece the guarantee needed (one lock for every writer, no lock takeover, the doctor check, the install checks). Split now, both halves would need a fresh review, and neither half is useful to revert alone.

## Tests

- `telemetry/config.lock.test.ts`, on the real file system with a real second process: the other process takes the settings lock and saves a No after a pause; the conditional yes waits for it and keeps the No. A settings write from a copy read before a No keeps the No, and a No saved elsewhere reads back in this process even when keeping it writes nothing.
- `commands/catalog.test.ts`: an unattended `--yes` answers a never-asked question and downloads; it keeps a recorded No and installs nothing; it keeps a No saved while the run was starting and installs nothing; when the answer cannot be saved it installs nothing and does not claim a No. A terminal with piped stdin, and a terminal in CI, are unwatched, so their `--yes` keeps a saved No. A person's No that cannot be saved is reported, in both places the CLI asks. A thin-results search in a terminal with piped stdin, or in CI, is not offered the download and saves nothing.
- `registry/localModel.test.ts`: a person's answer is recorded over whatever was saved; the assumed yes applies only to a question never asked.
- `media-use/lib/config-lock.test.mjs`, on the real file system: a failed release still returns the task's result; a lock left by a process that stopped is refused within a second, the message names it, and it is never removed; a live holder is waited for.
- `commands/doctor.test.ts`: no lock reports fine; a leftover lock is reported with the file to delete and left in place.
- `utils/autoUpdate.test.ts`: a background update whose pending record cannot be saved is not launched.
- `commands/catalog.test.ts`, the install checks: a routine update after a later No installs nothing; a No saved while the runtime installs stops the model download; a runtime missing beside a ready model installs only through the check; a person's unsaved yes installs nothing, in either prompt.
- `registry/localEmbedder.test.ts` and `utils/optionalPackages.test.ts`: the search's runtime loader never installs.
- `telemetry/config.lock.test.ts`: reading the answer waits for a No another process is saving; a leftover lock warns once in a terminal, never with `--json`, `--json=true`, piped output or CI.
- `telemetry/config.lock.test.ts`: a corrupt settings file, a directory where the file should be, and an answer saved as the text "false" all count as a No for an unattended yes.
- `telemetry/config.test.ts`: a failed write returns the answer on disk, not the new one; a lock held past the timeout returns the No on disk and writes nothing; a write nested inside the lock does not wait on itself.
- `utils/autoUpdate.test.ts`, running the real generated script: it waits for another process's locked write and keeps the No it saved; it leaves a settings file it cannot read untouched; it starts one when there is none.
- `media-use/lib/telemetry.test.mjs`: the same three cases through media-use's `track`; the two media-use copies stay identical.

Results: CLI `src/telemetry`, `src/registry`, `commands/catalog.test.ts`, `commands/doctor.test.ts`, `utils/autoUpdate.test.ts`, `utils/optionalPackages.test.ts` and `commands/auth` 699 (1 skipped); `node --test` for the lock, media-use telemetry and the copy parity 20; the skills manifest check passes; the lock helper, bundled at the CLI's target, runs from its embedded source; `tsc`, `oxlint` and Fallow clean. Single mutations each fail a test: no lock, a stale copy's consent winning, an unconditional yes, a failed save reported as a No, a stale in-process copy after an unchanged answer, the auto-update step or media-use writing without the lock or over an unreadable file, a failed write reporting the new answer, a lock timeout treated as never asked or running unlocked, no re-entry guard, the old stdout-only terminal rule, no CI check, no stdin check, the thin-results offer on the old stdout-only rule, a person's unsaved No reported as saved, an unreadable or non-boolean answer read as never asked, a leftover lock taken over or waited on instead of refused, a routine update trusting the cached yes, no re-check after the runtime install, a person's unsaved yes installing, the search installing the runtime, no route for a missing runtime, the warning printed with `--json` or piped output or more than once, a failed release surfacing as an error, a non-exclusive lock create, doctor staying silent about a leftover lock, and no re-entry guard.
