title: fix(studio-server): uncopied HEVC clips no longer stall Studio while their preview copies are made
body:
## What changes for a user

Opening a project with several videos the browser cannot decode (HEVC, ProRes) no longer freezes the rest of Studio while their preview copies are made. Before, every such clip held one of the browser's six connections to the Studio server for the whole transcode, so saves, API calls and other assets queued behind them for many seconds. Now the server answers at once, the preview asks again until the copy is ready, and the clip switches to its copy as soon as it lands.

## How

- **Server** (`packages/studio-server/src/routes/preview.ts`): a `?hf-proxy=` request for a clip whose copy is not ready yet answers `202` with `Retry-After: 2` and `Cache-Control: no-store` instead of awaiting the transcode. It reuses the existing `waitForProxy` with a zero wait, so a cached copy still wins (it resolves before any timer fires). The transcode keeps running and concurrent asks still share it. `recordProxyRequest()` moves after the wait, so it counts served proxies only (a 304, a 202 or a failure serves none).
- **Failures reach the client** (`packages/studio-server/src/helpers/proxyTranscoder.ts`): an ask that got a 202 only hears a failure if the transcoder remembers it. Its failure cache now remembers every failure except a full queue (which already surfaces in the same turn as a 503). ffmpeg missing and HDR filters missing used to be skipped on purpose so that installing ffmpeg recovers without a restart. They are now kept for 10 s (five times the 202's `Retry-After`, one shared constant), so recovery still takes seconds. Everything else, including non-transcode errors such as a failed rename, keeps the existing 60 s.
- **One owner of the proxy URL** (`packages/core/src/runtime/mediaProxy.ts`, `proxyWait.ts`): the preview runtime is the only code that makes `?hf-proxy=` URLs. It now asks for one byte of the copy (a media element never sees an HTTP status), waits out each 202 or 503 per `Retry-After`, and only then puts the proxy URL on the video and reloads it. Per-source sync state (drift offsets, seek-retry latches, volume tracking) is evicted first, because state measured on the original would read the new file's buffering as drift. Until then the video keeps its original `src`. So nothing that reads a clip's `src` ever gets a copy still being made: the player's parent media mirror, the timeline filmstrips and the timeline duration probe all read a URL that works. None of them needs its own retry. A copy that cannot be made is diagnosed once and the clip stays on its original. A failed one-byte ask (the request drops, or an error status such as a restart race) is asked again after 2 s, up to 3 times, inside the same wait, so a clip still has one wait at a time. A wait whose video leaves the page is dropped, and one whose video is pointed at another file is dropped too, while the new file gets its own wait.
- **The player's parent media mirror follows its clip** (`packages/player/src/parent-media.ts`): it copied each clip's `src` once, when the timeline became ready, and never looked again. It now also watches `src`. A clip that is re-pointed while the parent owns playback is followed at once. Otherwise the mirror keeps its file until the parent takes over playback, and then re-points every entry to its clip's current `src`. Following eagerly downloaded every finished copy a second time, while the preview was downloading it too, and doubled the stall below (A/B in the table). One proxy per file still holds: a clip re-pointed onto a file another clip already plays is heard through that clip's proxy, a proxy's file being where its clip points now (so two clips that swap files keep both), a clip that leaves takes only its own proxy with it, and a clip that replaces another on the same file gets its own (a clip that left the page owns no file).
- **Studio's timeline follows the swap** (`packages/studio/src/player/hooks/timelinePlayerSync.ts`): the runtime re-posts its clip list when a clip's `src` changes, but Studio only accepted a new list when an id, timing, track or source length changed. A clip that only changed its URL kept the original in the timeline, so its filmstrip could keep decoding the file the copy exists to replace. The URL is now part of that check.
- **Thumbnails and snapshots** (`packages/studio-server/src/routes/thumbnail.ts`, `packages/core/src/runtime/mediaProxy.ts`): a frame capture holds for a clip's pending copy up to the same 5 s it already allowed a loading video (`HOLD_CAP_MS` in `media.ts`), because the copy now arrives after a round-trip instead of at once. A composition card rendered while any copy in the project is being made (or starts or lands during the render) is returned but not cached, so the next open renders it again.

## Before

![Before](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3b2ff4fe-918e-4c9c-b501-4b31d042e9e1)

main, 8 generated 720p HEVC clips (30 s each), Studio in headless Chromium on Linux (no HEVC decode, so every clip swaps to its copy). The proxy cache is cleared before each run and the transcoder uses default settings (2 at a time). In this run the copies took longer than the timeline's 30 s thumbnail timeout, so the timeline shows "no preview" and the composition card says "Preview unavailable".

## After

![After](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a162c926-bae9-4826-a46c-9e976e57ed66)

Same fixture, same machine, this branch: all 8 preview tiles paint from their copies and every timeline clip draws its filmstrip. The composition card was rendered while the copies were still being made, so it is partial and not cached. The Lint badge is the fixture's own info finding (its clips are HEVC), the same on main. Reopened:

![Composition card reopened](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5cce36bb-1024-4440-b8f7-6f24ebf1bd7c)

On main a cold card is also missing tiles (2 of 8 in my run). The thumbnail browser has the same 6 connections, and a capture waits at most 5 s per video.

## What I measured

An unrelated same-host `GET /api/projects`, fired one after another from the moment the page opens until every tile paints, with a fresh cache every run:

| run | worst unrelated fetch | all 8 tiles painted | timeline filmstrips |
|---|---|---|---|
| main 1 | 18.4 s | 67.2 s | not counted |
| main 2 | 16.6 s | 36.3 s | 42 frames, 0 "no preview" |
| main 3 | 8.5 s | 41.0 s | 0 frames, 7 of 8 "no preview" (thumbnail timeout) |
| this branch, run 1 | 4.8 s | 31.9 s | 30 frames at 8 s and 20 s after paint, 0 "no preview" |
| this branch, run 2 | 5.0 s | 35.1 s | 42 frames at 8, 20 and 40 s after paint, 0 "no preview" |

Every media request for a `?hf-proxy=` URL, by the frame that asked and the answer, in the same fixture:

| | preview frame `<video>` | top frame `<video>` (player's parent media mirror) |
|---|---|---|
| a previous head of this PR (which put the proxy URL on the video at once) | 8 answered 202, then 12 answered 206 on retry | **8 answered 202, never retried** |
| this branch | 8 answered 206, none 202 | none while the composition owns playback; re-pointed to the served copy when the parent takes over |

The previous head's run reproduces the review finding: the mirror copies the video's `src` once, when the timeline becomes ready, and never retries. On this branch, the only requests that see a 202 are the runtime's own one-byte asks.

On this branch the worst fetches are one or two stalls of about 5 s right after the copies land, while the preview's videos and the filmstrips download the finished copies. Apart from those and about 1 s while the page opens, every fetch took 0.35 s or less. The same stall appears on main (5.9 s at that point in one run), usually hidden inside the longer transcode wait. The filmstrip count varied between runs of the same code (30 or 42 frames), which I also saw once on an earlier head, and never showed "no preview".

Mirror A/B, same tree and fixture, alternating, two rounds each: following eagerly gave a worst unrelated fetch of 10.6 s and 10.3 s (tiles painted at 41.6 s and 48.1 s); not following gave 4.9 s and 5.1 s (31.7 s and 37.7 s). Following lazily, as shipped, gave 4.8 s and 5.0 s.

Tests (each file run alone, exit code 0 each):
- `packages/studio-server/src/helpers/proxyTranscoder.test.ts`: 23 passed. The new tests (a failure that lands after a zero wait gave up is heard by the next ask, whether it is an ffmpeg error or any other error; a full queue is not remembered) fail without the failure-cache change.
- `packages/studio-server/src/routes/preview.test.ts`: 62 passed. The new test fails on main with "a cold copy must not hold the request for the transcode".
- `packages/core/src/runtime/mediaProxy.test.ts`: 44 passed. The new tests (the original `src` stays until the copy is served; the original's own events are ignored while waiting; a failed copy is diagnosed once; a wait stops when the video leaves; a video pointed at another file gets one new wait) fail against the previous head, which put the proxy URL on the video at once. The newest (a dropped ask and an error answer are each asked again; a copy that cannot be made is diagnosed once after 4 asks, with the original's own events firing during the wait as a browser fires them) fail against the previous head, and fail again with the retry removed. Reading a 202 as served fails four others.
- `packages/studio/src/player/hooks/timelinePlayerSync.test.ts` (new): fails without the URL in the check. In my browser fixture Studio's timeline already ended on the copy's URL for all 8 clips even without it, because each clip's source length changed in the same update; the test covers the case where only the URL changes.
- `packages/core/src/runtime/init.swapScenes.test.ts`: 45 passed; the whole `packages/core/src/runtime` folder: 1544 passed. The two capture tests (a capture holds until a served copy shows its first frame; it holds no longer than 5 s for a copy still being made) fail without the hold, and the second fails without the cap.
- `packages/studio-server/src/routes/thumbnail.test.ts`: 23 passed. The two new tests (a card rendered while a copy is being made, and one during which a copy starts or lands, are not cached) each fail with its check removed; the transcoder test for the activity mark fails when the mark never moves.
- `packages/player/src/parent-media.test.ts`: 22 passed; the 6 newest (a re-point onto another clip's file, the same at takeover, two clips swapping files while the parent owns playback, swapping or chaining before takeover, a twin clip leaving, a clip replacing another on the same file) fail against the previous head or with their rule reverted. Earlier: the 4 new tests (keeps its file while the composition owns playback, re-points when the parent takes over, follows at once while the parent owns playback, drops a re-pointed clip when it leaves) fail against main's mirror. The whole `packages/player` suite: 452 passed.
- One mutation per new guard, each caught by its test. One guard was dead (a mutation left every test green) and I deleted it.
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on the changed files, `tsc --noEmit` in core, player, studio and studio-server, the comment ratchet and the comment-citation check: all exit 0.

## Independent review

An adversarial review of each head found one blocker. Failures the transcoder deliberately did not remember (ffmpeg missing, HDR filters missing, a failed rename) answered 202 forever, because the zero wait gave up before they landed and nothing remembered them. It was reproduced with the real transcoder and fixed in the failure cache, with a regression test that fails without the fix. A code review then found a fourth reader of the proxy URL (the player's parent media mirror). Instead of adding a retry to each reader, the runtime now publishes the URL only once the copy is served, and the per-reader waits added earlier are gone. The adversarial review of that design found the mirror would then keep the original for the whole session (silent for a clip whose original audio the browser cannot decode), so the mirror now follows its clip's `src`, lazily, as measured above. A later code review found two more: Studio's timeline could keep the original URL after the swap, and a single failed one-byte ask left a clip on its original for good. Both are fixed as described in How. The adversarial review of that fix showed that letting a later event retry never happens in a real browser, because the original's events all fire while the first wait is still running, so the retry lives inside the wait instead. The diagnostic for a copy that could not be made keeps its existing reason code (`proxy_playback_failed`), which `hyperframes check` and hosts already read. The composition card then showed a regression: a card rendered while copies were still being made was cached for good. A first fix made captures wait for every copy; the adversarial review showed that wait was unbounded (a capture could hang for a whole transcode), so it is now capped at main's 5 s, and cards rendered while copies are pending are not cached.

## What I did NOT exercise

- The `hyperframes play` route and the CLI's static project server still await the transcode. Switching them to the same 202 measured no better in `play`, because there the browser's connections fill with the videos' own downloads, so that change is parked.
- A host app that embeds `@hyperframes/studio-server` and loads `?hf-proxy=` URLs straight into its own `<video>` elements, without asking for one byte first, will now get a 202 it has to retry.
- While a copy is being made, the video plays its original: sound for HEVC, no picture off macOS, as before the swap.
- Playback through the parent media mirror (the parent owning audio) was covered by unit tests only, not in a browser; neither was a ProRes clip whose original audio the browser cannot decode. A clip the mirror re-points when the parent takes over starts loading from zero, so expect a short silence for it right after takeover (takeover only happens when autoplay is blocked).
- A clip re-exported while the preview stays open: its proxy URL goes cold again after the swap, and the clip is diagnosed rather than re-proxied.
- A failure is kept for 10 s (ffmpeg or its filters missing) or 60 s (anything else). A hidden browser tab whose timers are throttled to about once a minute can outlast that window. It then retries about once a minute until it is visible again, and the next ask reports the failure.
- If a finished copy is evicted from the cache after the swap, or between the one-byte ask and the video's own request (a cache over its size budget, swept in that gap), a reader could meet a 202 again.
- A video with no `src` attribute whose `<source>` child a script re-points while its copy is being made: the wait only watches the `src` attribute, so the late copy of the first file can replace the second.
- macOS Chromium, which decodes HEVC natively and never swaps, and real camera footage.
- A clip re-pointed by changing only its `<source>` child: the mirror follows a clip's `src` attribute, which is how the runtime re-points, so a `<source>`-only change is not followed.
- The card check ran on Studio's Vite dev server. The CLI Studio server uses the same thumbnail route and the same capture hold, but I did not run it in a browser. `snapshot` and the other capture commands were covered by the unit tests only.

title: fix(studio): keep a clip in sync when its head is trimmed at non-1x speed
body:
## What this fixes

Trimming the head of a video or audio clip in the Studio timeline, when that clip plays at a speed other than 1x, moved the clip's picture and sound slightly out of sync. Each trim moved it a little, and the error added up. After six head trims on a 0.25x clip, the source ran 60 ms early.

With this change a head trim never moves the clip's sync, no matter how many trims or which speed. At 1x nothing changes.

## Why it happened

A head trim changes three stored values together: the clip's start, its duration, and its in-point (where playback begins in the source). The in-point has to move by the start's change times the speed. That keeps the clip clock (`start - in-point / speed`) where it was.

The code rounded each of the three values to the centisecond on its own. After rounding, the start moved by one amount and the in-point by the speed times a different amount. The clock slipped by up to 5 ms x (1 + 1/speed) on every trim. On save, the in-point was rounded to the centisecond again, which added a second error of the same kind. That second rounding alone would still drift even if the math were right. At 0.5x the rounding lands on exact halves, so it tends to push the same way every time.

## The fix

- `applyClipStartTrimDelta` is now the one place that works out a head trim. It rounds the start once. It sets the duration so the clip's end stays put. It then computes the in-point from the rounded start: `in-point + (rounded start - old start) x speed`. Single-clip trims, multi-clip trims and trims that snap to a beat or clip edge all go through it. Before, the snap path did its own rounding to the millisecond. A snapped head trim now rounds its start to the centisecond during the drag too, which is what the save already stored.
- The in-point is saved to the microsecond (`formatTimelineMediaOffset`), not rounded to the centisecond. Start and duration still save to the centisecond, as before. For speeds with up to four decimals (0.25, 0.5, 0.8, 1.25, 2) the saved in-point is exact. For any other speed the error per trim stays under half a microsecond.
- A head dragged all the way left used to be able to round its start to a point just before the source's first frame. The in-point was then cut off at 0, and the clip moved by up to 5 ms. The start now rounds up to the next centisecond in that case, so the in-point never has to be cut off.
- A trim that snaps to a beat or a clip edge now uses the same limits as a normal drag. Before, a snap could shrink a clip to 0.05 s, while a normal drag stops at 0.1 s. The separate limit checks in the snap code are gone.
- Splitting a clip no longer rewrites the left half's in-point. That value did not change, but the split used to round it to the millisecond, which could move a slowed clip by up to a few milliseconds. The right half's new in-point is still saved to the millisecond, as before. That can move a slowed right half once by under 2 ms at 0.25x (well under a frame), and later trims do not add to it. Saving it more precisely would need a shared number formatter exported from the core package, which is more than this fix should add.
- A negative in-point written in the file (for example `data-media-start="-1"`) is now read as 0, the same way playback reads it. Before, Studio took it as written, and a head drag on such a clip could shrink it to zero length.
- When a group of selected clips is head-trimmed and one of them reaches its source's first frame, the whole group now stops together on the same centisecond. Before, that one clip could end up a centisecond out of step with the rest.
- A snap on a clip's tail edge now stops at the same 0.1 s minimum length as a normal drag. Before, it could shrink the clip to 0.05 s.

## Tests

- `timelineEditing.test.ts`: four head trims in a row at 0.25x, 0.5x, 0.8x, 1x, 1.25x and 2x. Each result goes through the saved-attribute formatting and is read back, the way a reload would. After every trim the clip clock and the clip end must match the originals to 1e-9. At 1x the saved in-point must be the same text as before this change.
- The same file checks that a multi-clip trim of a clip slowed to 0.8x keeps its clock. It also checks that a head dragged fully left at 1.5x lands on 1.34 s, not 1.33 s, and keeps its clock.
- `timelineClipDragPreview.test.ts`: a head trim at 0.8x that snaps to an off-grid beat keeps its clock. With the old snap formula it slips 0.6 ms.
- `timelineGroupEditing.test.ts`: a multi-clip trim at 0.8x and 1.25x, run through the real group preview, keeps each clip's clock. With the old rounding it slips 5 ms.
- `sourceMutationSplitAndGroup.test.ts`: a split leaves an in-point of `3.296375` on the left half exactly as it was. The old code rewrote it as `3.296`.
- `timelineDOM.test.ts`: a clip with `data-media-start="-1"` reads as in-point 0, and a 0.1 s head drag leaves it 0.9 s long.
- `timelineEditing.test.ts`: a group head trim where one clip reaches its source's first frame moves every clip by the same amount and keeps every clock.
- `timelineClipDragPreview.test.ts`: a tail snap that would leave a clip at 0.07 s is refused, so the clip stays at 0.1 s.
- Checked on the unfixed code: with the old trim math the test fails (`expected -9.99 to be close to -10`, a 10 ms slip on the first 0.25x trim). With only the old centisecond save it fails the same way.

## Before

![Saved source before the fix: in-point 3.17](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bea1bb05-fa4e-4b82-9e4e-1a16bf5e29ee)
![Timeline before the fix](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b4afba00-a401-40a0-aadb-d64dbac40055)

The same fixture clip at 0.25x (start 2, in-point 3), after six head drags in headless Studio. The saved in-point is `3.17`. It should be `3 + (2.62 - 2) x 0.25 = 3.155`, so the source is 60 ms off.

| trim | start | in-point | clock slip |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.31 | 3.08 | -10 ms |
| 2 | 2.18 | 3.05 | -20 ms |
| 3 | 2.67 | 3.17 | -10 ms |
| 4 | 2.58 | 3.15 | -20 ms |
| 5 | 2.8 | 3.21 | -40 ms |
| 6 | 2.62 | 3.17 | -60 ms |

## After

![Saved source after the fix: in-point 3.155](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d92bdc2b-799a-47da-88ad-6b18b049ebbb)
![Timeline after the fix](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5e085554-55d5-4372-abbf-ac420469c9b0)

Same fixture and the same six drags. The saved in-point is `3.155`, and the clock slip is 0 ms after every trim. The same drags at 0.5x and 0.8x also stay at 0 ms. Without the fix they moved by up to 10 ms at 0.5x and 7.5 ms at 0.8x.

| trim | start | in-point | clock slip |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.31 | 3.0775 | 0 ms |
| 2 | 2.18 | 3.045 | 0 ms |
| 3 | 2.67 | 3.1675 | 0 ms |
| 4 | 2.58 | 3.145 | 0 ms |
| 5 | 2.8 | 3.2 | 0 ms |
| 6 | 2.62 | 3.155 | 0 ms |

## Not in this PR

These predate this change and are left for a follow-up about in-point readers:
- Splitting reads the in-point with a plain number parse, not playback's rule, so a clip with an unusual in-point (negative, or with a unit) can split with the wrong right-half in-point.
- The property panels read `media-start` before `playback-start`, the opposite of playback.
- A clip whose end is off the centisecond grid can still be head-trimmed to 0.09 s.
- Durations still save to the centisecond, so a clip whose end is off that grid can move its end by up to 5 ms on its first head trim. This does not affect sync.

title: fix(studio): timeline clip pictures fit the clip instead of zooming in
body:
## What this fixes

The pictures inside timeline clips were zoomed in about 1.6x and cut off at the top and bottom. The thumbnail components still sized each tile for a 66 px clip, but a clip is now 42 px tall (a 48 px track with 3 px above and below), so every tile was drawn for a taller box and cropped.

Now `VideoThumbnail`, `CompositionThumbnail` and `ImageThumbnail` read their box's width and height through one shared hook, `useThumbnailStripSize`, and size each tile from the height. The hook keeps its previous size when a resize reports the same one, so a report that changes nothing does not re-render the thumbnail. The two 66 px constants are deleted, and `computeThumbnailStrip` takes the height as an argument. Until the box has a size, it shows one tile.

A composition tile keeps a 48 px minimum width, so a square or portrait composition is narrower than its tile. Its picture is now fitted inside the tile (`object-contain`) instead of cropped to fill it, so it shows whole, letterboxed. A landscape tile's width already follows the picture's shape, so it draws the same either way.

The height is measured instead of taken from the timeline layout for two reasons. The box a picture sits in is 40 px, not the clip's 42, because of the clip's 1 px border. And the three components are exported, so a host can put them in a box of any size.

## Before

Main, a fixture film with a 2.7:1 composition, a 16:9 video and a 2.7:1 still, each with a red TOP band and a blue BOTTOM band. Only the middle of each picture shows; both bands are cut off, and the composition's label is cut in half.

![Before: clip pictures zoomed and cropped](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f0594aa3-9674-4590-a90e-9ea81fa7ec2f)

## After

This branch, same film: the still and video tiles show the whole picture, TOP band to BOTTOM band. The composition tile shows the whole of what Studio captures for it: its host box in the film, with the full TOP band. Its lower edge is the still that overlaps that box, not a crop.

![After: clip pictures whole](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bb8cc077-48bc-4fd2-bca0-d1f3a81e19c9)

A second fixture adds a 9:16 and a 1:1 composition, each with a red TOP band and a blue BOTTOM band.

Before (this PR at 7eeaad6d, which Tai reviewed): the 9:16 clip shows only its yellow middle and the 1:1 clip loses part of both bands.

![Before: portrait and square compositions cropped](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/96a348c3-2b1e-4dea-90e2-18ef678683e1)

After: every 9:16 and 1:1 tile shows TOP to BOTTOM, with dark gaps beside the narrower picture. The nested Portrait row's server picture is blank in this fixture, so it now shows as dark stripes with the clip colour between them.

![After: portrait and square compositions whole](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d178cb1-c4ce-4940-9e8c-4cee6226c64a)

## What I measured

- Tile widths in the 40 px box: main 174 / 117 / 178 px (composition / video / still), this branch 105 / 71 / 108, which is 40 px times each picture's aspect.
- Tests: a 2.7:1 picture in a 40 px box tiles 108 px wide in each of the three components (main gives 178), the tiles follow the height the resize observer reports, a 2.7:1, a 1:1 and a 9:16 composition each keep the whole picture (tiles 108, 48 and 48 px, fitted, not cropped), a 440 px video clip requests the frame count its measured height calls for, and a box that has not been measured yet shows one tile. The three component tests fail on main.
- Each run alone: `useThumbnailStripSize.test.tsx` (1), `thumbnailUtils.test.ts` (24), `VideoThumbnail.test.tsx` (7), `ImageThumbnail.test.tsx` (8), `CompositionThumbnail.test.ts` (10), `useRenderClipContent.test.ts` (15), `clipContentExports.test.tsx` (3). Typecheck, lint, format, the comment ratchet and the fallow audit green.
- Shorter tiles mean more of them: a 440 px video clip now decodes 8 frames where main decoded 4 (about 1 MB against 0.5 MB of the 64 MiB frame cache). The per-clip cap is unchanged, so the most a clip can decode is the same.
- No thumbnail cache change is needed: the composition picture request carries no size, video frames decode at a fixed height cap, and the number of video frames requested is part of that request's cache key.

## What I did NOT exercise

- The three exported components size tiles from their direct parent's height. A host that wraps one in a parent with no height gets one tile a pixel wide (no picture) for video and stills, one 48 px tile for a composition; main drew 66 px tiles there. Studio always gives them a sized box.
- Zoomed far in, a clip now holds up to about 1.65x more tile elements; the timeline's page-size check renders no pictures, so it does not count them.
- The cap on decoded video frames per clip still assumes 66 px tiles, so on a very wide clip some neighbouring tiles repeat a frame. Kept on purpose: raising it would hold up to about 1.7x more decoded frames in memory.

title: feat(cli): transcribe with Parakeet on macOS, Linux and Windows after an opt-in install
body:
## What changes for users

`hyperframes models install parakeet` downloads NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 speech model (int8, about 670 MB) and the sherpa-onnx runtime that runs it, with progress. After that, `hyperframes transcribe` uses Parakeet on macOS, Linux and Windows, with no Python.

Parakeet is more accurate than the Whisper `small.en` model most machines get today, and several times faster on CPU. Nothing downloads unless you run the command.

## How it works

- **Install.**
  - The runtime comes from npm: `sherpa-onnx-node@1.13.8`, plus its native package at the same exact version.
  - The four model files are pinned to one Hugging Face revision. Each downloads to a temporary name and is checked against its pinned size and sha256 before it is renamed into place, so a file under its real name is always complete.
  - Re-running is a no-op, and it repairs a broken install. It refuses up front on a system with no native package (it names the six supported targets), on musl, and on glibc older than 2.32 (the prebuilt's floor).
  - Ctrl-C stops the download or the npm install, keeps no partial file, and exits 130. The staging dir is named with the installer's process id, so one left by a killed install is removed by the next run.
- **Engine choice.**
  - `--engine auto` and `--engine parakeet` use this runtime when it is installed, then an installed `parakeet-mlx`, then whisper.
  - `--engine parakeet` with neither installed fails and names the install command.
  - **The rule when Parakeet is installed but fails:** an explicit `--engine parakeet` fails with the Parakeet error and the repair command (`hyperframes models install parakeet`), with no fallback. `--engine auto` falls back to whisper with a visible warning that leads with the Parakeet error and names the same repair. If the fallback fails too, the Parakeet error is what gets reported.
  - **An unreadable input is an input error, not a Parakeet failure.** The audio is prepared once, before Parakeet runs. If ffmpeg cannot read it (for example, a video with no audio track), the run fails with ffmpeg's error, gives no repair advice and does not fall back. A fallback reuses the prepared audio, so ffmpeg runs only once.
  - Under `--optional`, a broken Parakeet install exits 1 even when whisper is missing. A broken install is a real failure; a missing optional tool is not, and that case still exits 0, as before.
  - Ctrl-C during a Parakeet transcribe stops it (exit 130) instead of starting whisper. That includes Ctrl-C while ffmpeg is still preparing the audio. ffmpeg catches Ctrl-C itself, so a cancel is read from ffmpeg's own "received signal" line, not from its exit code: from ffmpeg 7 on, exit 255 also means a file was not permitted. Any other ffmpeg failure is reported with ffmpeg's own last line (for example "Error opening input files: Permission denied"). A failed or stopped ffmpeg leaves no partial temp file.
  - The output shape is unchanged: `engine: "parakeet"`, the same model label, the same word list.
- **Decoding** runs in a child process, in about 60 s windows cut at the quietest point near each boundary. Both are required:
  - past about 400 s in one pass, onnxruntime aborts the whole process;
  - long single passes also silently dropped a sentence;
  - fixed 60 s cuts split words (6.6% word error rate at fixed 60 s cuts, 1.5% with cuts moved to the quietest 100 ms within 5 s).

  The model sometimes silently drops a clause: at the start of a window at some window lengths (4 of 167 lengths between 55 and 60 s on a looped speech clip), and after a pause in the middle of a window. So each window is checked for a stretch of at least 1 s with no words that is as loud as speech. In one measured case a 61.91 s window lost its first 9 words, and that stretch was 0.94 times as loud as the window. Each such gap is decoded again on its own, with 0.5 s of audio on either side and 0.5 s of leading silence, and only whole words that start inside the gap are added. The re-decode often hears the gap's neighbours again, up to about 0.3 s off and split into different pieces, so a word within 0.3 s of a gap edge that matches its neighbour letter for letter is dropped. Nothing is doubled or glued onto a neighbour. If that finds nothing, the whole window is decoded again with 0.5 s of leading silence, as before. A window with no words at all (music, noise) is not decoded twice. Decoding with 1.5 s of overlap before each cut was measured too and was worse (2.62% against 0.98% on 573 s), so it is not used.

  Audio with no speech gives 0 words, not an error. 24-bit and float WAV go through ffmpeg first.
- **Credit:** Parakeet's CC-BY-4.0 credit is in `CREDITS.md`.

Also fixed, each with a test: the media-use transcribe script always reported an undefined word count on the whisper path, and the embedded-captions script labelled its output `whisper.cpp` even when Parakeet ran.

## Evidence

Measured on Linux x64 with LibriSpeech test-clean (speaker 1089). The built CLI ran inside a glibc 2.36 container:

| | Word error rate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Parakeet int8 via this command, 191 s clip | 1.18% | 509 words |
| Parakeet int8, 573 s clip (the same audio three times) | 0.98% | no crash; one pass would abort at about 400 s; the same with and without the gap re-decode |
| Parakeet int8, whole-clip decode, 191 s | 0.98% | earlier measurement |
| Parakeet fp32, 191 s | 0.39% | 3.5 GiB peak; int8 is 2.6 GiB whole, 1.7 GB windowed |
| whisper.cpp `small.en`, 191 s | 1.77% | decode about 4x slower than Parakeet int8 |

Timings came from a heavily loaded shared machine, so they are upper bounds.

Dropped clauses, measured through the command on clips built from the model repo's `test_wavs/en.wav`, before and after the gap re-decode. These runs, the 573 s row and the first two failure paths below used the source through tsx in the same kind of container, not the built CLI:

| Clip | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| en.wav plus 1.5 s of silence, looped 24 times (128 s) | 399 of 408 words: "Ask not what your country can do for you" missing at about 96 s | 408 of 408, word for word |
| 62 s of looped speech with a fade-out, cut into a 61.95 s window that drops its first clause | 272 of 272 (the old retry) | 272 of 272 |
| 120 s of pink noise, two runs each | windows with no words decoded twice: 44 s and 28 s | decoded once: 19 s and 17 s |

Failure paths exercised:
- a video with no audio track: fails with ffmpeg's error in `auto`, `--engine parakeet` and `--optional`, with no repair advice and no fallback;
- Ctrl-C to the whole command (as a terminal sends it) while a real ffmpeg 7.0.2 prepares an hour of audio: exit 130, "Transcription cancelled", no whisper, no temp file left;
- an input that cannot be read (permissions 000) and an output ffmpeg is not permitted to write (EPERM, exit 255 from ffmpeg): exit 1 with ffmpeg's reason, not a cancel;
- the runtime installed but its native file deleted: falls back with the loader's error;
- the decode child killed with SIGABRT: falls back with "Parakeet decoder crashed (SIGABRT)";
- glibc 2.31: the install refuses; `--engine auto` runs whisper.

## Not verified here

- The sherpa runtime on macOS and Windows. The npm packages ship prebuilt binaries for both, and the Windows ones import no Visual C++ runtime, but this PR ran them only on Linux.
- Progress rendering in a real terminal. It uses the same spinner as `browser ensure`.

## Tests

New unit tests cover:
- the silence-snapped cuts and the window-offset merge;
- install verification: a sha256 mismatch discards the file and leaves nothing installed, and a repeat install is a no-op;
- the pinned native package name for each platform;
- the glibc gate;
- the engine order;
- the fallback on a child crash;
- cancellation (the decode child, ffmpeg preparing the audio, told apart from a not-permitted error that exits the same way, and the model download), the partial audio file removed when ffmpeg fails, the repair message, the no-fallback rule for `--engine parakeet`, and the Parakeet error winning when the fallback fails too;
- an unreadable input failing as an input error with no fallback, and the fallback reusing the one prepared file;
- the empty transcript, the dropped-speech detector, the gap splice (whole words inside the gap added in order; neighbours re-heard in other pieces or case dropped; a real repeated word kept; a word shared by two gaps added once; a first word with no leading space kept as its own word), the decode worker's gap re-decode and its 0.5 s margin, padded retry and error paths (run as a real child with a stand-in runtime), and the `models` command's `--json` and error shapes.

Each fails with its guarded line removed.

title: feat(cli): add --require-beginframe to fail instead of falling back to screenshot capture
body:
## What

`hyperframes render --require-beginframe` (env `PRODUCER_REQUIRE_BEGINFRAME=true`) fails the render when a capture session would not run BeginFrame, instead of continuing in screenshot capture. The error names the reason:

```
✗  Render failed

   BeginFrame capture is required, but the HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame probe failed after 2000ms (beginFrame probe timeout during warm-up beginFrame). Browsers starting together on one GPU can miss this deadline, so fewer --workers may help; not falling back to screenshot capture.
```

Without the flag nothing changes.

## Why

A BeginFrame render can drop to screenshot capture and still exit 0. In #4584 every worker's probe times out once 6 workers start on one hardware GPU, the render takes twice as long, and only the summary line shows it. Scripts and CI that expect BeginFrame have no way to find out other than parsing that line. A render that should be fast or not happen at all can now say so.

## Related work

Refs #4584. The cause there (a probe deadline shorter than a GPU start under contention) is a separate fix; this PR only makes the fallback detectable. #2810 made the effective capture mode visible for distributed chunks; this does the same for local renders by failing early.

## How

- `EngineConfig.requireBeginFrame` (default `false`), read from `PRODUCER_REQUIRE_BEGINFRAME`. The CLI flag sets that variable through the render plan's environment, as `--low-memory-mode` does.
- `createCaptureSession` throws `BeginFrameRequiredError` when the session's capture mode resolves to screenshot: not Linux, no chrome-headless-shell, supersampling, transparent drawElement, a software GPU, or a caller that set `forceScreenshot` (alpha formats, render-mode hints, low-memory mode, the retry after a failed capture). This runs before any browser starts, so the producer's own screenshot retries also stop there.
- `launchBrowser` throws the same error when the BeginFrame probe fails, instead of relaunching the browser without BeginFrame flags. `requireBeginFrame` is part of the launch fingerprint, so a pooled browser that fell back is never handed to a session that requires BeginFrame.
- `BeginFrameRequiredError` is exported from `@hyperframes/engine`.

The flag does not change which capture mode a render asks for; it only refuses to continue in screenshot mode. It does not apply to `--docker` renders, which use SwiftShader.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated
  - `browserManager.test.ts`: a failing probe relaunches in screenshot mode by default, and with `requireBeginFrame` rejects with `BeginFrameRequiredError` after a single launch (Linux only, like the launch path it covers). The second test fails without the change.
  - `frameCapture-requireBeginFrame.test.ts`: a session forced to screenshot capture, and one on a software GPU, are refused with their reason before Chrome launches.
  - `config.test.ts`: the environment variable; `render/plan.test.ts`: the flag maps to it.
- [x] Manual testing performed, on Linux with an RTX 3090 (`--browser-gpu --gpu`, chrome-headless-shell 152.0.7977.30, the 10 s composition from the issue):

  | Command | Exit | Summary |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `--workers 6 --require-beginframe` | 1 | fails at "Starting browsers" with the error above, no output file |
  | `--workers 3 --require-beginframe` | 0 | `beginframe capture · hardware gpu` |
  | `--workers 1 --require-beginframe` | 0 | `beginframe capture · hardware gpu` |
  | `--workers 6` | 0 | `screenshot capture · hardware gpu` (unchanged) |

- [x] Documentation updated: the flag table in `docs/packages/cli.mdx`
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

`bun run lint`, `bun run format:check`, `bun run --filter '*' typecheck`, `fallow audit`, `check-comment-citations` and `comment-ratchet` pass. The engine and CLI suites pass except 4 engine tests (`videoFrameExtractor`, `ffprobe`: FFmpeg 9 no longer accepts `-vsync`, and the HDR PNG fixtures) and 3 CLI tests (`skillsManifest` `pruneOrphanedLockEntries`), which fail the same way on `main` on this machine.

title: fix(cli): a failed command sends one error report, naming its real cause
body:
## What this fixes

A command run outside a project sent two `cli_error` events for one failure: `resolveProject` reported the project error, then the top-level handler reported the same failure again as "Command failed". figma commands did the same: their own report with the Figma error code, then "Command failed". `browser`, `transcribe` and `remove-background` also reported inline before failing, so each of those failures counted twice.

Now `trackCommandFailure` owns "one failure, one report". A command that fails after printing its error now passes the original error along as the cause. `trackCommandFailure` reports that original error, remembers it, and skips it if it comes again:

- A failure the command reports where it knows the cause (`resolveProject`, figma with its error code and endpoint) sends that report only. The handler's later report is the same error and is skipped.
- A failure only the handler sees (`browser`, `transcribe`, `remove-background`, which no longer report inline) is reported by the handler under its real error, not "Command failed".
- Commands that catch the failure themselves and never reach the handler (`lint`, `check`, `preview` outside a project) keep the report `resolveProject` sends.
- `normalize-audio` and `media-treatment` rethrow a failure as their own; they now pass the original along, so it is reported once under its real name.

figma's error handler no longer flushes telemetry itself: its failure goes to the top-level handler, and the CLI flushes on the way out as for every other command.

Unchanged, as on `main`: failures other than a missing project that `lint`, `check` and `preview` catch themselves still send no event, and failures raised without a cause still report as "Command failed".

## Tests

`cli.lifecycle.test.ts` runs the CLI with the real reporting and counts the `cli_error` events it sends. Each case expects exactly one, with the real error:
- a failure outside a project that reaches the top-level handler;
- `lint` outside a project (it catches the failure itself);
- `normalize-audio` outside a project (it rethrows the failure as its own);
- a figma failure, reported by its code (`NO_TOKEN`).

The cases run with `--json`, so they skip the update check. The lint case still reads the telemetry config, like other CLI tests, until the CLI tests get a home folder of their own (a separate change).

Unit tests: `trackCommandFailure` reports the same error once, reports the original error through every wrapper, once, and takes a caller's error name and endpoint.

Results: `tsc`, oxfmt, oxlint and Fallow clean; the CLI tests pass. Each of these fails a named test: reporting without the repeat check, `resolveProject` without its report, `normalize-audio` or figma failing without passing the original error, and unwrapping one wrapper only.

title: test(cli): CLI tests run with a home folder of their own, never the user's
body:
## What this changes

The CLI builds its caches, config and state paths from the home folder: the registry cache (`~/.hyperframes/cache`), telemetry config, downloaded browsers and models, agent skill folders. A test that forgot to stub one of them read or wrote the real folder of whoever ran the suite. It happened: a test run cached a fake catalog list under the public registry's key in a real `~/.hyperframes/cache`, where it would have stood in for the real catalog for up to a day.

Both CLI test lanes now run with a home folder of their own. `packages/cli/scripts/test-home.mjs` is loaded before any test module: it makes a temp dir, removed when the run ends, the `HOME` and `USERPROFILE`, and clears the variables that point the CLI at a user folder directly (the `XDG_*` folders, the agent and HeyGen config folders, the catalog, media and Hugging Face cache overrides; the list is in the module). The CLI's vitest config imports it, and the skills lane (`test:skills` and its CI step, the `node --test` run of the media-use tests) preloads it with `--import`. Tests that set their own home keep doing so. The test reachability map carries the skills step's new command, since it matches runners by their exact text.

The tokenizer parity test reads its downloaded model from the user's real home, read-only, so it still runs where the model is present.

## Tests

- `testHome.test.ts` (vitest): the run's home folder is under the temp dir and is not the user's (`os.userInfo()` reads the real one from the OS, not from `HOME`); a registry read caches in that home and writes nothing to the user's.
- `media-use/lib/test-home.test.mjs` (skills lane): the same home check.

Results: `tsc`, oxfmt, oxlint, Fallow and the test reachability check clean; the full CLI suite and the skills lane pass with the temp home, and no temp folder is left behind. Without the vitest config's import both vitest tests fail; without the `--import` the skills test fails.

title: fix(cli): unattended transcribe and init never install whisper.cpp
body:
Stacked on #4583, which adds the `hyperframes models install parakeet` command this PR's hint names. The diff here is against that branch.

## What changes for users

When nobody can answer, `hyperframes transcribe` and `hyperframes init --audio/--video` no longer install whisper.cpp system-wide. That means no `brew install whisper-cpp` and no source build (git clone + cmake). A run counts as unattended when:
- stdin or stdout is not a terminal,
- `CI` is set,
- `--json` is passed, or
- init runs with `--non-interactive` (or the hidden `--agent`), even inside a terminal. Those flags say nobody will answer, so they get the same rule.

Such a run only looks for a whisper.cpp that is already installed. If there is none, it stops right away with:

> whisper-cpp not found, and unattended or --json runs do not install it. For much better transcripts, run: hyperframes models install parakeet. Or install whisper-cpp: <platform install instruction>

Where the message shows up:
- **Without `--json`:** `transcribe` now writes its spinner and this skip message to **stderr**, as `models install` already does. Scripts that shell the CLI and print stderr on failure now show the hint. stdout carries only `--json` output.
- **With `--json`:** the text is included as `error` in the existing `{"ok":false,"skipped":true,"reason":"whisper_unavailable"}` line.
- `--optional` still exits 0 on this skip.

Interactive `init` asks "Generate captions from audio?" first. When the person says yes, it installs whisper as before, so its "installing automatically" message stays true.

A person who answers yes to init's captions prompt, even through a pipe, still gets whisper installed; that is an explicit answer.

Bundled skill scripts that shell the CLI pass the reason on:
- The embedded-captions transcribe script prints the CLI's JSON `error`.
- TTS captions (Kokoro/ElevenLabs voices) record an anomaly when a line gets no word timings, instead of dropping them silently.
- Skill docs no longer promise that whisper.cpp installs on first use. They point at `hyperframes models install parakeet` or a manual whisper.cpp install.

Unchanged:
- At a real terminal without `--json` or `--non-interactive`, the automatic install still runs as before.
- The Whisper model download (small.en) still happens silently once whisper is present.
- When Parakeet is installed, `--engine auto` uses it and never touches whisper.
- `hyperframes doctor` only probes and installs nothing, so it is left as is.

## How

The check lives in `ensureWhisper`, the one function every installing caller goes through. It takes a new `mayInstall` option, which defaults to `isAttendedTerminal()`. `transcribe()` passes the option through.

Callers that set it:
- `transcribe` passes `false` under `--json`.
- init's non-interactive path passes `false`.
- init's interactive path passes `true` after the person confirms captions.

## Tests

- `whisper/manager-resolution.test.ts` runs on both a Linux-style (`which`) and a Windows-style (`where`) host:
  - an unattended run records no brew or git/cmake call and fails with the Parakeet hint;
  - `mayInstall: false` at a terminal does the same;
  - an attended run still tries brew, then a source build.
- `commands/transcribe.test.ts`:
  - `--json` passes `mayInstall: false` and puts the reason into the JSON `error`;
  - without `--json`, the reason reaches stderr and not stdout.
- `commands/init.whisper.test.ts`:
  - `--non-interactive` at a terminal probes with `mayInstall: false`;
  - interactive init installs once the person says yes.
- `commands/init.test.ts`: `init --non-interactive --audio`, with fake `brew`/`git`/`cmake` on PATH and a fresh HOME, calls none of them and prints the Parakeet hint. It is skipped when whisper-cli is already installed or `HYPERFRAMES_WHISPER_PATH` is set. On Windows the install-log check is skipped, because the fakes are shell scripts.
- `embedded-captions/scripts/transcribe.test.mjs`: a failing CLI's JSON `error` reaches stderr.
- `media-use/audio/scripts/lib/tts.test.mjs`: a failed transcription returns an explanation instead of a bare `null`, and a run that found no words gives no install hint.
- `media-use/scripts/transcribe.test.mjs`: a failed run reports only the CLI's last few stderr lines (the reason), not thousands of spinner redraws.

Each fix was reverted on its own, and its test failed; the other tests kept passing.

## Verified by hand (Linux, glibc 2.31, so no sherpa-onnx; fresh HOME, no whisper-cli)

- `transcribe voice.wav --json </dev/null | cat`: exits 1 in about 2 s with the message above, and no git, cmake or brew process shows up.
- `transcribe voice.wav` without `--json`: stdout is empty, and stderr has "Captions skipped — …" with the same message. Exit code 1.
- `init proj --non-interactive --audio voice.wav` under `script` (a real TTY): prints "Transcription skipped: …" with the message. No git, cmake or brew process starts.
- `transcribe voice.wav` under `script` (a real TTY, no flags): `git clone … whisper.cpp` starts within a second, so the attended path is untouched (stopped by hand).

title: fix(studio-server): a write through a link lands on the file the system resolves
body:
## What

A Studio edit through a symlink whose target contains `..` could write a different file than the one the link shows. Example: `sub -> deep/nested` and `m/x.txt -> ../sub/../y.txt`. The system resolves `m/x.txt` to `deep/y.txt`, but saving `m/x.txt` in Studio wrote `<project>/y.txt`.

The cause is node's JS `fs.realpathSync`, which resolves `..` inside a link target as text rather than after following the link. `realFilePath`, which picks the file an edit writes, used it. Core already had a private real-path helper that asks the system (`realpathSync.native`, with a fallback for Windows volumes that refuse it). This exports that helper and routes every real-path lookup on these decisions through it: the edit target, composition insertion, the proxy source check, the codec check, and the catalog install (its root, every installed path, and the file list `add` and `catalog` print). The install root and the installed paths must come from the same resolver, or the relative paths Studio mounts break on a project folder typed in a different letter case.

A link like this that lands outside the project was already refused by a later check. That stays covered by a test.

## Tests

- studio-server, "writes the file a link resolves to when its target climbs out of a linked folder": fails on main (it writes `y.txt`), passes here.
- studio-server, "refuses a write through a link whose target climbs out of a folder linked outside": a guard; it passes on main too.
- CLI, "publishes through a leaf alias whose target climbs out of a linked folder to the file it resolves": fails on main (it writes the decoy).

title: fix(studio): list and grade only real compositions, not generated preview files
body:
## What

Studio's Variables tab listed the preview document the CLI server writes into the project (`.hyperframes/preview/<hash>.html`, a built copy of the film) under "Other compositions", with the film's own variables. Editing a variable there edited that generated file.

The server already sends the project's compositions: `.html` files outside dot and vendor folders whose content is a composition. The Compositions panel uses that list. Two places re-derived their own list from every `.html` in the file tree, and both now use the server's list, so there is one owner for "which files are compositions":
- the Variables tab's "Other compositions";
- project-wide color grading, which patched the generated preview copy too and counted it in its changed files and undo history. The handler moves into `useApplyColorGradingScope` so this wiring is testable.

In the master view, "Other compositions" now leaves out the project's real main composition instead of assuming `index.html`.

Project-wide color grading now covers exactly the files Studio lists as compositions. It no longer touches `.htm` files or HTML without `data-composition-id`, which the composition rules already require.

## Tests

- Studio, "leaves out the main composition in the master view when it is not index.html": fails with the old exclusion.

title: perf(studio): a film with no manual edits skips the edit reapply on each seek
body:
## Summary

Playing a film that has never been edited in Studio stops re-applying manual edits on every frame. Films
with edits behave exactly as before.

## What changed

- The manual-edit reapply runs after every timeline seek, so on every playback frame. It ran six document
  queries plus the motion rebuild even when Studio had never edited the film.
- One combined query now answers "any edits?" first (`hasStudioEdits`) and returns early when there are
  none.
- The seek reapply moves from `manualEditsDom.ts` into a new `manualEditsSeekReapply.ts`, keeping that file
  under the 600-line limit. `manualEdits.ts` re-exports it, so callers are unchanged.

## Proof

- `reapplyPositionEditsAfterSeek.test.ts`:
  - a film Studio never edited triggers no per-edit document queries;
  - a legacy double-prefixed edit mark is still migrated;
  - a motion timeline left registered after an undo removed its marks is still killed. This one fails when
    the skip stops treating that timeline as an edit.
- The existing reapply tests (`reapplyBoxSizeAfterSeek`, `anchoredResizeReleaseShift`) pass with the
  imports updated.
- Seeks per frame in the playback gate are unchanged (1).
- Timing: the earlier +10% came from 3 runs per side, and its 95% interval for the difference (-0.69 to
  +1.33 ms) includes zero. Measured instead in Chrome 153, with both builds' edit reapply on one page in
  alternating blocks, at 4 reapplies per frame. A film with no edits costs 1.2 µs per reapply against 5 µs on
  main at 43 elements, and 0.3-0.6 µs against 6-13 µs at 1.5k elements. A film with one edit is unchanged:
  6.0-6.6 µs against 6.3-8.2 µs, with 7 lookups on both.

## Before

Studio playing the repo fixture `studio-playback` on main, with a counter of the preview-document queries the
manual-edit reapply makes (counted by call stack while playing; the reapply runs about 4 times per frame):

![main, film without edits: 28 queries per frame](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/06dd694a-e658-46f7-8773-8268f4db8527)

The same fixture with one manual path offset added (the orange box):

![main, film with a manual edit: 28 queries per frame](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a01bee63-df19-4c84-b080-d365ad4f69e0)

## After

Film without edits: 0 queries per frame. The "any edits?" answer is cached per document, so a
steady film makes no lookup at all.

![this PR, film without edits: 0 queries per frame](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/56075c12-429a-49d6-8f97-4414b61f3cc3)

Film with a manual edit: 28 queries per frame, the same as main, and the box holds its edited
position.

![this PR, film with a manual edit: 28 queries per frame](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e2cd680f-4bcc-4d19-abd6-29c8f1e80e18)

## Follow-up

None.

## Known limits

- The "any edits?" answer is cached per preview document and worked out again only after a MutationObserver
  sees an edit mark added or removed, or an element inserted or removed (seven single-attribute lookups,
  1-4 µs on 1.5k elements). A steady film, edited or not, does no extra lookup per seek; a film that replaces
  elements every frame (for example captions rebuilt on each animation frame) recomputes about 13 times a
  second.
- A document with no window, and so no MutationObserver, skips the cache and checks on every seek.

title: perf(studio): playback no longer relayouts the timecode and playhead every frame
body:
## Summary

During playback Studio stops redoing layout for the timecode and the timeline playhead on every frame. Both
look and move exactly as before.

## What changed

- `PlayerControls.tsx`: the timecode is written only when its text changes. It showed MM:SS but was
  rewritten on every playback frame.
- `useTimelinePlayhead.ts`, `TimelineCanvas.tsx`: the playhead moves by a composited
  `transform: translateX(...)` instead of `style.left`.
- The new `timelinePlayheadTransform.ts` wraps the same position function. While playing it keeps fractional
  pixels, as main's `left` did, so slow motion stays smooth. At rest (paused, or a settled seek) it rounds to
  device pixels the way layout rounds the ruler ticks, so the 1px line is crisp and sits on its tick.

## Proof

- `PlayerControls.test.tsx`: the timecode node is not rewritten when the formatted text is unchanged.
- `Timeline.test.ts`: the existing playhead tests now expect the position in the transform. A new test plays
  to a fractional position and expects a fractional transform, then pauses and expects the rounded one.
- `timelinePlayheadTransform.test.ts`:
  - playing, 121 samples at fit zoom give 121 distinct positions; resting, the same samples collapse to a few
    device pixels;
  - at rest the line lands on the same device pixel as the ruler tick for the same time, at 1x, 1.5x and 2x;
  - at t=0 the line sits on the first tick.
- Playhead probe, a 120 s film at fit zoom, 120 animation-frame samples while playing:

  | | main | previous head | this head |

  | Distinct positions, 2x | 120 | 42 | 120 |

  At rest at t=0 the line paints the same device columns as its tick, as on main: column 84 at 1x (main

title: perf(core): playback housekeeping runs on a timer, and rebinds stop re-sampling silent media
body:
## Summary

Playing a film no longer repeats bookkeeping work per frame (so twice as often on a 120 Hz display). It also
no longer stalls for 50-140 ms when the runtime re-binds the timeline mid-play.

## What changed

- **Sizing.** The composition observer now also watches `data-width` and `data-height`, so a size edit is
  applied while playing and while parked. Main only picked it up on its 20-frame counter while playing, and
  missed it while parked.

- **Housekeeping.** While playing, the transport re-posted the clip manifest every 20 frames and re-bound
  media every 30, counted in frames. On a 120 Hz display it did both twice as often, for a film that was not
  changing.
  - Now, while playing, those jobs run when the composition changes (rate-limited as before), plus a
    one-second poll for anything nothing pushes (`timelineRebindPolicy.ts`, `init.ts`).
  - Paused behaviour is unchanged.
  - Some clip edits reach no observer: `data-track-index`, `data-timeline-label` or an inline `z-index` on an
    existing clip (watching `style` would fire on every GSAP frame). On the poll the runtime builds the
    manifest and posts it only when it differs from the last one posted, so such an edit lands within a
    second and a steady film posts nothing. The tick where playback stops runs the same diff once, so an edit
    made just before a pause is not lost (main lost it too).
- **Volume probe.** A rebind re-probed every media element's volume by seeking the whole timeline 60 times
  per second of clip, about 1,500 seeks and 50-140 ms in one frame.
  - The probe seeks with events suppressed, so what can move the volume is a tween naming `volume` on that
    element, or a tween on a non-DOM object whose tweened property is a setter (a gain proxy, or a class
    with a `volume` setter), found along the prototype chain.
  - Those fall back to the full probe, as on main. Everything else is answered from the timeline's tweens
    without seeking (`mediaVolumeEnvelope.ts`), including the `tl.to({}, {duration})` spacer the generator
    and the runtime emit, `tl.call` and `add(callback)`, and a counter tweened on a plain object.
  - A tween that does automate volume is still sampled exactly as before.
  - This is a structural check rather than a cache of "no automation". A cache would be unsound here: the
    first probe can run before the root timeline has any children.

## Proof

- Regression tests:
  - `transportPark.test.ts`: the manifest is not re-posted while playing a film that is not changing;
  - `transportPark.test.ts`: a playing clip's track, label and z-index changed to 7, "After" and 9 arrive in
    the next poll's post. It fails without the manifest check;
  - `transportPark.test.ts`: a label edited while playing and paused before the next poll is posted. It
    fails without the check on the stop, and on main;
  - `mediaVolumeEnvelope.test.ts`: no probe seeks for an element whose volume no tween names, and a
    keyframed volume tween is still sampled;
  - `mediaVolumeEnvelope.test.ts`, with real GSAP: a gain tweened 0 to 0.75 through a plain-object proxy that
    writes the element's volume reads 0.375 at 0.5 s, and a class instance with a `volume` setter is sampled
    too. Both fail without the setter fallback, and the class also fails if only own properties are read;
  - `mediaVolumeEnvelope.test.ts`, with real GSAP: a `{}` spacer, a `tl.call` and a plain `{n: 0}` counter
    each make 0 probe seeks on a 25 s clip. All three fail if any non-DOM target falls back, and the counter
    fails if any property, not only a setter, does;
  - `timelineRebindPolicy.test.ts`: while playing, it checks on the poll timer, not the frame counter;
  - `transportPark.test.ts`: a `data-width` change applies while playing, and a `data-height` change while
    parked. Both fail when the observer does not watch them.
- Core runtime suite: 63 files, 1512 tests pass.
- Red/green: with main's runtime sources and these tests, 8 of the 14 new tests fail (the four no-seek
  cases, the poll timer, the steady-film no-repost, the parked `data-height` and the edit before a pause). The other 6 guard behaviour
  main already has: the three volume samplings, the rate limit, the playing metadata post and the playing
  `data-width`. On this branch all 56 tests in the three files pass.
- Render parity: three fixtures (studio-playback, added by the gate PR, plus studio-open and design-panel-qa) render byte-identical to
  main. Main was rendered twice to confirm it is deterministic, and this branch once, all matching. They were
  rendered again after the sizing fix, with the CLI rebuilt around the new runtime, and still match.
- Timing, quiet window 2026-09-27 09:30-09:45Z, one box, Chrome 153 uncapped, main and this branch in
  alternating runs (3 rounds each, load 8.6-11.8):

  | Per frame | main | this PR |
  |---|---|---|
  | Main-thread CPU (median) | 6.77 ms | 6.19 ms (-9%) |
  | Frame time, median | 10.68 ms | 6.45 ms |
  | Frame time, p95 | 25.09 ms | 8.93 ms |
  - Main's p95 includes its mid-play rebind, which re-probes media volume by seeking; this branch has no such
    frame.

## No visible change

Runtime-only: no visible change, so no captures.

## Follow-up

None.

## Known limits

- Something that changes the film without touching the DOM is picked up by the one-second poll, not on the
  next frame.
- `onUpdate` and `call` volume changes are missed, as on main: the probe suppresses events.
- A tween on a non-DOM object that writes volume without a setter on the tweened property (an ES `Proxy` with
  a `set` trap) is missed; main sampled it.
- A tween on an object whose tweened property is a setter (for example a Three.js rotation) still takes the full
  volume probe on a rebind, as on main; one registry block does this.
- A film that changes its DOM every frame now attempts a rebind up to 3 times a second while playing, instead
  of once a second at 60 Hz. Each attempt returns early once the timeline is bound.

title: fix(engine): renders show the video frame the preview shows at each output frame
body:
## What

Renders now show the video frame the preview shows at each output frame. The main gains are when the render frame rate is below the source's (for example a 60 fps clip in a 24 fps render) and when a clip starts partway into its source.

## Why

Frame extraction sampled with ffmpeg's `fps=N` filter. That filter rounds each source timestamp to the nearest output slot and keeps the last frame that lands in the slot, so it picks a frame from up to half a slot in the future. The preview shows the frame on screen at that time. Measured with a 60 fps clip whose frames carry their own index:

| render fps | slot times | main picks | preview picks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 0, 0.1 s | 2, 8 | 0, 6 |
| 24 | 0 .. 4/24 s | 1, 3, 6, 8, 11 | 0, 2, 5, 7, 10 |

The same holds on ffmpeg 5.1.9 (Debian bookworm) and 7.0.2. A 29.97 fps source rendered at 30 fps was also one frame ahead in every slot after the first.

## How

For constant frame rate sources (VFR and the one-frame path are unchanged):

- `fps=N:start_time=0:round=up` puts in each slot the last frame that starts at or before the slot time.
- `-noaccurate_seek` keeps the frame on screen at the seek point. An accurate seek drops it when the start time falls between two frames, which made slot 0 of a trimmed clip one frame late.
- `settb=intb/2,setpts=PTS-lte(TB\,0.001)` shifts timestamps back by half a tick on timebases of 2 ms per tick or finer. WebM and MKV store whole milliseconds, so a 30 fps frame due at 66.67 ms reads 67 ms and would otherwise miss its own slot, making a WebM rendered at its own rate drop one frame in three. Timebases where each frame lasts a whole number of ticks (AVI, an MP4 whose timescale equals its frame rate) store exact frame times; ticks coarser than 2 ms are not shifted.
- The extraction cache schema moves to `hfcache-v6-`. The cache key carries no filter identity, so without a bump, entries main wrote under `v5` (from #4564) would keep serving the old sampling's frames.

## Evidence

A 1 s composition with two copies of a 60 fps index clip, one from the start and one with `data-media-start="0.37"`, rendered at 24 fps as a PNG sequence. Each rendered frame is mapped back to its source frame index. ffmpeg 7.0.2, fresh extraction cache for each render:

| | slots showing the preview's frame |
|---|---|
| main | 0 of 48 (every slot one source frame late) |
| this branch | 48 of 48 |

Sample slots (from-start clip / trimmed clip, source frame index):

| frame | t | main | this branch | preview |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 1 / 23 | 0 / 22 | 0 / 22 |
| 1 | 0.0417 | 3 / 25 | 2 / 24 | 2 / 24 |
| 4 | 0.1667 | 11 / 33 | 10 / 32 | 10 / 32 |

A 30 fps VP9 WebM rendered at 30 fps shows all 30 of its first 30 frames, in order.

A direct ffmpeg probe covered:
- 11 sources: mp4 at 60, 24 and 29.97 fps; mkv at 30 and 29.97 fps; webm at 30 and 60 fps; mp4 with timescale 30 and 24; avi at 30 fps; and mp4 29.97 with timescale 600.
- output rates 10, 24, 25, 30, 50 and 60, and start times 0, 0.01, 0.37 and 1.23 s.

Against the frame on screen at each slot's nominal time: 288 wrong or missing of 4400 slots here, 2727 on main. Results were identical on 5.1.9 and 7.0.2. The remainder:
- **Unaligned starts on coarse timebases:** ffmpeg rounds `-ss` to the tick, shifting the whole window (see Known limits).
- **Millisecond or 1/600 timestamps at 29.97 fps:** near-ties where the stored timestamp cannot say which side of the slot a frame starts.

## Test plan

- New test `frame sampling at the output frame rate` in `videoFrameExtractor.test.ts`, four cases:
  - mp4 60 fps at 24 fps from 0
  - mp4 60 fps at 10 fps from 0.37 s
  - mkv 30 fps at 30 fps
  - mp4 30 fps with timescale 30, at 60 fps
- Main fails the two mp4 60 fps cases. Removing each part of the change fails its own case:
  - `round=up`: both 60 fps cases
  - `-noaccurate_seek`: the 0.37 s case
  - the shift: the mkv case
  - the 2 ms bound: the timescale 30 case
- `videoFrameExtractor.test.ts`: exit 0, 182 passed at this head (167 before the rebase, on ffmpeg 7.0.2 and 5.1.9).
- `extractionCache.test.ts`: exit 0, 36 passed.
- Engine `tsc --noEmit` clean; oxlint 0 errors; pre-commit lint, format, fallow and typecheck green.

## Regression baselines

Regenerated in the pinned test image (`Dockerfile.test` with `--update`), `output.mp4` only, for the four fixtures that fail against the old baselines: `style-12-prod` (3 checkpoints under the 30 dB floor), `style-13-prod` (4), `style-15-prod` (1), `style-18-prod` (3). All four play 25 fps sources at 30 fps; for 25 into 30, main picked one source frame ahead in 2 of every 6 output frames.

**Each new baseline shows the source frame the rule picks.** For every failing checkpoint, output frame k should show source frame floor(k x 25/30); main picked the next one. The source frames were decoded with ffmpeg and compared with both baselines over the pixels where the two baselines differ and the video is not under an overlay:

| Fixture | Output frame | Expected source frame | New baseline vs expected / vs main's pick | Old baseline vs expected / vs main's pick |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `style-12-prod` | 80 | 66 | 38.0 / 15.1 dB | 15.1 / 38.3 dB |
| `style-12-prod` | 109 | 90 | 38.9 / 15.8 dB | 15.9 / 39.1 dB |
| `style-12-prod` | 122 | 101 | 25.7 / 15.3 dB | 17.0 / 28.3 dB |
| `style-13-prod` | 38 | 31 | 38.8 / 16.2 dB | 16.3 / 38.6 dB |
