In all 11, the new baseline best matches the expected frame among its neighbours (expected -1 to +2), and the old baseline best matches main's pick.

- Each regenerated fixture passes against its new baseline with 0 failed checkpoints.
- The CI regression run at this head is green across every shard, including the video fixtures not re-checked by hand.

## Known limits

Found by independent review, not fixed here:

- **Unaligned starts on coarse timebases:** some rows are worse than main. The seek point is rounded to the tick and every frame lands just after its slot. Example: an AVI at 30000/1001 starting at 0.37 s. The same sources are better than main overall.
- **Coarse ticks that do not divide the frame duration:** such timebases (1/250, 1/400) are not shifted and drop one frame in three at their own rate. No common writer produces them: MP4 writers pick at least 10000, Matroska/WebM/FLV use 1/1000, QuickTime 600, MPEG-TS and Android 90000, AVI 1/fps.
- **Millisecond timestamps:** a start time that is not on a whole millisecond is rounded before the half-tick shift, so a slot can take a frame up to about one tick after its time. This is still fewer wrong slots than main.

## Notes

- Rebased on main after #4564, which took `v5`; this PR takes `v6`.
- When a slot time sits exactly on a frame boundary that is not a whole microsecond (for example 60 fps footage at 1/30 s), a paused Chrome seek shows the earlier frame. This change follows the engine's own lookup rule for those ties: the frame that starts at that time.

title: fix(studio): a clip edit keeps the film as long as its animation, and a hand-set length stays
body:
## What this fixes

Moving, resizing or deleting a clip in Studio sets the film's length to the furthest clip end. It ignored where the animations end. So moving the last clip left could save a film shorter than its own animation: the rest of the animation was cut from the render, and, now that preview stops at the declared length too, from the preview on the next open.

Now that length is the later of the furthest clip end and where the preview's animations end. Media with no known length still does not count.

Studio reads the animation end from the runtime's `window.__hf.animationEnd()` (#4541). Where it reads nothing, Studio behaves as it did before.

## Decided behaviour

- **A repeating animation counts one cycle.** The runtime reports each animation's first cycle, so a tween with `repeat: 40` counts once and an author who overshoots a repeat to fill the film never balloons it.
- **A length set by hand wins.** Nothing new is written into the file. A length counts as derived when it equals where the content ended before the edit (the later of the furthest clip end and the animation end); any other length was set by a person or an agent. A derived length follows the content both ways. A hand-set length is never shortened and never grown for an animation.
- **Except a clip newly placed past it.** An edit that places a clip past a hand-set end grows the film to that clip's end, not to a later animation end. A clip that already ran past a hand-set end does not grow it on an unrelated edit.
- **One decision per file in a group edit.** Moving or resizing several clips at once decides the length once per file, from the file before and after the whole edit, so the result does not depend on the order of the clips.
- **One undo step.** A move, resize, group move or group resize writes the new length in the same save as the clips, on both save paths (the film view and a composition opened on its own), so one undo restores the clips and the old length together and one redo brings both back.
- **Decided again once the preview has caught up.** Moving a clip can move the animations tied to it. After a move or resize, once the preview runs the new timing in place, the length is decided again with the new animation end; usually nothing changes. A preview that had to reload fully, or whose script is still waiting on a plugin, is not treated as caught up. An animation end that was known before the edit and reads as unknown after it never shortens the film.
- **Only the film's own clips.** Inside the preview the runtime gives untimed elements with an id (a background, a logo) the film's full length, and inlines a nested scene's clips on the scene's own clock. Neither counts as a film clip: a scene counts by its host clip. So neither can make a hand-set length look derived or stop a derived one from following its content.
- **Scene files read like any other.** A scene file keeps its composition inside `<template>` (plain, or wrapped in `<html data-composition-id>` as installed registry components are), which Studio's file readers used to skip. They now read it, so a scene opened on its own keeps its length at its clips instead of dropping to its animation end. A root that does not wrap its clips (a `<meta data-composition-id>`, as in the quickstart template) keeps all its clips.
- **One place finds the root tag.** The length writer, asset drop, block install and the paste fallback now find the composition's root tag the same way, skipping HTML comments. In a registry component scene, dropped or pasted content used to land after `<html …>`, outside the template, where the preview never showed it; it now lands in the scene's root. Comments (malformed and unclosed ones too) and script or style bodies are skipped as the browser skips them, so a mention of `data-composition-id` inside one no longer captures the length write or an insertion.
- **A preview that has not caught up shows the file's length.** When the soft reload is waiting on a plugin or could not verify, the readout and the preview's root take the length in the file and nothing is written. If the file's length changed during the gesture (typed in the code panel, say), the re-decision leaves it alone.

Paste, asset drop and block install keep their grow-only behaviour. Because the readers now see inside `<template>`, they also grow a scene file when content lands past its end.

## Before

Main, a 5 s composition whose dot animates for the full 5 s, with clips A (0 to 2 s) and B (3 to 5 s). Clip B is dragged one second left, then the project is reopened: the film is saved as 4 s, the Dot animation track is cut at 4 s with its last keyframe past the cut, and the dot never reaches the end.

![Before: after moving the last clip left the film is 4 s and the animation is cut](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/92c90170-b40d-4518-9b52-a7f52044e0d7)

Main, a 6 s film whose length follows its content (clip B ends at 6, the dot animates to 5). Clip B is dragged to end at 4: the film is saved as 4 s and the dot's animation is cut at 4.

![Before: a derived length shrinks past the animation to 4 s](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cde76d74-e2d2-4da1-8da1-08bb20de9469)

## After

This branch, same project and drag: the film stays 5 s, the Dot track runs the full length, and the dot reaches the end. The saved root reads `data-duration="5"` and nothing else was added.

![After: the film stays 5 s and the animation plays to its end](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/63b2d4a0-bf48-4995-92a5-9171895d3498)

This branch, same drag: the length shrinks with the content but stops at the animation's end, 5 s.

![After: a derived length shrinks to the animation's end, 5 s](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d3e182bd-218c-446f-995f-36aca6c29f21)

## What I measured

- Studio tests that fail on main and pass here: a derived length is not shortened below the animation end on move, resize, group move, group resize and delete; a hand-set length is kept on each of those; an animation does not grow a hand-set length; a repeating animation counts its first cycle; a length counts as derived only when it equals the content end; a group edit decides once per file whatever the clip order; a clip that already ran past a hand-set end does not grow it; a move, resize, group move or group resize undoes and redoes the clips and the length in one step on both save paths; a host with no active composition gets the same length from a group move as from a single move; a length another writer changes after a move, resize, group move or group resize starts, before its save reads the file, is kept on both save paths, as is one set back to its old value just before the preview catches up; two moves saved at once decide the length from the file each save reads; an element the runtime stamped does not make a hand-set length look derived; a nested scene's inner clips neither cut a hand-set length nor stop a derived one following content; a template scene file keeps its length at its clips, with or without a declared length; a registry component scene and a `<meta>` root keep their length at their clips; an unverified or deferred soft reload leaves the readout on the file's length; a length changed on disk mid-gesture is kept; drop, paste and block install into a registry scene land inside its root; a comment mentioning `data-composition-id`, a malformed or unclosed comment, or one inside a script or style body captures neither the length write nor an insertion, and the root tag scan stays linear (inputs that took seconds to minutes before, such as a tag with no closing `>` followed by many mentions, now take a few milliseconds at 2 MB); every edit type re-decides on each of two edits in a row, including on a film with no declared length.
- Guards proven by breaking the code, each failing a test: converging on any soft-reload result but "applied", treating an unverified soft reload as caught up, reporting a plugin wait as "applied", dropping the unknown-reading guard, ignoring the new animation end after the preview catches up, ignoring the file's clip end then, counting stamped elements, counting a nested scene's inner clips, not unwrapping `<template>`, not syncing the readout on an unverified reload, syncing it after a full reload too, and escalating a plugin wait in the script-commit path.
- Each run alone (`packages/studio`): `useTimelineEditing.test.tsx` (200), `timelineTimingSync.test.ts` (31), `timelineEditingHelpers.test.ts` (16), `useTimelineDeleteOps.test.tsx` (8), `useTimelineGroupEditing.test.tsx` (2), `timelineEditingGsap.test.ts` (9), `patchDocumentRootDuration.test.ts` (6), `timelineAssetDrop.test.ts` (42), `rootDuration.test.ts` (36), `useClipboard.test.ts` (23), `useTimelineAssetDropOps.test.tsx` (6), `blockInstaller.test.ts` (2), `gsapSoftReload.test.ts` (31), `useGsapScriptCommits.test.tsx` (24), `gsapUndoRestore.test.ts` (18), `useTimelinePlayer.test.ts` (29), `useTimelineSyncCallbacks.test.ts` (17), `clipboardPayload.test.ts` (10), `studioHelpers.test.ts` (20), `sdkEditTransaction.decline.test.ts` (3), `sdkCutover.test.ts` (74), `sdkCutover.gate.test.ts` (3), `sdkEditTransaction.test.ts` (1), `timelineQuickSaves.test.ts` (6), `canvasQuickSaves.test.tsx` (2). Typecheck, lint, format, the comment ratchet and the fallow audit green.
- Real Studio: headless Chrome, Studio's dev server on main and on this branch with the runtime from #4541, real mouse drags in the timeline, each file read back after reopening. A hand-set 8 s film (with and without `data-start` on its root) stays 8 after a move and after its animation grows to 9; a derived 6 s film whose clip is dragged to end at 4 becomes 5, its animation end (main: 4); a derived 5 s film with a 1 s tween repeated nine times becomes 4 (one cycle counted); the fixture above stays 5. The runtime stamps `data-start="0"` on every live root; the tests now model that.

## What I did NOT exercise

- Delete ends in a full preview reload, so its length is decided with the animation end from before the clip's animations are removed. The next edit corrects it.
- Edits that end in a full reload have no point where the preview has caught up, so they keep the length decided when the edit was saved.
- If an agent changes animation timing between two Studio edits, the next edit sees a length that no longer equals the content end and keeps it as hand-set: kept, never cut.
- A hand-set length grown to a newly placed clip equals the content end afterwards, so a later edit treats it as derived: set 8, drag a clip to end at 9 (the film grows to 9), drag it back to 5, and the film follows it to 5. Keeping the author's 8 would need the file to remember it, and this change writes nothing new into files.
- A composition edited from another composition's view (a scene file, plain or in `<template>`, edited from the film) counts only its own clips, not its own animations, as on main.
- When the right length is only known after the preview catches up (a moved clip whose own tween the edit shifts past the old end), that correction is a second save. It joins the edit's undo step when the animation rewrite lands within 300 ms of the clip's save and the correction within 10 s of the rewrite. Otherwise the first undo can restore the animation and the length while the clip stays moved, as a slow animation rewrite already does on main.
- An undo that lands after an edit but before the preview catches up restores the old length, which the re-decision then reads as the edit's own and may resize with the animation end from before the undo. The next edit corrects it.
- Padding an author wrote into their own timeline (for example `tl.to({}, { duration: 10 })`) counts as animation.

title: feat(studio): a refused undo names the later change and offers to undo it first
body:
## What this changes

Undo is per author: Cmd+Z undoes your own last change. When a later change by someone else, such as an agent turn, touched the same file, Studio refuses the undo so it does not overwrite that change. Until now the refusal only said "Can't undo: index.html changed since that edit.", which left you guessing what changed it and what to do next.

Now the refusal names the later change and offers to undo it first:

- The toast reads "Can't undo: Agent turn changed index.html since that edit." and has an "Undo Agent turn" button. Clicking it undoes that turn, and the next Cmd+Z then undoes your edit. If your own edit during the turn split it into parts, the button undoes the part that changed the file, and a further refusal names the other part.
- The Undo button's tooltip names it as well: "Undo Moved Title, changed since by Agent turn".
- The change named is the newest later one that is not itself an undo and whose content is still on the file your edit is blocked on. If another of its files moved on since, undoing it is refused in turn and names that later change, so the chain continues. After you undo your own later edit, the refusal still names the agent's turn, not your undo. If a later undo already put back an older version of the file, nothing qualifies and the old message shows.
- A refused redo offers nothing. Offering to undo the other change there would make the next Cmd+Shift+Z replay that change instead of your redo.
- If undoing the named change is itself refused because a still later change touched the file, that refusal names the next one, so the chain continues.
- Offer toasts stay until dismissed. The same offer twice shows one toast. A click while the toast is leaving does nothing. Switching projects clears offers from the previous one. Clicking an offer after opening another composition reloads the editor for the composition open at that moment.

The history engine adds an optional `changedSince: { id, label, paths }` to a refused step or undo, worked out while it refuses, and the server adds it to the history state. So `hyperframes history undo --json` reports it with or without a running preview. Studio undoes the named change with those paths, so it locks and soft-applies the right files even when the change landed after Studio last read the history. Older clients ignore it, and a newer client on an older server shows the old message.

## Before

On `main`, after a person edit and then an agent turn on the same file, Cmd+Z shows the generic refusal with no way forward.

![Before: Can't undo, index.html changed since that edit](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5f4b7680-0624-4d16-9850-d57b2379ad10)

## After

The same steps name the agent's turn and offer to undo it.

![After: Can't undo, Agent turn changed index.html since that edit, with an Undo Agent turn button](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/04c2bfe5-9521-4f21-818a-e84219d9cbaf)

Clicking "Undo Agent turn", then Cmd+Z, undoes the agent's turn and then the person's edit.

![After: both undone](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a735bd5c-4b79-4080-af91-d753a2d125a5)

## Tests

- `projectHistory.test.ts`: the later change named is the agent's turn after your own later edit was undone (E1, agent turn, E2, Cmd+Z, Cmd+Z), and after the agent undid its own later turn; the refusal itself carries the name; a change still on the blocked file is named though another of its files moved on; nothing is named when a later undo already put back an older version, or for a change still pending.
- `routes/history.test.ts`: the history state and a refused step name the change since, including after the person undid their own later edit; a refused redo names the later change too (Studio offers nothing for it); a refused undo names the next later change.
- `useEditHistoryActions.test.tsx`: the refusal names the agent and offers to undo its change first; a refused redo offers nothing; clicking the offer after switching composition reloads the editor for the composition then open.
- `useToast.test.tsx`: offers persist, the same offer twice is one toast, switching projects drops offers but keeps errors, a leaving toast ignores clicks.
- `usePersistentEditHistory.test.ts`: a refused undo names the agent's later change, and undoing that first lets Cmd+Z through; the offer undoes an agent turn Studio has not seen yet, locking and soft-applying its file.

Results: `tsc` for studio, studio-server and cli, oxfmt, oxlint and fallow clean; studio-server history and route tests 122, studio history hook and toast tests 24, and CLI history tests 32 pass. Each fix, taken out, fails a named test.

title: fix(engine): forced-SDR renders show tone-mapped HDR footage as Studio does
body:
## What

Forced-SDR renders (`--sdr` on HDR footage) now show the tone-mapped footage with the colours Studio's proxies have. This is the remaining part of #4549, after #4564.

1. **Tone-mapped frames are tagged sRGB.** The zscale/hable tone map wrote BT.709-tagged frames, and Chrome colour-managed them the way #4549 describes for SDR footage. They now carry the same sRGB tag, plus for jpg the BT.601 full-range matrix, as every other SDR frame since #4564.
2. **macOS uses the same tone map as Linux when it can.** The engine checks at runtime whether ffmpeg has the zscale filter (Homebrew's ffmpeg normally does). If it does, macOS decodes in software and uses the identical zscale/hable tone map. If it does not, the old VideoToolbox path stays, and the render prints one warning per process naming the difference. The two paths have separate extraction-cache keys (`hdr2sdr-hable-srgb`, `hdr2sdr-videotoolbox-hdr`), so a cached frame from one never serves the other.
3. **HDR footage with no matrix or primaries tag tone-maps.** zscale reads each decoded frame's own tags and finds no conversion path without them, so such an extraction failed, on main as well. Before the tone map, every frame is now tagged with the probed matrix, primaries and transfer, with BT.2020 where the matrix or primaries are missing. From ffmpeg 8.1, ffprobe can report container tags (including a PQ or HLG transfer) that the video stream lacks, which is why the tags are set on the frames rather than only when the probe is empty. Without the transfer tag, such a clip failed on 8.1 where macOS VideoToolbox used to render it.

Fixes #4549

Credit to @sontiac for the diagnosis in #4549, which this finishes.

## Decisions

- **zscale on macOS when present, VideoToolbox only as the fallback.** VideoToolbox on ffmpeg 8.1 does not tone-map: its frames stay HDR (cICP BT.2020 HLG), and Chrome then tone-maps them itself. One frame came out 2a737d where the zscale/hable reference is 388d96. Using zscale whenever it exists gives one look on every platform. Without zscale the look differs, and the warning says so rather than shipping a macOS-only look silently.
- **The warning prints once per process**, at extraction time, including renders served from the cache.
- **Untagged HDR is treated as BT.2020.** HDR transfer functions (PQ, HLG) come with BT.2020 in every consumer format; a missing matrix or primaries tag is a muxing omission, not a different colourspace.

## Measurements

HDR fixture clip, forced-SDR render with `--frames-cache-dir off`, on Linux with ffmpeg 7.0.2 and chrome-headless-shell 152. The reference is the zscale/hable tone map of the source, as Studio's proxies make it.

| Frames | Tone-map reference | main: Chrome paints | this PR: Chrome paints |
|---|---|---|---|
| png | 388d96 | 2d8790 | **388d96** |
| png (highlight) | ffd9c0 | | **ffd8c0** |
| jpg | 388d96 | | within 2 codes |

On macOS with Homebrew ffmpeg 8.1.1 (zscale present), the extracted frames are identical to Linux's on 5.1.9 and 7.0.2, tagged sRGB.

## Known costs

- On macOS, the zscale path decodes in software instead of on VideoToolbox: about 2x the CPU for forced-SDR extraction.
- The zscale probe lives in `utils/psnrFilterAvailability.ts`, generalized to `isFfmpegFilterAvailable(name)`. The file name is older than this use; renaming it is left out to keep the diff small.
- A failed probe is remembered for the whole process.
- HDR VFR extraction keeps a single ffmpeg process, like main, so on ffmpeg below 6.1 a trailing still can lose frames. That has its own follow-up (the two-process path from #4564 would drop HDR10 light levels).

## Test plan

- [x] `videoFrameExtractor.test.ts`, forced-SDR block (runs where zscale exists):
  - an HLG clip tone-maps to the zscale/hable reference, tagged sRGB with no cICP, with jpg within 3 codes;
  - macOS with zscale takes the same path (platform spoofed);
  - macOS without zscale takes VideoToolbox with its own cache key and warns exactly once;
  - HLG clips missing the matrix, the primaries or both in the video stream, and a PQ clip missing both, tone-map byte-identically to the fully tagged clip; an HLG clip tagged only in the container does too where ffprobe reports that tag (8.1 and later; before that ffprobe reads it as SDR, as on main);
  - a VFR HDR10 window matches the single-process command.
- [x] `psnrFilterAvailability.test.ts`: one shared `-filters` probe per process.
- [x] Each piece reverted fails its test, checked by an independent review:
  - the sRGB tag;
  - a shared cache key;
  - the warning printed on every call;
  - macOS ignoring zscale;
  - the jpg matrix (8 codes against a limit of 3);
  - VideoToolbox left on with zscale;
  - the HDR guard on the two-process path;
  - no frame tags before the tone map (the extraction fails, on ffmpeg 5.1.9 and 8.1.3);
  - no transfer tag (the container-only clip fails on 8.1.3).
- [x] Six engine test files on bookworm ffmpeg 5.1.9, rebased on current main: 493 passed. The forced-SDR, untagged and VFR tests also pass with ffmpeg 8.1.3 (60 passed). Typecheck, oxlint, oxfmt, `comment-ratchet` and `check-comment-citations` are clean.

title: fix(studio-server): history saved by 0.8.78 survives the update with every entry
body:
## What this fixes

Updating from 0.8.78 to 0.8.79 or 0.8.80 threw away every project's edit history. On the first open after the update, the history came up empty, and the project's `.hyperframes/history-id` was overwritten with a new id. The old entries stayed on disk, but nothing pointed at them any more, so the loss was permanent once the new version had run.

The cause: 0.8.78 recorded each history's folder as `{ dir }`. 0.8.79 records `{ dir, ino, born }`, so it can tell a moved folder from a new one on a reused inode, and it refused any record without them. Every 0.8.78 record failed that check, and the project was given a fresh history.

Now:

- A record from 0.8.78 is judged the way 0.8.78 judged it: it belongs to this folder unless another folder at the recorded path still carries the same id, which makes this folder a copy. A project opened in place, through another path to the same folder, or after a rename keeps its history, and a copy still gets its own. A record 0.8.78 left empty or unreadable keeps the history too, as 0.8.78 did. The record is then rewritten with the folder's identity. Opening the same project with an older `hyperframes preview` in between keeps working: the older version writes `{ dir }` again, and it is adopted again.
- The history id is only ever written when the project has none. If `.hyperframes/history-id` exists but holds something this version cannot read, opening the history fails with a `HistoryIdError` naming the file, and the file is left as it was (`hyperframes history` reports it as a refusal, not a crash). Before, it was replaced with a new id. The CLI and the dev server already treat a failed open as "history is off for this run" and log the reason.
- The embedding contract for `history` on the Studio API adapter said to keep one history per project for the host's lifetime. A history refuses every call once its folder is replaced, so it now says to keep them in `historyCache`, which reopens.

Not in this change: projects already opened with 0.8.79 or 0.8.80 got a new id then; their earlier entries are still on disk but are not folded back in.

## Tests

`projectHistory.test.ts`:
- a history written by the published `@hyperframes/studio-server@0.8.78` (the fixture under `__fixtures__/history-0.8.78`: its log, blobs and `{ dir }` record) opens with both entries, at its recorded path and after a move, and its agent entry can still be undone;
- a copy of a 0.8.78 project gets a history of its own while the original still carries the id, and the original keeps its entries;
- a 0.8.78 record that is empty or `null`, or that names the folder through a symlink, keeps the history;
- a 0.8.78-shaped record written over a current one keeps the history and is upgraded;
- a history id that cannot be read, including one that points outside the history root, is refused and left alone.

Results: `tsc`, oxfmt and oxlint clean; studio-server history and route tests pass. `main`'s code fails every one of these tests. Each of these fails a named test: dropping the 0.8.78 rule, minting over an unreadable record, counting another path to the same folder as a copy, and replacing an unreadable id.

title: fix(studio-server): a save never recreates a project folder renamed away
body:
## What

If a project's folder is renamed or deleted while Studio has it open, later writes brought the old folder back: every one of them created its parent folders with a recursive mkdir. Repro: open a project in Studio, rename its folder in Finder, keep working (a preview reload, an upload into a subfolder, a render, a catalog install). A folder with the old name reappears, holding only Studio's own files.

Now a write may create folders only below a project folder that still exists:

- Core gains `mkdirWithinProject(root, dir)`. It creates the missing folders below `root` one level at a time, without `recursive`, so a root that is gone fails with `ProjectRootMissingError` instead of reappearing. That also holds when the folder is renamed between a check and the write. A folder outside the project (the Studio dev server's renders folder, a cache) is created as before, but only while the project folder exists.
- Every folder studio-server creates for a project goes through it, and so does the CLI's catalog install (the producer's two and the CLI's `media-use` are listed under Known limits): file saves, creates, renames and duplicates; uploads; the id-stamp record; the backup journal; the project id file; the preview document store; background-removal outputs; thumbnail and proxy caches; renders; and the catalog install (published files create their folders through the helper).
- Core also gains `realProjectRoot(root)`: the folder's real path, or `ProjectRootMissingError` when it is gone. The catalog install (`registryRoot`, which no longer creates the project folder) and the media proxy resolve the project through it.
- Studio shows the error: a write into a folder that is already gone answers `404 { error: "not found", why: "project_dir_missing" }`, the same answer the file routes already gave for a missing project, which the hosts handle. A middleware maps the error after any error handler has run, so an embedder's own handler still sees it. The upload and catalog install routes now check for the folder up front, as the file routes do, and `add`, the thumbnail route, the media proxy and the backup journal pass the error through instead of wrapping it in a generic failure. An upload checks again after its body is read and its files written, so a folder renamed mid-upload answers the 404 instead of `201` with no files. A folder that vanishes while some other request is running can still get that route's own answer (a `409` from a save, a `422` from a media proxy whose codec probe then fails); the stacked follow-up #4617 answers the 404 for those too.

## Behaviour change

`hyperframes add <item> --dir <folder that does not exist>` now fails with "Project folder not found" instead of creating an empty folder. `hyperframes init` creates its folder before installing, so it is unaffected. The registry cache creates its own folder.

`createPreviewDocumentStore(projectDir, salt)` in `@hyperframes/studio-server` now takes the project folder and keeps its documents in `.hyperframes/preview` inside it; before, it took the store folder itself. The type did not change, so a caller outside this repo that still passes a store folder has every write refused (a failed write only costs a rebuild, so nothing errors). The CLI, the only caller in this repo, passes the project folder.

## Known limits

The producer still creates two folders recursively, without knowing the project folder: a render's output folder, and `.hyperframes/prepared-assets` when a film has GIFs. The render route now creates the output folder through the helper before the producer starts, so only a rename in the seconds before a render starts, or during a GIF preview step, can still bring a folder back. Closing that means passing the project folder into the render job.

The CLI's `media-use` commands (`resolve`, and anything writing the project's `.media/manifest.jsonl`) still create their folders recursively, so pointed at a renamed project with `--project <old path>` they recreate it. That code is unchanged from `main`; it needs its own change. The same holds for the CLI's `transcribe` output folder.

Undo and redo write through the history store, which creates parent folders recursively after checking the project folder, so a rename in that short gap can still bring the folder back, and a history write into a folder that is already gone answers a generic error rather than `project_dir_missing`. That code is unchanged from `main`.

A background removal on a folder that is already gone answers `403` here; #4617 turns that into the 404.

The media and thumbnail folder creation moved to the helper without a test of their own; the helper's own tests and the render, upload, proxy and backup-journal tests cover the rule.

## Tests

Each fails on main unless noted:
- core, `mkdirWithinProject`: creates folders below an existing root; "does not bring back a project folder that was renamed away"; creates a folder outside the project as before.
- studio-server, "does not recreate a project folder renamed away while Studio has it open": a save, an upload into a subfolder, a catalog install and a render after a rename all answer `project_dir_missing` and the folder stays gone. On main the upload answers 403 and the render recreates the folder. The save leg already passed on main and stays as a guard.
- studio-server, "does not recreate a project folder renamed away while its preview is open": main's preview document store recreates it.
- CLI, "answers that the project folder is gone, and does not recreate it, after a rename": through the real catalog install route.
- CLI, "answers that the project folder is gone when it is renamed while the item downloads": the folder vanishes mid-install; fails with a 500 if `add` wraps the error again.
- CLI, "does not recreate a project folder renamed away before an install": main's `registryRoot` creates it.
- studio-server, "answers that the project folder is gone when it is renamed while a proxy is requested": the folder is renamed during the codec probe; answered 502 before.
- studio-server, "answers that the project folder is gone when it is renamed while an upload is being read": answered 201 with no files before.
- studio-server, "answers that the project folder is gone when it is renamed while a file is read": the rename lands while an uploaded file's bytes are read; answers 201 with no files if the route's second check is removed.
- studio-server, backup journal "lets the missing-folder error through instead of reporting a failed backup": reported a failed backup (a 500 at the route) before.
- core, "creates no folder outside the project once the project folder is gone", and studio-server, "does not start a render into an outside folder once the project folder is gone": the render started (`200`) and created its outside folder before.

title: feat(studio-server): a host can make Cmd+Z undo the newest change, whoever made it
body:
## What this changes

Since 0.8.79, Cmd+Z in the project history undoes only your own changes (and outside edits): an agent's turn is the agent's to undo. That is right for Studio, where the agent is a separate author. A host whose agent acts for the person wants Cmd+Z to undo the newest change, whoever made it, as it did in 0.8.78: you ask the agent for a change, don't like it, press Cmd+Z, and the agent's change is what goes.

`openProjectHistory` takes a new option for that host:

```ts
openProjectHistory({ projectDir, historyRoot, undoScope: "everyone" });
```

- `"own"` (the default): unchanged, Cmd+Z and Shift+Cmd+Z step over your own changes.
- `"everyone"`: they step over every finished change, newest first, whoever made it.

An agent turn that is still open is left alone either way, so Cmd+Z while an agent is working reverts your own last change, not the agent's writes in progress. A new change by anyone ends Shift+Cmd+Z, as in a single undo stack. Studio's own hosts (`hyperframes preview` and the dev server) keep the default.

One limit: a host that calls `claim()` directly as the agent, with coalescing, can see the Undo button name an older entry while Cmd+Z takes the agent's held edit first. Studio's routes always claim as the person, so they cannot reach it.

## Tests

`projectHistory.test.ts`, with `undoScope: "everyone"`:
- after a person's edit and then an agent turn on the same file, Cmd+Z undoes the agent's turn, then the person's edit;
- Shift+Cmd+Z brings them back in turn, and a new change by anyone ends it;
- while an agent turn is still open, Cmd+Z reverts the person's edit and leaves the agent's writes.

The per-author tests are unchanged and pass.

Results: `tsc`, oxfmt and oxlint clean; studio-server history tests pass. Ignoring the option fails the first two tests; letting it reach an open turn, or not recording which entries belong to an open turn, fails the open-turn test.

title: fix(cli): commands exit right away even when the network or DNS is broken
body:
## What changes for users

A finished `hyperframes` command now exits right away, even when the network or DNS is broken. It no longer waits for the update check, the skills check or the telemetry upload.

Measured on a Linux box, `hyperframes lint` on a small project, TTY, empty caches, 3 runs each:

| Network | Before (main) | After |
|---|---|---|
| DNS that never answers | 2.05 s | 0.53-0.57 s |
| npm, GitHub and PostHog hosts pinned to an unreachable IP | 15.2-15.4 s | 0.68-0.71 s |
| Normal network, telemetry off | 0.85-0.92 s | 0.50-0.51 s |

Notices work as before. The update notice, the skills nudge, auto-install, `_meta.updateAvailable` and `doctor` all read the same 24 h caches as before. The caches are now refreshed by a background process, so something that process finds shows up on the next run.

## How it works

- **Background checks.** At startup the CLI works out, from the environment and the two caches, whether an update check or a skills check is due. If either is, it starts one detached, unref'd child (`backgroundChecksWorker.js`, a new build entry, spawned the same way as the render setup worker) and tells it which checks to run. The child refreshes the caches and exits. The CLI itself only reads the caches.
- **A failed check is retried at most once an hour.** Before it starts the child, the CLI records when it last tried each check. A check is due only when its last success is over 24 h old and its last try is over an hour old. So a dead network costs one child an hour, not one per command. Two commands started at almost the same moment can still both run the skills check, which is harmless because they write the same fields. A try stamp dated in the future, as after a clock correction, is ignored. If the settings file cannot be written (for example a stale settings lock), the stamp is lost and each command starts a child, as before this change, and the CLI prints that settings are locked.
- **Same opt-outs.** The child is only started when the CLI would have run the check before this change. That means not in dev mode, not under `CI=1`/`CI=true`, and not with `HYPERFRAMES_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`. For skills it also means not with `HYPERFRAMES_SKIP_SKILLS=1` and only when notices print (a TTY). A test runs through that whole list.
- **Auto-install stays in the CLI.** It is scheduled from the cached result, as it already was when the cache was fresh. The child never installs, because installer detection reads the path of the running script.
- **Exit telemetry.** `finalizeCli` no longer awaits the telemetry flush. The exit handler already calls `flushSync()` every time, which hands anything still queued to a detached sender. So every tracked command now hands its queued telemetry to a detached `node -e` child at exit. Before, that only happened after a failed in-process send. This builds on the unmerged `fix/cli-exit-without-waiting-on-telemetry` branch, re-applied on current main.
- **Windows.** The exit-time sender and the skills check's `git ls-remote` now pass `windowsHide`, like every other spawn in the package. Both now run from a process with no console.
- **Other places that waited on the upload.**
  - The `events` beacon now calls `flushSync()` alone. It has no exit handler of its own.
  - `feedback` and the `figma` error path stop awaiting `flush()`, because the exit handler delivers their events.
  - Render's eager `void flush()` stays. It is what delivers render events from a long-running preview process. It keeps the DNS probe, because a pending system lookup would hold render's forced exit.
- **The DNS probe (`hostAnswers`) stays**, for that eager flush and inside the child, where it bounds how long a child lives on a dead resolver.
- **The skills cache write and the stale-pin notice's write now read the settings file fresh.** Writing back a copy read at startup could otherwise undo what the other process wrote in the meantime. The update check already did this.

## From the post-merge review of #4556

These follow-ups come from @jrusso1020's review, and each one has a test:

- **Env proxy and AAAA.** The probe says yes when Node's fetch uses an env proxy (`NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`/`--use-env-proxy` with `HTTPS_PROXY`). It says no when either address family times out, because the system lookup waits for both. His UDP-server test for the probe is included.
- **Update check timer.** The request and `res.json()` now share one try/finally, so a request that fails fast leaves no 3 s timer, and a stalled reply body has a deadline.
- **Telemetry reply.** `sendQueued` cancels the reply body it never reads.
- **Missing tests.**
  - A flush behind a failed send keeps the batch for the next send.
  - The one-attempt cap is tested both when the send fails and when DNS does not answer.
  - A flush queued behind an empty one still sends.
  - The `events` beacon queues the event before it hands it off.
- **Nits.**
  - `printStalePinNotice` now calls `updateCheckDisabled()` instead of repeating the rule.
  - `checkSkillsForUpdate` and its `force` flag are gone, so the out-of-date JSDoc is gone with them.
  - The docs now say the version cache is refreshed in the background, and never under CI or `HYPERFRAMES_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`.
  - The PR-body wording he flagged was in #4556's own description, so it does not apply here.

## CI smoke harness

`scripts/ci/cli-telemetry-e2e.mjs` records telemetry by wrapping `fetch` in the CLI process, and it relied on the flush at the end of each command. Without that flush, the events leave through the detached `flushSync()` sender, which skips the wrapper. The `add` checks then fail, and CI would send real events. The harness preload now also catches that sender and runs its request through the same wrapper. With the old harness against this branch, 3 checks fail ("one event per installed item", got `[]`). With the new one, every check passes, including "exactly one render_complete event".

## Verified

- Every changed and new test file passes on its own, along with the neighbouring files: autoUpdate, stale pin, upgrade, events, figma, feedback, CLI commands and posture refresh.
- 21 mutants each fail a test, from finalize awaiting the flush and the CLI running the check itself to each gate, unref, the fresh read and patches A to D.
- Checks: `tsc`, oxlint, oxfmt, fallow audit, the comment ratchet and the CLI process-ownership check.
- The telemetry e2e passes on the built CLI.
- With a normal network, the child wrote `latestVersion` and the skills fields about 0.13 s after the CLI exited.
- On a dead network the child lives about 2.6-2.8 s (silent DNS) or about 15 s (unreachable IP) after the CLI exits, and then goes away.
- Three back-to-back `lint` runs on silent DNS with one settings file started one child in total (both attempt stamps came from the first run), and none were left after 4 s.
- Each new guard has a test that fails when it is removed: the attempt limit, each attempt stamp, the stamps surviving a settings read, the worker file name versus its build entry, both `windowsHide` flags and the stale-pin fresh read.

## Not verified

- macOS and Windows. The detached worker, the exit-time sender and `git ls-remote` all pass `windowsHide`, but I did not see it on Windows.
- Settings writes are still read-modify-write outside the settings lock. The fresh reads narrow the window to one synchronous step; they don't close it.

## Not in this PR

- The exit-time sender puts the whole batch on one `node -e` command line. A 1 s draft render produced about 35,000 characters, over Windows' 32,767-character limit, and a failed spawn drops the batch. This was already true for `render` on main. The fix is to pass the payload through stdin or a temp file.
- The whole CLI suite. I ran only the files listed above; CI runs the rest.

title: chore: release v0.8.81
