title: fix(studio): tone-map HDR preview proxies with the render tone map
body:
## What changes

Studio's preview proxy now tone-maps HDR footage the way renders do, with one shared builder: `hdrToSdrToneMapFilter` in `@hyperframes/core`. Studio no longer keeps its own copy of the zscale/hable chain. Three visible fixes follow:

1. **HDR footage that tags only its transfer now previews.** HLG or PQ footage with its primaries and matrix left unspecified used to fail: the proxy transcode exited with zscale's `no path between colorspaces`, and the preview route answered 502. Renders tone-map that footage as BT.2020 since #4600. Studio now does the same.
2. **BT.2020 SDR footage is no longer tone-mapped.** Studio tone-mapped anything with BT.2020 primaries, including SDR, so its preview came out darker than the render. The proxy now tone-maps only a PQ or HLG transfer, like renders. Studio's HDR label and colour-grading flag are unchanged.
3. **Tone-mapped proxies use the colour matrix they are tagged with.** The tone map ends in RGB, and the proxy's scale step converted that to YUV. ffmpeg 5.1 does that conversion with BT.601 unless told otherwise, while the file is tagged BT.709, so saturated colours shifted. The scale now names BT.709. ffmpeg 7.0 and 8.1 already read the tags, so their output is unchanged. 6.x (what CI runs) was not measured.

`PROXY_PARAMS_VERSION` goes from v4 to v5, so proxies cached under the old rules are made again.

## How

- `packages/core/src/hdrToneMap.ts`: one builder. zscale reads each frame's own colour tags, so the builder sets only the tags the first shown frame lacks: from ffprobe (which may see them in the container), else BT.2020 for the matrix and primaries. A stream that switches from HLG to PQ keeps each frame's transfer, as Studio did before. Then it runs the existing zscale/hable chain to BT.709.
- The first shown frame's tags are read with one `ffmpeg -frames:v 1 -vf showinfo` frame (`firstFrameColourArgs` and `parseFirstFrameColour` in core, used by both callers). ffprobe's packet-bounded reads return nothing on stream-copy trimmed files, which open on edit-list pre-roll.
- Engine (`videoFrameExtractor.ts`): #4600's private copy is replaced with a call to the builder, with the same per-frame rule.
- Studio (`proxyTranscoder.ts`): calls the builder, tone-maps only a PQ or HLG transfer, and names the BT.709 matrix when converting the tone map's output.

## Tests

- `proxyTranscoder.test.ts`, real ffmpeg: writes an H.264 clip with primaries and matrix unspecified and an HLG transfer, then compares the proxy's mean luma with a reference built in the test (the render tone map's RGB, converted with BT.709). The difference must be under 1. It skips when ffmpeg lacks zscale; CI's apt ffmpeg has it.
- `proxyTranscoder.test.ts`, real ffmpeg: one stream with HLG frames, then PQ frames. The mixed proxy's PQ frames must match the PQ-only proxy (above 36 dB; read as HLG they land near 31). The engine keeps #4600's mixed and trimmed-file tests.
- `proxyTranscoder.test.ts`, mocked: BT.2020 footage without a PQ or HLG transfer gets no tone map.
- `proxyTranscoder.test.ts`, mocked: the tone-map branch names the BT.709 matrix, which covers every ffmpeg version.
- `hdrToneMap.test.ts`: no tags set when the first frame carries them all, only the missing ones otherwise, and the BT.2020 defaults.

Each deliberate break was run on ffmpeg 5.1.9 and 8.1.3:

| Change | 5.1.9 | 8.1.3 |
|---|---|---|
| This branch | 22 passed | 22 passed |
| main's `proxyTranscoder.ts` | real test fails (transcode exits 1) | fails |
| gate back on the HDR flag | mocked test fails | fails |
| HLG not tone-mapped | real test fails | fails |
| matrix not named | mocked check and real test fail (off by 2.9) | mocked check fails; the real output is unchanged because 8.1 reads the tags |

The engine's `videoFrameExtractor.test.ts` passes unchanged (184 tests, 5.1.9).

## Known limits

- A stream whose first frame is fully tagged but whose later frames lack tags still fails in zscale, as on main.
- BT.2020 SDR proxies keep BT.2020 matrix values under a BT.709 tag on ffmpeg before 8 (the plain branch has always relabelled non-BT.709 SDR this way). A follow-up will name the probed matrix there.

Stacked on #4600.

## Before

Studio on main, previewing a fixture with two HEVC clips at 2 s (headless Chrome proxies HEVC). Left: HLG with only its transfer tagged; its proxy request answers 502 (zscale "no path between colorspaces"), so the clip stays black. Right: BT.2020 SDR, tone-mapped anyway and too dark (mean luma 85 against the source's 126).

![Before: Studio on main](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c5328a3f-b382-41cb-ba10-1007fca0a8e6)

## After

This PR at 098674e3, same fixture and time. Both proxies answer 206. Left: the HLG clip previews, tone-mapped (mean luma 117). Right: BT.2020 SDR at full brightness (126). The studio server used ffmpeg 7.0.2.

![After: Studio on this PR](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e8de12ad-5aad-4f0e-93f5-c2880a2bf7c6)

title: fix(skills): keep plugin workflows on their installed release
body:
Plugin workflows currently refresh standalone skills from main before running, so an installed plugin can mix skill releases. Add a bundle-relative launcher that selects the manifest's CLI version, suppresses standalone skill refresh, and passes the release version to Node helpers. Each published skill links to the plugin execution contract; standalone installation keeps its existing behavior.

Validation: 9 launcher regression tests; skill lint and manifest generation; live CLI version check at 0.8.80. A title-card fixture passed browser checks and rendered a 10-second 1080p MP4 through the launcher.

Stack: this is the execution foundation. #4608 adds portable/Gemini manifests, release packaging, native-client setup and migration docs, and scaffold guidance. No marketplace submission or release is performed by this PR.

Review follow-up: suppress cached skill notices in the CLI and suppress all update notices in the launcher so older pinned CLI releases also stay quiet. Pass a distinct plugin-version variable to plugin-aware helpers. The Windows launcher test now uses real Windows paths with spaces and runs in this foundation PR’s Windows job. The stale-cache notice regression and all nine launcher tests pass.

title: feat(plugins): ship portable agent bundles and installation guides
body:
HyperFrames has vendor manifests but no portable Agent Plugins or Gemini extension entry point, and its README and quickstart primarily advertise standalone skill installation. Add both manifests, keep their versions in the existing release workflow, and build a compact committed-source ZIP with source SHA and checksum. Releases attach the portable artifact after npm publication.

Document Claude, Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini, Codex, and OpenCode setup/update behavior, migration from standalone skills and core-skills, and the maintainer release checklist. Put the full plugin first in the marketplace: native Copilot otherwise identifies the shared directory by the legacy core-skills entry. Preserve that legacy install ID for migration. Scaffold guidance respects plugin ownership, and the media resolver shim works without a monorepo checkout.

Foundation #4607 is merged. This PR now targets main; the approved packaging diff was reapplied unchanged, then the two new manifests were aligned with main's existing 0.8.81 release.

Validation:
- Packaging/version tests, launcher/helper tests, 27 init tests, skill lint/fingerprint/import-boundary checks, CI test reachability, lint/format, required typechecks, and Fallow audit pass.
- Mintlify build validation and broken-links check pass.
- Claude Code 2.1.283: isolated installation discovers 21 skills; a Git-backed test plugin upgrades 0.8.80 to 0.8.81 while a SHA-pinned profile stays on 0.8.80; uninstall succeeds. These are local fixture releases, not public releases.
- Copilot CLI 1.0.88: isolated marketplace install discovers 21 skills, lists the correct enabled identity, and uninstalls.
- Gemini CLI 0.61.0: isolated extension install/discovery and uninstall succeed.
- Pinned HyperFrames 0.8.80: browser check passes; title-card renders 1920x1080, 300 frames, 10 seconds. Portable media resolver --help succeeds.
- Portable and Codex ZIPs build at about 11.9 MB; contributor-only skills are excluded.

Limits: Cursor and VS Code native UI flows are documentation-backed, not tested here. Background auto-update timing is not tested. Public marketplace approval and publication are separate from these repository changes; Codex submission is deferred. No new release or Codex submission is included.

Review follow-up: captions matting, transcription, and shell rendering resolve the pinned launcher from ZIP or unbuilt Git installs. Document project-owned Sharp/Puppeteer/GSAP prerequisites and allow caption helpers to resolve them from that project. An extracted-archive CI regression exercises all three CLI boundaries and failure propagation without a checkout. A synthetic 2-second render/composite produces final.mp4 under an isolated HOME; prepare succeeds with cached synthetic matte/transcript inputs and project-local Sharp. This does not test fresh model downloads or speech quality. Media resolver regression preserves contributor local CLI behavior when only the helper-package override is set. Update-policy wording now distinguishes tracked-branch skill changes from CLI version pinning, and asset paths normalize before deduplication.

Render completion: remove the shell watchdog and its size-based timeout recovery rather than attempting process-tree ownership through racy portable snapshots. The helper runs the pinned CLI in the foreground and composites only after a zero exit status and output-file existence. CLI cancellation/cleanup stays with the renderer; HF_TIMEOUT_S is no longer used, as documented in the skill. The extracted-ZIP tests cover normal completion, a failing CLI with a >1 MB partial file, terminal Ctrl-C and group TERM/HUP, plus explicit contributor CLI overrides. They do not claim arbitrary detached-daemon ownership or a new cleanup guarantee for terminating only the parent shell.


Retarget validation: 14 launcher/resolver/packager tests and all 6 freshly extracted ZIP caption tests pass. Lint/format and skill fingerprints pass. Local typecheck could not resolve built workspace dependencies in the temporary worktree; the Fallow findings in the captions tests were resolved by extracting fixture helpers, and the explicit audit now passes. The final artifact assertion also verifies successful output exists. Fresh main-base CI must pass before merge.

title: test(engine): real-ffmpeg tests get a 60 s ceiling so a stalled Windows runner stops flaking them
body:
## What this fixes

The Windows engine test lane failed at random on unrelated PRs. The test "survives the encode -> mux -> faststart chain that produces a delivered mp4" ran into vitest's 5 s default timeout, and its cleanup then failed with `EBUSY` on `audio.m4a`. When a test times out, vitest does not stop the ffmpeg it started, so the mux was still reading that file when `afterEach` tried to delete it.

A normal run of that test takes about 0.35 s on the Windows runner: 10 runs in a row took 343 to 409 ms each. So the failure was a stall of more than ten times its usual time, most likely from a loaded runner. The engine and CLI test pools share it, each with their own ffmpeg processes. The engine suite had no timeout of its own, so every test that runs a real ffmpeg was exposed to the same stall: HLS packaging, the audio mixer, audio effects, volume envelopes and frame extraction as well.

Now:
- The engine's vitest config sets one 60 s ceiling, the same knob the CLI's config uses for the same reason. A hang still fails, just at 60 s instead of 5 s. Tests that set their own timeout keep it.
- The cost: a change that makes many engine tests hang now fails slowly, 60 s per test; about twenty hung tests would reach the job's own time limit, and the job would show as cancelled rather than listing them.
- The provenance tests' cleanup retries on `EBUSY`, so if a test does time out, the timeout is the failure reported, not a locked file.

## Tests

- A throwaway test that sleeps 6 s passes with the new config and fails with "Test timed out in 5000ms" without it.
- The chain test, repeated 10 times on the Windows runner, passed every run at 343 to 409 ms.

Results: engine `tsc` and oxfmt clean; the engine suite passes on Linux, except four `ffprobe` tests that need an LFS fixture that checkout did not have (they fail the same way on `main` there).

title: fix(producer): gif renders survive rgb frames among transparent ones
body:
## What

Transparent GIF renders no longer fail when some frames are fully opaque, and they now stay correct after those frames.

- **The crash:** a transparent GIF with a shader transition, for example, used to stop with `FFmpeg exited with code 190`.
- **Stale frames:** once rendered, pixels that turn transparent again after an opaque frame showed that frame instead of the page behind.

## Why

- Captured frames are PNGs. A fully opaque frame can arrive as an RGB PNG among RGBA ones: every shader transition frame does.
- When the pixel format changes mid-sequence, ffmpeg rebuilds the filter graph. `paletteuse` does not survive the rebuild and fails with `Internal bug, should not have happened` (exit 190 on ffmpeg 7, exit 1 on 4.2).
- The failure is a race, so the same frames fail on most runs, not all. On a 16-frame sequence alternating RGBA and RGB, main's arguments failed 12 to 17 runs in 20.

## How

- **The crash:** both GIF passes (palettegen and paletteuse) read the frames with `-reinit_filter 0`, so ffmpeg converts a frame of a different format instead of rebuilding the graph. Alpha is kept: a sequence that starts with RGB frames still decodes its later RGBA frames with their transparency.
- **Stale frames (only transparent GIFs that go from an opaque frame to a see-through one):**
  - **Cause:** ffmpeg's GIF encoder picks each frame's disposal from that frame alone. A fully opaque frame is marked "leave in place" and cropped to what changed, so later transparent pixels keep showing it. ffmpeg master has the same logic.
  - **When it applies:** after the normal encode, the producer reads the GIF's frame headers (`gifClearsAfterLeavingFrameInPlace` in core, built on the existing GIF block walker). Only a "leave in place" frame followed later by a "clear" frame can show a stale frame. Every other GIF, opaque or transparent, is left exactly as ffmpeg wrote it.
  - **Whole frames:** for those GIFs the palette pass runs again with `-gifflags 0`, so every frame is written whole. The palette is reused.
  - **Cleared disposal:** every frame is then set to clear before the next one (`clearGifFramesBeforeNext`).
  - **Transparent index:** frames on the shared colour table that name no transparent index get the one the other shared-table frames use. ffmpeg's own decoder, used by players such as VLC and mpv, clears a disposed frame to its transparent colour only when the frame names one; browsers clear to transparent either way. Frames with their own colour table are left alone, since the shared table's index can be a real colour in theirs.
- **File size**, the same captured frames encoded before and after this change:

  | Film | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | transparent shader-transition film from the repo fixture `page-side-shader-compositor-render-compat`, 20 frames | 547,348 bytes | 577,058 bytes (1.05x) |
  | repo fixture `transparency-regression`, 30 frames | 6,273 bytes | unchanged (never goes opaque then see-through) |
  | any opaque GIF | | unchanged |

  An earlier version of this PR wrote every transparent GIF whole, which cost up to 8x on flat-colour films. Only the GIFs that need it pay now, and films with motion pay little.

## Test plan

- New `gifEncodeArgs.test.ts`, in the producer's integration lane (the lane that installs ffmpeg):
  - It encodes 16 frames alternating RGBA and RGB five times. Each run must exit 0, and on ffmpeg 7 must not log a filter-graph rebuild. The GIF must keep all 16 frames, with the first one transparent.
  - With main's arguments it failed every run we tried: on ffmpeg 6.1.1 (CI's version), 7.0.2 and 4.2.7.
- Same file, on the real encode stage:
  - Frames that go transparent, opaque, opaque with a small change, then transparent decode with every frame's transparent pixels intact (2304, 0, 0, 2304 per frame). It fails if the header check, `-gifflags 0`, the disposal rewrite or the transparent-index step is removed.
  - An all-opaque sequence and a transparent-throughout sequence come out byte-identical to the plain two-pass encode.
- `encodeStage.test.ts` (unit lane):
  - The argument tests cover the new input option.
  - A one-frame alpha GIF is left byte-identical (two ffmpeg calls).
  - A two-frame GIF that goes opaque then see-through gets a third call with `-gifflags 0`, and both frames come out set to clear.
  - A GIF that can't be read back fails the encode instead of skipping the fix.
- Core `gif.test.ts` (unit lane): the header check fires only on "leave in place" then "clear", and never hands an image the control block of a plain-text block before it; the rewrite sets disposal on every frame, takes the transparent index only from shared-table frames, and refuses bytes that are not a GIF.
- Checked by hand:
  - The fixed arguments failed 0 of 40 runs on ffmpeg 7.0.2, and encode the same sequences on 4.2.7.
  - On 7.0.2, RGB-first, 16-bit, gray, gray+alpha and palette PNG mixes decode to the source colours.
  - On 7.0.2, `-reinit_filter 0` on its own leaves opaque JPEG and all-RGBA GIFs byte-identical to main's output. With the whole change, GIFs that never go opaque then see-through get exactly the previous output (pinned by the integration test).
- End to end, on a transparent composition with a shader transition rendered as GIF:
  - Main's GIF arguments fail with `FFmpeg exited with code 190`.
  - This branch exits 0. The opaque transition frames have no holes, and after them the transparent area comes back in full. Pillow, ImageMagick and ffmpeg's decoder agree.
- `tsc --noEmit` clean; oxlint 0 errors; test classification check green.

## Not in this PR

- **Opaque shader transitions:** every shader writes full opacity, so transition frames of a transparent GIF are opaque. This is a separate decision.

title: fix: run the configured ffmpeg and ffprobe everywhere and say when an upload was not checked
body:
## What this fixes

`HYPERFRAMES_FFMPEG_PATH` and `HYPERFRAMES_FFPROBE_PATH` choose which ffmpeg and ffprobe HyperFrames runs, for example a bundled build instead of whatever is on `PATH`. Most spawns already resolve through the one shared resolver (`findFfBinary`). These did not:

- **Distributed renders** read the ffmpeg version from `ffmpeg -version` on `PATH`. The version goes into the plan hash, so a host with a configured ffmpeg planned and checked renders against a different binary than the one that encoded them.
- **Studio's upload check** ran `ffprobe` from `PATH`. With no ffprobe there, it silently accepted the upload unchecked, and nobody was told.
- **media-use** probed, analysed and doctor-checked media with the ffmpeg and ffprobe on `PATH`.

Now:

- The distributed version check runs the configured ffmpeg (through the engine's `getFfmpegBinary`), cached per binary. A missing binary fails with `ffmpeg not found at "<path>": install FFmpeg or set HYPERFRAMES_FFMPEG_PATH.`
- The upload check runs the configured ffprobe. When no ffprobe is configured or found, the upload is still accepted, so people without FFmpeg are not blocked. The upload response now lists it under `unchecked`, with the reason, and Studio shows it as an info notice (the add succeeded): "Added clip.mp4, not checked: ffprobe was not found. Install FFmpeg or set HYPERFRAMES_FFPROBE_PATH." The response change is additive; older clients ignore the new field.
- A path set in `HYPERFRAMES_FFMPEG_PATH` or `HYPERFRAMES_FFPROBE_PATH` that cannot run is an error, never a quiet fallback: the upload is rejected with "HYPERFRAMES_FFPROBE_PATH names \"<path>\", which cannot run: fix it or unset it", media-use commands (including `--json` runs, which answer `{"ok":false,"error":...}`) stop with the same message instead of reporting unknown metadata, and the doctor fails that check and says to fix or unset the variable. media-use checks a set path once per run by running it with `-version`: it must start, exit 0 and print `ffprobe version` (or `ffmpeg version`). So a missing path, a folder, a script whose interpreter is missing, a broken binary or the wrong tool all fail the same way. A relative path is resolved from the working folder, so the file checked is the file run. Local text-to-speech checks the path before it starts generating, and a resolve that fails for this reason names the setting instead of saying no provider could resolve it. Studio's rejected-upload notice now gives each file's reason ("Not added: clip.mp4 (<reason>)") instead of only "Unsupported media skipped".
- The distributed version check's not-found error keeps `code: "ENOENT"`, so callers that branch on it are unchanged.
- media-use spawns the configured binaries everywhere (probe, local TTS duration, grade analysis, doctor) through one small helper. It is plain `.mjs` with no package imports, so it reads the two variables itself rather than importing `findFfBinary`.

## Before

On `main`, with no ffprobe available, uploading a video gives no message: the file is added and its media check was silently skipped.

![Before: the upload is added with no message](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b703353-016f-450c-b9d4-3d191d1184c9)

## After

The same upload is added, and an info notice says it was not checked and how to fix that.

![After: an info notice says the upload was not checked because ffprobe was not found](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/38df4b8e-1aac-4ef0-a7e2-5e586992d1f6)

With `HYPERFRAMES_FFPROBE_PATH` set to a path that does not exist, the upload is not added and the notice says which setting to fix.

![After, broken setting: the upload is not added and a notice names the setting](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a9472790-a661-45f8-aa30-accdd4e0017d)

## Tests

- `shared.ffmpegVersion.test.ts`: the version is read from the ffmpeg `HYPERFRAMES_FFMPEG_PATH` names; a configured binary that is missing gives the named error with `code: "ENOENT"`.
- `mediaValidation.test.ts`: the configured ffprobe is the one run; with none found the upload is accepted with the "not checked" reason; a configured one that cannot run rejects the upload, naming the setting.
- `useFileManager.upload.test.tsx`: an upload answered with `unchecked` shows an info notice; rejected uploads each show their own reason.
- `resolve.test.mjs`: the doctor reports the version of the configured ffmpeg and ffprobe, and fails a configured path that is missing or does not run; `--analyze` and `--adopt` answer `ok:false` with the named error instead of reporting unknown metadata, and `--adopt` registers nothing; a local-voice resolve with a broken setting names it.
- `probe.test.mjs`: media probing runs the ffprobe `HYPERFRAMES_FFPROBE_PATH` names, runs a relative one from the working folder rather than from `PATH`, and refuses a missing path, a folder, a script whose interpreter is missing, one that exits with an error, and another tool.

Results: `tsc` for studio-server, studio, producer and cli, oxfmt and oxlint clean; the tests above and the studio-server upload route tests pass. `main`'s version of each changed file fails its tests.

## Notes for reviewers

- The distributed plan hash now includes the configured ffmpeg's version. A host whose configured ffmpeg differs from the one on `PATH` will see a version mismatch for plans made before this change and re-planned after it; plans made and run on the same side of the upgrade are unaffected.
- An upload is listed as unchecked only once it is written, under its final name. Only a name-collision race can tell the order apart, so there is no test for it.
- A system lookup is cached for the process lifetime (as before), so installing ffprobe while Studio runs needs a restart; setting the variable does not.

title: fix(studio): quick saves no longer refuse each other as outside changes
body:
## What users saw

Two saves close together on the same file could refuse each other. Hiding two tracks in quick succession is one example. Others: starting a move while a volume save is still writing, moving an animated clip twice in a row, and nudging an element on the canvas while a timeline save is in flight. The second save got a 409 and Studio showed "Save conflict: index.html changed outside this Studio session". When Studio is embedded, the host reads that 409 as an outside edit and blocks further edits until a reload. Some combinations failed without any message: a color grade that started while a move was writing put the clip back where it was.

## Why it happened

Each file has a mutation queue, and `saveProjectFilesWithHistory` joins it. Most callers, though, read the file and built the new content before joining the queue. They then handed the queue a finished string, plus a `readFile` that returned the copy they had read earlier. If a save for the same file was still in flight, the second save's base was already out of date:

- when that stale copy was also passed as the base, the write was refused as a conflict;
- when the base was re-read inside the queue, the write went through but wiped out the earlier edit.

An earlier fix did this correctly for the single-attribute save (volume and automation). No other caller did.

## The fix

The fix is in `saveProjectFilesWithHistory` itself, not in each caller. `files` now maps each path to a builder, `(content) => nextContent`. The owner reads each file after the save has its turn in that file's queue, runs the builder on what it read, and writes with that same content as the base. Callers no longer hold a content string they could pass in, so they cannot read outside the queue.

Every caller now uses the builder:

- timeline move/trim, single clip and batch (`persistTimelineEdit`, `persistTimelineBatchEdit`)
- track and clip visibility (`setElementsHidden`)
- audio group create
- asset drop onto the timeline
- paste and duplicate
- block/component insert
- color grading (source file and project scope). A project-wide grade now reads the files one at a time inside the queue, where it used to read them in parallel.
- code editor save. It still writes the editor buffer as the whole file, so its builder ignores the current content. That is unchanged behavior: the editor buffer is the file.
- the single-attribute save, which was already inside the queue and now passes a builder too.

Three callers have the server rewrite the file before the history entry is saved: delete element, delete timeline clip, and group/ungroup. They now go through one helper, `saveServerRewriteWithHistory`, which runs the read, the server call and the history entry as one step inside the file's queue. Before, the server call could land between another save's read and its write, and that save would 409. Undo still returns to the content from before the server call. The write still expects what the server wrote. Group/ungroup now passes the server's content to the writer as the expected base. Before, it expected the pre-call content and relied on the writer accepting a 409 whose current content already matched.

Other writers went around `saveProjectFilesWithHistory` altogether, and they now take their turn in the queue too:

- **GSAP timing rewrites after a move or resize.** When a moved clip has tweens aimed at it, the server shifts or scales them in a second step. That step, its ownership check and its rollback now hold the queue of every file they touch (single clip and group). Before, move A's rewrite could land between move B's read and write, and B was refused. This is the common case for animated clips. The server-mutation client moved to its own file (`gsapMutationClient.ts`) so the timing-sync file stays under the size cap; the moved code is unchanged.
- **Canvas edits** (nudge, drag, style, text, attribute commits). The read, the server patch, the optional follow-up write (the injected `@font-face` for a custom font) and the history entry run as one step in the file's queue. Before, the server patch could land while a timeline save held its read. That save's write then went out on a stale base and was refused.
- **Layer reorders** (the multi-file atomic patch). These queue on every file they touch.
- **The id assigned before adding a GSAP animation** to an element that has none.
- **Block background write** for a newly installed component.
- **Block parameter commits.** These now queue on the block file, which replaces their private promise chain.
- **The conflict dialog's "keep mine" overwrite.** Only a user's click starts it, never code that already holds the queue, so queuing it cannot deadlock.

Canvas edits that the in-memory document handles directly, including deleting an element through it, were already queued. That path joins the file's queue itself and re-reads there, so it was not wrapped again; nesting would deadlock.

The rule now covers every writer of a composition file: a save reads the file only once it has its turn in that file's queue, and nothing writes a composition outside the queue. The exceptions are three sidecar files, each written by a single writer that no other save touches:

- the legacy motion-file clear, which runs once when the project opens; only undo can also write that path;
- the beat-analysis cache, which only the beat analysis writes;
- the caption overrides file, which only the caption sync writes.

File create, rename, delete and duplicate are structural file-manager operations and are out of scope. The code editor save is queued, but it writes the whole editor buffer.

The live preview updates and failure unwinds still work as before. A builder that cannot find its target throws before anything is written, and the caller's existing unwind restores the preview. Undo entries record the content read inside the queue as "before".

## Tests

New `timelineQuickSaves.test.ts` and `canvasQuickSaves.test.tsx`. They use the real queue and a fake writer that refuses a stale base, the way the server does. The first save's write is held while the second save starts. Both saves must land with no refused write, and the file must contain both edits. Cases:

- two moves
- two trims
- a move started while a volume save is writing
- a color grade started while a move is writing (the lost-update variant)
- a move started while the previous move's GSAP rewrite is in flight
- a canvas commit started while a timeline save is writing (the real race)
- two canvas commits, the second started while the first one's `@font-face` write is held. In the app, canvas commits are already chained through the canvas-edit save queue, so this pair cannot race there. The test mounts the commit hook without that chain and guards that the file queue alone keeps them apart.

The same test files, run against main's versions of every changed source file:

```
     × lands both moves
     × lands both trims
     × lands a move started while a volume save is writing
     × keeps a move when a color grade starts while it is writing
     × lands a move started while the previous move's GSAP rewrite is in flight
AssertionError: expected [ 'index.html' ] to deeply equal []
AssertionError: expected [ 'index.html' ] to deeply equal []
AssertionError: expected [ 'index.html' ] to deeply equal []
AssertionError: expected '<div id="root"><video id="a" class="c…' to contain 'id="a" class="clip" data-start="3"'
AssertionError: expected [ 'index.html' ] to deeply equal []
      Tests  5 failed (5)

     × lands a second canvas commit started while the first one's font write is held
     × lands a canvas commit started while a timeline save is writing
AssertionError: expected [ 'index.html' ] to deeply equal []
AssertionError: expected [ 'index.html' ] to deeply equal []
      Tests  2 failed (2)
```

With the fix:

```
 ✓ two quick timeline saves on one file > lands both moves
 ✓ two quick timeline saves on one file > lands both trims
 ✓ two quick timeline saves on one file > lands a move started while a volume save is writing
 ✓ two quick timeline saves on one file > keeps a move when a color grade starts while it is writing
 ✓ two quick timeline saves on one file > lands a move started while the previous move's GSAP rewrite is in flight
      Tests  5 passed (5)
 ✓ canvas edit commits share the file queue > lands a second canvas commit started while the first one's font write is held
 ✓ canvas edit commits share the file queue > lands a canvas commit started while a timeline save is writing
      Tests  2 passed (2)
```

Two existing canvas-commit tests started two overlapping commits and expected both server patches to be in flight at once. The second commit now waits for the first, so those tests now fail the older commit first and then land the newer one. What they check is unchanged: a failed older commit never overwrites the newer value.

`studioFileHistory.test.ts` now uses builders, and one of its cases checks that the builder receives what an earlier queued mutation wrote. The GSAP case also fails against the source files of the commit before it, which has every other fix in this PR, so it proves the GSAP change on its own. The existing timing-sync tests now pass a writer, which the GSAP step needs to join the queue. I ran every test file that imports a changed module one at a time (29 files), and all of them pass.

## Before

Headless Chrome, 1440x900, a two-track fixture project. Both track eye buttons are clicked in the same moment. The first save lands (PUT 200). The second is refused (PUT 409) and shows the conflict toast, so only the title track is hidden on disk.

![Before: second track save refused with a save conflict toast](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7b14bd29-d7c0-49cd-97b8-be054aa6c209)

## After

The same steps on this branch. Both saves land (PUT 200, PUT 200), and both tracks are hidden on disk.

![After: both tracks hidden, no conflict](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/80e0a028-a893-4d6c-a604-ba0113d7fdc5)

## Not verified

- The timeline's own edit queue already makes UI moves and trims wait for each other's file save. What slipped through was the GSAP rewrite that follows each one. The captures use the track-visibility path, which had no queue at all. Move, trim and the GSAP rewrite are covered by the unit tests only.
- I could not capture a canvas nudge. In headless Chrome the element selected, but neither arrow keys nor a mouse drag produced a canvas commit, on main or on this branch. Canvas edits are covered by the unit tests only.
- I did not test inside an embedding host. The host-side "changed outside" state is inferred from the 409 the host receives.
- I did not run the full Studio suite locally. CI covers it.

## Not in this PR

- `pendingTimelineEditPathRef` is dead state, and older than this PR: saves add paths to it and one handler deletes them, but nothing ever reads it. This PR only moves the existing adds into the builders. Removing it belongs in its own change.
- A move's save and the GSAP rewrite that follows it are still two queued steps. Another save that joined the queue while the move was saving can land between them. That no longer causes a conflict or loses an edit, because every step reads the file after it gets its turn. But reading the history code suggests the move's undo could then take two presses (not run end to end). Making the save and the rewrite one step touches two save paths, so it is left for its own change.

title: fix: render names a folder composition source instead of crashing
body:
## What

When a composition's `data-composition-src` points at a folder instead of an HTML file (say `compositions/intro`, holding an `index.html`), `hyperframes render` crashed with a raw `EISDIR: illegal operation on a directory, read` stack from lint's project walk. The error never said which attribute or file was at fault. `hyperframes lint`, `hyperframes check`, `hyperframes compositions`, `hyperframes keyframes` and Studio's insert-composition route crashed the same way.

Studio already treats a folder source as missing: its bundler skips it and does not look for an `index.html` inside. So every other reader now agrees with Studio instead of resolving the folder:

- Lint's sub-composition check (used by render, `lint`, `check` and Studio's background lint) and the render pre-flight report `compositions/intro: it is a folder, not an HTML file`, the same way they already report a missing file. Lint's fix hint says to point the attribute at the HTML file inside, such as `compositions/intro/index.html`.
- The producer's inliner, `hyperframes compositions` and `hyperframes keyframes` skip a folder source, as they already skip a missing one.
- Studio's insert-composition route answers `400 Composition source is a folder, not an HTML file` for a folder source, or for a folder nested inside the source, instead of a 500.

Each reader checked "exists, then read"; now each checks "is a regular file, then read".

Real run on a fixture film with a folder source:

```
$ hyperframes render film -o out.mp4
Render failed ... compositions/intro: it is a folder, not an HTML file
```

## Tests

Each fails on main with `EISDIR`:
- producer, "compileForRender aborts naming a data-composition-src that points at a folder"
- lint, "errors, instead of crashing, when the referenced sub-composition is a folder" (also checks the fix hint)
- CLI, `parseCompositions` "treats a data-composition-src that points at a folder as inline instead of crashing"
- CLI, `collectCompositions` "skips a data-composition-src that points at a folder instead of crashing" (now exported for the test)
- studio-server, `insertCompositionIntoSource` "rejects a source, or a source's dependency, that is a folder"

The inliner's check has no test of its own: the render pre-flight stops a folder source before the inliner runs.

title: media-use audio engine ignores HYPERFRAMES_PYTHON, so local MusicGen BGM is skipped even though doctor reports it installed
fix(shader-transitions): shader transitions in renders keep scene layout, styles and animations
body:
## What

Shader transitions in renders now look like the composition:

- Scenes keep their own layout, fonts, colours and composition-scoped styles.
- A scene smaller than the frame stays in its box.
- Nothing of the transition is left behind once it ends.

This is the page-side compositor that default mp4 and GIF renders use for shader transitions.

## Why

The compositor copies the two scenes into staging canvases, draws them with `drawElementImage`, and blends them in WebGL. It had three defects:

1. **Ghost after the transition:**
   - The staging canvases sit behind the page (`position:fixed; z-index:-9998`) and kept their last bitmap.
   - Any transparent area of the composition showed a full-frame copy of the incoming scene for the rest of the film.
2. **Lost styles:**
   - Scene copies were appended straight under the staging canvas, a child of `<body>`.
   - They lost everything inherited from the composition root: fonts (text turned serif), `line-height`, custom properties such as `var(--accent)`.
   - They also lost every rule scoped under an ancestor. That is how sub-composition CSS is compiled: `[data-composition-id="…"] .word`.
3. **Stretched layout:** each copy was drawn into the whole canvas, so a scene smaller than the frame was stretched to full frame.

## How

- **Ancestor copies:** each scene copy is staged inside childless copies of its real ancestors below `<body>`. Their attributes and inline style carry inheritance, custom properties and scoped selectors. Ancestor effects also carry over: a camera zoom, a fade, a filter or a clip on a wrapper, and a border on the root.
- **Placement:** the copies sit in a full-frame box drawn at full frame, so they lay out against a sized containing block like the live page. Wrappers with no size of their own work.
- **Animations:** a freshly inserted copy restarts its CSS animations. Each copied animation, pseudo-elements included, is paused at its live counterpart's current time, and one whose live counterpart has finished is cancelled. A wrapper fading in no longer dims the transition, and animated inherited colours match. One subtree lookup per side does the matching, so the cost stays close to linear: a scene with 2,000 animated elements still renders.
- **Pin removed:** the old pin (`clonePinStyleFor`) set each copy to its live box. That box already includes any transform, so a scaled scene was scaled twice. The copies no longer need it, so it is removed.
- **Clearing:** both staging canvases are cleared in a `finally` after drawing and uploading, so no path leaves a bitmap behind.
- **Failed capture:** the overlay is now hidden, so the frame shows the live page rather than the previous transition frame.

## Evidence

Frames at 0.5 s (before the transition), 1.2 s (inside it) and 1.8 s (after it), mp4 at 10 fps. Main is on top, this branch below. Every film is built from the repo fixture `page-side-shader-compositor-render-compat`:

- **Text variant:** `#main { font-size: 20px; line-height: 1.2; --accent: #ffe000 }`, `.word { color: var(--accent) }`, a two-line word, and a `[data-composition-id=…] .word` outline rule.
  - Main: serif white text with no outline during the transition.
  - Branch: the yellow two-line word with its outline, matching the frame after the transition.
- **Transparent inset variant:** page background transparent, scenes `inset: 90px 160px`.
  - Main: stretches the transition to full frame and leaves a full-frame ghost behind the inset scene at 1.8 s.
  - Branch: keeps the transition in the scene's box and leaves nothing behind.
- **Wrapper variant:** the inset scenes sit in an unsized wrapper that fades in with a CSS animation, inside a bordered root.
  - Main: stretches the transition to full frame in serif and drops the border.
  - Branch: keeps it in the scene's box, at full brightness, with the border.
- **Unmodified fixture:** the transition text uses the composition's font instead of serif.

## Test plan

- `engineModePageComposite.test.ts`: exit 0, 14 passed. Its five new tests fail on main:
  - each scene copy inside unaltered ancestor copies, in a full-frame box
  - copied CSS animations held at the live time, pseudo-elements included, and ones finished live cancelled
  - a scene directly under `<body>` staged in the full-frame box
  - clearing after the upload
  - clearing and hiding the overlay when capture fails
- Mutations, each caught by a test:
  - no ancestor copies
  - no animation hold
  - pausing instead of cancelling a finished animation
  - clearing before the upload
  - no clear in `finally`
  - no overlay hide
- 37 layout cases rendered and compared: the last transition frame (shader at full progress, so only the incoming scene) against the next live frame. Cases include wrapper zoom, fade, scale, filter and clip; root transform, border and offset; unsized and `display: contents` wrappers; CSS keyframes on wrappers and the root; percentage and viewport units; fixed children; sub-composition hosts; back-to-back transitions.
  - Every case matches within ongoing motion, except the offset-root and `body >` selector limits listed below.
  - Examples of the mean difference (0 to 255 scale): wrapper scale went from 125 on main to 0.04; wrapper clip-path and filter from 69 to 0.08; root border from 37 to 0.22.
- `tsc --noEmit` clean; oxlint 0 errors; pre-commit lint, format, fallow and typecheck green.

## Not in this PR

- **Alpha during transitions:** every shader writes alpha 1.0, so transition frames stay opaque on alpha outputs. Keeping alpha needs a rule per shader, which is a separate decision.
- **Page outside the composition root:** the overlay covers the frame and fills it with the transition's background colour, so where a root smaller than the frame shows the body background live, the transition shows that colour instead, as on main.
- **Already the case on main:**
  - Selectors that depend on siblings or on `<body>` (`:nth-child`, `body > …`) match differently on copies.
  - A body margin or padding offsets the drawing (the runtime zeroes both).
  - Web Animations API animations and in-flight CSS transitions on ancestors are not carried to copies.
  - `<canvas>` content is not cloned.
- **Preview-mode captures:** the html-in-canvas scene capture in `capture.ts`, used by preview-mode captures such as thumbnails and snapshots, has the same staging gaps. It is a separate change.

![Text variant: main on top, branch below, at 0.5 s, 1.2 s and 1.8 s](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9516b51f-9e20-46d0-a8e3-ae2123639754)

![Transparent inset variant: main on top, branch below](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b510ce7d-242e-44b2-bc42-92349c43e326)

![Wrapper variant: main on top, branch below](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/240577cc-7d51-4ad4-81bc-108e9101af68)

![Unmodified fixture: main on top, branch below](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d9df02b8-24c3-42d2-9212-3af18d71866d)

title: fix(lint): a missing image, audio or mask file names the composition that references it
body: ## What `hyperframes lint` reports a missing image, video, audio or CSS mask file, but it never said which composition references it. The three project-wide checks (`missing_local_asset`, `audio_src_not_found`, `texture_mask_asset_not_found`) collected missing files across every composition into one finding, attached to the root `index.html` result and with no `file`. A tool that reads `hyperframes lint --json` could not tell a broken draft section from a broken film. Repro: a project whose `compositions/draft.html` has ``. Run `hyperframes lint --json`: the `missing_local_asset` finding has no `file`. Now each check groups what it finds by the composition that references it and sets `file` on each finding. That is the same absolute path the per-file findings already carry, so tools can match on it the same way. ## Behaviour change A missing file referenced from N compositions was one error and is now N, one per composition, each naming its own file. The error count in `hyperframes lint`, `check` and the render pre-flight summary grows to match. Every gate only asks whether there are errors, so nothing that passed now fails. ## Known limits - These findings still sit under the root `index.html` entry of the results. So Studio's lint panel, which labels a finding by its entry, and the CLI's text label for a finding without a line number, still show `index.html`. Moving each project finding under its own composition's entry fixes both, but the CLI suite reads these findings from the first entry in about 50 places; that is a follow-up. - `video_media_start_at_or_past_eof` sets a project-relative `file` (`index.html`); these three set the absolute path the per-file findings use. ## Tests - lint, "points a draft section's missing image, audio and mask at the draft, not the film": the three findings for the draft carry `compositions/draft.html`, and a missing image in `index.html` carries `index.html`. On main each `file` is undefined. - CLI, "reports a missing file once per composition that references it" and "reports the same missing src once per composition that references it" (were the two dedupe-across-compositions tests): one finding per referencing composition, each with its `file`. They fail on main.

title: fix(studio-server): a request that fails after its project folder vanished says the folder is gone
body:
Stacked on #4602 (its base branch); review that first.

## What

#4602 makes a write into a project folder that has been renamed or deleted answer `404 { why: "project_dir_missing" }`. A request whose folder vanishes while it is running still got whatever answer its route happened to give. Renaming the folder while a request's body is read, for example:

- a save answered a `409` conflict;
- a rename answered `403` "forbidden", as if the path were unsafe (the path check fails closed when the project folder is gone);
- a duplicate answered a bare `404` "not found", indistinguishable from a missing file;
- a route that throws on the missing folder answered `500`.

Now one rule in `createStudioApi` covers every project route: when a request under `/projects/:id/` fails with 403 or above and that project's folder no longer exists, the answer is the same `404 project_dir_missing` the rest of the API gives. A `400` (a malformed request) stays as it is. Only a folder that is really gone counts: one that exists but cannot be looked at (a locked parent folder, a failing network mount) keeps the route's own error. `folderGone` in `@hyperframes/core` owns that answer, and every "is the project folder gone" check in this API and in `mkdirWithinProject` now uses it instead of `existsSync`, which says "gone" for any error. Such a folder keeps the route's ordinary answer (for example `403` on a file route, or the `400` composition-path message on a render), which does not claim the folder is gone.

- The project is looked up before the route runs. On the Studio dev server the lookup stops returning a project once its folder is gone, so a lookup afterwards would miss exactly these requests. This costs one extra lookup per project request (cheap on both hosts in this repo; an adapter whose lookup is costly would want it memoized per request).
- The 404 replaces the failed response outright. Before, Hono carried the failed route's headers over, so a thumbnail's `ETag` could ride on the 404 and keep the image broken after the folder came back. #4602's existing missing-folder answer had the same carry-over and now uses the same helper.

On the CLI host with the folder gone, `GET /projects/:id` now answers `404 project_dir_missing` instead of a `500`.

Two path checks answered `400` for a vanished folder, so the rule above never saw them. When their check fails, both now ask whether the project folder is gone before answering `400`, so they still check the same path the renderer opens:
- a render that names a composition, which Studio's Render button always does, answered `400` "composition path must be within the project directory";
- inserting a composition answered `400` "escapes the project" if the folder vanished after the route read its target file.

For apps that mount this API inside their own Hono app with `app.route(...)`: the middleware reads the response headers before the route runs, so it can keep the host's own headers (CORS, cookies) on the 404. Once that happens, Hono copies headers the host set before the route onto every response, including routes that return a raw `Response`. A host header with the same name as a route header now wins over it, which is how Hono's own `cors()` already behaves. The CLI and the Studio dev server call the API through `api.fetch`, so neither is affected.

## Tests

On a host that keeps resolving the project and on one that stops once the folder is gone:
- "answers that the project folder is gone when it vanishes while a save / a rename / a duplicate reads its body": answered 409, 403 and a bare 404 before. The second host's rows also fail if the lookup runs after the route.
- "... while a render that names a composition reads its body": answered the 400 before, whether the folder vanished mid-request or before it.
- "keeps a malformed request's 400 when the folder vanishes": fails if the 403 threshold is removed.
- "keeps a save conflict's 409 while the folder is there": fails if every 403+ is rewritten.

And:
- "keeps a route's error when the project folder is there but cannot be looked at": answered the 404 with an `existsSync` check.
- "refuses a render composition that leaves a symlinked project folder through ..": a check against the folder's real path instead of the path the renderer opens would let `../<real name>/x.html` through.
- core, "folderGone": true for a missing path and for a path below a file, false for a folder that exists or that cannot be looked at. The studio-server tests run against core's built output, so this core test is what proves the unreadable-folder branch; the route test above proves the middleware keeps the route's answer.
- "says the project folder is gone rather than that the source escapes it" (composition insertion): threw the 400 before.

And, with the API mounted behind a host middleware that sets a CORS header:
- "keeps the host's headers but not the route's on the 404 when a route throws an error after the folder vanished / the missing-folder error": before, the 404 carried the route's `ETag`, and an intermediate version dropped the host's header.
- "answers that the project folder is gone when a rename makes the codec probe fail": the media proxy answered `422 unknown_codec` on #4602.

title: fix(lint): Studio's lint panel and the CLI label a finding by the composition it names
body:
Stacked on #4616 (its base branch); review that first.

## What

#4616 makes a missing image, audio or mask file name the composition that references it in `finding.file`. The finding itself was still filed under the root `index.html` entry of the lint results, so two surfaces kept saying `index.html`:

- Studio's lint panel, which labels each finding with the entry it sits under;
- the CLI's text output, which labels a finding that has no line number with its entry, e.g. `✗ [index.html] missing_local_asset: ...` for an image missing from `compositions/draft.html`.

Now `lintProject` files each project-wide finding under the entry for the file it names, at the one place those findings are handed out, and counts it there. A finding without a `file`, or naming a file that has no entry of its own, stays on the root entry as before. Totals are unchanged.

Side effects worth knowing:
- Studio's file-tree lint badges for these findings move from `index.html` to the composition that has the problem.
- The lint-streak telemetry now ties such a finding to its own composition's content, so an edit to `index.html` no longer counts as that finding surviving an edit. Streaks for these codes restart once after the upgrade.
- With "errors first" output, errors that moved to a composition print after the root file's warnings; the sort is per file.

## Known limit

Registry and figma snippet files under `compositions/` are not linted as compositions, so they have no entry of their own; a missing asset in one still names the snippet in `finding.file` but is filed under `index.html`. Giving snippets their own entry changes how they are linted, so it is left out here.

## Tests

- lint, "points a draft section's missing image, audio and mask at the draft, not the film": each finding now also sits under the entry for the file it names (`compositions/draft.html`, or `index.html` for the film's own image). On #4616 all four sat under `index.html`.
- CLI, "labels a draft section's missing image with the draft, not index.html": a real project run through `lintProject` and `formatLintFindings`. On #4616 the line read `[index.html]`.
- The CLI suite's reads of the four codes that carry a `file` now look across every entry instead of only the first, so none of them can pass by looking in the wrong place.


Out of scope: a missing file inside a registry snippet fragment still lands on `index.html`, as on main, because snippet fragments are not linted as entries of their own. With `hyperframes lint --json`, a moved finding now appears among its own file's findings instead of at the end of `index.html`'s; counts and `ok` are unchanged.


## Before

Studio's lint panel on main, fixture project with one missing image inside `compositions/draft.html`: the finding is labelled `index.html`, and the Compositions badges count it on `index`.

![Before: the missing image in the draft is labelled index.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/054d615e-243b-4db0-93df-08c9ad079cad)

## After

The same project on this branch: the finding is labelled `compositions/draft.html`, and the badge moves to `draft`.

![After: the missing image in the draft is labelled compositions/draft.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cbc74de9-d1d8-4795-a08a-d082746b6752)

title: fix(producer): renders use the font named in a var() fallback
body:
## What

A composition that names its font only inside a `var()` fallback, such as `font-family: var(--font-body, Inter, sans-serif)` with `--font-body` never defined, renders in that font in the browser. The producer's deterministic font injector did not read `var()` fallbacks, so it injected no font file, and Linux renders fell back to DejaVu. 28 registry items render this way today (found by compiling every item, not by a text search).

The injector now resolves `var()` the way the browser does:

- An undefined property uses its fallback, including nested `var()`s in the fallback.
- A defined property whose value is itself a `var()` is followed, up to 8 levels.
- An empty substitution, such as `var(--x,)`, makes the declaration invalid, so the browser inherits and nothing is requested.
- `normalizeSystemFontPrimaryFamilies` sees `var()` fallbacks too, so `var(--font, -apple-system, ...)` gets Inter first, as a direct system-font stack already does.

## Which fonts can fail a render

- A family named directly, or one defined `var()` away, stays required, as before.
- A family reached only through a `var()` fallback or a chain of `var()`s is optional. A definitive not-found (no source serves the family) is skipped. A transient failure (5xx, network error, timeout) gets one retry; if it still fails, the render uses the fallback font and logs a warning that names the font.
- A family that is both optional somewhere and named directly elsewhere stays required.

While Google Fonts is reachable, no composition that compiles on main fails here, and the plan check rejects nothing new. When a transient failure skips an optional font, the compiled HTML leaves its faces out, so that render (and a distributed plan's hash, which is computed from the compiled HTML) differs from one where the font loaded; the warning is the record. All font requests in a compile share one time budget; required families fetch first, so an optional font that hangs cannot fail a required one; it can only lengthen the compile, up to that budget.

The catalog's recorded font responses (`scripts/catalog-fetch-mirror`) gain the Inter request that `var()`-fallback items now make; three entries no current item requests are dropped.

## Verification

- `deterministicFonts.test.ts`, `deterministicFonts-failClosed.test.ts` and `render/planValidation.test.ts` pass, along with the other font test files (184 tests across 13 files). New cases:
  - fallback-only and chain-reached families tolerate a not-found;
  - on a 503, a network failure or a hang they make two attempts, then warn and render the fallback; a caller's cancel still aborts;
  - Inter behind a `var()` fallback keeps its bundled faces and warns when the top-up fetch fails;
  - a required family is fetched before hanging optional ones spend the budget;
  - a family also named directly, one defined level away, or named after a leading `var()` stays required;
  - `var(--x,), serif` and `var(--x,), system-ui` pass the plan check;
  - `var()` fallbacks with system fonts get Inter first.
- Each rule turns a test red when it is broken.
- Independent review, over three rounds, with real-network probes and a sweep of every HTML file in the repo:
  - Tailwind v4 compiled CSS compiles and embeds Inter and Noto Color Emoji.
  - 16 of 770 files change, and every one uses a `var()` fallback.
  - None newly throws or is newly rejected.
  - 30,000 generated documents showed no newly required font and no new plan-check rejection against main.
- Typecheck, lint, format and the audit gate pass.

title: fix(studio): an unsaved picker edit reverts and says why; edited values keep $ codes
body: Stacked on #4576; review the commits after its head (85379714f4). ## What this fixes **An edit that the picker cannot save is no longer silent.** After #4576, `useElementPicker` saves an edit only when the picked element's `data-hf-id`, or else its id, names exactly one element in its source file. When neither did, it saved nothing, but the preview kept the change, so the screen showed an edit the file never got. An element with an id and no `data-hf-id` took an older path that still wrote a repeated id's first element. Now every element goes through the same rule, preferring the file it was served from, and when nothing names one element it: - puts the preview back exactly as it was: the whole `style` attribute (so `!important` and shorthands survive), the data attribute, or the element's original child nodes; - shows the toast "Couldn't save that change: the element isn't uniquely identifiable in its file." through the `showToast(message, tone)` option. This is the same signature Studio's other hooks take, so a host passes its existing toast function; nothing new is drawn. `useElementPicker` is exported for apps that embed Studio and has no caller inside Studio, so a host that does not pass `showToast` gets the revert without a message. An element found in no saved file stays as before (nothing saved, no toast): that case is out of this change. When the element's hf-id is in no file and its id is in more than one, the save prefers the file the element was served from; that file is worked out from the preview and can be a guess, which is the same trust the hf-id path already places in it. **Edited values containing `$&`, `$$`, `` $` `` or `$'` are written as typed.** The source patcher built each patched tag as a string and passed it to `String.prototype.replace`, which reads those sequences as replacement codes. Saving `alt="R$&D"` wrote `alt="Ramp;D"`, a broken tag, into the file. Every such replacement now passes a function, so the text is used literally. The same pattern is fixed where other Studio editors write user values into source: the block parameter panel, `mergeStyleIntoTag`, the imported-font `

title: docs(motion-graphics): add Quiver asset source option
body:
## What

Add an optional Quiver asset-source path to the HyperFrames `motion-graphics` skill.

## Why

Users should be able to request Quiver vector artwork while making a motion graphic, then continue through HyperFrames' existing composition and preview workflow without manually moving assets between tools.

## Related work

Uses the official [QuiverAI skill and MCP integration](https://github.com/quiverai/cursor-plugin). No overlapping open Quiver PR was found.

## How

- Extend Director and shot-plan guidance to identify Quiver asset needs.
- Add a Source procedure for capability checks, authorized calls, result retrieval, and local SVG/PNG handoff with provenance.
- Keep provider calls and final verification with the invoking agent; handle uncertain provider outcomes without blind paid retries.
- Derive motion checks from the intended shot, including a deliberate final hold.
- Preserve the existing preview/render approval flow.

Six workflow documents plus the generated skills manifest. No new runtime, client, parser, or dependency.

## Test plan

- [x] Formatting check on the six changed documents.
- [x] `bun run lint:skills` (exit 0) and `bun run test:skills` (exit 0; 718 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped).
- [x] `git diff --check`.
- [x] Generated skills manifest check: 21 skills in sync.
- [x] Project skill mirror check: 24 files byte-identical.
- [x] Agent package tests (3 passed), caption package tests (6 passed), and both Agent/Codex plugin builds.
- [x] Fresh-agent existing-asset reuse through a checked HyperFrames preview.
- [x] One authorized Arrow 2 generation, one result, zero generation retries, followed by local asset handoff and checked preview. This run resumed after a model-capacity interruption; it needed no external artifact or code repair.

The generated SVG in the new-generation case contained internal CSS animation. Its original bytes were preserved; the composition used a locally derived transparent static PNG for whole-object motion and a stable final hold. The case does not establish direct SVG animation compatibility.

Native Quiver animation, REST editing, video export, offline operation, and provider reliability remain unvalidated. Ready for maintainer review. GitHub Actions requires approval from an upstream maintainer before it can run; local checks are not a substitute for that CI gate.

title: test(studio-server): undo keeps a write that lands between Studio's read and its patch
body:
## What this adds

A test, no behaviour change. It pins a case that looked like it could lose work, so a future change to the history engine cannot break it quietly.

The case: Studio reads a file, another writer (an agent turn, or anything outside Studio) changes it, and then Studio's element patch lands on top. Studio records its edit in history with the version of the file it read, which is now stale. If history trusted that version, undoing Studio's edit would write back the stale content and erase the other writer's change.

It does not happen today. When history splits the pending change between the writers, it walks the server's own write receipts back to the exact bytes the patch replaced, so the other writer's change stays theirs whatever version Studio sends. Undo then restores the other writer's content, not the stale read.

The test runs the real routes for both an outside write and an agent turn: read, other write, `patch-element`, `/claim` with the stale version Studio sends, then undo. It expects the other writer's content back.

## Tests

`routes/history.test.ts`: "keep the outside write …" and "keep the agent turn write … that landed between Studio's read and its patch when Studio's edit is undone".

Results: studio-server `tsc`, whole-tree `oxfmt --check` and `bun run lint`, fallow clean; the history route tests pass. With the receipt walk switched off, both new cases fail: undo writes back the stale read over the other writer's change.

title: fix(studio): playback keys do nothing while a dialog is open
body:
## What

With a modal dialog open over Studio (the lint results, for example), the player's playback keys still reached the player: Space, the arrow keys, J/K/L, M, I/O and A/E played and seeked the film behind the dialog.

The playback shortcut filter (`shouldIgnorePlaybackShortcutEvent`) now ignores keys while a modal dialog (`role="dialog"` with `aria-modal="true"`) is shown, wherever focus sits, including inside the preview frame. A dialog counts only when it is visible, not inert, and not left outside a fullscreen preview: the console-errors dialog can open behind fullscreen, where nobody can see or close it, so it must not take the keys.

## Why here

Every playback key goes through one handler (`usePlaybackKeyboard`), attached to the Studio window and to the preview frame, and that handler asks this one filter. So the check lives in the filter, not per key or per handler.

Not in this change: Studio's app shortcuts (F fullscreen, S split, Delete, tool keys) use a separate handler that does not ask the playback filter, so they still fire behind a dialog.

## Verification

- `useTimelinePlayer.test.ts`: two new cases fail on main (focus behind the dialog, focus inside it) and pass here; hidden, inert, non-modal and no-dialog cases keep their keys.
- The test DOM has no layout, so the tests stand in for `checkVisibility` with the `hidden` attribute; real hidden, `display: none` and inert dialogs are covered in a real browser by the captures below. Where a browser has no `checkVisibility`, a shown dialog still counts.
- Fullscreen: a dialog inside the fullscreen element blocks keys, one outside it does not.
- Each of these turns a test red when removed: the modal check, the visibility check, the inert check, and the modal-only match (matching every `role="dialog"` fails a test).
- Studio typecheck, lint and format pass.

Lint results dialog open, focus inside it, then ArrowRight six times and Space: the film moves from 00:00 to 00:02 behind the dialog.
