title: fix(cli): preserve unrelated package versions during upgrades
body:
## What

Keep similarly named packages out of Hyperframes project-pin detection and upgrades. `npx @acme/hyperframes@1.2.3 preview` and `npx custom-hyperframes@1.2.3 preview` retain version `1.2.3` when `upgrade --project` bumps the project's real `hyperframes` pin.

## Why

On main `46f6cb356785bed79e1ce7b79d7e7accc697786a`, the word-boundary matcher also starts after a scope slash, hyphen, or dot. It therefore rewrites unrelated package versions in package.json scripts and project-root shell wrappers, and reports those versions as Hyperframes pins.

## Related work

#2304 introduced project-pin upgrades; #3042 extended them to root shell wrappers; #4417 uses the same reader for stale-pin notices. Checked the files of all 152 current open PRs and searched open/closed project-pin work; no overlapping implementation found.

## How

Exclude package-name and scope characters immediately before `hyperframes`. Keep the existing version validation and right boundary, with the version still in capture group 1. Standalone pins and `--package=hyperframes@<version>` keep working.

## Test plan

- [x] Five new regression cases fail on main; all 64 project-pin, upgrade and update-notice tests pass after the fix. Coverage includes scoped/hyphenated/dotted names, mixed scripts and wrappers, and unrelated-only projects in check and apply modes.
- [x] Built CLI manual check in disposable project directories: `upgrade --project --json --check` writes nothing; apply updates only genuine pins; an unrelated-only project's package.json and wrapper stay byte-identical. A synthetic registry response fixes the target version without installing packages or touching user configuration.
- [x] CLI build/typecheck, root lint, changed-file formatting, whitespace, test reachability, comment checks and normal commit hooks pass.
- Documentation: no command or option changes.

title: fix(cli): honor HTML attribute casing in frame-rate defaults
body:
A root with `DATA-FPS="24"` renders at 30 fps when `--fps` is omitted, although Chrome reads the declaration as 24. The CLI's linkedom lookups preserve attribute spelling and also select a later duplicate lowercase attribute over an earlier uppercase one.

Read composition IDs, explicit root markers, and frame rates using case-insensitive HTML attribute names, keeping the first duplicate attribute as browsers do. Root selection and frame-rate validation retain the existing precedence from #2008.

Validation:

- Nine new regression cases fail on main; all 229 tests across the FPS helper, render arguments, render plan, render command, and timeline description pass with the fix.
- Built CLI, Chrome 152, and FFprobe: a one-second 64×64 composition changes from 30 frames at 30 fps to 24 frames at 24 fps. An explicit `--fps 60` produces 60 frames at 60 fps.
- Native Chrome agrees with the duplicate-attribute and explicit-root cases. The reproduction passes `hyperframes lint` and `hyperframes check` with no errors or warnings.
- CLI build/typecheck, workspace lint, changed-file formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and normal commit hooks pass.


The current-main integration retains the shared cloud-FPS defaults (24, 25, 30 and 60; unsupported declarations warn and fall back to 30). Mixed-case coverage now calls that helper. All 240 FPS/render/timeline/plan tests pass after a full workspace build. Four native Chrome cases agree with the source helper, and rebuilt CLI outputs contain 24 frames at 24 fps or, with explicit `--fps 60`, 60 frames at 60 fps. Composition lint/check, CLI typecheck, lint, formatting, reachability, final comment checks and normal hooks pass. The GitHub-signed tree matches the tested merge.

title: fix(cli): tolerate invalid optional package cache manifests
body:
A malformed cached optional-package manifest makes `hyperframes doctor --json` exit with an error and no report. The version reader also returns non-string and absent versions despite its `string | null` contract, which can make dependency availability checks report a package as installed.

Read the cache manifest as `unknown`, return a non-empty string version only, and return `null` for missing, unreadable, or invalid manifests. A pinned package beside the CLI retains priority. This change only reads metadata; it does not load package entries or repair the cache.

Validation:

- Ten regression cases fail on main; all 112 optional-package, doctor, local-embedder, local-search, and local-model tests pass with the fix.
- Built CLI in an isolated production dependency layout: malformed JSON and `null` change from exit 1 with no JSON to exit 0 with the complete doctor report. A numeric version is reported as unavailable; a valid cached version remains `1.52.0 installed`. No optional package was downloaded or installed during these checks.
- CLI build/typecheck, workspace lint, formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and normal commit hooks pass.

Related: #4156 introduced the cache and #4507 added pinned packages beside the CLI. Both are merged; this corrects the remaining cached-manifest reader.

title: fix(cli): tolerate removed files during desktop catch-up
body:
When a project file is deleted between the directory listing and metadata read, `hyperframes catch-up --json` exits with `ENOENT` and prints neither the remaining changed files nor the chat history. Tolerate failed per-file metadata reads and confirm that each listed path is still a regular file, so the scan continues when a file disappears or becomes a directory.

Validation: both new regressions fail on main and pass with the fix; all 38 app-history, catch-up, and desktop-app tests pass. The built CLI reproduces exit 1 with no JSON before the fix and exit 0 with the remaining files and chat turn afterward in an isolated fixture. CLI build/typecheck, repository lint, changed-file formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and normal commit hooks pass.

Follow-up to the merged catch-up implementation in #5114. This preserves its existing directory traversal and seen-marker behavior; the file list remains a best-effort view of the project during the scan.

title: fix(engine): retain fresh frames when replacing an empty cache
body:
If an extraction cache loses its frames but retains `.hf-complete`, lookup correctly reports a miss. After re-extraction, the publisher still adopts the empty directory as a completed concurrent winner and discards the fresh frames. Every subsequent render fails the coverage gate with zero frames.

Require a published winner to have frames as well as the completion sentinel, using the same check as cache lookup. An empty entry then takes the existing stale-directory replacement path. Healthy winners remain reusable; frame-count and coverage checks stay in their existing layers. This completes the empty-cache recovery promised by merged #3434.

Validation: both new tests fail on main; all 45 cache, frame-index, and recovery tests pass with the fix. Six built CLI renders show the cold/recovery/warm sequence before and after: main's two recovery attempts fail at 0/30 frames; the fix produces 30-frame, one-second MP4s and identical extracted-frame bytes on all three runs. Engine/CLI builds, engine/producer/CLI typechecks, repository lint, formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and normal commit hooks pass.

The broader extractor suite cannot complete with this machine's FFmpeg 9 because two existing fixture setups use the removed `-vsync` option; both fail identically with the change reverted. The dedicated recovery test uses current FFmpeg options and runs successfully.

title: test: use supported FFmpeg flags for VFR fixtures
body:
FFmpeg 9 removes `-vsync`, so three VFR fixture commands fail during suite setup and prevent 43 existing engine and producer regressions from running. Use the per-output `-fps_mode vfr` option, already used by the production extractor, to preserve the fixtures' irregular timestamps and let the tests run.

Validation with FFmpeg 9.0.2: the unchanged fixture commands fail on main; with this update all 199 engine extractor tests and all 35 producer HDR resource tests pass, including the previously blocked suites. Engine/producer typechecks, repository lint, changed-file formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and normal commit hooks pass. Existing assertions are unchanged.

title: fix(engine): recognize spaced closing template tags
body:
The exported engine media parsers return no video, audio, or image elements for a single template wrapper closed with valid HTML whitespace, such as `</template >`. The unwrap helper's precheck recognizes only `</template>`, so discovery never reaches the template contents.

Accept HTML whitespace before the closing angle bracket. The existing DOM-based single-wrapper check still decides whether to unwrap; incomplete closing tags and multiple sibling templates retain their existing behavior.

Validation: eight regressions fail on main; all 89 selected media-parser tests and 140 producer compiler tests pass. The actual exported parsers change from zero to one discovered element for each media type. Native Chrome 152 agrees on seven valid closing-tag variants; malformed inputs remain untouched. Engine build, engine/producer typechecks, repository lint, formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and normal commit hooks pass. Current producer compilation already normalizes mounted templates and passes the same four compilation controls on main; this fixes direct engine media discovery.

title: fix(cli): WebGPU compositions work in snapshot, check and layout like render
body:
## What changes for a user

- **A WebGPU composition is recognised by every local command.** `snapshot`, `check`, `layout` and motion shots look at the bundled project to decide whether it declares `data-requires-webgpu`. The bundle starts with the inlined runtime script, and the detector read a run of that minified code (`<32||…`, which happens to contain the text `data-composition-id`) as the composition root, so it answered "no". These commands then never asked for WebGPU: on a host without a GPU, `snapshot` saved a black frame instead of drawing or refusing. The detector now scans real opening tags with the shared HTML tag scanner, which skips script and style content. Render's compile and probe stages call the same detector on compiled HTML, so they get the fix too.
- **They follow render's software-WebGPU opt-in.** With `PRODUCER_ALLOW_SOFTWARE_WEBGPU=true` and no GPU in use, render runs WebGPU on SwiftShader. `snapshot`, `check`, `layout`, motion shots and Studio thumbnails now read the same opt-in. Without it they refuse the composition clearly, as render does.
- **A GPU probe whose page never answers gives up after 15 s.** In `auto` GPU mode the commands launch a small Chrome to see whether hardware WebGL works. A report from a Linux host without a GPU shows `check` spending two minutes there (`browserGpuMode probe -> software (probe failed (Timed out after waiting 120000ms))`), Puppeteer's launch-time wait for Chrome's first page, which runs on the 120 s launch timeout. The probe now launches without waiting for that first page (`waitForInitialPage: false`), so Chrome's process start keeps the configured launch timeout while the page, from opening to answering, has its own 15 s limit. The probe page now gets 15 s, and a probe browser that will not close is killed; the launch itself keeps the configured launch timeout, so a host that starts Chrome slowly is not misread as having no GPU.

## Checked on a Linux host without a GPU

One composition whose root declares `data-requires-webgpu` and clears a canvas to green through WebGPU, run with `hyperframes snapshot --at 0.5`:

| | Opt-in set | No opt-in |
|---|---|---|
| Current release | black frame; the page saw no adapter | black frame, no error |
| This branch | green, drawn by the `google/swiftshader` adapter | refused: "declares data-requires-webgpu, but no hardware WebGPU adapter could be obtained…" |

`hyperframes check` on a small project still passes here, and the probe still reports its answer in seconds.

## How

- `compositionRequiresWebGpu` (engine) walks `scanHtmlOpeningTags` and reads attribute names, so script content and attribute values cannot pose as the root. Parsers exposes the scanner as `@hyperframes/parsers/html-attribute-spans`.
- `resolveLocalWebGpu(browserGpuMode, requiresWebGpu)` in the CLI's GPU policy builds the launch config from the engine's own `resolveConfig().allowSoftwareWebGpu` and asks the engine's `usesSoftwareWebGpu` whether this launch runs WebGPU on SwiftShader. Each launch passes that config to `buildChromeArgs` and the matching flag to `assertWebGpuAdapterAvailable`.
- The GPU probe launches with `waitForInitialPage: false` and races its page against 15 s through `rejectAfter`, which the BeginFrame probe's `awaitBeforeDeadline` now also uses, and closes through the existing bounded close that kills a wedged probe browser.
- Studio's shared thumbnail browser records whether it launched with software WebGPU, and each thumbnail's adapter check reads that instead of re-reading the configuration.

## Limits

- Studio thumbnails share one browser that launches before any composition is known. With the opt-in set and no GPU in use, that browser launches with software WebGPU for every thumbnail. This is the cost the opt-in already states: software WebGPU is slow and skips the compositor workaround for transformed layers. Relaunching per composition would close thumbnails already in flight.
- The probe fix bounds the probe's page only. On a host where every Chrome page hangs, `check` still fails afterwards, now after at most 15 s of waiting on the probe page.

- The engine now imports parsers' `html-attribute-spans` subpath, so the GCP Cloud Run image's BeginFrame contract stage copies `packages/parsers/` before it runs `browserManager.ts`. That job's CI path filter still lists no parsers paths; a later change to that file can skip the job.

## Tests

- `browserManager.test.ts`: the root is found after an inlined script whose code holds `<`, `>` and the marker name (fails on the old detector); an attribute value naming the marker is not a root. A probe whose page never answers and whose browser will not close resolves to `software` once the 15 s page budget passes, keeps the configured launch timeout without waiting for the first page, and kills the browser (fake timers; fails without the page budget).
- `browser/gpuPolicy.test.ts` (real engine): with the opt-in in software mode a WebGPU composition gets SwiftShader's Vulkan flags; without the opt-in, on a GPU, or without WebGPU it does not.
- `captureCompositionFrame.browserFallback.test.ts`: the snapshot launch passes the opt-in config to `buildChromeArgs` and the software flag to the adapter check.
- The motion-shot and Studio-server source checks pin the shared helper.
- Engine `browserManager.test.ts` 76 passed and the four CLI files 51 passed, three runs each; `tsc --noEmit` clean for engine and CLI; comment ratchet clean.

title: fix(cli): name the unzip errors when every Windows unzip tool fails
body:
Follow-up to #5329, from its review.

## What changes for the user

- On Windows, when both `tar.exe` and PowerShell `Expand-Archive` fail to unzip Chrome, `install()` throws "no zip archiver is available", which is wrong on a machine that has both. The errors those two tools reported now follow it in the message, so the user sees why each one failed. Before, they were shown only when the unzip "succeeded" with nothing written.
- One check now decides whether a Chrome file is usable: a non-empty regular file. The unzip check reports a folder as "is not a file" instead of accepting it, and the two cache lookups no longer treat an empty file or a folder as a cached Chrome, so `ensure` installs again instead of reporting a browser that cannot start. The warning for that case now says the cached binary is unusable (missing, empty or not a file) instead of "missing".
- The render engine's own cache lookup skips an empty cached `chrome-headless-shell` too, and uses the next older build. Before, it picked the empty newest build that the CLI had just refused. A build it cannot read (a permission error) is skipped the same way instead of ending the scan.
- `browser ensure` on Linux ARM64 no longer hangs when its browser lookup throws: the spinner stops, the reason is printed, and it exits 1.
- `render`'s setup worker starts its error line on a new line, so the reason is found even when the worker's last warning had no trailing newline.

## How

The captured unzip errors moved from the missing-executable message into the one wrapper every failed install goes through (`wrapDownloadFailureWithBrowserPathHint`), so they appear for both failure shapes and only once. They are cleared once the executable check passes, so a later failure (for example the move into the cache) is not blamed on an unzip tool that failed before another one succeeded.

Not taken from the review: setting `process.exitCode = 1` in the worker before the write. Only `cli.ts` may set the exit code (`scripts/check-cli-process-ownership.mjs`); the worker exits 1 by rethrowing after the write.

## Verification

Each file alone, 3 runs in a row, all green: `browser/manager.test.ts` (59), `engine/src/services/browserManager.test.ts` (76), `commands/browser.test.ts` (5), `renderSetupWorker.test.ts` (10), `utils/cancellableProcess.test.ts` (2), `browser/preflight.test.ts` (25). Each new test fails when its fix is removed:

- every unzip tool failed: the message names both tools' errors (red when the install error is wrapped without them)
- a folder where the executable should be is refused (red when only the size is checked)
- an empty cached executable is installed again, not reused (red when the cache lookup only checks that the path exists)
- an empty executable in the puppeteer cache is skipped (red when that lookup only checks that the path exists)
- the engine skips a cached build that is empty or a folder and resolves the next older one (red with the old existence check, and red when only the size is checked)
- the engine keeps scanning past a build it cannot read (red without the catch; skipped on Windows and as root, where permission bits do not apply)
- a failed move into the cache does not mention earlier unzip errors (red when the log is kept past the check)
- the worker's error line is found after a warning with no trailing newline (red without the leading newline)
- the ARM64 lookup throwing stops every spinner and exits 1 (red without the guard)

title: fix(core): prepare split-video offsets during preview preload
body:
An upcoming split video can be buffered while its decoded frame is still at source time zero. When preview reaches a split with `data-media-start="6"`, showing that video before its asynchronous seek completes can briefly paint frame zero.

Prepare paused upcoming videos at their authored source offset when the preview prefetch begins. Read the current offset when metadata arrives, cancel pending preparation when releasing the resource, and confirm that the clip remains connected and upcoming before seeking. Replay prepares a retained video again without another `load()`.

The current-main integration preserves the three-slot prefetch queue, scene-local deferral, release of passed downloads, and the exclusion of videos replaced by extracted render frames. Queued clips wait for a prefetch slot before preparing their offsets.

Validation on current main: 253 tests across the preload, runtime entry, media, video preseek and start-resolver suites pass, including regressions for queued split preparation and extracted-frame videos. A full workspace build, core/runtime typecheck, lint, formatting, test reachability, both comment checks and normal commit hooks pass. The built CLI browser check passes for the existing 12-second long-GOP fixture. Native Chrome 152 first play and replay each capture 12 split-boundary samples with no stale or seeking frame and no runtime errors; the preview server stops cleanly.

Refs #5344 for the video-frame symptom. The separately reported audio discontinuity and the reporter's Windows environment remain outside this verification.

title: fix(engine): preserve Windows RSS samples after a query failure
body:
On Windows, a failed `tasklist` query discards every RSS sample collected earlier in the batch and skips the remaining processes. Capture memory telemetry then receives no rows even when the browser or GPU query succeeded.

Catch failures per process so successful samples remain available, matching the existing Linux behavior. Queries stay sequential, preserve input order and deduplication, and never reject; the macOS/POSIX batch path is unchanged.

Validation: four new regressions fail on main. All 35 engine memory tests, 27 producer telemetry tests, and 91 CLI telemetry tests pass. The built sampler retains browser and GPU rows around a failed renderer query, and a real macOS process sample succeeds. Workspace/engine builds, repository lint, formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and all normal commit hooks pass. Windows query failures are exercised through the existing injected runner; no native Windows run was performed locally.

title: fix(cli): renders on Windows stop cancelling when an old parent's pid is reused
body:
## What changes for a user

On Windows, a local render could cancel itself a moment after starting, or partway through, with `Render cancelled: render_cancelled_parent_exited`, while the terminal that started it was still open. Renders now keep going unless a real parent exits.

## Why

At start, a render records its chain of parent processes and cancels if any of them exits. On Windows it builds that chain from one `Win32_Process` listing by following each process's parent pid. Windows never reparents an orphan, so a parent pid can point at a parent that died long ago, and Windows may have handed that pid to an unrelated process. The walk followed it past the real chain onto that unrelated process; when it exited, the render cancelled.

`recordsToAncestors` now stops when a "parent" was created after its child, which can only mean its pid was reused. On macOS the `ps` listing carries no start time and Linux does not build this list at all, so nothing changes there.

This is the failure behind intermittent `Windows render verification` reds on main, the merge queue and unrelated PRs since the check was added.

## Limits

The check trusts process creation times. If the system clock steps backwards between a parent's start and its child's, a real parent can look newer and the walk stops there. That render then stops watching its parents from that point up. A backwards step after the child starts can still let a reused pid look older, which is the old behaviour for that render, no worse.

## Tests

- `orphanCleanup.windowsHide.test.ts`: with `400 → 300 → 200 → 999` where 999 started after 200, the chain is `300, 200`. Without the fix it also includes 999, and the test fails. A parent created in the same tick as its child stays an ancestor (fails if the check becomes `>=`).
- The orphan-cleanup, process-tree and render-cancellation unit tests (28) pass three runs in a row; `tsc --noEmit` clean for the CLI.

Standalone on purpose: one root in the CLI's process-ancestry walk, unrelated to other open changes.

title: fix(catalog): compare search vectors by direction so the publish PR can pass
body:
## What

The catalog drift check compared `registry/catalog-artifact/*-vectors.bin` byte for byte. Those files hold the search model's Float32 output, which differs slightly between CPUs. So the generated catalog PR (#4340) only passes when the runner that checks it happens to match the one that published it: on different hardware the same inputs give different bytes, and the check fails with `stale: registry/catalog-artifact/local-vectors.bin`. It failed 6 of the last 11 publish runs, each time on that file alone.

## How

- `treeDifferences` still compares every file byte for byte. When a `*-vectors.bin` differs, it compares the vectors instead: same row count, and every row within cosine 0.99 of the generated one. The row width comes from the `dimensions` field of the `.json` beside it.
- The `.json` beside each vectors file (item names and the content revision) is still compared byte for byte, so a changed item, a renamed item or a reordered row still turns the check red.

## Verification

- **The real case.** On #4340's branch, `local-vectors.bin` regenerated on an Apple Silicon Mac differs from the committed one in all 446 rows (largest element difference 0.017, lowest row cosine 0.9963) while the content revision is identical. `treeDifferences` on those two files: before, `stale`; now, no differences.
- **Tests** in `scripts/catalog-drift.test.ts`: a row at cosine 0.995 passes; a row at 0.984 (below the closest two different catalog items, 0.9897) and a changed row count are `stale`. The noise test fails without the fix, and the tests fail if the tolerance moves to 0.999 or 0.98. 3 runs green.
- **The real check.** With the fix applied to #4340's tree, `bun run check:catalog-drift --committed` (the CI command) prints "Committed catalog matches generation." comparing Apple Silicon output with the published x86 output.
- `oxfmt` and `oxlint` pass.

## After merge

The publish workflow regenerates #4340 on the next push to main; its catalog check should then pass.

title: test(core): isolate local font fallback from system discovery
body:
The local-fallback case in `deterministicFonts-googleSubsets.test.ts` writes a fake font into the user's font directory and discovers it through the real system-font locator. On macOS that invokes `system_profiler`, whose five-second timeout can consume the test's own five-second deadline. The unchanged suite reproduces this locally with 22 passes and one timeout.

Keep the font fixture in the suite's temporary directory and stub only the system-font lookup with a typed result. Restore the spy after every test. The existing assertion still checks that the compiler embeds the fixture bytes, and the failed authored-link case now explicitly verifies that the system locator is not called.

Validation: all 23 tests in this file, all 258 font tests, and the full 4,401-test core suite pass. Disabling local fallback and ignoring the authored-link restriction each fail the intended assertion, confirming the isolated tests still detect both regressions. Workspace build, core typecheck, repository lint, formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and the normal pre-commit hooks pass. Production font resolution is unchanged.

title: fix(studio): the timeline viewport gate gives the same verdict on the same code
body:
## What

The "Studio: timeline viewport gate" gives the same verdict on the same code. The 58.3 ms p95 budget is unchanged.

Two changes to how it measures:

1. **Each step is timed from the frame the jump is made in.** A sample used to be `second rAF timestamp - performance.now()`, with the start taken partway into a frame. Samples then landed at "n frames minus however long that frame's earlier callbacks ran", and on slow runners one cluster sat right on the 58.3 ms (3.5 frame) budget. Now a step is a whole number of frames (33.3, 50, 66.7 ms), so no sample can sit at the budget, and a p95 under budget means 95% of jumps show within 3 frames, which is what the number was meant to say. This is stricter than before: every sample gets longer by the part of the frame that used to be left out.
2. **A head that misses the budget is compared with its base on the same runner.** The job also builds the base (the first parent of the checked-out commit, the same base `base-file.sh` reads) and serves it beside the head. If both timing attempts miss the budget, and only then, the gate measures head and base in alternating blocks (2 rounds; each block opens its build alone in a fresh Chrome, runs the usual 3 warm-up and 5 measured runs of 63 steps, then closes it) and fails when the head misses the budget on more steps than its base, or has more steps a frame past the budget, beyond 3 standard deviations of the difference of the two counts (interactions and frame intervals each). Long tasks, DOM size, direct scroll and memory are still judged on the head alone, and the comparison only runs when those all passed.

## Why

Same commit, two runs, opposite verdicts. On the head of #5158:

| run | attempt 1 | attempt 2 | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| first | 73.4 ms | 58.6 ms | fail |
| rerun | 72.7 ms | 57.8 ms | pass |

Both runs had 315 samples per attempt (5 runs x 63 steps, after 3 warm-up runs), so the sample count was not the problem. The per-step split shows why. The tail comes from one step, the 0.25 to 0.5 jump, which is 45 of the 315 samples. In attempt 2 of both runs, that step's 4-frame samples sat between 57.8 and 58.7 ms, right on the budget, and where in the frame the timer started decided the verdict.

On current main (after #5151) the gate still flips. Across 32 finished gate jobs since #5151, the on-arm p95 ranged from 33.1 to 61.3 ms (median 48.5). 3 first attempts failed, and 2 jobs failed both attempts, on a lint fix and an esbuild bump that cannot change timeline scrolling. Runners come in speed classes. Build steps that take 6 to 7 s on the fast ones take 9 to 11 s on the slow ones, and every failure was on a slow runner. Retrying on the same runner does not help: both failing jobs failed attempt 2 as well (61.0 and 60.4 ms).

Deeper sampling or more warm-up cannot fix a verdict that depends on which machine ran the job. Comparing with the base on the same machine can, and the budget still decides on any runner where the head meets it.

## How

- `timeline-virtualization.mjs`: `measureScrollInteractions` starts each step at the previous step's second rAF timestamp, which is the frame the next jump is made in. New `measureAgainstBase`: head, base, base, head, each block alone in a freshly launched Chrome. The original page is closed after the memory check so nothing else renders during the comparison. `openStudio` and `assertRowVirtualization` were pulled out of the main flow so every page goes through the same checks. Two earlier versions were dropped after measuring them. Keeping the head's original page as the head side made the second Chrome read about 2 over-budget steps per run worse on identical code. Keeping both pages open made the idle one load the runner: on a slow CI runner the off arm's p95 doubled from 83 to 166 ms.
- `timeline-viewport-verdict.mjs`: `judgeAgainstBase`, and `shouldCompareWithBase` / `timingPassed`, which share one rule: the comparison can only settle timing, never runs that failed long-task or DOM checks.
- `ci.yml`: a step builds the base in a worktree. Each arm serves head and base, and the base page is loaded only when the head misses a budget. The step summary prints the comparison line when it ran.

What changes for the unvirtualized arm (1000 rows, 75 ms budget): with whole-frame samples its steps read 66.7 or 83.3 ms, so 75 ms sits between two frame counts. On slow runners more than 5% of its steps take 5 frames, so that arm now usually misses the budget and is settled by the comparison, which adds about 2 minutes. That is the stricter measurement telling the truth about slow runners, and raising the budget to hide it is out of scope. The virtualized arm's 58.3 ms budget sits between 3 and 4 frames the same way.

Comparison rule, exactly: for each of interaction steps and frame gaps, count head and base samples over the budget and samples a frame past it. The head fails if any head count exceeds the base count by more than `3 * sqrt(head + base) + 1% of the steps`. The 1% is there because a slow stretch of a shared runner makes a run of steps late together, so steps are not independent. On the unvirtualized arm with the base at 38 of 630 steps over budget, a head passes up to 76 and fails at 77.

Known residual: the second block of the comparison (always a base block) reads about 5 to 14 over-budget steps lighter than the other three, including when both sides point at the same server. Its cause is not known. It counts against the head (the cautious direction) and stays well inside the allowance in every comparison measured. An earlier version also served the base fewer projects than the head; the base now gets the head's exact project set.

Tradeoff to read: if main itself drifts over the budget on a slow runner, a PR that matches main there passes with the comparison line in the summary instead of failing. The budget still fails a head that misses it on a runner where its base meets it, and any head clearly slower than its base (beyond the allowance above).

Decision on the unvirtualized arm (made here, reasoning for the record): keep its 75 ms budget and let the comparison settle it on slow runners. The alternatives were raising the budget to 83.3 ms or more, which would hide real tail growth, or going back to the old sampling, which is what made verdicts flip. A budget a slow runner cannot meet with main's own code should not decide a PR; the base on the same runner should. Fast runners still hold the arm to 75 ms outright.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests (`timeline-viewport-verdict.test.mjs`, 22/22): head and base missing equally, identical builds either side of the budget, head slower even where the comparison puts it under budget, same count but late steps a frame later, a slow stretch's extra steps on identical builds, frame gaps alone, the rule that the comparison only settles timing, and the exact summary line. Making `judgeAgainstBase` always pass turns 2 red; dropping the frame-later rule lets the 200 ms case pass.
- [x] Local headless runs, CI tier, 50k clips, Chrome 152 on an arm64 laptop (a fast machine, so the screen passes):

| run | code | result |
|---|---|---|
| before x5 | main script, main app | p95 32.3 / 32.8 / 33.0 (min / median / max), 5 of 5 pass |
| after x5 | this branch, main app | p95 33.4 on all 5 (exactly two frames), 5 of 5 pass |
| identical code through the comparison x3 | 35 ms busy-wait in the timeline scroll path of both head and base | both screen attempts fail every time; comparison 6 vs 9, 3 vs 5, 4 vs 3 steps over budget; 3 of 3 pass |
| injected regression | 35 ms busy-wait in the head only | both attempts fail; comparison: 540 vs 0 frame gaps over budget; exit 1, FAIL |

- [x] CI on this branch. The PR changes only test and CI files, so every run measures main's app code, and every comparison is head against identical code:

| | before (32 gate jobs on main-based PRs after #5151) | after (25 gate jobs on this branch, PR and dispatch runs plus reruns) |
|---|---|---|
| virtualized arm, first attempt p95 | 33.1 to 61.3 ms, median 48.5 | 33.4 (11 jobs), 50.0 to 50.1 (9), 66.6 to 66.7 (5, each passed on attempt 2) |
| jobs red on identical app code | 2 (both attempts at 61.0 to 61.3 and 59.7 to 60.4) | 0 |
| unvirtualized arm | p95 46 to 80, budget 75 | 50.0 / 66.7 on fast runners; 83.3 to 116.6 on slow ones, settled by the comparison in 13 jobs: head vs base over budget 49/38, 97/77, 72/58, 45/39, 53/42, 64/55, 72/56, 74/60, 56/44, 49/42, 49/44, 82/77, 44/41; all pass |
| forced comparison, virtualized arm | n/a | 62/58 and 12/15; both pass |

- [x] Independent adversarial review, iterated to this head (no blockers; findings fixed: count steps a frame past the budget, one owner for the "timing only" rule, fresh Chrome per block, summary names every count, labels by threshold).
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: fix(cli): accept already-exited Windows process trees
body:
When a subprocess exits just before Windows `taskkill /T /F` reaches it, `taskkill` reports status 128 (process not found). The process-tree helper currently rejects that result, so cancelled render setup and probes can report `taskkill exited with status 128` instead of the original error.

Treat only status 128 as completed teardown. Preserve rejection for other exit statuses, signal termination, and spawn errors. Caller tests verify that an output overflow retains `ENOBUFS`, a timeout retains `ETIMEDOUT`, and an abort returns the exact supplied reason when the child has already exited.

Validation: five new regression cases fail on unchanged main; all 92 related process, cancellation, orphan-cleanup, preflight, and preview-lifecycle tests pass with the fix. Workspace and CLI builds, CLI typecheck, repository lint, formatting, comment checks, test reachability, and normal pre-commit hooks pass. The Windows branches are exercised through the injected process seam locally on macOS; native Windows execution is left to the required CI lane.

Related: #5273.

title: fix(lint): check timeline registration before explicit font loads
body:
An empty GSAP timeline registered before a font-readiness callback can be mounted by a parent before its tweens are added. The existing error catches `window.__timelines["intro"]` with `document.fonts.ready`, but misses `window.__timelines.intro` and `document.fonts.load(...)`, the explicit font-loading pattern documented in #5203. It also treats a registry read before the callback as a registration.

Recognize dot and bracket assignments, including spaced member access, and both font-readiness forms. Require an assignment so an earlier registry read does not hide a correct registration at the end of the build. Update the diagnostic to mention explicit loads.

Validation: five added cases fail on unchanged main; all 197 GSAP tests, all 900 lint-package tests, and 100 CLI lint-path tests pass. Six controls through the rebuilt CLI flag early registrations and accept registration after the build. Workspace, lint and CLI builds, lint typecheck, repository lint, formatting, test reachability, comment checks and normal pre-commit hooks pass. The GSAP patch from #3953, which adds a separate network-fetch rule, still applies cleanly alongside this change.

Related: #5203.

title: fix(studio-server): a failed save reports its real error when a later file was never written
body:
## What

When a multi-file save fails because a later file cannot be written at all (for example its folder is read-only), the error now says what actually happened: the write failed and the earlier files were put back. It no longer claims "rollback did not complete" when every file on disk is in its original state.

## Why

`applyFileMutations` (used by Studio element edits and by `hyperframes timeline` apply, ids, undo and the single-row edit verbs) rolls back a failed batch by rewriting each attempted file's original bytes. It did that even for the file whose write had just failed and never landed. With a persistent failure, that rewrite fails for the same reason, so the call threw an `AggregateError` "File mutation failed and rollback did not complete" while disk was consistent: file 1 restored, file 2 untouched. Callers and users were told the project might be half-saved when it was not.

Reproduce on main: two files, the second in a folder made read-only with `chmod 555`, apply a change to both. Before this change the call throws the `AggregateError`; after, it throws the original `EACCES` and both files hold their original bytes.

## Related work

Found in review of the timeline undo batch work; independent of it.

## How

The rollback now decides per file from what is on disk:

- a file whose write completed is restored when it still holds our bytes (unchanged rule, so a save that landed afterwards is kept);
- a file whose write never completed is restored only when its bytes differ from the original. If it still holds the original bytes there is nothing to undo, and nothing is written.

Tradeoff, kept on purpose: when a never-written file's bytes differ from the original, the code cannot tell a writer that failed halfway (an injected non-atomic writer; the existing partial-write test pins restoring that) from another save that landed while the write was failing (on Windows the rename retries for about 100 ms while another program holds the file). It restores the original in both cases, as main did for every unwritten file. The production writer is atomic, so this only matters in that race. Main overwrote unconditionally, so this change narrows that window and does not widen it. Keeping such a save would mean dropping the partial-write guarantee, which is a separate decision.

A real rollback failure (a written file that cannot be restored) still throws "rollback did not complete". The rollback loop moved into its own function to keep `applyFileMutations` under the complexity gate; the repeated attempted-mutation and writer types each became one alias.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated
  - New: a two-file apply with the second file's folder read-only throws the real `EACCES`, not an `AggregateError`; file 1 is back to its original bytes, file 2 is untouched, and file 1's write receipt is cleared. Skipped on Windows and as root, where `chmod 555` does not block writes. Red on main with `expected AggregateError: File mutation failed and … to not be an instance of AggregateError`.
  - New: when a written file cannot be restored, the call still reports "rollback did not complete".
  - Existing: a failed write that left partial bytes is still restored to the original.
  - Putting back the old rollback condition fails both new tests; dropping the partial-bytes restore fails the existing partial-write test. 9/9 pass on three runs in a row.
- [ ] Manual testing performed
- [ ] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments": they say why, not what, and a bug fix says what the code must do and how to reproduce the bug

title: fix(cli): refuse undo when a target or backup is missing
body:
If a timeline undo receipt refers to a removed target or backup, the command exits 1 with a raw filesystem error instead of its normal refusal payload. A missing `index.html` also trips project discovery before the receipt is checked. This follows the nonblocking review feedback in #5279.

Catch missing-file errors while preparing the entire undo batch and return exit 2 with `{ok: false, reason, fix}` on stderr in JSON mode. Include the missing project-relative path and a recovery hint. Resolve undo projects without requiring `index.html` so a missing root target receives the same refusal. Preparation still completes before mutations begin.

Validation: six new single/batch cases fail on unchanged main, then all 109 timeline tests and seven atomic-write tests pass. Eight controls through the rebuilt CLI on Node 22 verify JSON and text refusals, unchanged source and backup bytes, and successful batch undo/redo. Workspace and CLI builds, CLI typecheck, repository lint, formatting, test reachability, comment checks and normal pre-commit hooks pass. The overlapping test patch in #5315 still applies cleanly.

Related: #5279.

title: fix(cli): mirror skills into every installed agent on Windows
body:
## What

On Windows, `hyperframes skills` could skip mirroring into an installed agent's skills folder at random. CI showed it as an intermittent failure of `skillsMirror.test.ts` on windows-latest (`expected [ 'bob', 'cursor' ] to include 'goose'`) while the same commit passed on another run.

## Why

Before mirroring, the CLI refuses any target that is the same folder as one of the two install-owned stores, and part of that check compares `statSync(...).dev` and `.ino`. On Windows the inode is a 64-bit NTFS file id, and Node returns it as a JavaScript number, which keeps only 53 bits. Two different folders created close together can then report the same `ino`, so a fresh agent folder looks like the store and is skipped as `aliases_install_owned_store`. Which folders collide depends on where NTFS places them, hence the randomness.

The same comparison guards `--shot` in `hyperframes motion`: on Windows a rerun could refuse to overwrite its previous PNG with "must not overwrite the composition source".

## How

- `sameExistingNode` (skills mirror) and `pathsReferToSameFile` (motion shots) read both stats with `{ bigint: true }`, so device and file id compare exactly.
- The existing mirror test now also asserts nothing was skipped, so a future failure names its cause instead of only a missing agent.

## Verification

- New `fileIds.windows.test.ts` mocks number-mode `statSync` to give every path one identity, as colliding Windows ids do, while bigint mode stays real. Without the fix, goose is skipped with `aliases_install_owned_store` and the shot rerun throws; with it, both pass.
- `fileIds.windows.test.ts` and `skillsMirror.test.ts`: 21/21, three runs in a row. CLI typecheck, lint and the fallow audit pass.

Not exercised: a Windows machine. The CI failure does not print the skip reason, so that the runner hit this collision is inferred from the mechanism and the symptom.

title: test(engine): real-ffmpeg tests and fixture cleanup get a 30 s budget
body:
## What changes

`packageHls against real ffmpeg` runs several real ffmpeg encodes per test (a test source, a locked-GOP encode, the HLS package, then ffprobe) plus a cold import of the encoder module, all under vitest's 5 s default. On a slow Windows runner a test can pass that limit: `writes a master and no audio playlist when there is no audio` timed out at 5 s in the `engine-cli` shard, and its cleanup then failed with `ENOTEMPTY` because the timed-out ffmpeg was still writing into the temp directory.

The block now carries a 30 s timeout, the budget other real-ffmpeg tests in this package already use (`runFfmpeg.test.ts`, `audioMixer.test.ts`, `streamingEncoder.test.ts`). On passing Windows runs these tests take under a second each; the failing run took 7.7 s on a loaded shard. A hang inside the async packaging call still fails at 30 s; a hang inside the synchronous `spawnSync` setup steps was never bounded by a vitest timeout and is unchanged here.

In the merge queue the same shard then failed in `videoFrameExtractor.test.ts`: the `afterAll` that deletes a real-ffmpeg fixture directory ran past vitest's 10 s hook default (`Hook timed out in 10000ms`). The five `afterAll` hooks that delete fixture directories now get 30 s: the budget four of their fixture setups already use to create those files, and the cli package's `hookTimeout`. The fifth fixture (forced SDR) creates its files in the tests and keeps the default setup budget.

## Tests

- `packageHls.test.ts`: 26 passed, three runs in a row. `videoFrameExtractor.test.ts`: passed three runs in a row.
- With the block's timeout set to 1 ms, all six real-ffmpeg tests fail, so the option governs the whole block.

Standalone on purpose: test-budget fixes for red CI shards, unrelated to other open changes.

title: fix(cli): check warns instead of failing on a still title card
body:
## What changes for the user

`hyperframes check` no longer fails a valid still title card. Before, a card of 3 s or more whose frame never changes failed with `sweep_static` ("Timeline did not advance under seek; every green verdict on this run is unreliable"), exit 1, even when its registered GSAP timeline followed every seek. Authors and agents padded cards with fake tweens to get past it, and those did not help either: a 0.999 to 1 opacity tween and an empty `tl.set` at the end both still failed.

Now:

- **Error, as before, now with a hint to put the animation on the registered timeline:** the frame never changes and a GSAP timeline or tween, or a CSS or Web animation, on the page holds the same time at every sample without having finished. That is direct proof the seek is not driving the page, for example motion on a paused GSAP timeline that was never registered.
- **Warning, exit 0:** any other frame that never changes, reading "Nothing on screen moved under seek." `--strict` still fails the run on it, and `data-no-timeline` still skips the guard. The audio-only warning is unchanged.

## Root cause

The guard inferred "the seek did not work" from "nothing on screen changed". A still card looks exactly like that, so `check` cannot tell the two apart from the picture alone. The runtime's own clock always moves on a seek, so it proves nothing either.

What does prove a broken seek is an animation `check` can see that never moved. At each layout sample the guard now reads the time of every registered timeline, every top-level child of `gsap.globalTimeline` and every CSS or Web animation, each tracked by identity across samples (so a tween created mid-run, or one that finishes and leaves the list, cannot shift the others). An animation that holds the same time at every sample where it exists, and never reports itself finished, is stuck. "Finished" comes from each clock's own completion state in the page: GSAP's repeat-aware `totalProgress()` (and `reversed()`; a timeline that only has `duration()`/`time()` falls back to those, and one whose time cannot be read, or whose methods are plain values, is left out rather than counted as stuck), a Web Animation whose time is a plain number (a scroll-driven one is left out): its `finished` play state, or its end in its own playback direction (a reversed animation is complete at 0, not at its end). Only a time and a done flag cross into Node, so an infinite animation's `Infinity` end never has to survive serialization.

## Decision and its cost

A frozen frame with no visibly stuck animation is now a warning, not an error. The cost: motion that `check` cannot see now gets that warning instead of failing, unless `--strict` is set. That covers an anime.js animation never registered with the runtime, a GSAP timeline from a module import or a second GSAP copy, an unregistered GSAP tween that autoplays and ends before the first sample, a tween aimed at a selector that matches nothing, and motion drawn by requestAnimationFrame, canvas, iframes or shadow DOM. A paused infinite CSS animation on a `::before` also warns now, because pseudo-element animations are not in `document.getAnimations()`. The alternative was keeping a hard failure on every valid still card. Still cards are common and a hard failure there sends authors to pad them with fake motion; a run that should move can still use `--strict` or a `keepsMoving` motion assertion.

## Verification

Real CLI on the devbox, built from this branch and from `main`, on thirteen 4 s cards (one `h1`, GSAP 3.14 from a CDN):

| card | `main` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| registered timeline with a 0.999 to 1 opacity tween (the reported card) | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| registered empty timeline | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| registered timeline that moves the title | passes | passes |
| moving tween on an unregistered paused GSAP timeline | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| the same, plus a tween created mid-run by `tl.call` | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| the same, plus a tween created mid-run by an interval | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| a tween delayed past the end of the run | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| a 0.1 s reveal that then holds | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| a CSS animation the author paused | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| an anime.js animation never registered with the runtime | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| an unregistered GSAP timeline from a module import, or from a second GSAP copy that replaced `window.gsap` (two cards) | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| an infinite paused CSS animation created mid-run that never moves | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| the same with a finite CSS animation | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| a reversed Web Animation created mid-run and paused at its start (its end time) | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| the same paused halfway | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| a registered timeline object with only `duration()`/`time()` that never moves | error, exit 1 | error, exit 1 |
| a registered timeline object with only `duration()` and `seek()` (no way to read its time) | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| a still card whose title has a scroll-driven CSS animation (`scroll(root)`, and `view()`; two cards) | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| a registered timeline object whose `duration` is a number, not a method | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |
| a finished repeat/yoyo GSAP timeline | error, exit 1 | warning, exit 0 |

The anime.js and module/second-GSAP rows are the cost described above: `check` cannot see those clocks. Finished Web Animations (reverse and forward) also warn on real cards, but there the runtime drives them so their clocks move anyway; their completion state is pinned by the Chromium test below instead.

Tests, 3 runs in a row, all green:

- `commands/check.test.ts` and `utils/checkBrowser.test.ts` (103). New cases, each red when its rule is removed: a still card whose timeline follows the seek, one with nothing that could move, one whose only animation already holds at its end, and one whose timeline is seen at only one sample, listed twice, all warn without failing (red when every frozen frame is an error; red when the end is ignored; red when a clock is counted per entry instead of per sample); a stuck animation next to a moving one, and a tween created mid-run that is stuck, both fail (red when a frozen frame is never an error).
- `utils/checkBrowser.chromium.test.ts` (2, new, runs in Chromium when `PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` is set; like the other `*.chromium.test.ts` files in this package, no CI job sets it yet; run 3 times in a row with Puppeteer's headless Chrome): the page probe marks a finished yoyo timeline, a finished reversed timeline, a finished reverse Web Animation, one paused at its end and a reversed one paused at 0 done, an infinite CSS animation and a reversed one paused at its end never done, reads registered timelines that only have `duration()`/`time()`, done at their end and not done halfway, leaves out one with no readable time, scroll-driven CSS animations and plain-value `duration`/`reversed` without failing the read, keeps one id per animation when a new timeline appears in front of the others, and skips an empty timeline (red when the probe returns nothing, when ids are not kept between samples, when `reversed()` is ignored, when GSAP is never done, when the `finished` play state is ignored, when an animation paused at its end is not counted as done, when playback direction is ignored, when the `duration()`/`time()` fallback is removed, when an unreadable or non-numeric time is kept as a clock, and when a plain-value method is called without a guard).

title: fix(studio): a stalled font or asset no longer leaves the preview empty or drops reloads
body:
## What was wrong

Studio started its timeline sync only on the preview iframe's `load` event. One font or asset request that never finishes (a slow font host, a flaky network) keeps `load` from firing at all, even though the runtime has already booted and knows the duration (about 6 s in the fixture below; its own font wait gives up after 5 s). So:

- On first load the timeline stays empty and Play stays disabled ("Drop media here or describe your video to start").
- Every edit that needs a full reload loads in the hidden frame, never counts as loaded, and is dropped after the 45 s budget with "The preview did not reload (it took too long to load). The previous preview is still showing."

## Fix

- `Player.tsx` runs its load path (Studio's timeline sync, and promotion of a hidden reload) on the player's `ready` event (the runtime's own handshake) as well as on the iframe's `load`, once per document, whichever comes first.
- That decision has one owner. When the load path runs, Player announces `hf-preview-document-loaded` on the iframe (`announcePreviewDocumentLoaded`, `sceneSwap.ts`). `onPreviewContentReplaced` (Topology lens, Layers, colour grading, edit re-apply) and the console error capture now listen to that announcement instead of the raw `load` event. A page's own late `load` after a stalled font therefore no longer closes the Topology lens or wipes its console errors, and Retry on a stalled page re-applies edits as soon as the new page is ready.
- `ready` takes the load path only once the current page's runtime has booted (`__playerReady`, which the runtime sets before it posts any timeline). A late `ready` from the page Retry just replaced therefore leaves the new page to its own `load` instead of marking it loaded before its runtime exists.
- A host that embeds Layers or DOM editing with its own `<hyperframes-player>` gets no announcement from Studio's Player, so `announcePreviewDocumentLoaded` is now exported for it to call on each new preview page, and the `LayersPanelHost` doc says so.

## Verification

- Regression tests:
  - `Player.test.ts`: `ready` with no `load` starts the load path and announces it; a late `load` or `ready` for the same document does neither again; a new document does both. A `ready` before the page's runtime has booted does nothing, and that page's own `load` then runs the load path.
  - `sceneSwap.test.ts`: `onPreviewContentReplaced` fires on the announcement and on a scene swap, never on a raw `load`.
  - `useConsoleErrorCapture.test.tsx`: a raw late `load` keeps the page's errors; the next announced page replaces them; an announcement after the preview goes away captures nothing.
  - Moving Player off announcing, or either listener back to raw `load`, turns its own tests red.
- The touched files plus every subscriber's own test file (`Player`, `sceneSwap`, `useConsoleErrorCapture`, `NLEPreview`, `useTimelinePlayer.shadowReload`, `LayersPanel`, `TopologyLens`, `useColorGradingController`, `useDomEditPreviewSync`): 148 passed, three runs, exit 0. The comment ratchet and citation check pass, as do pre-commit typecheck, lint and format.
- Headless Studio on a fixture with two sub-compositions and a font whose host accepts the request and never answers. On main: an empty timeline, and the edit dropped at 45.1 s with the message above. On this branch: timeline and Play on first load, and the edit on screen within 20 s (re-checked at the final head: timeline on first load with the font still stalled, edit shown between 13 and 20 s, no failure message) (runtime ready at about 6 s plus the player's bounded asset wait).

## Not covered

- The "Composition timeline not found after 8s" reload error seen on older builds did not reproduce on main and is not changed here.
- Pages without the HyperFrames runtime still become ready only after `load`; the player's fallback probe starts there.
- The player does not check which document a runtime `ready` belongs to, so a `ready` from the old page arriving after Retry has navigated can start Studio's load path early; Studio's existing 5 s retry recovers. Narrow, Retry-only, and a player-side fix.

### Before

![Before: first load with a stalled font, empty timeline, Play disabled](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/59442419-e755-43b5-9b25-536b79cd7340)

![Before: the edit is dropped at 45 s, old preview kept](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/39f62791-3481-4d72-b90b-92a746db352f)

### After

![After: first load with the same stalled font, timeline and Play ready](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ffd5776d-2a33-4d80-8944-ce376ad9df66)

![After: the edit is on screen at 14 s](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c5f96239-7327-41cd-a14b-a2e92dc1451c)

title: fix(ci): keep the catalog publish PR when main changes nothing it generates
body:
## What

The standing catalog publish PR keeps its approval when main moves without changing anything the catalog generates. Today it can only merge if a reviewer approves it and the merge queue takes it before the next push to main lands.

Also here: a seven-line comment copied across five motion-blur sources is cut to three lines. The publish PR carries it into the generated pages, and it is held there on comment length.

## Why

`publish-catalog.mjs` decided whether the branch already held the right snapshot by comparing the branch's whole tree with "main plus generated catalog". Any push to main changes that tree, even one that touches no catalog source, so the bot force-pushed a new commit on every main push. With "approval of the most recent push" required, each rewrite dismissed the approval.

Two consecutive bot commits from this afternoon differ, among generated files, only in `registry/catalog-artifact/local-vectors.bin`. The embedding model's floats vary slightly between runs, which is why the drift check already compares vectors by direction rather than bytes.

## How

- The bot fetches the published branch and finds where it left main. It keeps the branch as is (no new commit, no force-push) only when all of these hold:
  - main has not changed any generated file since that point;
  - the branch carries nothing but generated files;
  - its generated files equal what this run generated. A modified `*-vectors.bin` still counts as equal when every row agrees within the drift check's cosine threshold.
- Anything else republishes exactly as before.
- The cosine rule moves to `scripts/catalog-vectors.mjs`, so the drift check and the publisher share one definition.
- A kept PR's body names the main commit its snapshot was built on.

A kept branch sits on an older main. The merge queue does not require it to be up to date, and the first rule above means main changed nothing it would merge into.

Comment trim, the same three lines in each file: `registry/blocks/gooey-split/gooey-split.html`, `registry/components/motion-blur/{motion-blur,demo}.html` and `registry/components/shutter-slam/{shutter-slam,demo}.html`. Only comment lines change.

## Verification

- `catalog-publication.test.mjs`: the fixture now has a real `origin` holding the published branch. New tests:
  - an unrelated main push leaves the publication alone;
  - regenerated vectors nudged slightly keep it, and vectors that point elsewhere replace it;
  - vectors the publication lacks replace it;
  - a main commit to a generated file replaces it;
  - a publication carrying a non-generated file is replaced.
  21/21, three runs in a row.
- Non-vacuous: removing each of the three keep conditions fails exactly the test for it, and the publisher from main fails the new tests.
- `catalog-drift.test.ts` 4/4 after the move. Lint, format, typecheck and the fallow audit pass in pre-commit.

Not exercised: the workflow itself on GitHub. The fetch relies on the repository being public, since the checkout does not persist credentials.

title: fix(examples): the k8s chunk-runner image installs and loads the producer again
body:
## What changes for a user

The reference image in `examples/k8s-jobs/Dockerfile.example` did not build from a clean checkout: `bun install --frozen-lockfile` stopped because the workspaces the producer depends on were not in the image.

```
error: the root package depends on workspace "@hyperframes/player" (packages/player), which is listed in bun.lock but not on disk
error: workspace "@hyperframes/core" depends on workspace "@hyperframes/lint" (packages/lint), which is listed in bun.lock but not on disk
error: workspace "@hyperframes/core" depends on workspace "@hyperframes/parsers" (packages/parsers), which is listed in bun.lock but not on disk
error: workspace "@hyperframes/core" depends on workspace "@hyperframes/studio-server" (packages/studio-server), which is listed in bun.lock but not on disk
```

Once it builds, it had drifted from the image the repo actually ships (`packages/gcp-cloud-run/Dockerfile`) in ways that broke renders. Now the image builds and renders static, text-heavy and video compositions:

- **Workspaces.** It copies every workspace the producer reaches (`lint`, `parsers`, `studio-server`, besides `core`, `engine`, `producer`) and the `player` manifest the root package depends on.
- **Runs under bun.** In a workspace checkout the producer's exports point at TypeScript source, which bare `node` cannot load. The image keeps `bun` (pinned to 1.4.2, as the Cloud Run image is) and the usage line runs the producer with it from `packages/aws-lambda`. It builds only `core`, whose build generates gitignored files its source imports; without that the producer fails with `Cannot find module './generated/runtime-inline'`.
- **Chrome 148.** It pinned chrome-headless-shell 131, well behind the 148.0.7778.167 the Cloud Run and test images render with; it now pins 148, and the video composition below renders on it.
- **Fonts.** It installed only Liberation, so CJK and emoji drew as boxes; it now installs the Cloud Run image's font set.
- **Usage line.** It passed `-e PRODUCER_HEADLESS_SHELL_PATH=/opt/chrome/chrome-headless-shell`, a directory, overriding the correct path the image sets, so Chrome failed to start (`EACCES`). The line is dropped.
- **Build context.** A `Dockerfile.example.dockerignore` keeps local `node_modules`, `dist` and the producer's LFS test fixtures out of the image.

## Checked

Built from a `git archive` of each commit (no local build output in the context), on Linux:

| | Before (main) | After |
|---|---|---|
| `docker build` | fails at `bun install --frozen-lockfile` | builds |
| default command | (no image) | prints the producer version and the Chrome 148 path |
| header's `docker run` line, as written | (no image) | loads `renderChunk` |
| `plan`, `renderChunk` per chunk, `assemble` under `bun`, static fixture | (no image) | 3 chunks, 30 frames, h264 |
| same, `sub-composition-video` fixture | (no image) | 16 chunks, 390 frames, h264 1080x1920; a frame checked by eye shows the video and its caption |
| same, Japanese, Chinese, Korean and emoji text | (no image) | every glyph drawn; frame checked by eye |
| same image without the core build step | | fails: `Cannot find module './generated/runtime-inline'` |
| test fixtures in the image | | none |

The image is about 2.8 GB; most of the growth is the Noto font set (largest: `fonts-noto-extra`, about 340 MB), kept identical to the Cloud Run image's. The README's size line is updated. The `.dockerignore` next to the Dockerfile needs BuildKit, the default builder since Docker 23.

## Not changed here

Running the producer under bare `node` needs a published `@hyperframes/producer`, whose published exports point at `dist/`, not this workspace image.

Small and standalone on purpose: one example image and its README, unrelated to other open changes, so nothing else can carry it.

body:

title: fix(engine): long exports with many clips no longer stall at 90% or hide a timeout
body:
## What was wrong

Long exports with many video clips failed near the end.

- **Frame extraction ran one ffmpeg per clip, all at once.** `extractAllVideoFrames` started every clip's extraction together (an unbounded `Promise.all`), each with its own 300 s deadline. With 82 clips the machine was starved: processes stalled and 51 of them hit their deadline. The same export passes when extraction runs four at a time.
- **The final stage ignored the configured ffmpeg timeout.** The assemble stage called the audio normalize, mux, faststart and HLS steps without the render's `ffmpegProcessTimeout`, so each fell back to the fixed 300 s default whatever `FFMPEG_PROCESS_TIMEOUT_MS` said. When a long 4K mux hit that deadline the error read `Audio muxing failed: FFmpeg exited with code 255 ...`, with no sign that it had been killed for taking too long. The distributed assemble path had the same gap.

## Fix

- **One limit, at the one place extraction ffmpeg is spawned.** At most half the CPU count of extraction jobs run at once, across every clip and every long-clip segment, in every render in the process. This is the same formula the segment workers already used. A variable-frame-rate clip's two-process pipeline takes one slot. A queued extraction's deadline starts only when its ffmpeg spawns. The limiter wraps only the spawns, so nothing waits while holding a slot.
- **Cancel is prompt.** A queued extraction whose render is cancelled leaves the queue at once, without spawning. `runFfmpeg` and `runFfmpegPipeline` start no process when their signal has already aborted.
- **Every assemble step takes the configured timeout.** In process, the assemble stage receives `ffmpegProcessTimeout` and passes it to normalize (including its true-peak probe), mux, faststart and HLS packaging. The distributed assemble reads `FFMPEG_PROCESS_TIMEOUT_MS` the same way for its remux, concat, CFR re-encode, normalize, mux and faststart.
- **A deadline kill now says so.** `describeFfmpegFailure` leads with `FFmpeg timed out after N ms (ffmpegProcessTimeout; long renders can raise FFMPEG_PROCESS_TIMEOUT_MS)` and then the usual stderr tail. Other failures read as before.

## Behaviour to know

- Concurrent renders in one producer process now share the extraction queue, so a small render can wait behind a large one's queued clips. Before, they ran side by side and overcommitted the machine.
- The cap is `floor(cpus / 2)`: 4 on an 8-core machine, which is the value measured above; 6 on 12 cores, 8 on 16. Whether 6 to 8 at once also passes the 82-clip export is unmeasured. It uses `os.cpus()`, so a CPU-quota container sees host cores, as the rest of the engine does.

## Verification

- `videoFrameExtractor.concurrency.test.ts`: real extractions through a shim ffmpeg that records how many processes are alive as each starts, with two CPUs (one slot). Four short clips: every start sees one alive. Two 125 s clips, split into segments: every start sees one. Two variable-frame-rate clips through the two-process pipeline: never more than two. Removing the limit at each of the three spawn sites turns its test red. A fourth case holds the only slot with one extraction, queues a second and cancels it: the second fails as cancelled without starting ffmpeg while the first still runs; without the signal reaching the queue it waits for the first and times out. The shim is a shell script, so this file is skipped on Windows.
- `concurrencyLimit.test.ts`: never more than the limit at once, waiters start in order, a failing task frees its slot, a cancelled waiter leaves the queue without a slot, an already-cancelled task does not wait. Dropping the cancel handling turns the last two red.
- `runFfmpeg.test.ts`: an already-aborted run spawns nothing, alone or as a pipeline. Removing the check turns it red.
- `chunkEncoder.test.ts`: a mux and a faststart killed at a configured deadline (fake timers) report `FFmpeg timed out after ...`; an ordinary failure's message is unchanged.
- `assembleStage.test.ts`: the configured timeout reaches normalize, mux, faststart and HLS.
- `distributed/assemble.test.ts` (bun): with `FFMPEG_PROCESS_TIMEOUT_MS=1`, assembly fails with `FFmpeg timed out after 1 ms`. With the env ignored it passes and the test turns red.
- Runs on our test box, three each, exit 0: the four engine files 131 passed; the assemble stage 20 passed; `assemble.test.ts` and `audioPadTrim.test.ts` 51 passed.

## Not covered

- The 82-clip ProRes alpha export itself was not re-run on this branch. The four-at-a-time measurement came from the same cap applied by hand.
- Other fan-outs in the same export stay unbounded: the alpha-plane probe (three 8x8 frames per alpha source, 30 s cap, a failure only skips a warning), the HDR first-frame colour read, and the audio mixer's per-element reads. None can stall the export the way extraction did.

title: ci: image builds pull through a mirror instead of rate-limited Docker Hub
body:
## What changes

The regression shards, the BeginFrame image contract and the fast video validation build their Docker images with buildx on GitHub-hosted runners. Those runners pull `moby/buildkit` and `node:22.23.3-bookworm-slim` from Docker Hub anonymously, and Docker Hub has started answering with rate limits:

```
ERROR: failed to build: failed to solve: node:22.23.3-bookworm-slim: failed to resolve source metadata for docker.io/library/node:22.23.3-bookworm-slim: unexpected status from HEAD request to https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/library/node/manifests/22.23.3-bookworm-slim: 429 Too Many Requests
```

That turns shards red on main and on every PR, at random.

The three `docker/setup-buildx-action` steps now:

- start BuildKit from `mirror.gcr.io/moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1` instead of Docker Hub;
- tell BuildKit to pull `docker.io` images through `mirror.gcr.io`, Google's public Docker Hub mirror. BuildKit falls back to Docker Hub if the mirror misses.

The regression workflow's change filter now also matches `.github/workflows/regression.yml`, as `ci.yml` already lists itself for the BeginFrame contract job. Before, an edit to the regression workflow skipped the very shards it changed.

The Dockerfiles are unchanged, so anyone building them locally pulls exactly as before. The two `docker run` steps run the image the job just built and pull nothing.

## Checked

- `mirror.gcr.io` serves both images: `docker buildx imagetools inspect` resolves `mirror.gcr.io/moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1` and `mirror.gcr.io/library/node:22.23.3-bookworm-slim`.
- The pinned `setup-buildx-action` accepts both `driver-opts` and `buildkitd-config-inline`.
- `actionlint` reports the same findings on the three workflows before and after.
- This PR's regression shards start BuildKit from `mirror.gcr.io/moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1` (the job log shows the pull) with the mirror config loaded, and no shard hit a 429. BuildKit logs image names as `docker.io/...` whichever host answers, so the routing was checked on a Linux box with a debug builder and this exact config, building `FROM node:22.23.3-bookworm-slim` with `--no-cache`: the manifest request and every layer went to `mirror.gcr.io/v2/library/node/...`, and Docker Hub got no requests. With the mirror pointed at a bad path, BuildKit logged `trying next host after status: 404 Not Found`, pulled from Docker Hub and the build succeeded.
- Docker Hub and the mirror return the same digests for both images, so build cache keys are unchanged.
- A manual dispatch of the fast video validation workflow on this branch built its image the same way and passed.

Small on purpose: one CI setting in three places, so nothing else can carry it.

title: render --docker: the first image build gets killed after 10 minutes and the error says to check Docker is running
body:
### Describe the bug

The first time you run `render --docker`, the CLI builds the renderer image with a 10 minute timeout (`timeout: 600_000` on the `docker build` call in `packages/cli/src/commands/render.ts`). If the build takes longer, it gets killed and you see `spawnSync docker ETIMEDOUT` plus "Check Docker is running: docker info". Docker was running fine. The build was just slow.

### Minimal reproduction

Any project, no cached `hyperframes-renderer` image, Docker VM with 2 CPUs (colima's default):

    npx hyperframes@0.8.78 render . --docker --output out.mp4

### Steps to reproduce

1. Remove any `hyperframes-renderer:*` image.
2. Run the command above.
3. Here one first build went past 10 minutes and got killed during `npm install -g hyperframes` (step 10/13). Another one, for 0.8.143, took about 8 minutes, so it depends on the machine and the connection.

### Expected behavior

The build finishes, or the error says it timed out and that running the command again picks up from the cached layers.

### Actual behavior

    ✗  Docker image build failed
       Failed to build Docker image: spawnSync docker ETIMEDOUT
       Check Docker is running: docker info

Running the same `docker build` by hand with no timeout finishes, and after that `render --docker` works.

### Environment

hyperframes 0.8.78 and 0.8.143, macOS 26 on an M4 Pro, colima with 2 CPUs and 4 GiB, Docker 29.4.0.

### Additional context

Either dropping the timeout for the build (the output already streams unless `--quiet`) or catching `ETIMEDOUT` with a message that says what happened would fix it. Happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer.
