title: feat(producer): frame cache that skips capture and encode of unchanged sections
body:
> **This is a suggestion, opened as a draft to start a discussion.** CONTRIBUTING asks for substantial features and changes to defaults to be discussed first, and I found no issue covering this, so I am bringing a working implementation with measurements instead of an abstract proposal. The [open questions](#open-questions) are the decisions I would like maintainer input on; I am happy to change the scope, make it opt-in, split it, or drop it.

## What

A frame cache for the disk-capture render path. A render keeps its encoded video, a hash of every captured frame and fingerprints of the composition in `renders/.hf-frame-cache/`. The next render captures and encodes only the sections of the timeline that changed, and stream-copies the rest from the cached video.

Measured on a 60 s, 1080p, 30 fps composition with three scenes (`hyperframes render -w 4`, mp4, standard quality):

| Render | Total | Frames captured | Frames encoded |
|---|---|---|---|
| First render, empty cache | 53.2 s | 1800 | 1800 |
| One scene edited | 21.6 s | 660 | 570 |
| Nothing changed | 3.6 s | 0 | 0 |

## Why

Editing a composition usually touches one scene, but every render captures and encodes the whole timeline. Capture is the larger part of a render (31-49 s of capture against about 20 s of encode on the composition above), so reusing only the encode saves little. This PR skips both.

## Related work

I found no open issue or PR for this. It is a substantial feature and, as written, it is on by default for disk-path renders. That default is a placeholder for the discussion, not a request; see "Open questions" below. Both parts can be switched off: `HF_FRAME_CACHE=false` (no cache) and `HF_FRAME_CACHE_SKIP_CAPTURE=false` (reuse encodes, capture every frame).

## How

Five steps per render, all in `packages/producer`:

1. **Fingerprint** (`clipFingerprint.ts`). Before capture, on a planning session, the loaded page is hashed: one SHA-256 per top-level `[data-start]` clip over its elements (attributes, text, computed style, pseudo-elements) and the GSAP tweens that target them, and one global hash for everything else plus the bytes of every file the page loaded.
2. **Probe** (`captureSkip.ts`). Up to 32 frames spread over the timeline are captured on that session and hashed.
3. **Plan.** Runs the fingerprints predict unchanged are cut to whole GOPs of the cached render, two seconds or longer. A run is skipped only when every probe inside it equals the probe the cached render stored for that frame.
4. **Capture** (`renderOrchestrator.ts`). Only the remaining runs are captured, each through the existing capture stage with its `frameRange` input.
5. **Encode** (`frameCache.ts`, `frameDiff.ts`). Captured frames are compared with the cached hashes, so unchanged GOPs inside a captured run are reused too. `reuse` segments are split out of the cached video with `-f segment -segment_frames`, `render` segments are encoded, and everything is merged with the concat demuxer.

Design decisions worth a reviewer's attention:

- **Reuse is per closed GOP of one second.** A stream copy can only cut on a keyframe. Cached renders are therefore encoded with a keyframe every second (every frame for ProRes, the segment length for HLS), which makes files larger: 10.6 MB against 7.6 MB here.
- **The cache stores hashes, not images.** 32 bytes per frame plus one copy of the video. An earlier version that compared only part of each file's bytes reused 1140 of 1800 wrong frames in a test with a small changing corner, so the comparison is a full-file SHA-256.
- **Probes are compared with probes, not with the workers' frames.** A frame captured by jumping to it and the same frame captured in sequence by a worker were different bytes for 5 of 14 frames I checked, while five different jump orders gave identical hashes. Comparing a jump-captured sample with a worker's hash made unedited renders capture everything.
- **A prediction alone never skips a capture.** A page with content the fingerprint cannot see into is not fingerprinted at all: `<video>`, `<canvas>`, `<iframe>`, embedded objects, SVG / Lottie / CSS / WAAPI animation, shadow DOM, registered frame sources, functions in tween vars, cross-origin files, more than 5000 elements. Ease functions are the one exception (the runtime hands every tween a parsed ease); they are fingerprinted by 33 samples of the curve.
- **The cache can never fail a render.** A cache-path error falls back to the existing encoder. If frames were skipped and the cache cannot supply them (for example `--quality` changed since the cached render), the orchestrator captures them and encodes again.
- **Not touched:** `packages/engine`, `captureStage.ts`, streaming / segmented / HDR capture, png-sequence, gif, GPU encoders, `PRODUCER_ENABLE_CHUNKED_ENCODE`.

### Benchmarks

Same composition, one run each on a shared 10-core Mac; other processes were running, so compare rows within a table only.

Through `executeRenderJob`, 4 workers:

| Render | Total | Capture | Encode | Frames captured |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First | 71.8 s | 50.9 s | 20.3 s | 1800 |
| Last scene edited | 25.4 s | 18.4 s | 6.8 s | 630 |
| No change | 2.4 s | 2.2 s | 0.0 s | 0 |
| Middle scene edited | 26.3 s | 18.0 s | 8.1 s | 660 |
| Same composition, capture skipping off, empty cache | 66.6 s | 38.4 s | 27.8 s | 1800 |

For comparison, the encode-only version of the cache (every frame captured) took 44-63 s for an edited render, and a single-worker streaming render without the cache took 42.6 s.

Cost on a first render: about 1.5 s for 30 probe frames (50 ms each).

Output of "middle scene edited" against a full render of the same composition: 1800 frames, 60.0 s; 1356 frames decode to identical pixels, the rest are at PSNR 56.6 dB or higher. The "no change" output is byte-identical to the render before it.

## Known limits

- The CLI's default render and `--workers 1` stream frames into the encoder and never reach the cache. It needs `--workers 2` or more.
- Capture skipping needs screenshot capture. With BeginFrame or drawElement capture only the encode is reused.
- Output is not byte-identical to a full render.
- A change outside every clip (root element, stylesheet, script, asset file) captures the whole timeline.
- Tested on one GSAP composition, JPEG frames, macOS. Not tested: PNG (alpha) output, Linux, compositions with overlapping clips or sub-compositions.

## Open questions

1. **Is this wanted in the producer at all?** If incremental rendering belongs somewhere else (studio, a separate command), I would rather hear that before polishing this.
2. **On by default, or opt-in?** I would suggest opt-in (a `--frame-cache` flag or `HF_FRAME_CACHE=true`) for a first release, because it changes output bytes and writes to the project directory.
3. **Should a render that would stream take the disk path when a cache exists?** Without that most CLI users never reach the cache, but a first render on the disk path was slower than the streaming render here (about 53 s against 43 s).
4. **Are the one-second GOP and the larger files acceptable for cached renders?**
5. **Is the fingerprint's list of disqualifying content the right one?** It is deliberately conservative. `computeStaticFrameSet` in the engine already makes a similar judgement and may be a better place to share it.
6. **Would you prefer this split?** The encode-only cache (`frameCache.ts`, `frameDiff.ts`) stands alone; capture skipping (`clipFingerprint.ts`, `captureSkip.ts`) builds on it.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated: `frameCache.test.ts`, `frameDiff.test.ts`, `clipFingerprint.test.ts`, `captureSkip.test.ts`; `frameCache.integration.test.ts` runs the real FFmpeg split, encode and merge and is registered in `scripts/test-classification.mjs`.
- [x] Manual testing performed: the benchmark renders above through the rebuilt CLI and through `executeRenderJob`; frame count and PSNR against a full render; the fallback when the cache cannot supply skipped frames (render at `-q high` over a `standard` cache).
- [x] Documentation updated: "Frame cache" and "Capture skipping" in `docs/packages/cli.mdx`.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments": `check-comment-citations.mjs` and `comment-ratchet.mjs` pass.

Not covered by an automated test: the in-page fingerprint code and the orchestrator wiring run in a browser and were exercised by the manual renders only.

Local results: `bun run lint`, `bun run format:check`, producer typecheck and the pre-commit hooks pass. Producer unit lane: one failing file, `captureHdrResources.test.ts`, which fails the same way without this change on my machine (the local FFmpeg rejects `-vsync`). The producer integration lane (other than the frame cache test) and the regression harness were not run locally.

The commit is not signed yet. I will sign it and force-push before this leaves draft.

title: fix(media-use): transcript-cut video renders without repeated frames or a keyframe warning
body:
## What

Video cuts made with `transcript-cut` now have their frames exactly on the source's frame times, and a keyframe every second.

## Why

In #5417 a cut made with `transcript-cut` stutters when it is used as footage in a composition. The script wrote each kept range to a temporary `.mkv`, and ffmpeg writes Matroska timestamps in whole milliseconds, so a 30 fps frame that belongs at 2/30 s was stored at 0.067. The last step copies the video stream as it is, so the output kept those timestamps, and the renderer shows the previous frame whenever one of them is a hair late.

The same issue points out that the renderer warns about sparse keyframes on footage this script has just written, because nothing set a keyframe interval.

I ran the repro from the issue on `main`: 352 of the 528 frames were off the frame grid, a real `hyperframes render` of that cut showed the previous frame in 97 of them, and the render printed the sparse-keyframe warning. With this change the frames are all on the grid, the render shows every frame where it belongs, and the warning is gone.

## Related work

Fixes #5417

The `.mkv` files came in with #4179, which moved the audio of each range to PCM so it is encoded only once. Before that the temporary files were `.mp4` and the frames were already on the grid.

#5426 and #5325 touch the same script for other bugs. They don't overlap with this change, but whichever merges later has to regenerate the manifest hash.

## How

The temporary files are now `.mov`, which holds the frame times exactly and also carries PCM, so the audio work from #4179 stays untouched.

Each temporary file is also written at a constant frame rate. Without that, ffmpeg 7 and later start a range that begins between two source frames one frame late, which is what the first push of this PR tripped on in CI.

The encode of each range also asks for a keyframe every second, which is what the renderer's own warning recommends. On the clips I tried the output grew between 3 and 9 percent.

To make sure nothing else moved, I ran the old and the new script over more than a dozen sources: different frame rates, cut points in the middle of a frame, a variable-frame-rate clip, a rotated clip, 5.1 audio, no audio, and HEVC and VP9 sources. The audio came out identical every time.

One thing stays as it was: if you ask for the output itself as `.mkv`, it still has millisecond timestamps, because that is what ffmpeg stores in that container.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added in `transcript-cut.test.mjs`. Three check that the frames of a video cut sit on the frame grid with no gaps, at 30, 29.97 and 60 fps, and one checks that keyframes are no more than a second apart. All four fail on `main`. One more checks that the audio of a video cut isn't padded at each splice, so the fix from #4179 is also covered for video outputs.
- [x] The tests in this file pass with ffmpeg 6.1, 7.1 (the build CI pins) and 9.0. `bun run test:skills` passes with 7.1 (866 passed, 2 skipped). Lint, format and the comment checks are clean.
- [x] Manual testing: the renders described above, running the CLI from source with ffmpeg 7.1.
- [ ] Documentation updated (not applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: media-use: ElevenLabs TTS helper reads the text with the locale encoding on Windows (non-ASCII becomes mojibake)
body:
**Environment:** Windows 11, Python 3.14 (locale encoding cp1252, UTF-8 mode off), skills installed from `heygen-com/hyperframes` on 2026-10-10, CLI 0.8.145.

`skills/media-use/audio/scripts/lib/tts.mjs` writes each line with `writeFileSync(p, text)` (UTF-8). The inline Python helper (`ELEVENLABS_PY`) then reads it with `open(sys.argv[1]).read()`, which on Windows uses the locale encoding unless `PYTHONUTF8=1` is set. Every non-ASCII character reaches ElevenLabs as mojibake, so German, French, Spanish etc. voiceovers are spoken wrong.

**Repro (no API call needed):**

```
node -e "require('fs').writeFileSync('line.txt','Größe, Grüße und Übergabe')"
py -3 -c "import sys; print(ascii(open(sys.argv[1]).read()))" line.txt
# -> 'Gr\xc3\xb6\xc3Ÿe, Gr\xc3\xbc\xc3Ÿe und \xc3œbergabe'
```

**Fix:** `open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8")` in `ELEVENLABS_PY`.

**Related:** the same helper hardcodes `model_id="eleven_multilingual_v2"` and ignores the `model` argument that `synthesizeOne()` receives, so a caller cannot pick e.g. `eleven_v3`.

title: media-use telemetry ignores telemetryEnabled: false from ~/.hyperframes/config.json

It never reads the shared config the CLI writes, so `transcribe.mjs`, `transcript-cut.mjs` and `audio-duck.mjs` still post to PostHog for a user who opted out through the CLI. When `~/.heygen/credentials` exists, `identifyAccount()` additionally sends the account email as the distinct id.

**Expected:** `optedOut()` also returns true when the shared config has `telemetryEnabled: false`, so one opt-out covers the CLI and the skills.

title: media-use tts.mjs leaves one hf-txt-* temp directory per synthesized line

body:

4. **Deprecated command.** `hyperframes-animation/adapters/animejs.md:123` still uses `npx hyperframes validate`; `hyperframes-cli/SKILL.md` says to use `check`.

title: [Feature Request] Support custom AI providers via configurable API endpoint and API key
body:
### Problem

### Description

It would be great if HyperFrames allowed users to configure their own AI providers by specifying a custom API endpoint and API key, instead of being limited to predefined providers.

### Benefits

- **Flexibility:** Use any OpenAI-compatible provider.
- **Self-hosting:** Connect to locally hosted or private models.
- **Cost control:** Choose providers based on pricing and performance.
- **No vendor lock-in:** Avoid depending on a fixed list of supported providers.

### Expected Behavior

Users should be able to provide a custom base URL, API key, and model name, and have HyperFrames use that provider without requiring changes to the source code.

### Proposed solution

Allow users to define a custom provider through configuration or the app.

For example:

```json
{
  "provider": "custom",
  "baseUrl": "https://api.example.com/v1",
  "apiKey": "${CUSTOM_API_KEY}",
  "model": "my-custom-model"
}
```

Ideally, this would support OpenAI-compatible APIs, making it possible to use self-hosted models, private inference endpoints, and third-party AI providers.

### Alternatives considered

_No response_

title: fix(audio): master bus follow-ups: a scene renders with its own chain; long mixes render in windows
body:
## What changed and why

Follow-ups to #5420, from the two non-blocking notes in @miguel-heygen's review.

### 1. A scene rendered on its own uses its own master chain

The audio-effects reference says a sub-composition file rendered on its own is the top-level root, so its `data-fx-chain` is the master bus. The code did not do that: the standalone wrapper built for a scene file reused the project index's root attributes, so the index's chain became the master bus.

The wrapper now carries the scene root's own `data-fx-chain`, or none when the scene declares none. Studio preview of a scene alone goes through the same function and gets the same fix. No docs change was needed, since the docs already described this behavior.

### 2. Master-bus exports past about 93 minutes

The master pass read the whole mixed WAV with `readFileSync`, which Node refuses past 2 GiB ("File size is greater than 2 GiB"). A stereo 48 kHz float mix reaches that at about 93 minutes. The browser page also held the whole track twice.

`applyAudioFxChain` now reads, renders and writes inputs above 512 MiB of samples in 5 minute windows:

- each window is rendered with 10 s of preceding and 1 s of following audio, which is discarded, so stateful effects arrive warm;
- the last window keeps the chain's tail, as the whole-file render does;
- a fresh browser page is opened per window, so the browser holds one window at a time;
- the output header is patched at the end;
- inputs below the threshold keep the existing whole-file path unchanged.

Parameter automation is clocked from the start of the file and is not windowed. An input past 2 GiB that carries automation now fails with an `AudioFxRenderError` that says so, instead of Node's raw file-size error. The master bus has no automation, so it is not affected.

`writeWav` was split into a header builder and a sample encoder so the windowed writer shares them. `writeWav` output is unchanged.

## Tests

- `standaloneEntry.test.ts`: the wrapper carries the scene's own chain, and drops the index's chain when the scene declares none.
- `audioFxRender.test.ts`:
  - segment planning tiles the input exactly, with pre and post roll at the edges;
  - on a sparse 2.5 GiB file, `readWav` throws the 2 GiB error while the header read succeeds;
  - a windowed render of a 4.4 s stereo mix never calls `readFileSync` on the input, and matches the whole-file render;
  - a volume envelope with a step lands on the file's own clock across window boundaries;
  - automation on a file past 2 GiB fails with the named error.

Mutations, each turns its test red:

- force the window gate off (every input takes the whole-file path): the no-whole-read test fails;
- do not trim the preroll from each window: the whole-vs-windowed comparison fails;
- set preroll to 0: the segment planning test fails;
- remove the wrapper's set/remove of `data-fx-chain`: both wrapper tests fail;
- remove the over-2-GiB automation check: its test fails.

Changed test files only: `standaloneEntry.test.ts` (8 tests), `htmlBundler.test.ts` (with it, 191), `audioFxRender.test.ts` (31). The test-reachability check and the comment ratchet pass.

## Measured

- Windowed render of a 4.4 s stereo mix through the true-peak limiter (ceiling -6 dBTP, 3 ms lookahead), 1 s windows with 1 s preroll, against the whole-file render: maximum sample difference 0, excluding the last 10 ms (see the note below).
- A 30 minute stereo 48 kHz float mix (691 MB, over the 512 MiB threshold, so 6 real windows with the default settings) through the same limiter: 225 s, on a shared machine at load 15 to 18. The output is the same size, with a valid header. Peak Node RSS 744 MB, which includes the memory left from generating the test input.

## Not exercised

- A real end-to-end render of an input past 2 GiB. Only the header read and the reader were exercised on a sparse 2.5 GiB file; a full run would be over 100 minutes of audio.
- WAV files past 4 GiB (about 186 minutes of stereo float). The sum that feeds this pass is written by ffmpeg as a plain WAV, and I did not test how it behaves past the 32-bit RIFF size limit. The windowed writer clamps its size fields to 0xFFFFFFFF, and the header reader treats a declared size beyond the file as "to the end", but neither was run against a real 4 GiB file. Treat about 3 hours as the supported ceiling until that is checked.
- Effects other than the true-peak limiter compared window against whole. A reverb or a long-release compressor could differ at a window seam if its memory exceeds the 10 s preroll.
- Parameter automation on inputs past 2 GiB. It now fails with a clear error and is not supported.
- Windowed rendering through `processCompositionAudio`. It was exercised through `applyAudioFxChain` directly; the master pass uses the default limits.

## Separate finding, not changed here

On the existing whole-file path, a lookahead limiter's last few milliseconds can come back as zeros depending on the input's length. Measured on unmodified `applyAudioFxChain` with a stereo 300 Hz tone through the true-peak limiter: 52800 frames gives 0 trailing zero samples, 100800 gives 192, 67200 gives 320, 48000 gives 320, 211200 gives 0. The comparison test above leaves the last 10 ms out for this reason. It looks like an issue in the offline render or the limiter worklet and deserves its own issue.

— Jerrai

Nothing directly: this adds a check. The 0.8.148 fix (#5458) for a talking-head video that went black while Studio preview played is now guarded by a real project played in Studio's real preview, not only by unit tests. If the preview ever again forces a script-hidden backdrop visible, CI goes red.

## Before (the #5458 visibility change reverted)

![Before, playing: the dark backdrop covers the video, only the caption shows](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2ae30b52-1ceb-41e6-97ef-42ecba543e09)

## After (main)

![After, playing: the video shows under the caption](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b6e0a5d9-6023-4d02-89bd-ca487d28b221)

![After, playing inside the backdrop's own window: the backdrop shows, so the check cannot pass by the backdrop never appearing](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dbd31df9-e303-46df-8bfb-dedfe3a30074)

`aroll-backdrop.mjs` plays it in Studio and reads the preview's pixels and the element on top at the frame's centre: the video must show paused at the start, while playing at about 1 s, and paused after the backdrop's window; the backdrop must show while playing inside 6-8 s. Every wait is on a condition (Play enabled, the video has a frame, the playhead inside a range). Studio can re-fit the preview just after a pause, so a screenshot taken across that reflow is retaken (up to 5 times).

It runs in the existing `studio-timeline-viewport` job, in the same step as the trim-snap check (`ci.yml`), which also runs on `packages/core/**` changes.

- On main: exit 0, three runs in a row, no failures.
- oxfmt, oxlint, comment checks clean.

## Not covered here

- Run on Linux headless Chrome for Testing only; not yet on the CI runner's Chrome (this PR's CI run is that check).
- It does not fail if a future Studio stops stamping the backdrop at all; it records that in its output.

title: fix(media-use): clean up temporary TTS text directories
body:
## What

Clean up the per-call `hf-txt-*` directory used by the ElevenLabs and Kokoro paths in `synthesizeOne`. Add isolated regression tests and refresh the media-use skills manifest.

## Why

Each synthesized line creates a temporary text directory. The text must remain available until its subprocess finishes, then only that call's directory should be removed, including when writing or synthesis fails.

## Related work

Fixes #5466.

#5469 separately changes ElevenLabs Python text decoding to UTF-8. This PR does not include or replace that change.

## How

- Scope allocation, writing and the awaited provider call inside `withTmpText`, with cleanup in `finally`.
- Keep existing synthesis results and original write/spawn errors. Cleanup is best effort: a removal failure must not replace those results or errors.
- Test success, nonzero exit, missing output/executable, thrown spawn, allocation/write/removal failures, and overlapping calls without touching another call's or a pre-existing directory.
- No credentials, real provider requests or model downloads are used by the new tests.

title: fix(audio): keep the pitch shifter's tail; no silence after a bitcrush seek
body:
## Summary
Two follow-ups from the review of #5474.

- **Pitch shifter tail.** The offline render padded its source with silence only for the true-peak lookahead. Once a source ends, its worklets stop being fed, so the pitch shifter's grain ring never drained and the last ~90 ms of a clip was cut off. The source is now padded for the whole render (clip + chain tail + latency). That length is computed once and also sizes the `OfflineAudioContext`.
- **Bitcrush after a seek.** A bitcrush node built part-way into a clip seeds its hold counter from the clip position, but its held value started at 0. A preview seek could therefore play up to `samples - 1` frames of silence before the counter wrapped. The held value is now primed from the first input sample, quantised. The counter seed is unchanged, so render windows still line up with a whole render.

## Tests
- `audioFxWorklets.test.ts`: "does not open with silence when its hold counter starts part-way through a hold". The hold is 250, the counter is seeded one frame in, and the input is a steady 0.5. All 128 output samples must be above 0.4. Before the fix it fails with `expected 0 to be greater than 0.4`.
- `audioFxRender.test.ts`: "a pitch shifter keeps the last 90 ms of its input". A 0.4 s steady clip is rendered at +7 semitones with mix 1. The output must be longer than the input, the RMS over 0.31–0.40 s must be above 0.2, and the RMS over 0.40–0.45 s must be above 0.1. Before the fix it fails with `expected 0 to be greater than 0.1`.
- The existing window-seam test (bitcrush, modulation, delay, reverb and compressor state across window seams) still passes at its 0.001 tolerance, which is unchanged.
- `packages/core/src/audio` (17 files, 367 tests) and the full `audioFxRender.test.ts` (41 tests, browser cases included) pass. oxfmt, oxlint, the comment ratchet and the comment-citation check are clean.

## Not exercised
- No listening pass in the Studio preview. The seek fix is covered by the worklet unit test only.
- The primed value is the first input sample, not the sample the hold actually started on before the seek. That is the closest value available without pre-roll.

— Jerrai

title: ProRes `mov` output carries 8-bit levels in a 10-bit container (the docs say "10-bit color")
body:
## Summary

The docs describe `format: "mov"` as "ProRes 4444 + `yuva444p10le` → true alpha channel + 10-bit color. Sized for editor ingest (Premiere, Final Cut Pro, DaVinci Resolve)" (`@hyperframes/producer`, the `format` doc comment in `dist/services/renderOrchestrator.d.ts`; the README table says "True alpha + 10-bit"). The file is 10-bit, but what goes into it is an 8-bit screenshot widened by the encoder: the two extra bits hold no information.

On a plain composition that costs something an editor or colourist will see after a strong lift of the shadows: **blurred shadows and glows show contour rings** (Chrome does not dither them), and **CSS gradients show a fine dither pattern** (Chrome does dither those, so they do not band hard, but the dither is the only thing standing in for the missing bits). Details and numbers below. It does not matter for web delivery.

I would ask for two things: **(a)** a sentence in the `mov` description and the render docs saying the ProRes output carries the 8-bit capture, and **(b)** your view on an opt-in improvement for ProRes output: a cheap deband step (which visibly smooths the rings, with a cost on steep gradients), or a higher-precision capture (I tested supersampling and report where it works and where it does not). I can send a PR for either, if you tell me which direction you prefer.

## What the code does in 0.8.140 (from the published dist files)

- Frames are Chrome screenshots: `Page.captureScreenshot` as PNG (`@hyperframes/engine/dist/services/screenshotService.js`; the render log of a `mov` says `needsAlpha: true`). The BeginFrame and drawElement routes also return 8-bit images. `alphaBlit.d.ts` on `decodePng`: "Chrome's Page.captureScreenshot always emits this format" (RGBA, 8-bit per channel).
- `@hyperframes/engine/dist/services/chunkEncoder.js`, `getEncoderPreset`: `mov` → `codec: "prores"`, `preset: "4444"`, `pixelFormat: "yuva444p10le"`. `streamingEncoder.js`: the ProRes branch is `-c:v prores_ks -profile:v <preset> -vendor apl0 -pix_fmt <pixelFormat>`, fed PNG through `image2pipe`.
- A 16-bit input exists: `rawInputFormat: "rgb48le"` (set in the layered compositor, `producer/dist/index.js`, which runs for HDR content and also for SDR compositions with shader transitions, `shouldUseLayeredComposite`). Even there the DOM layers enter at 8 bits: `alphaBlit.js` builds a 256-entry LUT per transfer function (`lut[i] = i * 257` for sRGB; "sRGB 8-bit value → HDR 16-bit signal value" for HDR). `mov` cannot use the HDR route at all: the `format` comment says alpha output disables HDR.
- Motion blur averages N samples per frame (`engine/dist/services/motionBlur.js`, `MotionBlurAccumulator`): float32 premultiplied sums ("far more precisely than the 1/255 quantum the result is rounded to"), and `finish()` rounds them into a `Uint8Array` before encoding. So even an average of 16 captures is rounded back to 8 bits before a 10-bit encoder sees it.

So a ProRes file from an ordinary composition holds 8-bit levels in a 10-bit container.

## What I measured

Composition (attached, 1920x1080, 1 s, no media, no scripts): three 640x1080 panels: **A** `linear-gradient(180deg, #0b1d3a, #1e3c72)`, **B** `radial-gradient(circle farthest-corner at center, #3a3a3a 0%, #101010 60%, #060606 100%)`, **C** a `box-shadow` glow (`0 0 160px 70px rgba(255,150,70,.42)`) on a dark ground. Rendered with the producer's programmatic API (`render.mjs`):

```js
createRenderJob({ fps: { num: 30, den: 1 }, quality: "high", format: "mov" })   // @hyperframes/producer 0.8.140, executeRenderJob(job, projectDir, out)
```

I decoded frame 0 with ffmpeg to 10-bit planar RGB (the precision the encoder was given) and read the values back (`measure.mjs`). For A and B the ideal ramp is known exactly (CSS interpolates in sRGB codes, sampled at pixel centres), so `reference.mjs` draws it with ffmpeg's `geq` at 16 bits and encodes it with the same ProRes settings (`prores_ks`, 4444, `yuva444p10le`): "the same gradient rendered at 16 bits by a non-Chrome reference". A control quantises the same drawing to 8 bits first (`reference.mjs <out> 8`).

**Blurred shadows are not dithered.** `glow-gain4-capture_debanded.png` (left: the glow panel of the capture, right: the same after the deband step of option (b) below) is shown after a x4 gain on the code values (a strong shadow lift), at 8 bits, 1:1. On the left: concentric contour rings in the falloff. Along the glow's left falloff (180 pixels, row 540) the green channel takes 75 distinct codes and the values form clean stairs, the longest flat run being 8 pixels. (Both halves show a vertical seam about 500 pixels into the panel: a Chrome tile seam of 11 codes, about 3 levels, at x = 1779 of that row; it is a rasterisation seam, not a bit-depth effect.) I have no ideal reference for a blur, so I report the crop and the codes, not an error.

**CSS gradients are dithered.** Along the vignette (centre to bottom edge, 540 pixels), green channel, 10-bit codes; "fill" is distinct codes divided by the span they cover (1.0 = every code used):

| frame | distinct codes (fill) | largest difference to the 16-bit reference, 10-bit codes | share of pixels on the 8-bit grid |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ProRes from the HyperFrames capture | 139 (0.71) | 4 | 0.47 |
| the same drawing quantised to 8 bits (control) | 72 (0.37) | 3 | 0.46 |
| the same gradient drawn at 16 bits (reference) | 190 (0.97) | 0 | 0.20 |

"Share of pixels on the 8-bit grid": the panel is neutral, so a pixel's luma code is `Y = 64 + 876·v/255` for an 8-bit level `v`; this is the share of the panel's pixels whose `Y` lies within ±0.1 of a whole level. Data with real 10-bit values lands there by chance, 20 % of the time (the reference does); an 8-bit signal reads higher but not 1.0, because one level is 3.435 luma codes and rounding to a whole code moves it off the grid (the plain 8-bit control reads 0.46). The capture matches the control (0.47 vs 0.46), not the reference. The sky (panel A) agrees: green channel, capture 120 codes and a largest difference of 5 codes to the reference (control 72 codes and 3; reference 126 codes). Full tables, all channels: `results/`.

What the capture's values look like (green, vignette, 16 pixels down the column x = 960 from y = 700): `160 160 157 160 157 159 156 156 157 156 156 156 153 156 153 155`, against the 16-bit reference `161 161 160 160 159 158 158 158 157 157 156 156 156 155 155 154`. The capture alternates between neighbouring 8-bit levels in an ordered pattern: Chrome dithers CSS gradients. That is why it has *more* distinct codes than the control, and why its error is larger than plain 8-bit quantisation: dither trades band edges for noise. After a x4 gain on the code values the pattern is a fine two-pixel checkerboard that is visible in a dark vignette and absent in the reference: `vignette-dark-4x-capture_supersampled_reference.png` (left the capture, right the 16-bit reference, the middle one is described below; each enlarged 4x with nearest-neighbour).

## Why anyone would need it

ProRes is chosen for the handoff to an editor or colourist and for archival masters, and the `mov` description targets exactly that. Those users lift shadows, add exposure, push curves or apply a LUT on the file, and CSS gradients, blurs, shadows, vignettes and fades are exactly the content with smooth ramps. At normal brightness the dither hides the problem; after a strong lift it shows as a dither texture (gradients) or contour rings (blurs and shadows). The docs promise 10-bit colour: the samples are 10-bit, the levels are 8-bit.

## What would help

**(a) Document it**: a sentence in the `mov` description, the README table and the render docs that ProRes output carries the 8-bit capture (10-bit only in the container). Zero risk.

**(b) A deband step, opt-in, for ProRes output.** The cheap thing that exists: ffmpeg's `deband` on the capture before the ProRes encode (`deband.mjs`, three settings, run on the decoded 10-bit frame). It is mixed. On the glow it visibly smooths the rings (right half of `glow-gain4-capture_debanded.png`): along the falloff the longest flat run drops from 6 / 8 / 10 pixels (R / G / B) to 4 / 4 / 4, and the fill rises from 0.42 / 0.45 / 0.76 to 0.52 / 0.73 / 0.92 (setting c; the other two settings give 0.50–0.55 / 0.73–0.75 / 0.94–0.96). On the steep dark vignette it hurts: the largest difference to the 16-bit reference rises from 4 to 7 (setting c), 11 and 15 codes, because it blurs a steep ramp; the sky improves by at most one code. It interpolates between levels, which is right for a soft falloff and wrong for a steep ramp, so it would have to be opt-in and tuned.

**(c) A higher-precision capture, opt-in: your view?** I do not know the best route and would defer to you: I do not know whether Chrome can rasterise ordinary DOM content into a deeper surface. Two routes I can see in the code, one of them tested:

- *Keep the average at 16 bits for motion blur.* The accumulator already sums in float and rounds in `finish()`. Returning 16-bit output for ProRes would carry whatever sub-level information 16 dithered captures contain. I have not tested it.
- *Supersample.* I tested the cheapest version available today: render at 2x device scale (`outputResolution: "landscape-4k"`, `render.mjs ... --resolution landscape-4k`) and downscale to 1920x1080 in 16 bits (`supersample.mjs`: ffmpeg `scale=…:flags=area` on `gbrp16le`, so each output pixel averages four captured pixels), then the same ProRes encode. Vignette, same table:

| frame | distinct codes (fill) | difference to the reference, 10-bit codes | share on the 8-bit grid |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| capture at 2x, averaged in 16 bits | 192 (0.99) | 2 | 0.20 |

  The values are off the 8-bit grid (0.20, the chance level, as for the reference), the codes fill the span, the error halves, and the enlarged crop (middle panel of the three-panel image) is as smooth as the reference. The sky improves the same way (largest difference 2 to 4 codes instead of 5 to 6). So the dither Chrome applies to gradients does carry the missing bits, and averaging recovers them. **But it does not help the blurs, which are the worse case:** at 2x device scale Chrome (software GL) drew the blurred shadow with visible rectangular tile seams (on the 4K row 1080 the green channel jumps by 36 codes, about 9 levels, at x = 2795 and again, downwards, at x = 3557; the 1x capture has one seam of 11 codes) and a shorter falloff than at 1x, so supersampling through `outputResolution` is not safe for large blurs. I did not investigate why. It also costs more capture work: 30 frames of this static composition took 17 s at 2x device scale against 6.7 s at 1x here (software GL, one machine).

## I can send a PR

I am happy to send a PR for (a), and for (b) or (c) if you tell me which direction you prefer (an opt-in deband step, the motion-blur average, supersampling for the content it suits, or something you know about Chrome that I do not). The sketch, not implemented:

- **Where.** The pieces exist: `outputResolution` already scales the capture by `deviceScaleFactor`; `decodePng` in the engine decodes the 8-bit frames; `MotionBlurAccumulator` already holds a float sum; the streaming encoder takes raw 16-bit frames (`rawInputFormat`, today `rgb48le` without alpha, from the layered compositor) and has a ProRes branch. New: a 16-bit RGBA path to the encoder (`rgba64le`, alpha-weighted averaging, since `mov` carries alpha), fed either by `finish()` or by a `k×k` block average of a supersampled capture; for the deband option, an ffmpeg `deband` filter on the encoder's input chain for ProRes only.
- **Opt-in.** A new optional render setting (for example `precision: "high"` or `deband: true`), ignored unless the output is `mov`, off by default, changing nothing when absent: the default path stays byte-identical.
- **Tests.** (1) With the setting off, a render of the existing regression compositions is byte-identical to before (hash of the frames or of the output, whatever your render regression harness already compares; I have not read it, so I would follow its conventions). (2) With it on, a synthetic gradient composition is compared with its analytic 16-bit ramp by PSNR and by distinct-code count, as in the attached scripts, and must improve over the 1x capture. (3) A unit test of the average on synthetic buffers, including an alpha edge.
- **What I would not change.** The default capture path and output bytes, the HDR route, video and audio handling, the Chrome launch flags and GPU/software mode, `h264`/`h265`/`webm` outputs, and the public `RenderConfig` for anyone who does not set the new field.

## Limits, and what I did not test

- This does not matter for web delivery. Scope it to ProRes (and any other mastering-oriented output).
- One machine, one Chrome (154.0.8037.92 headless shell, software GL, screenshot capture), HyperFrames 0.8.140, one composition, frame 0 of a static render. I did not test Linux, the BeginFrame or drawElement routes (all return 8-bit images, per the code), a GPU-backed Chrome, `png-sequence`, `mp4`/`webm`, ProRes profiles other than 4444, or real footage; and I did not check whether the dither pattern differs between Chrome versions.
- I do not claim banding is visible at normal brightness: the dither hides it for gradients. The claim is about headroom after a strong lift, and about the description of the format. "A x4 gain on the code values" is a strong lift (more than two stops of light at mid levels), not a calibrated exposure change.
- `mov` cannot use the HDR route (alpha disables it), so HDR does not help here.
- My readings of the code come from the published `dist` files of 0.8.140, not from the TypeScript sources.

## Reproduction

`npm i @hyperframes/producer@0.8.140`, ffmpeg and Node 22+ on the PATH; the attached folder holds everything (relative paths only):

```
node render.mjs capture.mov                 # 30 frames; composition/index.html (data-no-timeline: it has no timeline, which the producer would otherwise poll for 45 s)
node reference.mjs reference.mov            # ffmpeg only: the same A and B panels drawn at 16 bits
node reference.mjs control8.mov 8           # the control: the same drawing quantised to 8 bits
node measure.mjs capture.mov "capture" --ref reference.mov --crops crops
node render.mjs capture4k.mov --resolution landscape-4k       # the same composition at 2x device scale
node supersample.mjs capture4k.mov supersampled.mov && node measure.mjs supersampled.mov "2x averaged" --ref reference.mov --crops crops
node deband.mjs capture.mov debanded && node measure.mjs debanded-c.mov "deband c" --ref reference.mov --crops crops    # settings a, b and c
# the two crops of the issue: capture | 2x averaged | reference, and capture | debanded
ffmpeg -i crops/vignette-dark-zoom4x-gain4-capture.png -i crops/vignette-dark-zoom4x-gain4-2x-averaged.png -i crops/vignette-dark-zoom4x-gain4-reference.png -filter_complex hstack=inputs=3 vignette-dark-4x-capture_supersampled_reference.png
ffmpeg -i crops/glow-gain4-capture.png -i crops/glow-gain4-deband-c.png -filter_complex hstack=inputs=2 glow-gain4-capture_debanded.png
```

(`measure.mjs` names a crop after its label: `capture`, `2x averaged`, `deband c`; the vignette crop is the dark part of panel B enlarged 4x with nearest-neighbour, the glow crop is panel C 1:1, both after a x4 gain on the code values.) `render.mjs` uses the signature in the installed `renderOrchestrator.d.ts` (`executeRenderJob(job, projectDir, outputPath)`); the README example for 0.8.140 shows a different shape. If no Chrome is installed the producer downloads one; I pointed `PRODUCER_HEADLESS_SHELL_PATH` at a headless shell I already had, so nothing was fetched.

title: fix(ci): catalog publishing skips runs whose only change is vector noise
body:
## What

"Publish catalog" on main stops failing with HTTP 422 "No commits between main and bot/catalog-publish", and stops opening pull requests whose only change is float noise in `local-vectors.bin`. It has failed on 9 of the last 12 main pushes, including the v0.8.147 release merge.

## Why it failed

Regenerating the catalog rewrites `local-vectors.bin` with tiny float differences. `sameVectors` already treats those as equal, but `publish()` only cleared when zero files changed, so a noise-only run was treated as a real publication. That broke in two ways:

1. **Branch missing.** Branches are deleted on merge, so after a publish PR merges, the next noise-only run commits the noise and opens a PR. That is how #5435 came to change only `local-vectors.bin` (+0/-0).
2. **Branch is plain main.** When that PR is closed, the branch is reset to main. On the next noise-only run, `keptSnapshotBase` sees no generated difference and opens a PR from a branch with no commits of its own, and GitHub answers 422.

Signature in the failing logs: `Catalog publication: 1 files, 1 signed commit batches.`, followed by the 422.

## How

`publish()` now decides "nothing to publish" by comparing the regenerated catalog with main through the existing `sameGenerated` check (vector noise counts as equal), instead of counting changed files. A noise-only run takes the same path as a no-change run: close any open publish PR and move the branch to main. Real changes, including real vector changes, publish as before.

## Test

Three new cases in `scripts/catalog-publication.test.mjs`:
- Noise over a standing branch already in main: the only write is the branch reset.
- Noise after the branch was deleted: no writes at all.
- Vectors that point elsewhere than main's: the run still publishes.

Results:
- 24/24 pass, 3 runs in a row.
- With main's `publish-catalog.mjs`, both noise cases fail (22 pass, 2 fail).
- With the check forced to always clear, the "still publishes" case fails (with 6 existing publish tests).
- `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint` and `fallow audit --base origin/main` are clean.

Known and left alone: on a noise-only run, the log still prints "Catalog publication: 1 files" before "No unpublished catalog changes", and `--dry-run` stops before the new check.

Follow-up worth doing separately: the "nothing to publish" decision now uses `sameGenerated`'s tree diff, while the publish list still comes from `catalogChanges`. CI's fresh checkout keeps the two in agreement. Deriving both from one diff would leave a single owner.

title: fix(registry): clear the product-promo example's lint errors
body:
## What

Clears the four `gsap_css_transform_conflict` lint errors in the `product-promo` example (`registry/examples/product-promo/compositions/scene2-4-canvas.html`). Rendered frames don't change.

## Why

`hyperframes init --example product-promo` gives a project that fails its own `hyperframes lint`:

```
✗ scene2-4-canvas.html:525 gsap_css_transform_conflict: ".dragged-card" has CSS `transform: scale(0.9)` …
✗ scene2-4-canvas.html:539 gsap_css_transform_conflict: ".stamped-cards" has CSS `transform: translate(-50%, -50%)` …
✗ scene2-4-canvas.html:545 gsap_css_transform_conflict: ".checkmark" has CSS `transform: scale(0)` …
✗ scene2-4-canvas.html gsap_css_transform_conflict: ".web-frame, .cursor, .dragged-card, .stamped-cards, …" …
◇ 4 error(s), 0 warning(s)
```

Because a lint error switches off the browser audits, `hyperframes check` on this example also reports "Browser session never ran" and `0/0 text checks`. Anyone who starts from it gets no layout or contrast feedback.

## Related work

## What

`skills/embedded-captions/scripts/hf-cli.cjs` gains a launcher of last resort: a new `standalone-cli.cjs` beside it that runs the published CLI through `npx hyperframes@<version>`, the same way `skills/hyperframes/scripts/plugin-cli.mjs` does for plugin installs. `HYPERFRAMES_CLI_VERSION` pins the version (default `latest`). `skills-manifest.json` is regenerated for the changed skill.

## Why

A skills-only install (`npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`, or `hyperframes skills`, landing in `.agents/skills/`) ships no plugin manifest and no built `packages/cli/dist/cli.js`. In that layout `hfCli()` throws `HyperFrames CLI unavailable`, so `matte.cjs`, `transcribe.cjs` and `render-and-composite.sh` cannot start. `plugin-cli.mjs` cannot stand in because it needs a manifest to pin a version. The only workarounds were a built source checkout via `HYPERFRAMES_ROOT`, or installing the plugin instead of the skills.

Found while vendoring the skills into a repo shared by Claude Code, Codex and Copilot, where the plugin route only covers one agent.

## Related work

No existing issue found for this. Tiny self-contained correction.

## How

- `hf-cli.cjs`: after every existing lookup fails (explicit checkout, `HYPERFRAMES_ROOT`, plugin manifest, skill-tree checkout, `~/Downloads/hyperframes`), return `standalone-cli.cjs` if it exists, else throw as before. Plugin installs and checkout users resolve exactly as before; the manifest branch still comes first.
- `standalone-cli.cjs`: exports `invocation(args, env, platform, node)` mirroring `plugin-cli.mjs`, including the Windows `npx-cli.js` lookup, and when run as a script spawns it with inherited stdio and exits with the child's status. Sets `HYPERFRAMES_SKIP_SKILLS=1` and `HYPERFRAMES_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` so a CLI call from inside a skill never re-installs skills or nags.

A hermetic standalone layout (launcher three levels below a manifest-less root, `HOME` without a checkout) resolves to the fallback; `HYPERFRAMES_ROOT` still wins; `invocation()` builds the npx command and honours the version pin.

title: fix(skills): measure embedded-captions audio volume before removing the scratch file
body:
## What

`skills/embedded-captions/scripts/transcribe.cjs` now runs the no-speech volume probe (`meanVolumeDb`) before it deletes the scratch `audio.mp3`, not after.

## Why

When a project has no `audio.mp3`, the script extracts a scratch copy from the source and removes it once transcription finishes, so a stray file can't make lint call the render silent. The no-speech guard then ran `meanVolumeDb(audio)` on that already-deleted path. ffmpeg could not open it, the probe returned `null`, and the `meanDb != null && meanDb < -45` check never fired. On a silent clip, Whisper's confident hallucination (e.g. the whole clip as "Thank you.") therefore passed with no `NEAR-SILENT AUDIO` warning. That is exactly the case the guard exists for, and it is the default path for a fresh project.

Projects that already had an `audio.mp3` were unaffected, because the file is not scratch and is never deleted.

## Related work

No existing issue found. Tiny self-contained correction. Independent of #5482, which touches a different file in the same skill.

## How

The probe moves above the cleanup and its result is kept in `meanDb`. The warning still prints in the same place, after the transcript is written, so output order is unchanged.

## Test plan

It fails before this change and passes after; the two existing cases still pass (3/3). It needs ffmpeg, which the `Test: skills` job already installs.

title: embedded-captions: occlusion gate records PASS when check-occlusion times out before its verdict
body:
## Bug

In `skills/embedded-captions/scripts/render-and-composite.sh`, the occlusion + overflow gate runs `check-occlusion.cjs` under a watchdog. When the watchdog fires because **no verdict was printed within 150 s** (analysis stuck, not the known sharp/libvips teardown hang), the kill branch still sets:

```bash
if grep -q 'cap(s) FAIL' "$OCC_LOG"; then OCC_RC=2; else OCC_RC=0; fi
```

The incomplete log has no `cap(s) FAIL` line, so `OCC_RC=0`. The gate then appends `occlusion+overflow PASS` to `_gates.txt` and the render continues, even though the analysis never completed. It also logs the misleading "hung after verdict (sharp teardown)" message.

The `verdict_at` marker (set when the `[v2] … word-fail≥` header appears) already distinguishes the two cases, but the kill branch does not consult it.

## Reproduction

Extract the gate block (the `if [[ -f "$PROJECT/plan.json" && -d "$PROJECT/frames_fg" ]]` … `fi` section) into a harness, lower `occ_t0 > 150` to `> 4`, and stub `check-occlusion.cjs` with a process that never prints, e.g. `setInterval(() => {}, 1000);`. On current `main` the harness exits 0 and `_gates.txt` reads `occlusion+overflow PASS`.

## Suggested fix

Treat a pre-verdict timeout as a failed gate, keeping the post-verdict teardown tolerance and the existing `OCCLUSION_SKIP=1` override:

```diff
       kill -9 "$OCC_PID" 2>/dev/null
+      if [[ -z "$verdict_at" ]]; then
+        # No verdict: the analysis never finished, so it cannot count as a pass.
+        OCC_RC=3
+        echo "[render] occlusion gate timed out before its verdict — killed; analysis incomplete (rc=3)" >&2
+        break
+      fi
       if grep -q 'cap(s) FAIL' "$OCC_LOG"; then OCC_RC=2; else OCC_RC=0; fi
```

Checked in the same harness with stub analyzers:

| Scenario | Current `main` | With the fix |
|---|---|---|
| Hangs before any verdict | PASS (wrong) | aborts, rc 3 |
| Verdict, no FAIL, then teardown hang | PASS | PASS |
| Verdict + `cap(s) FAIL`, then hang | aborts, rc 2 | aborts, rc 2 |
| Pre-verdict timeout with `OCCLUSION_SKIP=1` | PASS (wrong) | continues, recorded as OVERRIDDEN |

No permanent test is included: the skill has no harness for its shell scripts, and a fast test would need the 150 s budget to be configurable. Happy to open a PR with or without that if useful.

Found by automated review while vendoring the skills into a downstream repository (related: #5482, #5483).

title: feat(registry): add filmed-screen component
body:
## What

A new registry component, `filmed-screen`. It films a live-DOM scene the way a phone camera films a monitor:

- a tilted screen plane in perspective, with a slow handheld drift and a push-in per shot;
- depth of field that follows an element you name (36-tap golden-angle bokeh, highlights weighted);
- chromatic fringing toward the edges, LED sub-pixels, bloom, vignette, grain;
- a 5-colour palette per shot (or true colour), with an optional hue-preserving invert so light pages read as dark screens;
- shots that glide into each other (camera, grade and colour mode ease over `glide` seconds), or cut with a horizontal tear when a shot asks for `transition: "cut"`;
- focus that racks instead of snapping: the focus box is a Hann-weighted average of where it was over the last `rack` seconds, so a new target eases in on an S-curve. It is a pure function of time, so any seek order renders the same frame.

The element in focus stays legible: inside its box the pass turns off blur, LED-cell snapping and fringing, and the camera look fades back in over ~160 px around it. There are no overlays; the only thing on screen is the author's scene.

The shader is a port of the virtual-camera pass in [ff-tracking](https://github.com/mrsarac/ff-tracking) (`lens.sksl`, built on fframes), with one change to its maths: the bokeh average weights each colour channel by its own sample. The original weights all three by the green sample, which tints blurred texture green; its thermal palette hides that, a grey one shows it.

## The demo

Three scenes in the style of other compositions, a code editor typing a line, an analytics card counting up with a bar chart, and a chat thread, cross-fade inside one filmed screen. Each gets its own shot and grade (amber, true colour, night blue); the camera glides between them and racks focus to whatever just changed.

## How it plugs in

Paste-in snippet, like `motion-blur` and `grain-overlay`. The author puts their scene inside a static `<canvas layoutsubtree>` and lists shots:

```js
HFFilmedScreen.mount({
  canvas: ".hf-filmed-screen",
  shots: [
    { until: 3, palette: [...5 hex], tilt: [0.16, -0.22, 0.03], zoom: [1.0, 1.2], blur: 1.0,
      focus: (t) => document.getElementById(t < 1.4 ? "title" : "sub") },
    { until: 6, palette: null, focus: (t, local) => tiles[Math.min(2, local | 0)] },
  ],
});
```

Each frame it reads the focus element's box from the live DOM in `__hf_page_composite_prepare`, then captures with `drawElementImage` and shades in `__hf_page_composite_resolve`, the same handshake `data-vfx-chain` uses, composed with any prior owner. Shot times come from the owning composition's timeline, so it works inside a `data-composition-src` sub-composition. A plain canvas (p5, three.js) can be passed instead and is sampled directly.

Why not a `<template data-slot>` primitive like `ascii-render-pass`: the point is the live DOM. Focus follows elements as they animate and video plays through it, which a once-rasterized slot cannot do.

## Verified (CLI 0.8.147, renderer Chrome 152)

- `node scripts/lint-registry-items.mjs filmed-screen`: 0 errors.
- `bun run check:catalog-drift`: passes; the catalog page generates (`/catalog/components/filmed-screen`). Generated files are not committed.
- The demo, as a composition: `check` passes (0 layout issues, 27/27 text checks WCAG AA), `snapshot` and full `render` correct, screenshot capture.
- Inside a sub-composition starting at 1 s: `snapshot` and `render` correct; frames match the root render shifted by 1 s.
- Without HTML-in-Canvas (`drawElementImage` removed): the scene is moved back into the page and renders unfilmed, with one console warning.
- Earlier versions of the same pass, rendered on three existing projects (DOM with `<video>`, a light editorial page, a p5 canvas), were deterministic: 180/180 byte-identical frames across two renders.
- Not verified: `hyperframes add filmed-screen` end to end, since `add` reads from `main`.

## Things found while building it, worth knowing outside this component

- **Inside a sub-composition, `window` is a Proxy that returns functions bound.** The compiler runs sub-composition scripts with a scoped `window`, and reading `window.__hf_page_composite_prepare` back through it never equals the function you assigned. An "is this still my hook?" check therefore re-wraps on every seek, and a wrapper that reads a shared `prior` variable ends up calling itself: `Maximum call stack size exceeded` in snapshot/render, while preview is fine. This component installs engine hooks on `globalThis`. Anything else that owns the composite protocol from a sub-composition is exposed to the same thing.
- **`__hf.seek` is an accessor that wraps whatever is assigned**, so a marker property on a wrapper never survives; a hooker that polls for the seek functions must track what it hooked separately.
- **`check` reports filmed text as occluded.** The layout audit honours `data-layout-allow-occlusion` on the text element only (the contrast audit uses `closest`), and text inside a `canvas[layoutsubtree]` is never painted directly. The component stamps the attribute on the scene's elements at mount; a follow-up could have the audits skip `canvas[layoutsubtree]` descendants instead, which would also cover `data-vfx-chain` scenes.

## Costs and limits

- Compositions that declare a `layoutsubtree` canvas render with screenshot capture on one worker, so this is slower than drawElement capture.
- `.hf-filmed-screen-scene` needs an explicit pixel size; `inset: 0` inside a layoutsubtree canvas measures 0×0.
- Elements added to the scene after mount are not stamped for the occlusion audit.

title: fix(studio): an edit the history could not record says why in the log
body:
## What changes

When Studio saves an edit but its history server refuses to record it as the person's undo step, the console line now starts with `[history]` and carries the HTTP status (0 when the server could not be reached):

`[history] 409: "Move clip" was not recorded as your edit: <server reason>`

Before, the line started with the edit's label, so a host that only forwards known tags (HyperFrames Desktop's error reporting keeps a fixed tag list, which already has `history`) reported it as a bare "Error". With the tag a host can forward the line, and with the status it can tell a refusal from an unreachable server once its own filter reads the status. Behaviour is unchanged: the edit still lands as an outside change, as before.

title: fix(skills): reject occlusion timeout before verdict
body:
## What

Abort the embedded-captions occlusion/overflow gate when its analysis watchdog expires before a verdict is printed. An incomplete analysis no longer records `occlusion+overflow PASS` or allows rendering to continue without an explicit override.

## Why

A hanging analyzer produces no `cap(s) FAIL` line. The watchdog treated that absence as success even when the analyzer had never reached its verdict, silently bypassing the layout gate and misreporting the timeout as a sharp teardown hang.

## Related work

Fixes #5485.

No overlapping implementation PR was found in the open inventory or searches for #5485 and occlusion. #5482 and #5483 address separate embedded-captions CLI/audio concerns; they are not changed here.

## How

Use the existing `verdict_at` marker to distinguish an analysis timeout from a post-verdict teardown hang. A timeout without a verdict sets `OCC_RC=3`, emits an analysis-incomplete diagnostic, and enters the existing abort/`OCCLUSION_SKIP=1` handling. The render script still exits 2 when the gate aborts. Watchdog budgets and post-verdict pass/fail interpretation are unchanged.

The new Node tests execute the production shell gate against controlled analyzer processes. Only the test harness advances Bash's clock, in ten-second steps for hanging analyzers; normal-exit fixtures use short real polling. No production timeout configuration or new dependency is introduced. The required pre-commit hook also updates only the embedded-captions fingerprint and file count in skills-manifest.json.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated: eight cases cover silent/partial pre-verdict timeouts, explicit override, passing/failing teardown hangs, normal passing/failing exits, and analyzer errors. The three timeout/override regressions fail on unchanged main. The revised suite passed 30 consecutive local runs and 20 independent reviewer runs on macOS Bash 3.2.
- [x] Manual testing performed: `bash -n`, `bun run build`, `bun run lint`, `bun run test:skills` (869 passed, 2 skipped), standalone skill import checks (2 passed), additional skills CI guards (17 passed), test reachability, formatting, comment checks and `git diff --cached --check`. Normal contributor pre-commit and commit-message hooks passed, and the commit is SSH-signed.

Validation limits: no full caption-video render or Linux execution was performed. title: Long renders with injected video frames: renderer memory grows by every frame and capture eventually stalls
body: ## Summary During a render, each capture worker's renderer process grows by roughly the size of every video frame injected into the page, and never gives the memory back. On a long render with large source videos the page eventually stops making progress. The workers stay alive and the job keeps reporting "stage still running", but no new frames are written. ## Environment - `@hyperframes/producer` 0.8.140 - Chrome for Testing headless shell 154.0.8037.92 (mac-arm64) - macOS 27, Apple silicon - Node 26.0.0, ffmpeg 9.0.2 ## Reproduction (attached: `make-media.sh`, `project/index.html`, `render.mjs`, `watch-rss.sh`) These scripts are a condensed standalone version of the setup we measured with; the numbers below come from the same composition shape. 1. `sh make-media.sh`: two synthetic 1920x1080 30 fps clips with film-like grain (no real media). Each extracted PNG frame is several megabytes, as camera footage is. 2. `project/index.html`: a 1920x588 composition holding the two clips side by side, each shown at 960x540, for 106.7 s (3,200 frames). 3. `node render.mjs`: `createRenderJob({ fps: 30, format: "png-sequence", workers: 2, videoFrameFormat: "png" })` and `executeRenderJob`. PNG extraction keeps the source frames lossless. The default extracts non-alpha videos as JPG, which makes each frame smaller, but each injected frame is still kept. 4. `sh watch-rss.sh` in a second terminal: the resident size of each Chrome process every 30 s. **Expected:** each capture worker's memory stays roughly flat. A frame injected for one capture is released once the next one replaces it, and the render finishes. **Actual:** each worker's renderer process grows by roughly the bytes of every frame injected, and never shrinks. The render slows down as memory grows. On a long render with camera-like footage the page runs out of memory before the end: the workers stay alive, checkpoints keep arriving, and no new frames are written. ## Measurements The same layout with two smaller synthetic sources (960x540 each, so a quarter of the bytes per frame), 6,180 frames, two workers (about 3,100 captures per page), completes. But each renderer process grows linearly over the run: | time | captures per page (approx.) | renderer RSS per worker | | --- | --- | --- | | 120 s | 650 | 646 MB | | 300 s | 1,550 | 1,231 MB | | 510 s | 3,000 | 1,539 MB | That is about 0.5 MB per capture for two 960x540 frames per capture. The browser and GPU processes stay flat (about 115-125 MB). One injected 960x540 video at the same frame count peaks near 250 MB, and a page with no video stays near 120 MB. With two 1920x1080 smooth synthetic sources (small PNG frames), 3,200 frames and two workers complete. The renderer reaches about 1,840 MB per worker at about 1,500 captures per page, about 1.1 MB per capture. With two 1920x1080 sources carrying film-like grain, each extracted PNG frame is several megabytes, as with real footage. The same 3,200-frame render does not finish within 12 minutes. Each renderer process grows to about 10.9 GB by only about 580 captures per page: about 17 MB retained per capture, roughly the two base64 data URIs injected per capture. Throughput falls to about 2.4 frames per second. | time | captures per page (approx.) | renderer RSS per worker | | --- | --- | --- | | 300 s | 150 | 4.4 GB | | 450 s | 300 | 7.4 GB | | 570 s | 440 | 9.2 GB | | 690 s | 580 | 10.9 GB | So the memory retained scales with the injected PNG bytes, and a long render with real footage runs the page out of memory long before it ends. ## What we read in the code (not verified by experiment) In the producer bundle, `createVideoFrameInjector` reads each frame file and turns it into a `data:image/png;base64,...` string. `createFrameSourceCache` is used without a `frameSrcResolver`: the render path passes only the cache limits. `injectVideoFramesBatch` then sets that string as the `src` of the sibling `` on every frame and awaits `img.decode()`. Each frame is a new, unique data URL. It looks as if the renderer keeps the decoded images (or the URL strings) for the page's lifetime. ## Possible directions - Serve frames by URL from the file server the render already runs (the cache already has a `frameSrcResolver` hook), so the page fetches small URLs and its image cache can evict. - Or release the previous frame's image explicitly before setting the next. - Or recycle a capture page after a number of captures. Any of these would let a long render with large injected videos finish in one pass. Our workaround meanwhile: render shorter frame ranges as separate renders and join their frames. We would be glad to send a pull request for whichever direction you prefer (serving frames by URL looks the smallest to us). What we are asking for is a fix, or a documented limit (frames or bytes per capture page). We are not asking for a rewrite.

title: docs(lint): add a reference page for every lint finding code
body:
## What

Adds `docs/reference/lint-rules.mdx` (859 lines, 12 groups): one `###` anchor section per lint finding code, each giving its severity, one sentence on what it catches, and how to fix it, grouped by the rule file the code comes from. Links it from the top of "What the Linter Catches" in `docs/packages/lint.mdx` and adds `reference/lint-rules` to the "Composition reference" group in `docs.json`.

## Why

`hyperframes lint` and `check` print finding codes, but the docs only describe categories — there is no per-code reference, so the user has only the message itself to go on. The codes live as `code: "..."` literals scattered across `packages/lint/src/rules/*.ts` (121 codes) plus 11 project-level codes in `packages/lint/src/project.ts`, `hyperframeLinter.ts` and `hevcPreviewLint.ts` that reach users through the same `lintProject` pipeline.

A note on the count in the issue: the issue's 120 comes from its own suggested grep, `code: "[a-z_]+"`. Exactly one code contains a digit (`base64_media_prohibited`), which that character class cannot match. With `code: "[a-z_0-9]+"` the count is 121 — and it was 121 with an identical set already at b20f3f7ad, the commit two minutes before the issue was filed, so nothing merged since.

## Related work

Fixes #5385. Claim: [comment on the issue](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/issues/5385#issuecomment-6121515593). No overlapping PR found (open-PR search returned nothing for this).

## How

- Every code gets a `### \`code\`` anchor section: severity, what it catches, and a fix. Content is drawn from the rule's own message and fixHint, then tightened into prose. The 11 project-level checks get the same treatment under "Project-level checks".
- Severities were read back from the source, including the conditional ones: four codes are "Error / warning" (severity depends on how the finding arises) and four structure checks are "Warning or error" (warning from the CLI, error when Studio lints the file it is editing).
- Discoverability: `docs.json` "Composition reference" group gains `reference/lint-rules`, and `docs/packages/lint.mdx` links to it from "What the Linter Catches".

## Test plan

Coverage (the issue's acceptance criterion):

- `git grep -hoE 'code: "[a-z_0-9]+"' -- 'packages/lint/src/rules/*.ts' ':!*.test.ts' | sort -u` → 121 unique codes; the 11 project-level codes come from `project.ts` / `hyperframeLinter.ts` / `hevcPreviewLint.ts`, zero overlap with the rules set.
- Looping over all 132 codes greping `^### \`code\`$` in `docs/reference/lint-rules.mdx` → 121/121 rule codes and 11/11 project codes hit, 0 missing.

Docs checks (the same commands `.github/workflows/docs.yml` runs, under `timeout 300` since they need more than the default 120 on this machine):

- `cd docs && npx mint validate` → exit 0, "success build validation passed".
- `cd docs && npx mint broken-links --check-redirects` → exit 0, "success no broken links found".

title: fix(engine): bound injected video frame resource retention
body: Long renders retain a new multi-megabyte image data URL for every injected video frame in Chrome, independently of the bounded Node LRU. Deliver extracted frame bytes through page-scoped CDP interception with `Cache-Control: no-store` instead. Only short synthetic URLs reach the DOM; frame responses bypass the HTTP connection pool used by source-video downloads. Release registered response bytes after each batch, including decode failures and hidden-video skips. The existing decoded `` remains available to canvas, color grading and GPU texture uploads. Caller-provided frame URLs pass through unchanged. This shared engine path covers local and distributed capture without restoring file-server frame requests. Capture-owned pages also cap Puppeteer's original CDP session's inspection response-body buffer at 32 MiB total / 16 MiB per resource, instead of Chrome's 200 MiB total default. Network events and error diagnostics remain enabled. The runtime getter is guarded because Puppeteer omits it from the public Frame types; if unavailable, capture continues with the no-store transport and the default inspection budget. Caller-owned pages are unaffected by this extra optimization. Closes #5492. Validation: - All engine tests: **2,231 passed, 3 skipped** (before the added cross-origin browser case); final focused run including capture setup/rollback: **108 passed**. The final test-only cleanup rerun passes all four setup/rollback cases. Browser cases ran on Chrome and chrome-headless-shell 152. - Regression witness failed on the original inline source path. Browser tests check PNG/JPEG pixels, PNG alpha, GPU texture upload, no-store responses, expired/failed-frame cleanup, external URL compatibility, and capture while six same-origin downloads remain blocked. The alpha/GPU case also runs from a fresh `about:blank` page; removing either the CORS response header or anonymous image mode fails this cross-origin case. Unit tests cover overlapping batches and protocol/init failures. - Actual producer smoke: two noisy **1920×1080** source videos, **1920×588** output, **2 workers**, PNG extraction and PNG-sequence output: **60/60 frames completed**, no capture retry or browser error. Fixture lint/browser check passed. A second instrumented producer run confirms the memory limit is applied to both actual capture workers. - Engine build/typecheck, changed-file lint/format and all commit hooks passed; fallow reports no new dead code, complexity or duplication. Memory probe (Chrome 152 on Linux, two noisy 960×540 frame images): | Path | Work completed | Active renderer RSS | | --- | --- | --- | | Original | 200 frame updates; screenshots every 20 | 122 → **1,841 MiB**, safety limit reached | | No-store transport | 1,000 frame updates and PNG captures | **840–894 MiB** after warmup; **849 MiB** at completion | | No-store + inspection buffer cap | 500 frame updates and PNG captures | **675–683 MiB** after warmup; **680 MiB** at completion | The no-store probe transferred 1,786 MiB of PNG bytes using 400 deterministic source files repeatedly and a fresh URL for every update. The optimized probe transferred a further 865 MiB of PNG bytes. The first captured PNG is byte-identical across all three paths. The lower inspection budget cuts about 20% from the no-store-only renderer footprint in this probe; throughput comparisons are not controlled because other verification ran concurrently. Chrome still warms its decoded-image cache; this removes cumulative inline-source retention rather than eliminating normal image-cache memory. The reported macOS/Chrome 154 environment has not been run locally.

title: fix(embedded-captions): treat pre-verdict occlusion timeout as a failed gate
body:
Fixes #5485

## Problem

In `skills/embedded-captions/scripts/render-and-composite.sh`, the occlusion + overflow gate runs `check-occlusion.cjs` under a watchdog. When the watchdog fires because **no verdict was printed within 150 s** (analysis stuck, not the known sharp/libvips teardown hang), the kill branch still sets `OCC_RC=0`, recording `occlusion+overflow PASS` even though the analysis never completed.

## Fix

Check `verdict_at` after the kill: if no verdict was printed, set `OCC_RC=3` and abort with a clear message. The post-verdict teardown tolerance and the `OCCLUSION_SKIP=1` override are unchanged.

## Testing

The fix matches the suggested diff in #5485. No permanent test is included (the skill has no harness for its shell scripts).

title: feat(registry): filmed-screen curves, orbits and follows typing by default
body:
## What

A follow-up to #5487. It adds four options to `filmed-screen`, retunes its defaults, and replaces the demo. The defaults were tuned on a white page, filmed the way Vox shoots screens.

| option | default | before |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vignette` | 1.0 | fixed 0.42 |
| `aberration` | 2.2× | fixed 1×, none on the focused text |
| `curve` | 0.15 | none |
| `led` | 0.45 | fixed 0.9 |
| `rack` | 0.3 s | 0.7 s |
| shot `blur` | 0.45 | 0.9 |
| shot `tiltTo` | = `tilt` | (new) |

- **Curve:** a barrel bend on the camera's view. It's normalised so the frame's corners stay in place: the middle swells toward the camera and straight lines bow outward, and the page edge never enters the shot. The vignette is computed before the curve, so it stays even.
- **Aberration:** a quarter of the fringing now stays on the focused text, so it still reads as glass. Blur and LED-cell snapping are still off there.
- **LED grid:** it now fades in only once a cell spans about 4 output pixels. Below that, on a light page, it aliased into strong moiré.
- **`tiltTo`:** the tilt eases from `tilt` to `tiltTo` across a shot. Two shots chained through a glide give one continuous orbit.
- **`rack` 0.3:** fast enough for focus to follow text as it's typed.

## The demo

A white search homepage for a made-up engine, "lumen", with its own wordmark and copy. It's a neutral brand, so nothing here imitates a real site. A query types letter by letter: the camera follows each new letter while it orbits from one side of the screen to the other, and earlier letters soften as it moves on. Everything runs on the defaults; the mount passes no effect options.

## Verified (CLI 0.8.147)

- `filmed-screen.test.mjs`: 6/6, including the composite co-owner test, the second-mount test and the test that the demo's pasted library matches the snippet.
- `lint-registry-items`, oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
- `check` passes on the demo: no layout issues and 67/67 text checks at WCAG AA. Decorative chrome that sat permanently in the vignette (top links and the footer) was removed, because the audit read its contrast after the lens.
- A full render: 8 s, no browser errors.

The catalog poster and video will be refreshed on the CDN from this demo.

title: fix(registry): clamp filmed-screen's curve and vignette
body:
Fix-forward from Rames's post-merge review of #5499 ([review](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/pull/5499#pullrequestreview-5495532750)).

- **`curve` clamped at 0.** A negative value samples outside the frame and folds over below about −0.32. A new test mounts with `curve: -1` and checks that the shader gets 0; it fails without the clamp.
- **Vignette factor clamped at 0** (`max(0.0, 1.0 - uVig * dot(v, v))`). Above `vignette` ≈ 1.11 it went negative in the corners.
- **README:** a "previous look" line with the values from before #5499 (`blur: 0.9`, `rack: 0.7`, `vignette: 0.42`, `aberration: 1`, `led: 0.9`, `curve: 0`). It notes that the LED fade-in threshold and the trace of fringing on the focused element are hard-coded and can't be restored by options.

- **Catalog page preview:** `registry-item.json` now sets `preview.video` and `preview.poster` (the CDN files). The catalog builds this item's payload as needing `canvas-draw-element`. With no recorded video it showed the flag notice, under a "Recorded preview" caption, with nothing playing, whatever the visitor's flags were. Regenerated locally, the page now gets `video=`/`poster=` instead of `needsFlag`; the generated files themselves are left to the publish bot.

The demo's output is unchanged: at the defaults neither clamp is reached (the 16:9 corner factor is about 0.10). `filmed-screen.test.mjs` passes 7/7, and lint-registry-items, oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
