title: docs(cli): say capture needs direct internet and ignores HTTPS_PROXY
body:
## What changes

The `capture` docs now say that capture needs direct internet access and does not use `HTTPS_PROXY` or `HTTP_PROXY`.

Since 0.8.164 (#5668), Chrome's traffic goes through capture's own proxy, which dials each checked public address directly. Where the only way out is a proxy (some sandboxes and corporate networks), every page fails with `net::ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED`, while `curl` through the same proxy succeeds.

## Why docs, not code

Routing capture through the environment's proxy would loosen the public-address guard #5668 added. The decision is to keep that guard and document the requirement.

## Verified

Reproduced in a network namespace whose only way out is an HTTPS proxy:

- `curl https://example.com` through the proxy: 200;
- `capture https://example.com` on 0.8.164 to 0.8.166: fails with `net::ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED`;
- the same capture on 0.8.163: succeeds, and the proxy logs Chrome's `CONNECT example.com:443`.

`format:check` passes.

title: feat(media-use): source sound effects from Openverse with the bundled library offline
body:
## What changes

Sound effects now come from [Openverse](https://openverse.org)'s free audio API (no key, mostly Freesound) instead of HeyGen's audio library, with the bundled 21-file library kept as the fallback. Both SFX paths route through it:

- **Skill engine** (`skills/media-use/audio/scripts/lib/sfx.mjs`, behind `audio.mjs` and every workflow's `fetch-sfx`): each cue is searched on Openverse first. A cue with no usable match falls back to the bundled file for that cue; once Openverse is offline, rate limited or erroring, every remaining cue in the run uses the bundled library. No match anywhere: skipped with an anomaly, never blocks a render. Volume stays at 0.35.
- **CLI resolver** (`hyperframes media-use resolve --type sfx`): the provider list is now `openverse.audio` then `bundled.sfx`. `--local-only` and `--provider bundled.sfx` never call Openverse. The HeyGen sound-effects provider, its install/update advisory on bundled hits and the sfx-specific "needs the heygen CLI" miss are gone. Music stays on HeyGen, untouched.
- **Hosts** get one entry point: `findSoundEffect(query, { hyperframesDir, sfxLibDir? })` in `skills/media-use/audio/scripts/lib/sfx.mjs` returns `{ sound: { file, source, duration_s, license?, credit? } | null, anomalies }`, with the file saved under the project's `assets/sfx/`.

## Licences and credits

`packages/cli/src/media-use/lib/openverse.mjs` owns the rule: only `cc0` and `by` (no NonCommercial, ShareAlike or NoDerivatives). Openverse is asked for `license=cc0,by` and each result's `license` field is checked again. The standalone skill gets a byte-identical copy through `scripts/generate-skill-module-copies.mjs`.

Each CC BY sound is written to a credits file in the project (`assets/sfx/CREDITS.md` from the engine, `.media/audio/sfx/CREDITS.md` from `resolve`), one line per file with Openverse's attribution text and the source page. Two `resolve` runs at once write that file under the project's media lock (`.media/.lock`, the one id allocation already takes), so neither drops the other's line. The standalone media-use copy of `manifest.mjs` carries the same lock helper, so the copy-parity test holds. The skill engine writes its credits synchronously in one process, so its writes cannot overlap. Openverse entries in `audio_meta.json` carry `license` and `credit`; the three workflow adapters pass both through.

## Ranking

One search per distinct effect name, 20 results. The pick keeps Openverse's relevance order, drops anything over 15 s or not mp3/wav/ogg/flac, adds a penalty per second past 4 s, and adds 2 positions for CC BY so CC0 wins when the two are close.

## Things to know

- Anonymous Openverse use is limited to 20 requests a minute and 200 a day (its `x-ratelimit-*` headers). A run with more than 20 distinct effects gets the bundled library for the rest.
- `category=sound_effect` returns nothing for common queries and `result_count` is capped at 240 for anonymous calls, so neither is used.
- The resolver's local media index step still runs after both providers miss, as before.

## Evidence

Live run of the engine on a fixture project with 5 named cues (`audio.mjs --only sfx`), all from Openverse:

| Cue | File | Licence | Length | Openverse title (creator) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| door knock | `assets/sfx/door-knock.mp3` | CC0 | 2.12 s | Door knocking (Angry).wav (Macif) |
| typewriter ding | `assets/sfx/typewriter-ding.wav` | CC0 | 1.06 s | 406243 stubb typewriter-ding-near-mono (_stubb) |
| thunder | `assets/sfx/thunder.mp3` | CC0 | 2.79 s | Thunder rumbling, underwater, outdoors (carroll27) |
| crowd cheer | `assets/sfx/crowd-cheer.mp3` | CC BY 3.0 | 3.70 s | small crowd cheering and clapping.wav (Tomlija) |
| heartbeat | `assets/sfx/heartbeat.mp3` | CC BY 4.0 | 0.26 s | Heartbeat. (urupin) |

The credits file it wrote:

```
# Sound effect credits

These sounds are licensed CC BY: credit them wherever the video is published.

- `assets/sfx/crowd-cheer.mp3`: "small crowd cheering and clapping.wav" by Tomlija is licensed under CC BY 3.0. To view a copy of this license, visit https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/. Source: https://freesound.org/people/Tomlija/sounds/99634
- `assets/sfx/heartbeat.mp3`: "Heartbeat." by urupin is licensed under CC BY 4.0. To view a copy of this license, visit https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Source: https://freesound.org/people/urupin/sounds/92036
```

A second live run (whoosh, ui click, glass shatter, camera shutter, cash register) also resolved 5 of 5 from Openverse, all CC0; ffprobe reads every file as audio of the stated length.

Fallback with the network cut (`unshare -rn`), cues whoosh, click, pop, chime, riser: 5 of 5 from the bundled library, one anomaly `Openverse unreachable (fetch failed): the remaining SFX cues use the bundled library`, exit 0. The CLI resolver offline: `bundled.sfx`, with `media-use: Openverse unreachable (fetch failed); using the bundled sound effects` on stderr. The CLI online for "crowd cheer": `openverse.audio`, licence `by`, and the credit line in `.media/audio/sfx/CREDITS.md`.

## Tests

Every test stubs the HTTP layer; none touches the network or waits on a timer. The spawned resolver tests stand Openverse in with a `--import` preload instead of a new setting. Three runs in a row, all exit 0:

| File | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/cli/src/media-use/lib/openverse.test.mjs` (new) | 11 passed |
| `packages/cli/src/media-use/resolve.test.mjs` | 62 passed |
| `packages/cli/src/media-use/lib/manifest.test.mjs` | 26 passed |
| `packages/cli/src/media-use/lib/registry.test.mjs` | 20 passed |
| `packages/cli/src/media-use/lib/heygen-cli.test.mjs` | 24 passed |
| `skills/media-use/audio/scripts/lib/sfx.test.mjs` | 11 passed |
| `skills/media-use/audio/scripts/audio.test.mjs` | 11 passed |
| `skills/faceless-explainer/scripts/audio.test.mjs` | 18 passed |
| `skills/product-launch-video/scripts/audio.test.mjs` | 22 passed |
| `scripts/check-media-use-copy-parity.test.mjs` | 3 passed |

Each of these breaks turned its test red, then was reverted: allowing `by-nc`; asking Openverse again after a 429; skipping the CLI credit write; putting the bundled library ahead of Openverse; dropping the per-cue bundled fallback; ranking by relevance alone. The new two-resolves-at-once test holds each run just after its credits read until both have read; with the credit write outside the media lock it fails 3 of 3 runs (one of the two lines survives).

`oxfmt`, `oxlint`, `gen-skills-manifest --check` and `generate-skill-module-copies --check` pass on the changed files.

title: perf(core): playback and jumps do only the work on screen
body:
## What changes for the user

Long films keep playing smoothly deep into the timeline, and a jump does less work before its frame shows. On a 9-minute test film with 512 clips and about 90 scene timelines, playback from 3:00 and from 8:00 held 46-56 fps in every run, against 8-46 fps before. Jumps do about 18% less main-thread work.

This PR is now only the playback and jump scheduling. The rest of what was folded in here moves back to its own PRs, so each one can be reviewed and reverted alone:
- Play puts a sped-up or looping video in place in one seek: #5800.
- Capture stills load only the media near their moment: #5787.
- Holding far scenes' scripts until the playhead nears (and its boot-order repairs): #5719.

The consolidated head is kept on the branch `perf/playback-consolidated-backup` (`cc0e77e4`).

## Why it was slow

Every frame did work for the whole film, not for what is on screen:

1. **Visibility pass.** It re-decided all 512 timed elements every frame.
2. **Scene timelines.** Every registered scene timeline was seeked every frame, even long after its clip had ended.
3. **Timeline registry check.** The registry signature was rebuilt over every timeline, up to three times per frame.
4. **Clip-list posts.** A full clip-list post (about 258 KB) went to Studio during playback, and Studio re-read it in full.
5. **Layer optimizer (the run-to-run swings).** The preview's layer optimizer re-walked whole scene groups each time the runtime marked a clip as coming up or hidden. It wrote a mark between style reads, so every read forced the page to restyle.

## What this PR does

1. **Visibility.** While playing, an element is decided again only when the playhead crossed one of its edges (start, end, look-ahead or release edge, or an edge of a timed ancestor), when a loop is near, or when a script changed its visibility. A jump, a backwards step or a timing change still runs the full pass: the frame on which the timing revision changes re-decides every element.
2. **Scene timelines.** A scene timeline already resting at the frame it would be seeked to is left alone.
3. **Registry check.** While playing, the timeline registry is checked on the existing playing-poll timer (once a second) instead of every frame. The tick reads the timing revision once and hands it to the media index and the timeline seek.
4. **Clip-list posts.** The runtime holds clip-list posts while playing and sends one when playback stops. Studio skips its DOM re-scan while the preview reports playing. Product effect, accepted: a track, label or z-index edited inside the page while it plays reaches the timeline on pause. The hold covers the whole post, so the same applies to everything that post carries: live root-duration growth, a late root-timeline rebind and the scene-swap repost. An embedded player and Studio show the previous duration and clip list until pause. The runtime's own clock is updated, so playback still ends at the right time.
5. **Layer optimizer.** It ignores the clip attributes the runtime toggles during playback; the runtime's own rules on them only hide things and never restack. It also decides every mark in a changed subtree before writing any.

Not needed: a design item excluding runtime media writes from the timing revision turned out to be a no-op. Those writes already run inside `withoutOwnTimingRecords`.


## A jump paints first

1. **The video is asked first.** A paused jump used to render the whole page at the target (every registered timeline, scene discovery, overlays) and only then set the on-screen video's time. Now the media sync runs first, so decoding overlaps the page work. Measured in the page: the video's time is set 2-4 ms after the jump reaches the runtime.
2. **The clip list is rebuilt after the frame lands.** A jump that mounts scenes near its target triggered a full clip-list rebuild (all clips, with computed-style reads up each clip's ancestors), twice per jump: once from the scene mount and once from the transport tick. It cost 90-430 ms per jump inside the seek. While a jump's seek completions are pending, `postTimeline` now holds the post and sends one after they settle and the frame paints. The hold applies only after a jump: at load, posts (and `window.__clipManifest`) land at once, and render capture is never held.

`seek-dispatch` gains two read-only helpers (`hasPendingSeekCompletion`, `seekCompletionsSettled`), so the hold never consumes a failure that `waitForSeekCompletion` reports.

## Tests

Each new test fails without its change.

- `init.playbackScope.test.ts`
  - Over a scripted 300-frame play, every clip's visibility matches its window, and frames that cross no edge decide nothing.
  - A finished scene is not seeked again.
  - The registry is checked at most 3 times in 40 frames.
  - No clip-list post while playing, one after pause.
  - A non-timeline registry entry doesn't throw.
  - A clip whose timing moves it onto the playhead mid-play (moved start, stretched duration) shows on the next frame. Re-checked on this head: removing the one-line fix fails exactly this test (1 of 6).
- `init.seekOrder.test.ts`
  - On a paused jump, the on-screen video's time is set before the page's timeline is seeked.
  - A jump with a pending completion posts no clip list until the completion lands, then posts exactly one.
  - With a completion pending but no jump, the post lands at once.
- `previewRasterHints.test.ts`: runtime clip toggles cause no style reads (0, against 163 without the change); no style read after the first mark write.
- `previewMessageRouter.test.ts`: no enrich while playing, one when stopped.
- `transportPark.test.ts`: the label/track/z-index test now expects the post on pause.

On this head, rebased on current main: core runtime suite exit 0, 2123 passed in 85 files; core typecheck exit 0; `previewMessageRouter.test.ts` exit 0, 1 passed.

## Measurement

These numbers come from the original runs of each part on its own base (#5741 for playback, #5754 for the jump). They have not been re-measured on this rebased head yet.

Setup: headless Chrome on a shared 8-core Linux box, Studio's own Play button, whole CLI builds swapped, served runtime checked by hash on every run, runs alternated.

| Run | 0:00 | 3:00 | 8:00 | Jumps, median / p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base (#5741) | 15-47 fps | 10.5-46 fps | 8.5-38 fps | 0.90-1.39 s / 1.24-2.11 s |
| playback part, 3 runs | 37.3-55.7 fps | 46.2-56.3 fps | 49.2-54.5 fps | 0.84-1.02 s / 1.25-2.18 s |

Jump part alone, 12 jumps per run: median 843-874 ms to 801-859 ms; CPU for 12 jumps 5.5 s to 4.4-4.8 s; playback fps unchanged.

## No visible change

Nothing on screen changes. The Studio diff is 6 lines in `previewMessageRouter.ts`: the timeline's DOM re-scan waits while the preview reports playing.

title: fix(cli): snapshot no longer transcodes every iPhone clip it never plays
body:
## What a user can do now

Snapshot a project full of iPhone clips (HEVC, 4K, long) in seconds. Before, a snapshot transcoded every one of those clips in full first and could run for many minutes.

## Why it was slow

`snapshot` served Studio's media proxies by default (`--proxy`, on unless turned off). Its page server therefore pre-warmed an H.264 copy of every browser-hostile clip as the page loaded, and HEVC counts as browser-hostile. A snapshot never shows those copies: every video frame it captures is extracted from the original with FFmpeg and injected into the page. So the transcodes were pure cost, scaling with the length and resolution of each clip, and several 4K clips meant several full 4K transcodes running beside the capture.

## The fix

`serveCapturePage` in `snapshot.ts` decides whether the snapshot page gets preview copies: only when `--proxy` is passed. `media.autoProxy` in `hyperframes.json` keeps controlling preview, play and the other surfaces, but no longer turns proxies on for snapshots. The media guide says so in one sentence.

## Before / After

Same fixture clips, same timestamps, wall time of `hyperframes snapshot`. Before is the current release with its default; after is the same release with proxies off, which is the path this change makes the default.

| Fixture | Before | After | Frames |
|---|---|---|---|
| one 13-minute 4K HEVC clip, `--at 5,390,775` (Apple Silicon) | 553 s, wrote a 10.6 GB `.transcode-cache`, 0 proxy requests | 19 s, no cache | identical |
| four 20 s 4K HEVC clips, all graded, one at 2x speed, plus a wav bed, `--frames 10` (Apple Silicon) | 93 s, 4 transcodes (956 MB) | 59 s | all 10 pixel-identical (PSNR inf) |
| one 6 s HEVC clip, `--at 1,3,5` (Linux, where Chrome cannot decode HEVC) | 34 s, page requested and waited for the copy | 19 s | all pixel-identical |
| a 9-minute project with 140 4K HEVC clips, cold cache (Linux, one run each) | frames written at about 50 s, then the CLI never exited: 16 background copies (3.2 GB of transcodes) kept it alive until a 900 s cap killed it | exits 0 in 111 s | not compared |

## Tests

- `snapshot.proxy.test.ts` starts the snapshot page server for a project whose `hyperframes.json` turns proxies on, with an HEVC clip: by default the page gets no media codec map (the step that pre-warms transcodes), a direct `?hf-proxy=h264` request answers 404, and no transcode is requested. With `--proxy`, the codec map is injected. Passing the old value through (the project setting) turns the default-case test red.
- `snapshot`, `snapshot.proxy` and `staticProjectServer` tests, three runs in a row on main. CLI typecheck clean.

## Rebased onto main

This was stacked on #5811 (`check` judges hostile video from originals), which closed without merging. Nothing here needed it: main's snapshot already paints every video frame from the original with FFmpeg. The rebase keeps only the snapshot change; `check` is untouched and still follows `media.autoProxy`.

title: refactor(core): one owner for the distributed fps set
body:
## What changed

The integer frame rates the distributed renderer (Lambda, Cloud Run) accepts were written out by hand in about 25 places: type unions, runtime checks, error messages, CLI help, harness gates and a test's own copy. Adding 25 in #5423 had to touch 28 files and still missed a few. They now come from one owner in `@hyperframes/core`, next to `Fps`:

```ts
export const DISTRIBUTED_FPS = [24, 25, 30, 60] as const;
export type DistributedFps = (typeof DISTRIBUTED_FPS)[number];
export function isDistributedFps(value: unknown): value is DistributedFps;
```

- **producer**: config validation, the plan v2 manifest reader, render request mapping, plan types and the parity and regression harnesses use the owner. Error messages are built from the constant.
- **aws-lambda / gcp-cloud-run**: the plan result `Fps` field derives from `SerializableDistributedRenderConfig["fps"]`.
- **cli**: `lambda` and `cloudrun` checks, `--fps` help text and the `data-fps` default read the owner. `readAllowedCompositionFpsFromDir` no longer takes an allowed list. Its test passed `[24, 30, 60]`, a stale copy without 25.
- **engine**: `EngineConfig.fps` and the snapshot validator still said `24 | 30 | 60`, so a distributed render that passed an engine config snapshot with fps 25 was refused. They now use the owner.

Core is the owner because it already owns `Fps`, and the CLI bundles it, as do engine and producer. The adapters see it through producer's types. No new dependency edges.

Error wording changes from "must be 24, 25, 30, or 60" to "must be one of 24, 25, 30, 60".

## What I measured

Ran each changed or covering test file on its own, with exit codes:

| File | Result |
|---|---|
| core `parseFps.test.ts` (new `isDistributedFps` cases) | exit 0 |
| engine `config.test.ts` (new snapshot fps cases) | exit 0 |
| cli `compositionFps.test.ts` (new 25 fps case) | exit 0 |
| producer `plan-parity-harness`, `planV2`, `regression-harness-distributed`, `renderRequest`, `regression-shard-plan` | exit 0, 6 / 62 / 18 / 20 / 21 pass, 0 fail |
| aws-lambda `validateConfig`, `renderToLambda` | exit 0, 36 / 11 pass |
| gcp-cloud-run `validateConfig`, `renderToCloudRun` | exit 0, 18 / 8 pass |

`tsc --noEmit` is clean in core, engine, producer, cli, aws-lambda and gcp-cloud-run.

Mutations:
- Owner changed to `[24, 30, 60, 50]`: all 13 files above fail, which shows every consumer reads the owner.
- Engine enum put back to the literal `[24, 30, 60]`: only "accepts every distributed fps, including 25" fails.

## What I did NOT exercise

- No cloud render. This is a type and validation refactor; the render path is unchanged.
- Studio's local render settings still offer 24 / 30 / 60. That is the in-process renderer, not the distributed set, so it stays out of this PR.
- The CLI still falls back to 30 without a warning when `data-fps` is outside the set (for example 50 or 30000/1001). That is a behaviour change and gets its own PR.

title: fix(cli): warn when a cloud render ignores the composition's fps
body:
## What changed

`hyperframes lambda render`, `lambda render-batch` and `cloudrun render` pick the composition's `data-fps` when `--fps` is not passed. When that rate is not one cloud renders support (for example `50` or `30000/1001`), they rendered at 30 fps without saying anything, so a 50 fps project came back at 30 fps with no hint why.

They still render at 30 fps, but now print a warning naming the declared rate, the supported set and `--fps`. The 30 fps default moved into the helper (`defaultCloudFps`), so the three call sites no longer each carry their own `?? 30`.

I chose a warning over an error so existing renders keep working; turning it into an error is a one-line change if that is preferred.

## What I measured

- `packages/cli/src/utils/compositionFps.test.ts`: exit 0, 15 passed. New cases: supported rates (24, 25, 30, 60) return themselves with no warning; 48, 50 and 30000/1001 return 30 and warn once naming the declared value; no `data-fps` or no `index.html` returns 30 with no warning.
- `tsc --noEmit` in `packages/cli`: clean.
- Mutation: removing the warning makes exactly the three "falls back to 30 and warns" cases fail (3 failed, 12 passed).

## What I did NOT exercise

- No real `lambda` / `cloudrun` render; the change is in the CLI's fps default only.

title: fix(cli): check's overlap audit skips scenes the runtime hid
body:
## What

`check`'s content-overlap audit no longer walks inside scenes the runtime has hidden. On a long composition, almost every element sits in a scene that is off screen at any given sample, and the audit was reading styles and geometry for all of them on every sample.

## Why

The dense overlap pass seeks to up to 600 times and runs this audit at each one. The audit walked `root.querySelectorAll("*")`, so its cost per sample grew with the length of the film, not with what was on screen. On a 9-minute composition with about 430 scenes, 7,348 of 7,806 elements were inside runtime-hidden clips at a typical sample, and `check` ran past its deadline. In a CPU profile of 100 samples, the per-element visibility test in this audit was the largest single cost.

The runtime hides an inactive clip with `data-hf-clip-hidden` plus inline `visibility: hidden`. Its rule `[data-hf-clip-hidden][style*="visibility: hidden"] * { visibility: hidden !important; }` (core `timedClipHide.ts`) keeps every descendant hidden. So nothing inside such a clip can be on screen, and skipping the subtree changes no finding.

## Related work

Part of making `check`'s browser work independent of film length. Bounding the number of dense overlap samples follows in a separate PR.

## How

- `elementsOnScreenScenes(root)` walks with a `TreeWalker` that rejects runtime-hidden clips, so their subtrees are never visited. It matches the same selector as the runtime rule.
- `collectSolidTextBlocks` uses it. That is the walk behind `__hyperframesOverlapAudit` (every dense sample) and the overlap part of the full layout audit.
- An author-hidden ancestor without the runtime marker is still walked, so `visibility_escapes_segment` behaves as before (its existing test is unchanged and passes).

## Test plan

- [x] Unit test `never reads inside a scene the runtime hid`: the overlap audit returns nothing and never reads styles of an element inside a runtime-hidden clip. With the walk put back to the whole page, it fails (`expected [ { …(9) } ] to deeply equal []`).
- [x] `layout-audit.browser.test.ts` passes 3 runs in a row. oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
- [x] Same findings: `check` on the 9-minute composition, before and after, gives identical layout findings (80 of 80, same code, selector and time). The audit's share of the overlap pass dropped 2-3x. Wall times were taken on a loaded machine and are not quoted.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: fix(cli): keep check from waiting on project history another process holds
body:
## What changes

`hyperframes check` records its report to the project's history, and that recording could hold up the check itself. When another process owned the project's history (a running editor with the project open, or another CLI command), the check waited up to 5 s for that owner before giving up with `Check report was not recorded: This project's history is open in another process`, and only then started checking. The rule this PR enforces: recording the report never blocks, slows or replaces the check's own result.

- `captureArtifactRevision` (shared by `check`, `render` and `snapshot`) opens history with no owner wait: busy history is skipped at once with the same warning. `withOwner` takes the wait as an option; every other history command keeps its 5 s.
- `check` starts the history capture beside the check pipeline instead of before it, so opening history and checkpointing overlap the check rather than adding to it. The capture still has to finish before the report is saved with its revision.

## Evidence

Reproduced on `main` with a fixture project (14 scenes, 90 audio clips, a 52 s 1080x1920 composition, 14 MB) and a second process holding the project's history open. Alternating `main` and this branch on the same machine, three runs each:

| History held by another process | Warning printed at | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | 5.6 s, 5.7 s, 5.8 s | 16.1 s, 16.1 s, 17.0 s |
| this branch | 1.1 s, 1.0 s, 1.1 s | 11.6 s, 12.3 s, 10.1 s |

Every run returned the check's JSON with `ok: true` and exit 0. With nobody holding history, totals on the shared machine ranged 11 to 18 s on both sides, too noisy to claim a number for the overlap.

## Tests

- `checkArtifacts.test.ts`: the held-history test used to set the owner wait to 0 first, which skipped exactly this stall. It now sets a 60 s wait the check must not take.
- `checkCapture.test.ts` (new): the history capture only answers once the check has started, so a check that waits for the capture never runs.

Both fail on `main` (timed out at 20 s) and pass here.

## Not yet run

The three-in-a-row run of `checkArtifacts`, `checkCapture`, `artifactCapture`, `history` and `snapshot-contactSheet` tests and a full typecheck with built packages. The local typecheck hook was skipped: this worktree has no built `@hyperframes/core` dist, and `packages/cli` `tsc --noEmit` reports only `Cannot find module '@hyperframes/core/audio-fx-runtime'` from engine, none in the changed files. Draft until those run.


PR_SIZE_OK=1: a lone production fix for `check`, targeted at 0.8.170; no open check PR can carry it.

title: perf(core): a jump starts its video first and rebuilds the clip list after the frame lands
body:
## What changes for the user

Jumping around a long film costs less work: in the 12-jump test, the page now does about 18% less main-thread work per jump, and the jump median improves about 5% (843-874 ms -> 801-859 ms on a 9-minute test film). This is the first of three seek steps; jumps are still bound by video decoding and the page's layout, which the next PRs address (preview proxies, then an instant still).

## What this PR does

1. **The video is asked first.** A paused jump used to render the whole page at the target (every registered timeline, scene discovery, overlays) and only then set the on-screen video's time. Now the media sync runs first, so decoding overlaps the page work. Measured in the page: the video's time is set 2-4 ms after the jump reaches the runtime.
2. **The clip list is rebuilt after the frame lands.** A jump that mounts scenes near its target triggered a full clip-list rebuild (all clips, with computed-style reads up each clip's ancestors), twice per jump: once from the scene mount and once from the transport tick. It cost 90-430 ms per jump inside the seek. While a jump's seek completions are pending, `postTimeline` now holds the post and sends one after they settle and the frame paints. The hold applies only after a jump: at load, posts (and `window.__clipManifest`) land at once, and render capture is never held.

`seek-dispatch` gains two read-only helpers (`hasPendingSeekCompletion`, `seekCompletionsSettled`), so the hold never consumes a failure that `waitForSeekCompletion` reports.

## Tests

`init.seekOrder.test.ts`. Each test fails without its change; I checked each by removing the change and rerunning:

- On a paused jump, the on-screen video's time is set before the page's timeline is seeked.
- A jump with a pending completion posts no clip list until the completion lands, then posts exactly one.
- With a completion pending but no jump, the post lands at once. This one fails if the hold applies to any pending completion.

Core runtime suite: 2099 tests pass. Typecheck, lint and the comment ratchet pass. The new tests pass 3 runs in a row.

## Measurement

Setup:
- Headless Chrome on a shared 8-core Linux box, load 0.5-3.9.
- 12 jumps per run, plus playback from 0:00, 3:00 and 8:00 to check nothing regressed.
- Whole CLI builds swapped, and the served runtime checked by hash on every run.
- Alternating with the base.

| Run | Jump median / p95 (12 of 12 land) | CPU for 12 jumps | Playback fps 0:00 / 3:00 / 8:00 |
|---|---|---|---|
| base, run 1 | 874 / 1183 ms | 5.5 s | 55.3 / 51.8 / 54.2 |
| base, run 3 | 843 / 1206 ms | 5.5 s | 56.0 / 56.5 / 47.0 |
| this PR, run 1 | 812 / 1181 ms | 4.5 s | 57.3 / 54.7 / 56.2 |
| this PR, run 2 | 859 / 1219 ms | 4.8 s | 47.5 / 54.2 / 55.5 |
| this PR, run 3 | 801 / 1192 ms | 4.4 s | 52.0 / 51.5 / 55.8 |

One base run was lost to a bug in my test rig: it clicked Play before Studio enabled the button (Play stays disabled for 0.2-1.9 s after the preview reports its duration). Fixed in the rig; not a Studio issue.

What a jump still spends, per profile:
- The video's own decode: 0.1-1.2 s. The test media has keyframes every ~8 s and is decoded in software.
- About 300 ms of page layout after the jump.
- Rendering the newly mounted scenes.

## Stacking

Stacked on #5754, which is stacked on #5741. Measured on a build that also includes the held-scenes stack (#5719, #5722, #5726): the hold covers the post at the end of `nestRanScenes` without changing that code.

title: perf(aws-lambda): run chunks through a Distributed Map to lift the 40-chunk cap
body:
## What changed

- **Chunk renders run in a Distributed Map** in both state machine definitions (`HyperframesRenderStack.ts` and `examples/aws-lambda/template.yaml`). The inline Map ran at most 40 chunks at once, so a 256-chunk render went in waves of 40. Each chunk is now a STANDARD child execution (EXPRESS children stop at 5 minutes; a chunk may run the Lambda's full 15). No tolerated failures: any failed chunk still fails the render, and the per-task retry rules inside each chunk are unchanged.
- **Fan-out is capped at the function's reserved concurrency** (`MaxConcurrencyPath` now reads a `MaxChunkConcurrency` value the `BuildChunkList` state sets from `reservedConcurrency` / `ReservedConcurrency`; 0 = no cap when unreserved). Before, the cap was the chunk count, so chunks past the reserved concurrency were throttled by Lambda (`TooManyRequestsException`), retried 4 times over about 30 s, and failed the render if the first wave took longer than that. Now they wait in the Map instead.
- **IAM**: the state machine role may start its own child executions and describe or stop them. CDK adds this itself for a `DistributedMap`; the SAM role gets the same statements, with ARNs built from `ProjectName` because `!Ref RenderStateMachine` inside its own role is a dependency cycle.
- **Progress costs at most 3 Step Functions calls per poll, whatever the chunk count**: chunk events now live in each child execution's history, not the parent's. Reading every child's history on every poll made `hyperframes lambda render --wait` crash with `Rate exceeded` at 225 chunks. `getRenderProgress` now makes `DescribeExecution` + `GetExecutionHistory` (parent) + one `DescribeMapRun` while the chunk Map runs. Frames come from the Map Run's item counts; once the Map exits, exact chunk frames and Lambda time come from the chunk results in the Map's output. A failed chunk's own history is read only when the counts show a failure (at most 5 children), so typed chunk errors such as `PLAN_HASH_MISMATCH` on `RenderChunkV2` still surface.
- **Chunk results carry `FramesEncoded` and `DurationMs`** (both definitions' `ResultSelector`), which is what lets the Map output replace the child histories. About 45 bytes per chunk in the state payload.
- **Progress polls back off on throttling**: the progress client retries `ThrottlingException` up to 8 times with the SDK's backoff instead of throwing after the default 3.
- **IAM for callers**: `hyperframes lambda policies` now lists `states:DescribeMapRun`. The stack roles do not need it; only the caller polling progress does.
- **What the progress numbers mean now** (while the chunk Map runs): frames are the succeeded share of total frames (exact once the Map exits); the running cost leaves out chunk Lambda time until the Map exits, then adds it exactly; `lambdasInvoked` counts started chunks, not retry attempts inside a chunk; `errors` lists a failed chunk's attempts, not transient failures inside chunks that later succeeded. Percent math, status and final totals are unchanged.
- SAM quotes any intrinsic it finds inside a `Definition`, so the SAM value goes through `States.StringToJson` to arrive as a number.
- **Throttles get their own retry**: `Lambda.TooManyRequestsException` now retries 10 times from 5 s, doubling up to 60 s, with full jitter (about 7 minutes in total), ahead of the 30 s catch-all, on all six Lambda tasks. With the cap a render should not throttle itself, but a second render on the same function can still take the reserved slots.
- **`CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` is terminal for Plan and PlanV2** in both definitions. #5765 produces that code at plan time, so retrying it cannot help.

Message for users when chunks exceed `--concurrency`: not in this PR. The planner-side lane owns the plan-time message; this PR only makes the state machine queue instead of fail. The CLI default of 8 is unchanged.

Sync between CDK and SAM: the existing snapshot test already compares the Lambda task payloads and terminal error lists of both. The new tests check Map mode, child type, label, concurrency path and IAM actions on both definitions. Nothing compares the full definitions; this PR does not add that.

## What I measured

- Progress fix: `getRenderProgress` 18 pass, exit 0, three runs in a row; snapshot 17 pass; policies 16 pass; `tsc --noEmit` exit 0. The four new tests (225 running chunks make exactly 3 calls; exact frames and cost from the Map output with 2 calls; a failed chunk's error surfaces from reading only failed children; a client built like the real one rides out 3 throttles) all fail on the previous head. One mutation each fails only its own test: always reading failed children, default SDK retries, dropping the failed-chunk errors, ignoring the Map output.
- Earlier: `bun test` (packages/aws-lambda): snapshot 17 pass, contract 6 pass, getRenderProgress 15 pass, exit 0, three runs in a row. `tsc --noEmit` exit 0. `fallow audit` pass, oxlint/oxfmt clean.
- RED on main's source with the new tests: snapshot 4 fail (resource count, Distributed Map mode, concurrency cap, IAM), getRenderProgress 1 fail (`framesRendered` 0, expected 150). The throttle-retry and terminal-code tests fail on the first commit's definitions (2 fail). Mutations: SAM-only `Mode: INLINE` fails only the Distributed Map test; dropping the child histories fails only the child-execution progress test.
- `sam validate --lint` (SAM CLI 1.169.0): valid. `sam` translate shows `MaxChunkConcurrency.$` becomes `States.StringToJson('${...}')` with an `Fn::Sub` over the `Fn::If`.

Real AWS, us-east-2, stack deployed with `hyperframes lambda deploy` from this branch. The render was a 2-minute 1080p30 composition (3600 frames, video plus audio) with `--max-parallel-chunks 60`:

| Reserved concurrency | Chunks | Peak child executions at once | Throttled tasks | Wall (submit to done) | Measured cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 60 | 60 (all started within 0.6 s) | 0 | 39 s | $0.147 |
| 8 (CLI default) | 60 | 8 (Map Run max concurrency 8) | 0 | 119 s | $0.117 |

- For comparison, the same composition on main earlier the same day split into 16 chunks at concurrency 8: 75 s, with 32 throttled task attempts. On main, a 30-minute render at concurrency 8 failed outright on `Lambda.TooManyRequestsException`.
- Both outputs are identical: same size and MD5, 3600 video packets, 120.0 s, audio present.
- `hyperframes lambda render --wait` progress advanced through the chunks (51%, 55%, ... 3600/3600 frames) with cost, read from the child executions.
- Stopping a render mid-Map aborted its 7 running children and left the other 52 unstarted, so the role's StopExecution grant works.
- Deployed definition checked: both Maps `DISTRIBUTED` / `STANDARD`, `MaxChunkConcurrency.$` resolved to `States.StringToJson('64')`, then `'8'` after the redeploy.
- The stack, both buckets and the log groups were deleted afterwards. Total spend about $0.28.

Real AWS, the progress fix, same region: fresh stack from this head (reserved concurrency 300), the same 2-minute composition with `--max-parallel-chunks 225` and `render --wait --wait-interval-ms 2000`, which is the interval that crashed:

| Run | `--wait` | SFN calls per poll (client-side counter) | Retries | Peak chunks at once | SFN wall | Measured cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | completed, exit 0 | 2 before and after the Map, 3 during it | 0 | 225 | 40.6 s | $0.364 |
| 2, with the previous poller beside it | completed, exit 0 | same, 3 at most | 0 | 225 | 29.8 s | $0.242 |

- Progress advanced on every poll during the Map: 10%, 39%, 66%, 84%, then 3600/3600 frames, then done. Outputs: 3600 video packets, 120.0 s audio.
- The previous poller, run on the same render as run 2: 93 then 228 calls per poll, then it died with `ThrottlingException: Rate exceeded` after 3 attempts on its third Map poll. The new `--wait` next to it never needed a retry.
- The CLI's own total ($0.328 / $0.240) reads the handlers' `DurationMs`, so it sits below the billed figure.
- Stack, buckets and log group deleted afterwards and checked empty. Spend for these two runs about $0.61.

## What I did NOT exercise

- The CDK construct was not deployed. It was synthesized and tested; the real runs used the SAM template, which is what `hyperframes lambda deploy` ships.
- No render above 225 chunks, and no 30-minute render on this branch.
- No chunk failure inside a child on real AWS. The failed-chunk error path is covered by the unit test only.
- The backoff was exercised by a unit test with a fake transport, not by a real throttle on the new poller (it never got throttled).
- The CDK construct was synthesized and snapshot-tested, not deployed, for the new `ResultSelector` fields too.

title: fix(cli): show the real import error when a cloud adapter is installed
body:
## What changed

`hyperframes lambda deploy|sites|render|render-batch|progress|destroy` load `@hyperframes/aws-lambda` on demand and print an install hint when it is missing. The check treated every `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` as "not installed", so a missing file or a missing dependency inside an installed adapter was reported as the adapter being absent, and the real error was hidden.

`hyperframes cloudrun` had a narrower check that matched `@hyperframes/gcp-cloud-run` anywhere in the message. Node's message for a missing dependency of the adapter names the adapter too, in the importer path:

```
Cannot find package 'google-auth-library' imported from /app/node_modules/@hyperframes/gcp-cloud-run/dist/sdk.js
```

Both commands now use one helper, `isMissingPackageError(error, pkg)`, which matches only `Cannot find package '<pkg>'`, and one `missingPackageMessage`. Anything else is rethrown with its real message.

## What I measured

- `packages/cli/src/utils/missingPackage.test.ts` (new): exit 0, 4 passed. Cases use Node's real message format (captured from Node 22 with an absent package and with an installed package missing its own dependency).
- `packages/cli/src/commands/cloudrun.test.ts`: exit 0, 6 passed.
- `tsc --noEmit` in `packages/cli`: clean.
- Mutation: going back to "package name anywhere in the message" fails exactly "is false when an installed package is missing one of its own dependencies".

## What I did NOT exercise

- No real `lambda` or `cloudrun` command run end to end against a broken install; the behaviour change is limited to which errors get the install hint.

title: fix(cli): check's dense overlap pass takes at most 240 samples, at clip windows first
body:
## What

`check`'s dense content-overlap pass now takes at most 240 samples, whatever the film's length. It spends them where an overlap can start or stop: one sample inside every stretch where the set of visible clips stays the same, then a uniform fill up to the total.

## Why

The pass sampled at 8 fps up to a ceiling of 600, and each sample is a seek plus an audit. On a 9-minute composition, 600 of them ran `check` past its fixed deadline: a long film always hit the ceiling and then paid for all of it. A smaller uniform ceiling alone would make it bounded, but at 240 samples over 9 minutes the uniform step is about 2.3 s, long enough to step over a caption that overlaps for half a second.

Overlap can only change when the visible set changes, so the clip edges the runtime already publishes say where to look. The result is deterministic: the same composition gets the same samples on any machine.

## Related work

Follows the change that makes the overlap audit skip scenes the runtime hid (cost per sample). This one bounds the number of samples.

## How

- The page driver gains `getClipEdges()`. It reads `window.__clipManifest.clips` (the runtime's timeline payload) and returns each non-audio clip's start and end.
- `buildOverlapSampleTimes(duration, clipEdges)` cuts the film at the edges and takes the midpoint of every stretch between two cuts. The midpoint avoids sampling at the instant a clip enters, when it is often still fading in. If there are more stretches than the budget, an even subset is picked. The remaining budget is a uniform grid.
- With no clip edges inside the film, the samples are the same uniform grid as before. Films short enough to sample at 8 fps within 240 samples (up to about 30 s) keep that density.
- With `--range`, edges are taken relative to the range, as the uniform grid already was.
- Severity still works on a long film. An overlap is an error only when samples no more than 1 s apart see it held for 500 ms (`CONTENT_OVERLAP_HELD_ERROR_MS`). With 240 samples over 9 minutes the step is about 2.3 s, so no overlap could reach that. When an overlap is seen and the next planned sample is more than 1 s away, the pass now samples again 0.5 s later. Those probes are capped at 60 and come out of the same 240: the grid takes at most 180. Films sampled at 8 fps never need one.

## Test plan

- [x] `keeps a long film's dense pass to a fixed number of seeks`: a 540 s film with 433 clips does at most 240 dense seeks.
- [x] `samples a short clip the uniform grid steps over`: a 0.3 s overlap inside a short clip on a 540 s film is found.
- [x] `still promotes an overlap held on a long film`: an overlap held from 200 s to 260 s on a 540 s film is an error, within 240 seeks.
- [x] fails without the fix: with the old 600 ceiling and no clip windows, both tests fail (`expected 600 to be less than or equal to 240`, and the short overlap is not found). With the hold probes set to 0, the held-overlap test fails (the overlap stays below error).
- [x] The existing dense-pass, scoped-check and crop-time tests pass unchanged. `check.test.ts` and `layoutAudit.test.ts` pass 3 runs in a row (136 tests). `tsc` is clean. oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: perf(producer): size distributed chunks to the worker limit and concurrency
body:
## What changed

A distributed render with no chunking flags used to split into a fixed 16 chunks, whatever the video length or the number of Lambdas available. For 30 minutes of 1080p30 that is 3,375 frames per chunk. On a real Lambda run of a simple test video, each of those chunks took 13 minutes against the 15-minute limit. A video about 15% heavier per frame times out, and every retry times out the same way until the run's 1-hour timeout. Meanwhile a deploy with more concurrency could not use it.

Now the planner picks the chunk count from two numbers the platform supplies:

- **Worker concurrency** (Lambda: the reserved concurrency set at `lambda deploy --concurrency`). The default plan is one wave as wide as that allows, up to the 256-chunk ceiling, with a floor on frames per chunk so the fixed per-chunk cost (cold start, media fetch) does not dominate short videos.
- **Worker time limit** (Lambda: the function's timeout, read from the invocation itself). If a chunk's predicted time would exceed 75% of the limit, the plan widens until each chunk fits.

When fitting the limit needs more chunks than there are workers, the render still runs (in waves) and the planner logs a message telling the user to raise `--concurrency` to the needed number. When even 256 chunks cannot fit, the plan fails within seconds with a new non-retryable `CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` error that names the predicted time, the limit and what to change. It no longer burns four timed-out retries.

Explicit `--chunk-size`, `--max-parallel-chunks` and `--target-chunk-frames` behave as before and skip the estimate. Callers that pass neither worker input (local, k8s, Cloud Run today) keep the old default of 16.

Plumbing:
- `DistributedRenderConfig` gets optional `workerTimeoutSeconds` and `workerConcurrency`, validated as positive integers.
- The Lambda handler fills in `workerTimeoutSeconds` from its own remaining time at plan start (plan and chunks share one function), unless the config already sets it.
- `lambda deploy` records the reserved concurrency in the local stack file; `lambda render` and `render-batch` pass it as `workerConcurrency`. Stack files written before this change leave it unset, so those renders plan for 16.
- The `--chunk-size` and `--max-parallel-chunks` help and CLI docs no longer claim fixed defaults of 240 and 16.
- The Lambda handler now maps `FORMAT_NOT_SUPPORTED_IN_DISTRIBUTED` to its code as the error name. The state machine already lists that code as non-retryable, but the error arrived under its class name and was retried. Cloud Run maps the new code to HTTP 400.

The per-frame cost is measured on one simple video, not on every composition. On a 10 GB Lambda, 0.11 s per output megapixel per frame (about 0.23 s per 1080p frame, from that 13-minute chunk) is used, plus 60 s of fixed cost per chunk, against 75% of the limit. Heavier compositions cost more, which is what the margin and the separate fixed cost are for. The frame floor (no chunk shorter than its fixed cost) is a tunable. It holds 30 minutes of 1080p at 204 chunks even when 256 workers are available.

Follow-ups for the Step Functions lane (not edited here):
- Add `CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` to the Plan state's non-retryable list in `HyperframesRenderStack.ts` and `examples/aws-lambda/template.yaml`. Until then, an impossible plan fails in seconds per attempt instead of 15 minutes, but is still retried.
- This PR owns the planner-side "raise `--concurrency`" message. The Step Functions lane does not need to add a second one. The message is logged by the Plan function. Showing it in the `lambda render` terminal would need the plan output to carry it, which is a follow-up.
- Cloud Run does not pass its worker limit yet (the Workflows request timeout lives in Terraform), so Cloud Run renders keep the default of 16.

## What I measured

All runs on a Linux test host, one file per command:

- `bun test src/services/distributed/plan.test.ts` (producer): 54 pass, 0 fail, exit 0 (three runs in a row)
- `bun test src/handler.test.ts` (aws-lambda): 17 pass, 0 fail, exit 0
- `bun test src/sdk/validateConfig.test.ts` (aws-lambda): 38 pass, 0 fail, exit 0
- `bun test src/server.test.ts` (gcp-cloud-run): 27 pass, 0 fail, exit 0
- `vitest run src/commands/lambda/render.test.ts` and `render-batch.test.ts` (cli): 5 and 14 passed, exit 0
- `tsc --noEmit` in producer, aws-lambda, cli and gcp-cloud-run: exit 0 in all four

The new tests fail without the change. With the branch's test files placed on main's source:
- planner tests fail to load: `Export named 'CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT' not found`
- handler: `plans against the function's own timeout` and `normalizes producer workflow codes` fail
- config validation: both new worker-field cases fail
- Cloud Run: `routes producer code CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` fails
- CLI: 2 of 5 and 1 of 14 fail

One deliberate break per new test, each restored afterwards, and each turned exactly its test red. The breaks: margin raised to 150%, warning removed, 256 cap removed, frame floor removed, explicit flags ignored, throw removed, planner unwired from `plan()`, handler timeout dropped, handler code mapping dropped (new code and the format code), validation off, Cloud Run mapping dropped, CLI concurrency dropped in each builder, old help text restored.

Planner output at a 900 s limit:

| Video (1080p30) | Workers | Chunks x frames | Predicted per chunk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 s | any | 1 x 300 | 128 s |
| 2 min | 8 | 8 x 450 | 163 s |
| 2 min | 256 | 13 x 277 | 123 s |
| 30 min | 8 | 21 x 2,572 (raise-concurrency message) | 647 s |
| 30 min | 256 | 204 x 265 | 120 s |
| 90 min | 256 | 256 x 633 | 204 s |
| 8 h | any | fails at plan time, `CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` | 830 s at 256 chunks |
| old default, 30 min | n/a | 16 x 3,375 | 830 s |

The budget is 675 s (75% of 900 s).

## What I did NOT exercise

- No render on real AWS or Cloud Run. The Lambda timeout comes from the invocation context, covered by a unit test that injects it, not by a deployed function.
- The per-frame estimate has not been checked against heavy compositions at 1080p. It is set to the slowest rate seen so far.
- The state machine still retries `CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` until its non-retryable lists include it (see follow-ups).

title: fix(core): scrubbing back across a scene no longer leaves its content hidden
body:
## What

Scrubbing the Studio preview past a scene, back before it, and then forward into it again left that scene's background on screen with its content hidden. It stayed that way until the scene's next step. The rendered export was always right. With this change the preview matches the export on every scrub path.

## Why

To reproduce: take a sub-composition whose script reveals its content with two steps at its own time 0, such as `tl.set(field, { visibility: "hidden" }, 0)` followed by `tl.set(field, { visibility: "visible" }, 0)` (common when a scene builds clones at load and shows them from its first frame). Seek past the scene, seek back to just before its start, then scrub forward into it. Before this change the field stays hidden until the scene's next visibility step. On the test fixture below that is about 1.2 s of an empty dark frame.

Cause: on every seek the runtime also seeks each registered scene timeline to its own time (`seekStandaloneRegisteredTimelines`). A scene that has not started yet is held at local time 0. When GSAP lands a timeline exactly on a time coming from a later time, it applies the zero-duration steps at that time in reverse authored order and marks them done. So "hidden, then visible" ends hidden, and the next forward move never applies them again. Plain GSAP 3.14.2 and 3.15.0 do this:

```js
tl.totalTime(1); tl.totalTime(0);   // field: hidden (steps at 0 applied in reverse)
tl.totalTime(0.5);                  // field: still hidden
```

The same happens at any later time a scene lands on exactly from above, e.g. two steps on a whole second. The root timeline already re-renders after every eventful seek, from just below the playhead, except at 0, where it steps down from above and so applies the steps at 0 in reverse too.

## Related work

Refs #5614, which made `seekGsapTimeline` the path every runtime GSAP seek takes and added the never-rendered redraw this extends.

## How

One function owns the repair, `reapplyStepsInAuthoredOrder`: it takes the zero-duration steps sitting exactly on the landing time from the cached step index (`landingMarksOf`'s structure-keyed index from #5674), renders each in authored order, and restores GSAP's own bookkeeping on it (`ratio`, `_zTime`, `_act`), so callbacks fire exactly as often as in plain GSAP. Two callers:
- `seekGsapTimeline`, when a timeline lands backward (a scene parked at 0, or scrubbed back onto a step). Nothing else is redrawn, so a backward seek costs what it did on main, plus a binary search.
- `rerenderGsapTimelineAt` at 0, after its existing step down from above and its keyframe priming, which stay as they were.

Both seek paths in `init.ts` now pass the same structure key (`gsapStructureOf`). Render capture keeps passing none, as before.

## Test plan

New cases in `packages/core/src/runtime/adapters/gsap.steps.test.ts`, run with real GSAP:
- a scene's steps at 0 after the playhead comes back to 0 from later (the empty dark frame)
- a scene nested in a root timeline, parked at 0 by the same seek order the runtime uses
- two steps on one later time, after the playhead comes back onto it
- the root's re-render at 0 keeps them
- keyframed tweens starting at 0 (array and percent forms) match plain GSAP across five root and scene seek orders
- a call on the landing time fires as often as in plain GSAP across back-and-forth seeks
- a backward landing never redraws the whole scene

Against main's `gsap.ts` and `init.ts`, the four symptom tests fail (exit 1, 4 failed). On this branch: 74 passed, green on every run. Mutations: removing the re-application on backward landings turns 3 tests red, removing it at 0 turns 1 red, a full redraw on backward landings turns 1 red, and dropping the bookkeeping restore turns the callback test red (7 calls vs 5).

`packages/core` `test:hyperframe-runtime-ci` (typecheck, build, contract, behavior, seek, parity, security, coverage): exit 0, 83 files, 2104 passed. `packages/producer` `firstFrameStartingState.integration.test.ts` (real render): exit 0, 2 passed. Studio edit accuracy gate in CI: 271 accurate, same as main.

## What I measured

Fixture: a 12 s, four-scene composition with generated images. The third scene clones a 3x3 field of windows full of pictures at load and reveals it with steps at 0, and the second ends in a zoom push with motion blur. Driven through the published Studio's own timeline with a real mouse drag (park at 8 s, drag from 4.5 s to 8 s), headless Chrome, GPU, device scale 2, recording the compositor's frames:

| runtime | frames recorded | frames showing the empty dark scene |
|---|---|---|
| main | 185 | 60 |
| this branch | 176 | 0 |

The same back-then-forward seek order on Linux (headless Chrome 152): main shows the empty scene from 6.1 s and no new frame through 7.0 s, while the fix shows the field at every step.

Cost in Chrome on the same fixture, main vs this branch, three alternating rounds. Per-seek main-thread time over forward, backward and forward sweeps at 0.1 s steps, then 5 s of playback:

| | seek p50 | seek p95 | backward-sweep seek p95 | playback fps | frame gap p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 0.3-0.4 ms | 0.5-0.6 ms | 0.4-0.5 ms | 60.2 | 16.9-17.8 ms |
| this branch | 0.3 ms | 0.5 ms | 0.4-0.6 ms | 60.2 | 16.9-18.4 ms |

On a 38,000-step timeline (the long-caption case from #5674), a backward root seek costs a median 12.07 ms on this branch vs 11.89 ms on main over 8 alternating rounds, and a backward scene seek costs 1.5-2.6 ms on both.

## Before / After

Studio preview during the drag, same times. Before: the third scene shows only its background. After: its window field.

![Before and after: Studio preview while scrubbing forward after coming back](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0770a1d8-9406-4e3d-8135-58a644162ada)

The frame that looks low-res during the second scene's exit is authored motion blur, and the export has it too. Studio preview with this change next to the rendered export:

![Studio preview with the fix next to the rendered export](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/de63c06e-a2ae-4c14-85f7-ed23be1a45e5)

## What I did NOT exercise

- The fix in an embedding host's preview after a release: it reaches embedders when they pick up the next core release.
- Real-GPU Linux: the Linux run used headless Chrome without a GPU, and ran on the first version of this fix, not this head.
- The edit accuracy suite locally: it passed in CI at this change.
- The screenshots below come from the first version of this fix. I re-ran the drag at this head (0 empty frames) and the frames match them.

title: perf(producer): distributed chunks download only the videos they show
body:
Distributed render chunks (plan v2, Lambda and Cloud Run) now download only the project videos they show. Before this, every chunk downloaded every video in the project.

## What changed

- **Router** (`planV2.ts`, `artifactTargets`). Chunks extract their own frames from deferred video sources. A deferred source that the project already ships under `compiled/` now goes only to the chunks that show it, as `video-sources/` files already did. Everything else under `compiled/` (HTML, images, fonts, CSS, videos the plan does not defer) still goes to every chunk. Lambda and Cloud Run both read these per-chunk lists, so neither adapter changed.
- **Chunk** (`renderChunk.ts`). A chunk skips the browser readiness wait for a deferred video it does not show. That is exactly the set the router no longer gives it, taken from the chunk's own frame extraction result. Without this, the chunk logs `media_load_failed` for a file it was not given on purpose. A video the chunk shows keeps today's readiness wait. A missing source for a shown video still fails the chunk (`MISSING_PLAN_ARTIFACT`, unchanged).
- **Test contract change.** The old test "keeps a deferred source the page itself loads in every chunk" pinned the old routing. Its reason was that a missing `<video>` src fails the chunk. In practice chunks run best-effort and only log a warning, and this PR removes that warning too. The test is replaced by "ships each compiled/ video source only to the chunks that show it", which uses two clips: one shown in a single chunk, one shown in both.

I tried and rejected giving chunks the size hints that local renders use (`collectVideoMetadataHints`). They set a `height` attribute that resizes a video styled with only a CSS width, so chunk 0 changed pixels. The before/after chunk hashes caught it. Local renders have the same behaviour today; that is a separate fix.

## What I measured

Linux host, a 60 s 640x360 composition at 30 fps in 4 chunks. It has a 60 MB video shown for 0-60 s and a 1 MB video shown for 0-10 s.

| | chunk 0 | chunks 1-3 |
|---|---|---|
| bytes downloaded, before | 61,240,267 | 61,240,267 each |
| bytes downloaded, after | 61,240,269 | 60,243,993 each |
| chunk mp4 sha256 | identical before and after | identical before and after |

- All 4 chunk outputs are byte-identical before and after. There were no `media_load_failed` warnings in either run.
- On this fixture the saving is the short clip in 3 of 4 chunks. It grows with the number of clips a chunk does not show.
- New tests fail without the change, one mutation each:
  - Router reverted: the planV2 test gets `"all"` instead of `[1]`, and the chunk test gets `"all"` instead of `[0]`.
  - Readiness skip removed: the chunk test fails on `media_load_failed`.
  - Skipping every deferred video: the chunk test fails, because a shown video must not be skipped.
- The new chunk test passed 3 runs in a row. `planV2`, `renderChunk`, `plan`, `planSizeCap`, `publicExports`, `chunkBoundary` and `renderChunkFallback` tests are green, as are the aws-lambda `handler` and Cloud Run `server` tests and producer `tsc --noEmit`.

## What I did NOT exercise

- A real Lambda or Cloud Run deploy. The measurement drives the same `listPlanV2ArtifactsForTarget`, `materializePlanV2Target` and `renderChunk` path locally.
- Videos the planner extracts up front (clips shown for about a second or less, VFR) are not deferred. Their source under `compiled/` still goes to every chunk even though no chunk reads it. Scoping those needs the plan to record their plan-relative path. That is a follow-up.
- A composition whose script draws a video that is not on screen (for example a WebGL texture of an off-screen clip) in a chunk that does not show it. That chunk no longer has the file.
- Reading only the byte range of a long video that a chunk shows. That is a separate change.

title: perf(producer): assemble in one pass and keep its disk use under one output copy
body:
## What changed

The distributed assembler used to write the video three times on local disk: concat the chunks into a full-size file, mux the audio into a second one, then rewrite that again for faststart (a no-op rewrite, since the mux already wrote `+faststart`). While the last pass ran, disk held the chunks plus three full copies of the output. On Lambda's 10 GB `/tmp` that caps a 1080p render at roughly 35-40 minutes at typical bitrates.

Now the join, the audio mux and faststart run as one ffmpeg pass that reads the chunks through the concat demuxer, writes into the private work dir and renames into place. Disk peaks at the chunks plus one output copy.

- `assemble.ts`: one pass for mp4/mov/webm, with and without audio. A single chunk is still read directly (not through a one-entry concat list), and every write still sets the output `-r`.
- Audio pad/trim needs the video's frame count before the joined file exists. It now sums the chunks' frame counts at the plan's fps, which is what probing the joined file returned.
- `muxVideoWithAudio` gains a `videoInputArgs` option so the mux can take a concat-demuxer input. It is the only engine change.
- The opt-in `cfr` re-encode reads the chunks directly instead of a joined intermediate. Its output is the same.
- Stage timers: assemble logs `[assemble] stage timings` (`cfrMs`, `audioMs`, `joinMs`, `totalMs`). The v2 Lambda assemble handler logs an `assemble_stages` event (`planMs`, `chunksMs`, `assembleMs`, `uploadMs`).

## What I measured

Fixture: a 30-minute 1080p30 H.264 video cut into 16 chunks (0.90 GB) plus 30 minutes of AAC audio. Real `assemble()` from `main` and from this branch, alternated, page cache dropped before each run. Ran on a Linux x86 machine with the same ffmpeg 7.0.2 static build the Lambda image ships. A wrapper ffmpeg logged each pass's wall time and the disk total at its exit.

| | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| Peak disk (chunks + audio = 0.87 GB) | 3.47 GB | 1.76 GB |
| Disk above the inputs | 2.60 GB (about 3 output copies) | 0.89 GB (one output copy) |
| Assemble, run 1 / run 2 | 33.0 s / 16.3 s | 16.8 s / 13.2 s |
| ffmpeg passes | concat 6.7-7.2 s, pad/trim copy, true-peak scan 5.2-7.7 s, mux 1.5-5.0 s, faststart 1.7-12.9 s | pad/trim copy, true-peak scan 5.1-5.3 s, one join 7.5-10.6 s |

- **Streams identical:** video and audio packets match across all 54,000 video frames and the whole audio track, including pts, dts, duration, size and payload hash (`ffmpeg -c copy -f framemd5` per stream).
- **What differs in the container:** only `moov/udta/meta`, which is 160 bytes smaller. `main`'s file also carried `major_brand`, `minor_version` and `compatible_brands` as `mdta` keys, copied from the joined intermediate. This branch writes only `hf_renderer`, `hf_version` and `encoder`. Atom layout is otherwise the same, and ffprobe format and stream fields match apart from size and bit rate.
- **Tests:**
  - New: `keeps local disk under the chunks plus one copy of the output`. It points `HYPERFRAMES_FFMPEG_PATH` at a wrapper that records disk use after every ffmpeg exit. On `main` it fails: 284 KB above the inputs for an 88 KB output. With this change it uses 100 KB.
  - New: `writes the same video and audio packets as separate concat, mux and faststart passes`. It rebuilds the old path from the engine's own `muxVideoWithAudio` + `applyFaststart` + `padOrTrimAudioToVideoFrameCount` and compares per-packet `framemd5`. Counting one frame short in the chunk sum makes it fail on the audio packets.
  - `assemble.test.ts`: 18/18, three runs in a row. Also green: `audioPadTrim` (38 + 2 integration), `planV2` (62), `aws-lambda` `handler.test.ts` (16), engine `chunkEncoder.test.ts`, and `tsc` for producer, engine and aws-lambda. oxlint clean.

## What I did NOT exercise

- No real Lambda run. The numbers above come from the dev machine, where the page cache can hold everything. On Lambda the saving should be larger, because it drops about two full-size writes and reads of the output, but I have not measured it there.
- Chunks are not deleted mid-join. A single ffmpeg process owns the concat, so there is no safe moment to drop a chunk it has finished reading. Peak disk is chunks plus output.
- `cfr: true` still writes the re-encode and then the muxed output (two copies). It is opt-in and off by default.
- The v1 Lambda assemble handler has no stage timer; v2 is the default.
- Windows: the disk-ceiling test skips there (it uses a shell wrapper).

title: fix(cli): check's overlap pass misses fewer overlaps within its 240 samples
body:
## What

`check`'s dense overlap pass, still at 240 samples, now misses fewer overlaps. Half the samples are a uniform grid. The other half go only to stretches between clip edges that the uniform grid steps over. The hold probe, which tells a held overlap from a passing one, is spent once per overlap instead of on every sighting.

## Why

#5764 bounded the pass at 240 samples, so `check` finishes inside its deadline on a long film. On a 9-minute composition, it still missed 16 of the 72 overlap-error elements that the old 600-sample pass found. The misses were overlaps held 0.9-2.8 s that sat between grid steps.

Measured on that composition, every variant at 240 samples and inside the deadline, counted against the 600-sample pass's 72 overlap-error elements:

| Sampling | Missed entirely | Overlap errors |
|---|---|---|
| Clip windows first, then uniform fill (#5764) | 16 | 55 |
| Uniform only | 16 | 36 |
| Clip and all tween windows, then fill | 37 | 35 |
| Half uniform, half clip and all tween windows | 40 | 29 |
| Half uniform, half clip and geometry-tween windows (merged within 500 ms) | 22 | 46 |
| **Half uniform, half clip windows (merged within 500 ms), one probe per overlap (this PR)** | **10** | **56** |

Tween boundaries were tried and dropped. A long composition has thousands of them, from letter-by-letter text and the like, and spending samples there starves the rest of the film.

## Related work

Stacked on #5764. Same goal as #5758 (the audit skips scenes the runtime hid).

## How

- Clip edges closer than 500 ms (the hold that makes an overlap an error) merge into one cut, so a run of short clips does not eat the budget.
- Half the grid is uniform. A clip window gets a sample at its middle only if no uniform sample falls inside it. Windows that do not need one hand their share back to the uniform grid.
- The hold probe moves into `holdProber`. It remembers which overlaps (code and selector) a probe has already shown held, and probes only when a sample shows one it has not. This also lowers `collectMotionOverlapSamples`' complexity.
- A clip shorter than 500 ms no longer gets its own window. An overlap that short is never an error (it is held less than 500 ms), so the most it costs is a warning.

## Test plan

- [x] `spends one hold probe on an overlap that stays the whole film`: an overlap present at every sample of a 540 s film costs one probe (at most 181 dense seeks).
- [x] `samples a short clip the uniform grid steps over` now uses a 0.8 s clip, longer than the merge distance.
- [x] fails without the fix: probing every sighting gives 240 seeks, and with no window samples the short-clip overlap is not found.
- [x] `check.test.ts` and `layoutAudit.test.ts` pass 3 runs in a row (137 tests). `tsc`, oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: fix(engine): local renders lay out width-only videos like the browser
body:
## What changed

A local `hyperframes render` drew a `<video>` that the page sizes with only a CSS width (or only a height, or only a max-width) in the wrong box. A 200px-wide 16:9 clip got a 200x360 box with the picture centred inside it, so it sat lower than in the browser preview and in distributed chunk renders, which draw it at 200x112.

Cause: local renders pass the probed size of every extracted video to the engine, and `applyVideoMetadataHints` wrote it as `width`/`height` attributes. Those attributes are CSS size hints, so whichever axis the page left unset took the hinted pixel value instead of following the video's shape.

The hint exists for videos whose metadata Chrome never loads (frames are injected, so Chrome would otherwise lay them out at 300x150). It now gives such a video a transparent SVG poster of the probed size instead. Chrome takes a video's natural size from its poster until the video's own metadata loads, so every CSS combination lays out exactly as it does with the real video. The explicit `aspect-ratio` fallback is gone for the same reason. A video that already has a poster is left alone.

`contain: size` + `contain-intrinsic-size` was tried first and rejected: it matches the simple cases but shrinks a bordered `width:100%` flex item (style-9-prod's layout) by the border width.

## What I measured

- New real-Chrome test `frameCapture-videoMetadataHints.browser.test.ts`: six 640x360 videos with no metadata (no size, width only, height only, both sizes with object-fit, max-width only, bordered flex item) must get the boxes Chrome gives the same markup once a real 640x360 video's metadata has loaded (measured separately: 640x360, 200x112.5, 160x90, 200x300, 100x56.25, 416x241).
  - On origin/main (with only the export added) it fails: width only 200x360, height only 400x90, max-width only 100x360, bordered flex item 416x376.
  - With the fix: passes 3 runs in a row. Mutation (contain-size approach instead of the poster): fails on no size and the bordered flex item.
- `frameCapture.test.ts`: 55 passed. Engine typecheck, oxlint and oxfmt clean.
- Render of a two-video page (width-only and height-only clips): before, the local frame put both clips in the wrong box; after, the local frame and a distributed chunk frame show the same layout (PSNR 50 dB, the encoder difference only).
- Every producer regression fixture with a video (28): loaded each `output/compiled.html` in headless Chrome and compared every video's box with old hints, new hints and no hints, with media loading and with media blocked. With media loading, old and new give the same box in all 28, so no baseline should move. With media blocked, new matches the loaded box in all 28; old was off for style-9-prod (1920x1087 instead of 1936x1096).
- Producer regression harness (Docker test image built from this branch) on the video-layout fixtures: render-video-overlay-stretch, style-9-prod, portrait-edge-bleed, sub-composition-video, pip-video-late-host, video-hfid-no-id, style-4-prod: 7 of 7 passed against the committed baselines. No baseline changed.

## What I did NOT exercise

- A video that already has an authored poster keeps that poster, so if its metadata never loads it lays out at the poster's shape (same as in a browser before the video loads).
- The test cannot observe the wait for the poster to decode: Chrome had applied the poster by the next CDP call even without it. A same-task probe showed the box is still 300x150 straight after setting the poster and correct after the decode, which is why the wait stays.
- Windows and macOS renders; the full regression suite (only the video fixtures listed above ran).

title: perf(cloud): move project bytes once through shared content storage
body:
## Package size after merging current main

`@hyperframes/producer` packs to 731,628 / 2,674,226 B after main's chunk-sizing change and this PR's URL reads, 2,248 B over its budget. None of the merged code is left unused, so the growth is real. ## Original report — #5774 at 62eb3c8d

## What changed

A Lambda render used to move a project's video three times before any chunk started: the SDK tarred and uploaded the whole project, the plan step downloaded and untarred it, then re-uploaded the video as a plan artifact under that render's own prefix. Nothing was reused across renders.

- **Shared content store.** The render bucket gets one content-addressed area, `cas/sha256/<first two hex>/<sha256>`, shared by every render. The key comes from the SHA-256 alone (`contentStore.ts` owns the prefix, the key and the retention numbers).
- **SDK uploads files once.** `deploySite` uploads each project file (the list from `listSiteFiles`) to the shared area, skipping any whose key already exists (HEAD), then writes a small `sites/<siteId>/files.json` mapping path to hash. No tarball, no gzip.
- **Plan reads the site, reuses the bytes.** The plan step rebuilds the project from `files.json`, verifying each file's SHA-256 as it downloads. Plan v2 artifacts now live in the shared area too, so the video the SDK already stored is found by HEAD and never re-uploaded. A `.tar.gz` `ProjectS3Uri` still works for hand-built uploads (`smoke.sh`, the README).
- **Integrity unchanged.** Every write to the shared area is still create-only (`IfNoneMatch: *`) with `ChecksumSHA256`, chunks and assemble still verify each artifact's SHA-256 on download, and an existing object is reused only when its stored digest and size match. `files.json` paths that escape the project are refused.
- **CLI.** `--site-id` builds its handle through one SDK helper (`siteHandleFromId`) instead of two hardcoded tarball URIs.

### Retention: 30 days, refreshed on reuse

- A lifecycle rule expires `cas/sha256/` after **30 days**, added to both the CDK stack and the SAM template. A test pins the SAM rules to the CDK rules and to the constants.
- S3 counts expiry from an object's last write, not its last read. So whenever the SDK or a plan reuses an object that is **7 days old or older**, it rewrites the object in place (server-side `CopyObject`, same bytes, same SHA-256 metadata and checksum). That restarts its 30-day clock.
- Every object a plan's manifest references has passed through that reuse check during the plan, so it has at least 23 days left when the chunks run. A render never loses a file mid-run.
- A site idle for more than 30 days heals itself. Before a render reuses a site (`render --site-id`, `render-batch`, or an SDK `siteHandle`), it HEADs every file in the site's `files.json`. That also refreshes any file older than 7 days. Any missing file is re-uploaded from the local project directory, after checking it against its recorded SHA-256. The CLI always passes the project directory, so it never fails on expiry. An SDK caller who passes a site handle without `projectDir` gets `SITE_FILES_MISSING`, with the missing-file count and the fix (run `sites create`, or pass `projectDir`).

### IAM

No change needed. The function already has read and write on the whole render bucket (CDK `grantReadWrite`, SAM `S3CrudPolicy`). That covers HEAD, GET, PUT and the in-place copy on the new prefix. Nothing was widened.

### Not changed

Cloud Run keeps today's tarball path. Chunk range reads (a sibling change) read deferred videos through a presigned URL to `<artifact prefix>/<aa>/<sha256>` and check S3's stored SHA-256. That key and checksum are exactly what the shared area holds, so it works against these objects unchanged.
