## Original report — #5776 at 2895705b

## What changed

On the AWS Lambda path (plan protocol v2), a chunk that extracts its own frames from a long project video no longer downloads and hashes the whole video before its browser starts. It reads the video straight from S3 by byte range: only the container index and the part its seek needs.

- The chunk handler signs a short-lived GET URL (1 hour; a Lambda invocation runs at most 15 minutes) for each deferred video source the manifest gives that chunk, and hands it to the chunk instead of a local file.
- FFmpeg's own HTTP client does the reading. On an input seek it asks only for the byte ranges it needs.
- Every other artifact is still downloaded whole and sha256-verified, as before.
- The chunk's browser cannot load a video it was never given, so for those videos the chunk skips the readiness wait and sizes the `<video>` from the plan's metadata. This is what a local render already does for every video whose frames it supplies (`collectVideoReadinessSkipIds` / `collectVideoMetadataHints`).
- Cloud Run is out of scope: its chunk worker still downloads every artifact. The producer side (`materializePlanV2Target(..., { remoteSources })`) is storage-neutral, so the same switch is available to it later.

### Why the bytes are still the right bytes

A deferred video is no longer hashed on the chunk, so integrity rests on how plan v2 stores artifacts:

1. **The key is the content hash.** Artifacts live at `.../artifacts/sha256/<2>/<sha256>`, and the manifest that names them is itself pinned by the `PlanHash` the state machine passes.
2. **Objects are written once, and S3 checks the bytes on write.** The publisher puts each blob with `If-None-Match: *` and `ChecksumSHA256`, so S3 rejects a body that does not hash to the key, and no publisher can overwrite it.
3. **S3 attests the object before the URL is signed.** The handler sends `HeadObject` with `ChecksumMode: ENABLED` and refuses (`PLAN_ARTIFACT_DIGEST_MISMATCH`) unless the stored SHA-256 and size equal the manifest's.
4. **A read that fails partway fails the chunk.** FFmpeg can exit cleanly after a refused read. I checked this with a server that refuses the seek: it produced zero frames, and the chunk failed (`zero_output`). The chunk already fails when any frame it needs is missing.
5. **FFmpeg verifies S3's certificate.** For an `https` input, ffmpeg and ffprobe get `-tls_verify 1 -ca_file <bundle>` (`urlInputArgs`). The bundle is the first of `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt` (the Lambda `nodejs:22` image, Amazon Linux 2023), `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` and `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` that exists. If none exists, the read fails with a clear error instead of going ahead unverified. Local paths and plain `http` are unchanged.

### The signed URL never shows up in errors

`extractVideoFramesRange` strips the query string from every http(s) URL in each string field of an error it throws (message, diagnostic, stack). It uses the same `redactUrlQueryStrings` that telemetry already uses, now exported from core. ffprobe diagnostics were already redacted.

- **Same frames, fewer bytes (unit test, real ffmpeg).** Extracting 15 frames from the middle of a 2-minute lossless 640x360 file, by URL versus by local path: identical JPEG bytes for every frame, and the server sent about 10-12 MB of a 71 MB file. Most of that is socket buffering past the seek, so the share falls as files grow.
- **Same chunk, byte for byte.** A real chunk render (Chrome + ffmpeg) of a plan-v2 chunk that shows a deferred video gives the same chunk sha256 whether the video comes from the plan or from a local HTTP server. Without the plan-metadata sizing it differs (mutation below).
- **Every new test fails without the change.** On the base branch with this branch's tests: the handler test sees the video downloaded, the URL extraction finds no source, the end-to-end render finds the video copied into the plan, and the two new helpers do not exist. - Output, checked with `ffprobe -count_packets`: h264 1920x1080 at 30/1, **54000 frames**, 1800.000 s. AAC audio is 1800.000 s (84376 packets) at a mean of -27.1 dB, the same as the baseline. Frames grabbed at 900 s and 1799 s show the right background timecode and title state.
- The local Range proof is the same 240-frame chunk extracted from a 1080p 4 Mb/s file once by path and once by HTTP: identical sha256 over all 240 frames.

The baseline was measured at 16 chunks, so the end-to-end times are not comparable. The window before browser launch is: it is spent on the download whatever the chunk length, and it is what this PR removes.

## What I did NOT exercise

- **Cloud Run.** Its chunk worker still downloads every artifact whole.
- **Short-lived credentials.** A pre-signed URL stops working when the Lambda's role session expires, even before its own 1-hour expiry. A chunk that hits that fails loudly and is retried.
- **Plain `http` inputs, and hosts whose CA bundle is somewhere else.** Plain `http` inputs get no TLS options; only the local test servers use them. A host with its bundle in another path fails with a clear error instead of reading unverified.

title: test: preserve browser cleanup and regression failure evidence
body:
## What

Preserve two independent test improvements from #5183: clean up and check both browsers in the managed-profile witness, and retain the actual rendered video when a regression fixture fails.

## Why

The profile witness records only the second browser PID, so its fallback cleanup cannot stop the first browser after an assertion or launch failure. It also continues into an unrelated third browser navigation after verifying profile ownership. Regression failure artifacts contain sampled frames but lose the complete render when the temporary render directory is cleaned up.

## Related work

Split out at [Miguel’s request](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/pull/5183#issuecomment-6229945606). Refs #5183 and #5102. The HDR stacking implementation and HLG golden remain outside this PR; #5728 covers that export fix. This PR does not resolve #5102.

## How

Record the first browser PID before launching the second, include both recorded PIDs in fallback cleanup, and assert both have stopped. The profile witness exits after its two managed launches; the separate deadline witness keeps the existing file-specific hang report, exit status and cleanup assertions. Production browser behavior and deadlines are unchanged.

Before a failed fixture’s temporary render is removed, copy its existing rendered video file into `failures/actual.<extension>`. Directory-based PNG output continues through the existing failed-frame extraction path.

## Test plan

Tested revision: `0d97fd407` (Node 22.22.3, Bun 1.4.2).

- Passed: full `bun run build`, root lint and format checks, producer typecheck, required commit hooks (including core/Studio/scripts typechecks and Fallow), comment citation/ratchet checks, and `git diff --check`.
- CLI focused run (`checkDeadline.process`, `checkDeadline`, `processTree`): 7 passed, 2 failed, 1 Linux-only skip. Both process witnesses fail at local Chrome launch (`Code: null`, empty stderr), so browser cleanup is not claimed verified locally.

title: perf(aws-lambda): upload project files once to a shared content-addressed area
body:
## What changed

A Lambda render used to move a project's video three times before any chunk started: the SDK tarred and uploaded the whole project, the plan step downloaded and untarred it, then re-uploaded the video as a plan artifact under that render's own prefix. Nothing was reused across renders.

- **Shared content store.** The render bucket gets one content-addressed area, `cas/sha256/<first two hex>/<sha256>`, shared by every render. The key comes from the SHA-256 alone (`contentStore.ts` owns the prefix, the key and the retention numbers).
- **SDK uploads files once.** `deploySite` uploads each project file (the list from `listSiteFiles`) to the shared area, skipping any whose key already exists (HEAD), then writes a small `sites/<siteId>/files.json` mapping path to hash. No tarball, no gzip.
- **Plan reads the site, reuses the bytes.** The plan step rebuilds the project from `files.json`, verifying each file's SHA-256 as it downloads. Plan v2 artifacts now live in the shared area too, so the video the SDK already stored is found by HEAD and never re-uploaded. A `.tar.gz` `ProjectS3Uri` still works for hand-built uploads (`smoke.sh`, the README).
- **Integrity unchanged.** Every write to the shared area is still create-only (`IfNoneMatch: *`) with `ChecksumSHA256`, chunks and assemble still verify each artifact's SHA-256 on download, and an existing object is reused only when its stored digest and size match. `files.json` paths that escape the project are refused.
- **CLI.** `--site-id` builds its handle through one SDK helper (`siteHandleFromId`) instead of two hardcoded tarball URIs.

### Retention: 30 days, refreshed on reuse

- A lifecycle rule expires `cas/sha256/` after **30 days**, added to both the CDK stack and the SAM template. A test pins the SAM rules to the CDK rules and to the constants.
- S3 counts expiry from an object's last write, not its last read. So whenever the SDK or a plan reuses an object that is **7 days old or older**, it rewrites the object in place (server-side `CopyObject`, same bytes, same SHA-256 metadata and checksum). That restarts its 30-day clock.
- Every object a plan's manifest references has passed through that reuse check during the plan, so it has at least 23 days left when the chunks run. A render never loses a file mid-run.
- A site idle for more than 30 days heals itself. Before a render reuses a site (`render --site-id`, `render-batch`, or an SDK `siteHandle`), it HEADs every file in the site's `files.json`. That also refreshes any file older than 7 days. Any missing file is re-uploaded from the local project directory, after checking it against its recorded SHA-256. The CLI always passes the project directory, so it never fails on expiry. An SDK caller who passes a site handle without `projectDir` gets `SITE_FILES_MISSING`, with the missing-file count and the fix (run `sites create`, or pass `projectDir`).

### IAM

No change needed. The function already has read and write on the whole render bucket (CDK `grantReadWrite`, SAM `S3CrudPolicy`). That covers HEAD, GET, PUT and the in-place copy on the new prefix. Nothing was widened.

### Not changed

Cloud Run keeps today's tarball path. Chunk range reads (a sibling change) read deferred videos through a presigned URL to `<artifact prefix>/<aa>/<sha256>` and check S3's stored SHA-256. That key and checksum are exactly what the shared area holds, so it works against these objects unchanged.

Stacked on the symlink fix: this uses its `listSiteFiles` as the only definition of "the project's files".

## What I measured

- `bun test`, one file at a time, in `packages/aws-lambda`. All pass: transport 14, deploySite 9, publisher 7, handler 18, CDK contract 6, CDK snapshot 13, renderToLambda 11, plus the untouched suites.
- I broke the code once for each new test, and each one failed: refresh disabled, existing keys never skipped, artifacts back under the per-render prefix, tarball-only plan fetch, path check removed, SAM lifecycle drifted, CDK lifecycle drifted.
- **Real AWS, 30-minute 1080p30 benchmark** (932 MB project, 902 MB video), with #5778 on top. The CLI uploaded the project as loose files in **14.8 s**; on main the tarball upload took about 46 s, including tar and gzip. Deploying the same tree again uploaded nothing (`uploaded: false`) in **2.8 s**, timed twice. After two renders the bucket held exactly one copy of the video (under `cas/sha256/`), and the deployed bucket showed both lifecycle rules (`renders/` 7 days, `cas/sha256/` 30 days). Numbers and the teardown are in #5778.
- Two tests cover expired files in a reused site. One re-uploads the missing file from the project directory and renders; the other, without a project directory, refuses with the missing count before starting. Both fail when the check is removed, and each fails under its own one-line mutation.
- Whole renders stay at about 16 minutes on this change alone (944 s vs 969 s on main), because the chunks take about 13 of them. That changes only with chunk range reads and the Distributed Map changes.
- Typecheck is clean for aws-lambda, cli and producer. The fallow audit and the comment ratchet pass against this branch's base.

## What I did NOT exercise

- No AWS run of this PR on its own. The real run used the follow-up PR (#5778) stacked on this one.
- The 7-day refresh was not exercised against real S3 lifecycle timing. Only the `CopyObject` request shape is tested.
- The GCP adapter is untouched and was not run.

title: perf(aws-lambda): chunks read only the byte ranges of a video they need
body:
## What changed

On the AWS Lambda path (plan protocol v2), a chunk that extracts its own frames from a long project video no longer downloads and hashes the whole video before its browser starts. It reads the video straight from S3 by byte range: only the container index and the part its seek needs.

- The chunk handler signs a short-lived GET URL (1 hour; a Lambda invocation runs at most 15 minutes) for each deferred video source the manifest gives that chunk, and hands it to the chunk instead of a local file.
- FFmpeg's own HTTP client does the reading. On an input seek it asks only for the byte ranges it needs.
- Every other artifact is still downloaded whole and sha256-verified, as before.
- The chunk's browser cannot load a video it was never given, so for those videos the chunk skips the readiness wait and sizes the `<video>` from the plan's metadata. This is what a local render already does for every video whose frames it supplies (`collectVideoReadinessSkipIds` / `collectVideoMetadataHints`).
- Cloud Run is out of scope: its chunk worker still downloads every artifact. The producer side (`materializePlanV2Target(..., { remoteSources })`) is storage-neutral, so the same switch is available to it later.

### Why the bytes are still the right bytes

A deferred video is no longer hashed on the chunk, so integrity rests on how plan v2 stores artifacts:

1. **The key is the content hash.** Artifacts live at `.../artifacts/sha256/<2>/<sha256>`, and the manifest that names them is itself pinned by the `PlanHash` the state machine passes.
2. **Objects are written once, and S3 checks the bytes on write.** The publisher puts each blob with `If-None-Match: *` and `ChecksumSHA256`, so S3 rejects a body that does not hash to the key, and no publisher can overwrite it.
3. **S3 attests the object before the URL is signed.** The handler sends `HeadObject` with `ChecksumMode: ENABLED` and refuses (`PLAN_ARTIFACT_DIGEST_MISMATCH`) unless the stored SHA-256 and size equal the manifest's.
4. **A read that fails partway fails the chunk.** FFmpeg can exit cleanly after a refused read. I checked this with a server that refuses the seek: it produced zero frames, and the chunk failed (`zero_output`). The chunk already fails when any frame it needs is missing.
5. **FFmpeg verifies S3's certificate.** For an `https` input, ffmpeg and ffprobe get `-tls_verify 1 -ca_file <bundle>` (`urlInputArgs`). The bundle is the first of `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt` (the Lambda `nodejs:22` image, Amazon Linux 2023), `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` and `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` that exists. If none exists, the read fails with a clear error instead of going ahead unverified. Local paths and plain `http` are unchanged.

### The signed URL never shows up in errors

`extractVideoFramesRange` strips the query string from every http(s) URL in each string field of an error it throws (message, diagnostic, stack). It uses the same `redactUrlQueryStrings` that telemetry already uses, now exported from core. ffprobe diagnostics were already redacted.

## What I measured

- **Same frames, fewer bytes (unit test, real ffmpeg).** Extracting 15 frames from the middle of a 2-minute lossless 640x360 file, by URL versus by local path: identical JPEG bytes for every frame, and the server sent about 10-12 MB of a 71 MB file. Most of that is socket buffering past the seek, so the share falls as files grow.
- **Same chunk, byte for byte.** A real chunk render (Chrome + ffmpeg) of a plan-v2 chunk that shows a deferred video gives the same chunk sha256 whether the video comes from the plan or from a local HTTP server. Without the plan-metadata sizing it differs (mutation below).
- **Every new test fails without the change.** On the base branch with this branch's tests: the handler test sees the video downloaded, the URL extraction finds no source, the end-to-end render finds the video copied into the plan, and the two new helpers do not exist. Each production change also has a mutation that turns exactly its test red: no URL from the handler, no checksum check, materialize copying or accepting any remote path, the extractor ignoring the URL, no stray-URL check, and no `<video>` sizing.
- **TLS verification is on and works on Lambda.** I redeployed this head and rendered the 2-minute fixture. It SUCCEEDED with 16 chunks, 0 failed tasks, 44 s in Step Functions and $0.065. Every chunk read its video by URL with verification on, and no log line contains a signed query. Output: 3600 frames, 120.000 s, audio intact, and the frame at 65 s is right. I listed the bundle inside `public.ecr.aws/lambda/nodejs:22` (Amazon Linux 2023): `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt` exists and `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` does not. With the bundled ffmpeg and ffprobe builds, `-tls_verify 1 -ca_file` accepts S3, rejects a self-signed certificate, and fails when the CA file is missing. Without `-tls_verify` the self-signed site is accepted, which is the gap this closes.
- **Tests for both fixes.** A test checks that the URL-input args carry `-tls_verify 1 -ca_file`. Another checks the refusal when no bundle exists, and a third checks that a failing ffmpeg run leaves no signed query in the error. Breaking each fix turns its test red.
- Lint, format, typecheck for core, engine, producer and aws-lambda, and the comment and fallow audits are clean. The changed test files pass 3 runs in a row.

**One real AWS Lambda render** of a 30-minute 1080p30 fixture: a 932 MB H.264 background video that is on screen the whole time, plus a GSAP title and AAC audio. I deployed this branch with reserved concurrency 300 and rendered with `--max-parallel-chunks 225`, giving 225 chunks of 240 frames.

| | Before (same fixture, earlier baseline on main) | This branch |
|---|---|---|
| Seconds from Lambda start to the chunk's first browser launch | about 45 s (the whole 932 MB video downloaded and hashed) | **median 2.9 s**, p90 5.2 s, max 5.7 s (all 225 chunks) |
| Bytes of the video each chunk reads | 932 MB | the moov box plus the byte ranges for its 8 seconds (locally: 17.5 MB of a 293 MB 1080p file for one 240-frame chunk, socket buffering included) |

- Whole render: Step Functions 302 s (plan 109 s, chunks 107 s, assemble 86 s), with 0 failed tasks and 0 retries. Chunk Lambdas took 19-24 s each. Measured cost was $0.83 for 227 invocations.
- The chunks did not run as one wave. Peak concurrency was 50, which is the state machine's own Map limit, not something this PR touches.
- Output, checked with `ffprobe -count_packets`: h264 1920x1080 at 30/1, **54000 frames**, 1800.000 s. AAC audio is 1800.000 s (84376 packets) at a mean of -27.1 dB, the same as the baseline. Frames grabbed at 900 s and 1799 s show the right background timecode and title state.
- The local Range proof is the same 240-frame chunk extracted from a 1080p 4 Mb/s file once by path and once by HTTP: identical sha256 over all 240 frames.

The baseline was measured at 16 chunks, so the end-to-end times are not comparable. The window before browser launch is: it is spent on the download whatever the chunk length, and it is what this PR removes.

## What I did NOT exercise

- **Cloud Run.** Its chunk worker still downloads every artifact whole.
- **Short-lived credentials.** A pre-signed URL stops working when the Lambda's role session expires, even before its own 1-hour expiry. A chunk that hits that fails loudly and is retried.
- **Plain `http` inputs, and hosts whose CA bundle is somewhere else.** Plain `http` inputs get no TLS options; only the local test servers use them. A host with its bundle in another path fails with a clear error instead of reading unverified.

title: perf(producer): overlap the plan step's audio work and hash files once
body:
On a 30-minute 1080p30 project the distributed plan step on AWS Lambda drops from about 112 s to about 88 s. The audio mix now runs alongside hashing and uploading the project files, instead of in front of them, and each file is hashed once instead of up to four times. Plan artifacts and final videos are byte-identical to main.

## What changed

- **The audio mix overlaps the rest of the plan.** Only the assembler reads the mixed audio. The plan used to run the full-length AAC encode first, then hash every file, then upload. Now `buildLocalExecutionPlan` moves `compiled/` and the video trees into their final places first. It then starts the audio stage and, in parallel, streams a hash of those trees. `planV2WithPublisher` adds a `whileAudioMixes` callback that uploads the `compiled/` blobs in that same window, using the existing 32-slot pool. `artifactTargets` ships every `compiled/` file to every chunk, so each pre-uploaded blob is in the manifest; the new test checks this.
  - The audio stage resolves sources from the final `compiled/` dir. Its contents are the same copy of the project, so the audio input bytes and ffmpeg args don't change.
- **Hash once.** A `PlanFileDigests` memo (sha256 by absolute path) is filled by that streamed prehash. It is then read by `freezePlan`, by the publication's plan-hash recompute, and by the per-artifact digests.
  - Freeze used to `readFileSync` each whole file, including the full 902 MB video. It now streams.
  - The S3 upload no longer re-hashes the local file before the PUT: the PUT already sends `ChecksumSHA256`, and S3 rejects bytes that don't match.
  - `S3PlanV2ArtifactPublisher.putBlob` returns early for a digest it already published, so blobs uploaded during the audio window are not checked again with a HEAD afterwards.
  - Chunks still verify every artifact they download.
- **Stage timers.** The plan logs one line per stage with its wall time (`[plan] stage {"stage","ms"}`): copy, compile, probe, extract, audio, prehash, prepublish, freeze, publication, upload, manifest. The Lambda handler adds `plan_stage` lines for download and untar.
  - Before this, the plan's 86 s after compile had no log lines at all.

## What I measured

All runs used the same 30-min fixture: a 902 MB H.264 background, 29 MB of AAC, and a GSAP title, 16 chunks. Everything ran on one 10 GB x86 Lambda stack, swapping only the function code. Each plan was a direct invoke of the `plan` action.

- **Main** was measured with bench-only stage timers added and no other change.
- **This PR**'s first commit was measured three times, and the final head twice more after the simplify pass.

| stage (ms) | main run 1 | main run 2 | PR runs (3 + 2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| download + untar | 17,181 | 19,294 | 14,933-18,370 |
| copy + compile + probe + extract | 4,745 | 4,221 | 4,613-5,868 |
| audio (prehash and prepublish run inside it) | 65,599 | 65,382 | 62,719-66,006 |
| prehash, overlapped | - | - | 2,732-3,195 |
| prepublish (compiled/ upload), overlapped | - | - | 9,790-9,936 |
| freeze | 3,512 | 3,453 | 120-125 |
| publication | 6,667 | 6,648 | 140-231 |
| upload | 13,623 | 13,048 | 446-471 |
| **Lambda Duration** | **111.8 s** | **112.5 s** | **85.8-90.5 s** |

- The tail after audio went from about 23.5 s to about 0.8 s. Peak memory went from about 5.1 GB to about 4.2 GB.
- The audio encode itself (about 64 s on Lambda) is now the critical path of the plan.

Byte identity:
- **Full renders.** The same 2-min project rendered end to end (plan, 16 chunks, assemble) on main, on the first commit and on the head. All three final MP4s have the same sha256 (138,129,659 bytes).
- **30-min plan on a Linux box.**
  - Every published artifact is byte-identical between main and this PR, including the mixed `audio.m4a`, except `meta/videos.json` and `plan.json`.
  - `meta/videos.json` embeds the planner's random staging directory, so it also differs between two runs of main. With that one path normalized it is identical. `plan.json` differs only because it carries the resulting hashes.

Tests (bun, each file 3 runs in a row):
- **New, failing on main:** the compiled tree is published while the audio mixes, and that publish produces the same manifest as a serial build.
- **New, failing on main:** a digest taken earlier in the plan is reused, not recomputed.
- **New, failing on main:** a local file that no longer matches its digest is rejected by the S3 checksum.
- **New, failing on main:** the handler logs download and untar timings.
- **New:** the S3 publisher sends nothing for a digest it already published. Deleting the early return fails it.
- Each new test was also checked with one deliberate mutation of the code it covers, and failed.

## What I did NOT exercise

- **30-min renders end to end.** I did not run one; output identity at 30 minutes rests on the plan artifacts being identical, plus the 2-min full renders.
- **The GCS planner.** It shares the overlap and the memo but was not run against real GCS. `gcsTransport` still hashes locally before its upload, since GCS has no SHA-256 check on its side.
- **The non-deferred plan path.** Here the prehash also covers extracted frame trees, and it was only exercised by the existing unit tests.
- **Downloaded or out-of-project videos.** These ship under `video-sources/` and are not pre-uploaded during the audio window, so they still upload after it. This fixture's video lives in the project, so it ships under `compiled/`.

title: perf(aws-lambda): the plan step probes project videos in place instead of downloading them
body:
## What changed

The plan step used to download every project video in full, only to read its header and its last second. Now a video stays in the shared content store (from the PR below this one), and the plan reads those two parts over HTTP.

- **Lambda plan.** When it rebuilds a deployed site, the plan step downloads only the non-video files. For each video (`.mp4 .mov .m4v .webm .mkv`) it passes a pre-signed GET URL (1 hour) with the file's SHA-256 and size as `remoteFiles` to `planV2WithPublisher`. A `.tar.gz` project and the v1 plan path behave exactly as before.
- **Planner.** Each such file is keyed by the local path it would have had. Three resolvers check that map: the compiler's duration probe (header only), the engine's video extractor (metadata, then the deferred last-second tail probe, both straight from the URL with no download) and the audio mixer. `meta/videos.json` records the project path, never the URL. `meta/remote-files.json` lists path, SHA-256 and size, so the plan hash covers those files.
- **Publication.** Those files become manifest artifacts under `compiled/<path>`, routed like any compiled asset. A new optional publisher method, `referenceStoredBlob`, confirms the object is already in the store (stored digest and size must match, and the 7-day age refresh applies) instead of uploading it. A local plan directory, or a publisher without that method, refuses remote files loudly.
- **Chunks** are unchanged. They fetch the artifact by digest from the shared store and verify it. Chunk range reads (a sibling change) read the same object through its own pre-signed URL.

### Two bugs fixed along the way

- `extractMediaMetadata` read the entire video into memory as a possible PNG whenever any of its three color tags was missing, which is common for H.264. It now does that only when ffprobe reports PNG. A regression test fails without the fix.
- Plan asset hashing used `readFileSync`, which Node refuses above 2 GiB. It now streams, using one shared hasher (`sha256FileHex`) for `freezePlan` and plan v2.

## What I measured

- A real planner run (ffmpeg present) on a 3-second H.264 video known only by URL. The plan defers the video, `meta/videos.json` points at `compiled/assets/clip.mp4` with no URL in it, the publisher references the digest and never receives its bytes, and changing the digest changes the plan hash.
- The Lambda handler test asserts the plan step makes no GET of the video's key and uploads only the manifest.
- I broke the code once for each mechanism, and a test failed each time: extractor lookup, source shipper, publication of remote entries, the `srcPath` mapping, the handler keeping videos remote, a missing object accepted, a referenced digest not counted as durable, and the PNG fix reverted.
- Existing suites pass, one file at a time: producer planV2 62, plan 46, renderChunk 19, htmlCompiler 142, publicExports 8; engine ffprobe 137, videoFrameExtractor 201, audioMixer 69; aws-lambda handler 18, publisher 8, transport 14, deploySite 9.
- **Real AWS run.** I deployed this head (stacked on #5774), with reserved concurrency 300, 10 GB x86, in us-east-2. The fixture was a 30-minute 1080p30 benchmark: one 902 MB H.264 video, 29 MB of audio, 1800 s. I rendered it twice, once as the first upload and once reusing the site, and compared against the same fixture on main.

| | main | run 1 (first upload) | run 2 (reuse) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plan step (Step Functions state) | 103.6 s | 70.7 s | 66.2 s |
| Plan reaches "compiled composition" | 16.9 s | ~5 s | |
| Plan peak memory, cold start | 5,138 MB | 1,013 MB | (warm start, not comparable) |
| Copies of the video in the bucket | one per render | 1 | still 1 |
| Submit to finished file | 968.8 s | 944.1 s | 937.9 s |
| Lambda cost per render | $2.09 | $2.09 | $2.09 |

  - The bytes moved: after both runs the bucket held exactly one object the size of the video, under `cas/sha256/`, last written at the CLI upload. Neither plan read it whole or re-uploaded it, and no render has its own copy.
  - Both outputs, checked with ffprobe: 54000 video packets, 1800.000 s, an AAC track of 1800 s, mean -27.1 dB.
  - Whole renders stay at about 16 minutes on this lane alone, because the chunks take about 13 of them (787 s Map). That changes only with chunk range reads and the Distributed Map changes.
  - The plan's remaining ~66 s is not timed by stage on this branch. The largest item is probably the audio mix of 1800 s (a separate change).
  - Everything I deployed was deleted afterwards, and a resource listing for the stack's name came back empty.

## What I did NOT exercise

- A video with an audio track (`data-has-audio`) is still fetched whole by the audio mixer when it needs that audio. That is correct but not faster; the plan's audio work is a separate change.
- Some header probes are not cached for URLs: about four per remote file.
- Media referenced only from a sub-composition whose duration needs the browser probe does not see the URL map.
- Cloud Run keeps today's path.

title: test(studio): the edit accuracy bench starts one server when node is a Volta shim
body:
## What

The edit accuracy bench now starts exactly one Studio server per case on machines where `node` on `PATH` is a version manager's shim, such as Volta. Before, such a machine either failed every case at once or started copies of the server without end.

## Why

`startServer` spawns the CLI with a bare `node` and replaces `HOME` with a per-case directory, so Studio's undo history stays inside the case. A Volta shim finds its toolchain through `HOME`. Under the per-case `HOME` it has no toolchain, and one of two things happens:

- it exits at once: `studio exited 126: Volta error: Node is not available`
- it runs another copy of itself as its own child, again and again. One case start became 195 identical `node <cli> preview <case> --port 5800 --no-open --foreground --force-new` processes in 30 s, each the child of the previous one. Left running, this exhausts the user's process limit.

The case's `HOME` gets a fresh `.volta` directory the moment the case starts, which shows the shim is what ran there. The CLI's `preview` is not involved: started directly, or by the bench where `node` is the real binary, it runs one server.

## How

`startServer` resolves the real node binary under the bench's own environment (`node -p process.execPath`), then spawns that absolute path with the per-case `HOME`. The server still runs under the per-case `HOME`; only the lookup of `node` moved.

## Test plan

New case in `server.test.mjs`: a fake `node` shim first on `PATH` that refuses to run under any `HOME` but the real one, as Volta does. One `startServer` call has to start exactly one server, and that server has to run under the case's `HOME`.

- With the fix: 2 passed, three runs in a row.
- With the spawn reverted to bare `node`: 1 failed, `studio exited 126: shim: no node under HOME=<case home>`.
- One real bench case (`move-keys-px-r0-root-z100-on`) on a Linux machine with Volta first on `PATH`, under a process cap:
  - before: either the 126 failure or the chain of copies
  - after: one server, and the case passes (1 of 1 accurate, 0 errors)

## What I did NOT exercise

- The new test on Windows: it is skipped there, because the fake shim is a shell script.
- Other version managers keyed on `HOME` (nvm, asdf): the fix doesn't depend on which manager it is, but I only ran it against Volta.

title: chore: release v0.8.168
body:
Release v0.8.168.

Scrubbing back across a scene in the preview now shows its content instead of an empty frame. Cloud renders size their chunks to the worker limit and assemble in one pass, so long videos finish faster.

Full notes: `releases/v0.8.168.md`.

## No visible change

Version bump and changelog only. Each change was captured and reviewed in its own PR.

title: fix(cli): Chrome starts inside an agent's macOS sandbox
body:
## What

Chrome now starts inside an agent's macOS sandbox. When `CODEX_SANDBOX=seatbelt` is set on macOS, every CLI browser launches as one process with DevTools over a pipe. When an unnamed sandbox refuses Chrome's mach service, the launch is retried once that way.

## Why

Codex runs agent commands in a macOS seatbelt (`CODEX_SANDBOX=seatbelt`). Inside it, Chrome's child processes cannot register their mach rendezvous, so a normal multi-process Chrome dies at startup:

```
FATAL:base/apple/mach_port_rendezvous_mac.cc:159] Check failed: kr == KERN_SUCCESS. bootstrap_check_in org.chromium.Chromium.MachPortRendezvousServer.…: Permission denied (1100)
```

`--no-sandbox` does not help, and `--no-zygote` does nothing on macOS. `--single-process` works.

The CLI already had that launch (pipe plus `--single-process`), but only when its project server could not listen. A seatbelt that allows the network lets the server listen, so the CLI launched the normal way and Chrome died. `check` then reported `Failed to launch the browser process: Code: null` and skipped every browser check.

## Related work

Follows the change that turned this crash into a "rerun with escalation" message. Now that the launch works, that message is left for launches that still fail after the one-process retry.

## How

- `browser/sandboxDenied.ts` owns the decision: `inAgentSandbox()` (macOS plus `CODEX_SANDBOX=seatbelt`), `oneProcessOverPipe()` (`pipe: true` plus `--single-process`, added once) and `machServiceDenied()`.
- `launchManagedBrowser`, the one owner of CLI browser launches, uses one process over a pipe when the sandbox names itself or the caller already asked for it. If a normal launch dies with the mach denial, it relaunches once that way. If that also fails, the error carries the escalation remediation as before.
- The project server's no-listen path and the GPU probe now call the same `oneProcessOverPipe()` instead of their own inline copies.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit: under `CODEX_SANDBOX=seatbelt` on macOS the first launch is one process over a pipe. A mach-denied launch relaunches that way once. The existing escalation and other-failure tests still pass.
- [x] fails without the fix: with the old launch decision both new tests fail (`expected { args: [ '--headless' ], … } to match object { pipe: true, … }`).
- [x] On macOS, the published CLI against this branch's build, `check` on a small composition:

| Sandbox | Published 0.8.167 | This branch |
|---|---|---|
| mach registration denied, network open (`sandbox-exec`, `(deny mach-register)`) | `Failed to launch the browser process: Code: null`, browser checks skipped | browser checks run, no errors |
| same, with `CODEX_SANDBOX=seatbelt` | same failure | browser checks run, no errors |
| `codex sandbox -P :workspace` (Codex's own workspace-write seatbelt, network off) | passes (server can't listen, existing path) | passes |
| no sandbox | passes | passes |

- [x] `src/browser/` and `captureCompositionFrame.test.ts` pass 3 runs in a row (197 tests). `tsc`, oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: fix(producer): plan hash no longer depends on the scratch folder
body:
## What changed

A distributed plan now gets the same plan hash every time it is built from the same inputs, including plans with a video.

`meta/videos.json` recorded each video's source as an absolute path inside the planner's temporary work folder. That folder has a random name on every run, and the file feeds the plan hash, so any plan with a video got a new hash each run. That broke the contract in `planHash.ts` ("two invocations with identical inputs MUST produce the same hash"), which replay short-circuits and cross-version checks rely on.

The source is now written without the work folder: `compiled/...` or `video-frames/...` relative to the plan, project-relative for project files, and unchanged only for files outside the project (those are real inputs, so they are already stable). Nothing reads this field to open a file: chunks rebuild frame paths from `video-frames/<videoId>`, and deferred extraction uses `deferredRange.sourcePath`, which was already plan-relative.

The test plans one project with a real (generated) video into two different plan folders and checks the plan hash, the `meta/videos.json` bytes and the recorded source. The existing determinism test used a composition with no video, which is why this was never caught. The two ffmpeg-fixture tests in the file now share one small helper.

## What I measured

- New test: passes 3 runs in a row; with only the `plan.ts` change reverted it fails on the plan hash itself (two different hashes).
- `plan.test.ts` 55 pass, `renderChunk.test.ts` 19 pass, `planV2.test.ts` 62 pass, `rebuildExtractedFrames.test.ts` 5 pass, all 0 fail. Producer typecheck, oxlint, oxfmt, the comment checks and the Fallow audit are clean.

## What I did NOT exercise

- A real cloud render. The field is not opened by any chunk code path (checked by search), so I verified at the plan level only.
- Plans made by older producers still parse: the field is still a non-empty string, and the plan hash already includes the producer version.

## Main integration after merge-queue failure

Current signed head `8129af41685c6c910d725d3522829876796645b2` merges main `7e00f37be2c76b4a9294c81aed79cf49667709f1`. Main and this PR each added the same `spawnSync` import to `plan.test.ts`; Git merged them textually, but the actual queue lint rejected the duplicate declaration. Removed only that duplicate import, retaining both branches' fixtures and all plan behavior.

- fails without the fix: oxlint on the integrated file reports `Identifier spawnSync has already been declared` at lines 18/20; this matches queue job117525476189. With one import, lint and format pass.
- Fresh combined branch: 56 plan tests pass, including the generated-video same-hash test and main's stitched-audio fixture; producer typecheck passes. Normal signed-commit hooks pass lint/format, core/Studio/scripts types, commit-message/large-file/artifact and Fallow gates; no suppressions added.
- A fresh full build was attempted. Producer, core and prerequisites built, but inspector could not resolve `eslint-scope` / `@jridgewell/trace-mapping` in the reused local dependency cache. This is not a full local build pass. No dependencies were installed or shared caches changed; current-head locked-dependency hosted CI remains required.
- Original independent approval applies to predecessor `b66afc69`; successor review and fresh hosted checks are pending.

title: perf(producer): mp4 chunks as fragmented pieces that join by concatenation
body:
> **Parked: waiting on a product decision.** Streamed from its S3 URL over a ~6 Mbps link, the 30-minute fragmented output does not become playable in Chrome or WebKit within 60 s (no duration). The same streams remuxed as a regular faststart MP4 are ready in 1.3 s (Chrome) and 6.3 s (WebKit). A downloaded file plays fine everywhere, and AVFoundation streams it fine. Adding a total duration (`mehd`) and a leading fragment index (`sidx`) fixes Chrome's start (0.9 s) but not WebKit. An alternative that keeps the S3 stitch and a ~2 s assemble: chunks upload raw sample data, and the assembler writes a regular `moov` (built from per-chunk sample tables) in front of chunk 0 as part 1. Full measurements are in the comment below.

## What changed

On the AWS Lambda path (plan protocol v2), `format: "mp4"` output becomes a **fragmented MP4** (ftyp + moov init segment, then one movie fragment per chunk). Each chunk now uploads a self-contained piece: its video plus the plan audio packets that start inside its frame range, muxed into one moof + mdat. Chunk 0's piece also carries the init segment. Fragment sequence numbers and decode times (tfdt) are rewritten to their place in the whole render, so the final file is the pieces' bytes in order. Assemble now just concatenates them, with no concat demuxer, audio mux or faststart pass. This PR is the format half. The follow-up stitches the pieces inside S3 with multipart copy, so assemble moves no video bytes at all.

- `plan`: the new `fragmentedMp4` option (set only by the Lambda plan handler, and ignored for other formats and with `cfr`) is locked into `meta/encoder.json`. With it, the plan fits the mixed audio to exactly `totalFrames / fps`, including the true-peak fix. Assemble used to do that, but every chunk now needs the fitted audio. The audio artifact is routed to every chunk instead of the assembler.
- `renderChunk`: after the usual encode, `buildFragmentedPiece` muxes the chunk with its audio packets. The audio packets come straight from the one continuous AAC encode, selected with input `-ss`/`-t` at half-packet cut points plus `-copypriorss 0`; chunk 0 keeps the priming packet and its edit list. It then patches the moof in place and drops the init for chunks after 0. It checks the sample counts it expects (video frames, audio packets) and refuses a chunk whose video does not start at media time 0. Chunks are encoded with `-bf 0`, and a B-frame delay would shift each piece differently.
- `assemble`: a fragmented plan is joined by byte concatenation.
- Unchanged: mov, webm and png-sequence, Cloud Run (it never sets the option), local `planV2()`, and v1 plans.
- The lambda-local harness's disk-usage sampler no longer crashes when a scratch file disappears between listing and stat. I hit that flake while testing this.

Audio has no seams: all chunks share one AAC encode, each packet appears exactly once, and the seams are packet boundaries of that encode. Decoded samples are byte-identical to today's output (below).

## What I measured

All on the Lambda's ffmpeg build (7.0.2-static):
- **Through the real Lambda handler** (lambda-local harness with a filesystem S3, `audio-mux-parity` fixture, 10 s 1080p30, 5 chunks): v2 fragmented against v1 today. 300/300 video frames identical (framemd5 hash and pts), decoded audio PCM byte-identical. `ffprobe -v error` prints nothing for either. Video reports 10.000000 s in both. The audio stream reports 10.021 s in the fragmented file against 10.000 s today, because fragmented MP4 has no edit-list end trim for the AAC padding. The decoded samples are the same.
- **Players**, same file, seeks to 1, 5 and 9.5 s:
  - ffprobe/ffmpeg: no errors.
  - AVFoundation (QuickTime's engine) on macOS: playable, frames at each time.
  - Google Chrome 113 (`<video>` over HTTP with Range): readyState 4, playback advances, every seek lands exactly, no `error`. It reports duration 10.021.
  - **WebKit, not Safari** (Playwright WebKit 26.6 on macOS): same checks pass, and it reports duration 10.000.
  - The frame at 5 s is the same in every player and matches today's output.
- `fmp4Piece.test.ts`: real x264 chunks (uneven sizes, a 1-frame tail) and real AAC, joined by `assemble()`, compared against today's `assemble()` on the same chunks. Frames, audio samples, video duration, box layout and sequence numbers all match. 3/3 runs green. Each of these mutations turns it red: no `-copypriorss`, audio tfdt not shifted, sequence numbers not rewritten, B-frame guard removed.
- `plan.test.ts`: with the option, `encoder.json` carries it, and the audio is fitted to 1.000 s with peak below -1 dB (removing the fit gives -0.1 dB, red). With `cfr`, the field is absent.
- `planV2.test.ts`, `assemble.test.ts`, `renderChunk.test.ts`, `audioPadTrim.test.ts`, aws-lambda `handler.test.ts`: green. Producer and aws-lambda `tsc` clean.

## What I did NOT exercise

- **Safari itself.** safaridriver needs "Allow remote automation" turned on, and I could not enable it on the test Mac. The WebKit run above stands in for it.
- A real AWS render. The follow-up PR (S3 stitch) deploys and runs the 30-minute benchmark end to end.
- h265 mp4 on Lambda. Its chunks are also encoded `-bf 0`, so the same path applies, but I did not run it.
- Known costs, left out on purpose:
  - Every chunk downloads the whole fitted audio (about 43 MB for 30 min, roughly 0.5 s, in parallel).
  - One extra `-c copy` remux per chunk, about 0.2 s.
  - Chunks after 0 copy their piece once to drop the 1 KB init.

title: perf(aws-lambda): stitch the final mp4 inside S3
body:
> **Parked: waiting on a product decision.** Streamed from its S3 URL over a ~6 Mbps link, the 30-minute fragmented output does not become playable in Chrome or WebKit within 60 s (no duration). The same streams remuxed as a regular faststart MP4 are ready in 1.3 s (Chrome) and 6.3 s (WebKit). A downloaded file plays fine everywhere, and AVFoundation streams it fine. Adding a total duration (`mehd`) and a leading fragment index (`sidx`) fixes Chrome's start (0.9 s) but not WebKit. An alternative that keeps the S3 stitch and a ~2 s assemble: chunks upload raw sample data, and the assembler writes a regular `moov` (built from per-chunk sample tables) in front of chunk 0 as part 1. Full measurements are in a comment on #5783.

## What changed

Stacked on #5783 (mp4 chunks become fragmented-MP4 pieces that join by byte concatenation).

On the AWS Lambda path, assemble no longer downloads the chunks, joins them and uploads the result. When the plan's mp4 chunks are fragmented pieces, the assemble Lambda builds the final object inside S3: one multipart upload whose parts are `UploadPartCopy` reads of the chunk objects, in chunk order. No video bytes pass through the function, so assemble time no longer grows with the size of the video.

- `s3Stitch.ts`:
  - `headObjectSizes` reads each chunk's size.
  - `canCopyAsParts` refuses when a chunk other than the last is under S3's 5 MiB minimum part size.
  - `stitchS3Objects` runs Create, then all copies, then Complete. If any copy fails, it waits for the other copies to settle, aborts the upload so no parts are left billed, and rethrows.
- `handleAssembleV2`:
  - Checks the chunk URI count against the plan manifest.
  - Stitches in S3 and logs `assemble_stages {mode: "s3-stitch", planMs, stitchMs, parts}`.
  - Falls back to the existing local join when a piece is too small, which happens on short renders with many chunks.
  - `FramesEncoded` comes from the manifest, and `FileSize` is the sum of the piece sizes.
- The plan download now returns the manifest it already parsed, so the stitch path does not read `plan.json` again.
- Unchanged: non-fragmented plans, mov/webm/png-sequence, Cloud Run, and v1 plans all keep the local join.

## What I measured

- `s3Stitch.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`, 3 runs in a row each, green. The handler tests use a fake S3 with real multipart semantics:
  - "stitches fragmented pieces inside S3 without downloading them": the output bytes equal the pieces concatenated, and no chunk is downloaded.
  - "joins locally when a piece before the last is under S3's 5 MiB part minimum": the local assemble runs instead.
- Mutations, each turns a test red: dropping the abort, dropping the 5 MiB check, ignoring the stitch result.
- aws-lambda and producer `tsc`, producer `publicExports.test.ts`, `assemble.test.ts`: green.
- Snapshot parity test for the abort grant: 3/3 green, and red with the grant removed.
- **Real AWS, 30-minute 1080p30 benchmark** (the same fixture as the main baseline: 1800 s, looping 902 MB background video, tone audio), deployed from this branch with `hyperframes lambda deploy --concurrency 300`, rendered with `--max-parallel-chunks 225`:
  - **Assemble: 1.8 s** Step Functions state. Inside the function: 0.42 s plan download, then **1.21 s to stitch 225 parts**. Main's baseline at 16 chunks: **81.5 s**. The old assemble downloaded about 2 GB, ran ffmpeg and uploaded 2 GB. That work is gone, and assemble no longer grows with video length.
  - End to end: 343 s in Step Functions (plan 127.8 s, render map 213.6 s, assemble 1.8 s); the CLI measured 397 s from submit to final file, including the site upload. Plan and chunk rendering are other work in flight.
  - Measured cost (Lambda REPORT lines plus Step Functions): **$1.62**. 227 invocations all OK, 0 failed, 0 timed out.
  - Output, downloaded and checked:
    - 2.07 GB; `ffprobe -v error` empty; a full decode of all 30 minutes reports no errors.
    - h264 1920x1080 30/1, **54000 frames**, video **1800.000 s**.
    - AAC **84376 packets**, the same count as main's output. Mean -27.1 dB and max -22.3 dB, as on main, and the last 2 s still at -27.1 dB.
    - 225 movie fragments with sequence numbers 1-225, continuous.
    - The audio stream and container read 1800.021 s. Fragmented MP4 has no edit-list end trim for the AAC padding (#5783 explains this); the decoded samples are unchanged.
  - Pictures at 5 s, 900 s and 1799 s show the right background timecode and title state, and match main's frames at the same times.
  - Chrome (`<video>` over HTTP with Range): plays, and seeks to 5, 900 and 1799 s land exactly.
  - No incomplete multipart uploads were left in the bucket. The stack is torn down and nothing remains.

## What I did NOT exercise

- Starting the chunk size lookups (HEAD requests) before the plan download finishes. They wait for it today; overlapping would save roughly 0.1 s.
- One producer-side "how to assemble" decision shared by `assemble()` and the handler. Today the handler asks `chunksAreFragmentedPieces` and the producer asks it again on fallback.

title: fix(gcp-cloud-run): the BeginFrame contract image resolves the engine's core import
body:
## What changed

The GCP Cloud Run image's `beginframe-contract` stage (the `GCP BeginFrame image contract` CI job) failed on main with `Cannot find module '@hyperframes/core' from '/app/packages/engine/src/config.ts'`. #5756 made the engine config import the distributed fps set from `@hyperframes/core`, and that stage copies only the `parsers` and `engine` sources before running the engine's `buildChromeArgs`.

Copying core's source into the stage alone is not enough: core's root entry re-exports `./generated/runtime-inline`, a build artifact this stage deliberately never builds. So:

- The fps set moves to its own core module, exported as `@hyperframes/core/distributed-fps` (declared in `package.json` exports, `publishConfig.exports` and `package-subpaths.json`, like `telemetry-redaction`). The core root still re-exports it, so no public import changes.
- The engine config imports the subpath, the same way the engine already imports `@hyperframes/core/audio-fx`, `audio-gain` and the other light core modules.
- The contract stage copies `packages/core/` next to `packages/parsers/`.

## What I measured

- `node scripts/package-subpaths.mjs`: "Package subpaths verified: 14 public workspaces."
- `check:gcp-cloud-run-dockerfile`: "GCP Cloud Run Dockerfile covers 15 workspace manifests."
- Real `docker build --target beginframe-contract -f packages/gcp-cloud-run/Dockerfile .` on a linux/amd64 host (Docker 24):
  - this branch: exit 0; the stage runs `buildChromeArgs` and the BeginFrame probe against the pinned headless shell.
  - main at the same moment: exit 1 at the same step with `error: Cannot find module '@hyperframes/core' from '/app/packages/engine/src/config.ts'` (the CI failure).
- `tsc --noEmit` clean in core, engine, producer and cli; `parseFps.test.ts` 25 passed, engine `config.test.ts` 113 passed.

## What I did NOT exercise

- The full `runtime` image target and a Cloud Run deploy.

title: fix(repo): lint and format hooks use the repo's pinned oxlint and oxfmt
body:
## What changed

The pre-commit `lint` and `format` hooks ran `bunx oxlint` / `bunx oxfmt`. In a checkout without `node_modules`, `bunx` fetches the latest release instead of the repo's pinned one (`package.json` devDependencies, `oxfmt ^0.41.0`), and even `bunx --no-install` falls back to bun's global `@latest` cache. A newer oxfmt orders `publishConfig` keys in `packages/core/package.json` differently from CI's, so the hook reformatted a correctly formatted file back to the shape CI's Format check rejects and re-staged it, leaving an empty commit.

Both hooks now:
- run the installed binary through `bun run`, which only resolves `node_modules/.bin` and never downloads, so `package.json` stays the one owner of the version;
- refuse when the package is not installed: `oxfmt is not installed in this checkout, run bun install` (exit 1, files untouched).

## What I measured

- Checkout without `node_modules`, a mis-formatted `packages/core/package.json` staged, `git commit`: the format hook prints the message and fails; the staged file's hash is unchanged and no commit is created.
- Same file staged after `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `lefthook run pre-commit`: the hook reformats and re-stages it (staged hash changes), and `bun run format:check` (the command CI's Format job runs) then reports "All matched files use the correct format." over the whole repo.
- `lefthook.yml` passes `oxfmt --check` with the pinned version.

## Not changed

`typecheck`, `fallow` and `commitlint` still use `bunx`. They only report and never rewrite staged files; moving them to the pinned binaries is a separate change.

title: perf(engine): long renders encode their audio in parallel segments
body:
## What changed

Renders longer than two minutes now encode their soundtrack on several cores at once. On a 30-minute render the cloud plan step's audio work drops from about 64 s to about 19 s, which shortens the whole plan step by about 42 s.

The audio stage was almost entirely one AAC encode: ffmpeg's AAC encoder runs on one core at about 60x real time, so 30 minutes of audio took about a minute on a Lambda core. Decoding and mixing took under a second on a Linux test machine.

- `engine/src/services/aacEncode.ts` (new) owns the AAC encode. Audio of two minutes or more is cut at AAC frame boundaries into one segment per minute, up to 8. The segments are encoded in parallel to raw AAC frames, each segment's own frames are kept, and the frames are joined and remuxed into `audio.m4a` without re-encoding.
- Each segment starts 10 s before its cut and ends 8 frames after it; those extra frames are dropped. The encoder's rate control takes about 10 s to settle (a fresh encoder's error is higher for its first 10 s), so a shorter warm-up leaves a measurable quality dip after every cut. That is measured below, and the test fails with a 2-frame warm-up.
- Joined raw AAC frames lose the encoder's 1024-sample start delay that an `.m4a` records. The remux puts it back with `-itsoffset -1024/48000`. Remuxing a single encoder's frames this way decodes to exactly the same samples as today's file.
- Joined raw AAC frames also lose the last packet's short duration, so a length that is not a whole number of AAC frames (most real renders) made `audio.m4a` claim up to 21 ms more than it holds (180.010 s instead of 180.000 s on a 3-minute track; decoded samples were already identical). The remux now sets that last packet's duration with `setts`, so the stream ends exactly where a single encoder's does. Found while measuring the joins below; the test now uses an unaligned length and checks the end.
- The segment count depends only on the duration, never on the machine's core count, so the same project gives the same `audio.m4a` bytes (and plan hash) on any machine.
- Under two minutes nothing changes: same single encode, same bytes. The master-bus path already summed to a float WAV before encoding; long renders without a master chain now go through that same path (sum to float WAV, then encode), and both use the new encoder. The AAC settings have one owner (`AAC_ARGS`).

The mixed audio's role and format are unchanged: still `audio.m4a`, AAC-LC 192k, 48 kHz stereo, same duration and frame count, so anything that consumes the plan's mixed audio keeps working.

**Not byte-identical for long renders, by necessity.** An AAC encoder carries rate-control state across the whole stream, so frames from an encoder started mid-stream never fully re-converge with a single encoder's (after warm-up only 10 to 30% of frames matched). Any parallel encode differs from today's at codec-noise level. Measured differences are below.

## What I measured

Real AWS, one 10 GB Lambda stack, same 30-minute 1080p30 fixture (one 902 MB H.264 video, a GSAP overlay, one 30-minute AAC soundtrack at volume 0.5), direct plan invokes alternating base (main) and this branch:

| | base run 1 | base run 2 | new run 1 | new run 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| plan `audio` stage | 63.7 s | 63.6 s | 18.6 s | 18.7 s |
| whole plan step | 87.7 s | 86.5 s | 45.5 s | 45.6 s |

These runs still describe the current head: the later end-duration fix leaves 30-minute and 2-minute output byte-identical (both are whole numbers of AAC frames; checked by hash).

Sound, base vs new plan `audio.m4a` from those runs:
- Each version wrote byte-identical audio on both of its runs.
- Same 84,376 AAC frames, 1800.000 s, same decoded sample count; mean volume -27.1 dB and max -22.3 dB on both; integrated loudness -24.8 LUFS on both.
- Decoded difference, new minus base: -76.3 dB relative to the signal, max absolute difference 0.00055.

A full 2-minute cloud render (2 segments) on each version: video packets byte-identical; audio has the same packet count, start and duration; decoded audio differs by -73.1 dB. The new render plays in ffprobe, AVFoundation, Chrome, and WebKit, checked by seeks at 5, 60 and 119 s.

### Segment joins

Measured on the 30-minute benchmark soundtrack (a pure 440 Hz tone, the most sensitive click detector there is) and on a 2-minute and a 3-minute tone, PR output against main's output decoded to PCM. The audio inside the join windows is the PR's own bytes. Join k is where the decoder overlap-adds segment k-1's last packet with segment k's first packet: input samples [(cut-1)·1024, cut·1024), where cut = round(k · packets / segments) and packets = ceil(seconds · 48000 / 1024) + 1, the same math as the code. Every window is 50 ms, centred on that block; mid-segment is the middle of the segment that starts at the join.

| Fixture | Join | Decoder block (samples) | |PR−main| peak, join / mid-segment | Coding error vs source at join, PR / main | 2 kHz high-pass peak of PR, join / mid-segment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 min (benchmark) | 1 | 10,799,104–10,800,128 (224.992 s) | -79.6 / -110.1 dBFS | -73.3 / -75.0 dBFS | -93.0 / -94.1 dBFS |
| 30 min (benchmark) | 2 | 21,599,232–21,600,256 (449.995 s) | -87.0 / -113.2 dBFS | -73.2 / -74.7 dBFS | -94.3 / -94.3 dBFS |
| 30 min (benchmark) | 3 | 32,399,360–32,400,384 (674.997 s) | -83.4 / -113.1 dBFS | -71.6 / -73.1 dBFS | -94.6 / -93.9 dBFS |
| 30 min (benchmark) | 4 | 43,199,488–43,200,512 (900.000 s) | -99.2 / -111.8 dBFS | -74.2 / -74.2 dBFS | -94.2 / -94.7 dBFS |
| 30 min (benchmark) | 5 | 53,999,616–54,000,640 (1125.003 s) | -100.0 / -111.9 dBFS | -75.9 / -75.9 dBFS | -93.6 / -94.5 dBFS |
| 30 min (benchmark) | 6 | 64,799,744–64,800,768 (1350.005 s) | -80.1 / -111.6 dBFS | -71.7 / -71.7 dBFS | -95.0 / -94.6 dBFS |
| 30 min (benchmark) | 7 | 75,599,872–75,600,896 (1575.008 s) | -99.6 / -110.8 dBFS | -73.9 / -73.6 dBFS | -94.8 / -94.1 dBFS |
| 2 min | 1 | 2,879,488–2,880,512 (60.000 s) | -84.5 / -114.3 dBFS | -73.6 / -74.3 dBFS | -92.6 / -94.9 dBFS |
| 3 min | 1 | 2,879,488–2,880,512 (60.000 s) | -84.5 / -114.3 dBFS | -73.6 / -74.3 dBFS | -92.6 / -94.9 dBFS |
| 3 min | 2 | 5,760,000–5,761,024 (120.011 s) | -102.9 / -113.9 dBFS | -72.0 / -72.0 dBFS | -93.5 / -92.5 dBFS |

| Fixture | Alignment offset | Decoded samples, PR / main | Stream duration, PR / main | High-pass floor of PR (median / 99.9th pct of 50 ms windows) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 min (benchmark) | 0 samples | 86,400,000 / 86,400,000 | 1800.000000 / 1800.000000 s | -94.0 / -90.9 dBFS |
| 2 min | 0 samples | 5,760,000 / 5,760,000 | 120.000000 / 120.000000 s | -94.0 / -91.2 dBFS |
| 3 min | 0 samples | 8,640,512 / 8,640,512 | 180.000000 / 180.000000 s | -94.0 / -91.3 dBFS |

Reading it:
- **No click at any join.** The 2 kHz high-passed PR output (a 440 Hz tone has essentially nothing there, so a click shows as a broadband spike) sits at the noise floor at every join (−92.6 to −95.0 dBFS against a −94.0 median). As a check that the detector works: the 30-minute source track is itself 2-minute AAC files joined by stream copy, and those joins read −53.7 dBFS in both PR and main outputs, 40 dB above the floor.
- **Join windows differ from main more than mid-segment does, but are not worse.** For a pure tone two encoders settle to nearly identical frames, so mid-segment |PR−main| is around −110 dBFS. At a join the PR is encoded differently, but its coding error against the source there equals main's own in the same window (−71.6 to −75.9 dBFS for PR, −71.7 to −75.9 for main; the file's median is −74.0).
- **Largest difference in the 30-minute file:** −65.2 dBFS, 0.28 s after join 2. There the PR's coding error is −65.8 dBFS against main's −76.4 dBFS, but its high-passed level is −94.2 dBFS (floor) in both: narrowband quantisation from the new encoder settling, about 40 dB under the tone, not a broadband click.
- The 2-minute and 3-minute rows for join 1 match because both tones are the same deterministic 440 Hz sine, encoded identically up to that point, and both cut at packet 2,813.
- Listening proxy: 2 s around the first 30-minute join, PR and main. Spectrograms are indistinguishable (a steady 440 Hz line, no vertical broadband stripe at the join), and the high-passed waveform boosted 60 dB stays flat through the join in both.

Quality against the source, 3-minute pink noise plus tone (the new test), versus one encoder: RMS coding error 0.4 to 0.7% higher, and the peak error within 4096 frames of each cut matches one encoder's at the same spots. With only a 2-frame warm-up the RMS error is about 3% higher and every cut shows the encoder's start-up spike.

Tests: `aacEncode.test.ts` (4 tests) passes 3 runs in a row and with Lambda's bundled ffmpeg. The click test encodes a pure tone in segments and checks, at each join, the 2 kHz high-passed peak and the residual against the source (each under 2x the file's median 50 ms window; measured 0.97x and 1.29x). Mutations, each fails: a frame dropped at every join (click test and quality test), kept frames off by one (both), 2-frame warm-up (both), start delay not restored, end duration not restored. Engine audio suites pass (`audioMixer*`, `audioFx*`, `audioAutomationRender`, `audioVolumeEnvelope`: 166 tests), as do producer `audioStage`, `plan.masterBus`, `planAudioCompat` and the ffprobe argv contract. Engine and producer typecheck, oxlint, oxfmt, the comment checks and the Fallow audit are clean.

**Why not about 10 s:** the encode is about 60 s of one Lambda core. Spread perfectly over a 10 GB Lambda's 6 vCPUs that is about 10 s, plus about 3 to 4 s of decode and mix that must happen first. The measured 18.6 s means about 4x effective parallelism. My guess for the gap (not measured): the vCPUs are hyperthreads, and the plan's own hashing and publishing overlap the audio stage. Getting to about 10 s needs the encode off the plan's critical path (for example each chunk encoding its own slice), not a faster split.

## What I did NOT exercise

- A full 30-minute end-to-end cloud render with this change (plan step measured directly; end to end at 2 minutes).
- Real Safari: the playback check fell back to WebKit.
- Compositions with a master FX chain longer than two minutes on AWS (covered by unit tests only; the FX output keeps the 48 kHz rate the encoder's frame math assumes).
- Disk: long renders write the mixed audio as a float WAV first (about 690 MB for 30 minutes), as the master-bus path already did. The Lambda stack provisions 10 GiB of `/tmp`; other hosts need that much free scratch space.
- A segment failure does not stop its sibling segments; they finish (seconds) before the error is returned.

title: test(player): the loading-overlay debounce test no longer races real time
body:
## What

The player test "debounces the loading overlay so a fast, nothing-pending wait never shows it" no longer depends on how fast the machine runs. It failed in CI on a PR that didn't touch the player: `expected "showAssetsLoading" to not be called at all`.

## Why

The test raced two clocks. The overlay shows after a real 150 ms `setTimeout`. The wait it debounces settles after a few animation frames, which happy-dom runs as `setImmediate` callbacks, microseconds apart. On a normal run the frames win by a wide margin. If the test process stalls for 150 ms or more inside that window (the failing CI run took 239 ms), Node's timers phase runs the overdue overlay before the pending frames, and the overlay shows.

## How

- The overlay delay now runs on fake time (`vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ["setTimeout", "clearTimeout"] })`). The iframe's own frames stay real.
- The test drains frames until the wait settles (capped at 600), instead of exactly six. Under load, the frame gaps can fail the quiet-frame check and need more than six.
- It then advances fake time past the delay and checks the overlay never showed.

The player code is unchanged.

## Test plan

- With CI's stall reproduced (a 40 ms busy wait before each of the iframe's frames, about 240 ms in all):
  - old test: failed 3 of 3 runs, with the CI error
  - new test: passed 3 of 3
- The whole `hyperframes-player.test.ts`: 249 passed, three runs in a row.
- The test still guards the debounce: showing the overlay at once makes it fail. Dropping the timer's "already settled" check does not, because settling cancels the timer; the old test didn't catch that either.
- CPU load alone did not reproduce it: up to 16 busy processes on a 0.3 CPU container, the old test still passed. The window is a single event-loop turn, so only a stall of 150 ms or more inside it flips the result.

## Not covered

- Under that extreme throttling, four other tests in the same file failed: three hit the 5 s test timeout, and "handles its iframe's load before a host's load listener runs" failed with `expected [] to have a length of 1`. They passed in every normal run here and are left for a separate change.

title: fix(cli): each start sweeps the running markers of CLIs that are gone
body:
## Problem

`~/.hyperframes/running` holds one file per live CLI process so the background installer can wait until no `hyperframes` command is running (#4637). Each file is removed in a `process.on("exit")` listener. A CLI stopped by Ctrl+C, SIGTERM or SIGKILL never runs that listener, so its file stays.

The only code that removes such leftovers is the installer's own sweep (`running()` in the script built by `installerScript` in `packages/cli/src/utils/autoUpdate.ts`). That sweep runs only when an update is being installed. When the installer skips (`[skip] Unknown install layout …` in `~/.hyperframes/auto-update.log`, which is what happens for a CLI bundled inside another tool's `node_modules`), nothing ever removes the files, and the folder only grows. On one machine it held 185 markers accumulated over 12 days, and none of them belonged to a live CLI.

### Reproduce

1. Run a CLI from a layout the installer skips (or set `HYPERFRAMES_NO_AUTO_INSTALL=1`).
2. Start `hyperframes preview`, then stop it with Ctrl+C. Repeat.
3. `ls ~/.hyperframes/running` keeps one file per interrupted run.

## Fix

`registerRunningCli` sweeps the folder right after writing its own file. It removes every other file that:
- is not named by a positive integer pid,
- names a pid that no longer exists (`process.kill(pid, 0)`; `EPERM` counts as alive), or
- has not been rewritten within `RUNNING_STALE_MS`. A live CLI rewrites its file every 30 s, so a live pid with an old file is a reused pid.

This is the installer's own criterion, applied at every start. The sweep never throws, so a failure cannot skip the heartbeat or the exit listener. The folder now stays bounded by the number of CLIs that are actually running.

## Verification

- New test in `runningCli.test.ts` covers a dead pid, a non-pid name, a live pid with a stale file (removed) and a live pid with a fresh file (kept). It fails before the change and passes after.
- `bunx vitest run src/utils/runningCli.test.ts src/utils/autoUpdate.test.ts` in `packages/cli`: 20 passed.
- The pre-commit hooks pass: oxlint, oxfmt, typecheck, fallow. `scripts/check-comment-citations.mjs` and `scripts/comment-ratchet.mjs` pass.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix(core): media-treatment --analyze finishes on long HDR clips
body:
## What changes for users

`hyperframes media-treatment --analyze` now finishes on several-minute HDR clips instead of failing with `spawnSync ffmpeg ETIMEDOUT`, and its grade reflects the whole clip rather than only the first 40 seconds.

## Root cause

`analyzeMediaGrade` (`packages/core/src/mediaGradeAnalyzer.ts`, and its vendored copy `packages/cli/src/media-use/lib/grade-analyzer.mjs`) ran one ffmpeg pass from the start of the file with an `fps` filter set to `5 / duration`, floored at 0.1 fps. For any clip longer than 50 s the floor wins, so ffmpeg decoded every frame of the first ~40 s, at full resolution and frame rate, to emit its five samples. The cost grows with resolution × frame rate, and a 4K60 10-bit HEVC phone clip goes past the fixed 15 s timeout. The same floor meant the five samples all came from the first 40 s.

## Fix

Each of the five samples seeks (`-noaccurate_seek -ss`) to the middle of one fifth of the clip and decodes a single frame from the keyframe there. Decode work no longer depends on clip length, resolution only scales the five decodes. The 15 s timeout (still overridable with `HYPERFRAMES_ANALYZE_TIMEOUT_MS`) now applies per sample, and on expiry the error names the sample time and the variable. Images and media with no probed duration keep the old single pass. `trim=end_frame=N` heads the filter chain: on ffmpeg 8, `-frames:v N` still lets one extra frame through the filter, so each sample counted twice (main's image path had the same leak: an animated GIF reported 6 frames).

`-noaccurate_seek` over an accurate seek: an accurate seek decodes from the keyframe up to the target, which on a long-GOP file (a screen recording with one keyframe) brings back a decode that scales with clip length. The sample lands on the keyframe at or before the target instead, within a GOP of it on camera footage.

## Before / after

Same machine (8-core Linux, shared and under load), same generated clips, wall time of `analyzeMediaGrade`:

| Clip (generated, 10-bit HEVC, HLG BT.2020) | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1080x1920, 30 fps, 240 s | 3.3-3.7 s | 0.73-0.75 s (3 runs) |
| 2160x3840, 60 fps, 180 s | **fails at 15.6 s: `spawnSync ffmpeg ETIMEDOUT`** (16.1 s with no timeout) | 2.08-2.13 s (3 runs) |

The measured stats agree to the decimal (yAvg 126.4 vs 126.4 on the 4K clip). The table times the media-use copy; the core module behind the command measured the same way: 4K60 clip main `ETIMEDOUT` at 17.5 s vs 2.4 s, 240 s 1080x1920 clip 5.7 s vs 0.8 s. Generated clips decode faster than camera footage; an independent rerun on a 60 s 4K60 synthetic clip measured 8.4 s on main vs 2.1 s here.

Known limits, deliberate: the per-sample timeout means a stuck run fails after up to 5 x 15 s instead of 15 s, with the sample named. On a file with one keyframe (some screen recordings) every sample lands on that keyframe, so the grade comes from fewer distinct frames; it still finishes.

## Tests

- `packages/core/src/mediaGradeAnalyzer.test.ts` (new, real ffmpeg, runs in the runtime test job): a two-minute 128x128 10-bit HLG HEVC clip, black then white. On main it fails with `expected 16 to be greater than 200` (all samples from the black first 40 s); on this branch the samples cover both halves. A second test sets the timeout to 1 ms and checks the error message.
- The media-use copy measures the same clip identically (runs in CI with ffmpeg; replacing its seek with a single pass turns it red), and the parity test checks both copies seek to the same times.
- 20/20 pass 3 runs in a row on ffmpeg 8.0.1 (the build CI pins) and once on 7.0.2; `media-treatment.test.ts` (34) and `grade-analyzer.test.mjs` (10) pass.

## Pre-review pass (independent reviewer)

| | |
|---|---|
| Blocker | new test red on ffmpeg 8 (`expected 10 to be 5`): extra frame per sample. Fixed in 5d5ef88c25, verified on 8.0.1 and 7.0.2 |
| Minor | single-keyframe files sample one keyframe; per-sample timeout ceiling; image-path timeout wording (fixed); media-use copy had no ffmpeg test in CI (added) |
| Audited | all three callers of both copies; 13 odd inputs (0.04 s clip, MKV with audio longer than video, MPEG-TS start offset, VFR, animated GIF/WebP, audio-only, truncated file, path starting with `-`): none worse than main, the 0.04 s clip and the long-audio MKV now work where main errored; six code mutations |
| Not exercised | Windows locally (CI covers it), real camera footage |

title: feat(preview): report when a playing video is hard-resynced, with its drift, codec and rate
body:
## What

One event when the preview runtime hard-resyncs a playing video, with drift, codec, rate and whether a copy was playing.

When a playing video drifts far enough from the playhead that the runtime seeks it back, the preview now emits `media_resynced`. Studio forwards it to its existing browser telemetry, so the next "my video resets while playing" report says whether this seek was the cause and on what kind of file.

## Why

A playing video that resets mid-playback is hard to diagnose without the file. The runtime's resync seek is one candidate, and until now it left no trace.

## How

- **Runtime** (`media.ts`): `syncRuntimeMedia` takes an optional `onResync(el, drift, reason)` and calls it when it seeks a `<video>` while the clock plays. `reason` is the branch that fired: `hard` or `strict`. A clip's first tick is its initial placement, so it is not reported. Paused seeks and the transport's own forced ticks (seek, play, loop) are not reported either.
- **Event** (`mediaProxy.ts`, `reportMediaResync`): this module already owns the codec map lookup and the proxy URL, so the event is built there. It carries `drift` (seconds, rounded to 0.1), `codec` (from the codec map entry, else null), `rate` (the element's playback rate), `copy` (the element is playing a `?hf-proxy` copy) and `reason`. It never includes file names or paths. Each element sends at most one event per 10 s.
- **Wiring** (`init.ts`): passes `reportMediaResync` as `onResync`. It goes out through the existing `emitAnalyticsEvent` bridge.
- **Host** (Studio `previewMessageRouter.ts`): forwards only `media_resynced` from the preview iframe to `trackEvent`. The other runtime analytics events stay local, as before. Properties are re-checked by type, and a codec that is not a plain codec name is dropped. Consent is the existing `browserTelemetryAllowed` policy, which already honours the CLI's telemetry setting. There is no new opt-out path.

## Tests

- `mediaProxy.test.ts`: a playing video that drifts past the threshold emits exactly one event with those properties. A paused jump emits none. The 10 s limit holds.
- `previewMessageRouter.test.ts`: the router forwards the event to the telemetry client. It drops an odd codec and ignores other events and other frames.
- `init.mediaResync.test.ts`: through the real player, at 1x and 2x, a seek while playing, a seek that keeps playing and a loop back to the start report nothing, and a video that falls behind on its own reports once. The 2x seeks reported a 6 s resync before forced ticks were excluded.
- Each test fails when its line is removed. Each passes three runs in a row. Core `src/runtime` and Studio `src/player` + `src/telemetry` are green. tsc (core and studio), oxlint, oxfmt and the comment ratchet pass.
