title: perf(aws-lambda): build the final mp4 inside S3 with its index up front
body:
Stacked on #5812 (the MP4 index builder), which is stacked on #5803 (chunks carry their audio). This is the AWS half: the final mp4 is assembled inside S3 as a regular faststart file, so browsers start it from a URL.

## What changed

On the AWS Lambda path, `format: "mp4"` renders (without `cfr`) now plan with `chunksCarryAudio`. Assemble builds a regular **faststart** MP4 inside S3: `ftyp`, one `moov` that indexes every sample, then one 64-bit `mdat`.

- `stitchMp4InS3` reads each chunk's `ftyp` and `moov` with two small ranged GETs and builds the header with #5812's `buildStitchedHeader`.
- One multipart upload writes the file:
  - Part 1 is the header plus just enough leading bytes of chunk 0 (downloaded) to reach S3's 5 MiB minimum.
  - Every other part is `UploadPartCopy` of one chunk's `mdat` byte range, so those bytes never pass through the function.
  - Part rule: every part but the last must be at least 5 MiB, and a copy reads one object. A range of at least 5 MiB is copied as it is. Anything smaller is downloaded into an uploaded part, which borrows the next range's head when the rest of that range can still be copied. Short renders take the same path, so there is no local fallback.
  - Any failure aborts the upload. The SAM template grants `s3:AbortMultipartUpload`, which `S3CrudPolicy` lacks; the snapshot test pins it.
- Audio layout: each chunk's audio packets sit inside that chunk's payload, interleaved with its video as ffmpeg muxes any MP4. A player streaming from the start reads audio and video from the same few MB.
- The lambda-local harness's disk-usage sampler no longer crashes when a scratch file disappears between listing and stat (hit while testing this).
- `chunksAreStitchedMp4`, `buildStitchedHeader`, `readMp4Layout` and `muxChunkWithAudio` are exported from `@hyperframes/producer/distributed` for this package.

## What I measured

Locally:
- `s3Stitch.test.ts`:
  - The part planner on exact sizes, and abort on a failed part.
  - 3 real x264 + AAC chunks through an S3 stand-in. It serves ranged reads, joins parts and rejects a non-last part under the minimum, which is set to 16 KiB so small chunks take every path that 5 MiB takes. Results: `ffprobe -v error` silent, boxes `ftyp, moov, mdat`, 91 frames and all audio packets. Frames, PCM and stream durations equal today's `assemble()`, and the local `assemble()` output is byte-identical to the S3 output.
- `handler.test.ts`: a plan whose chunks carry audio assembles through S3 and never calls the local join.
- 3 runs in a row green. Each mutation turns its test red: borrowing that leaves a short copy, no abort, the handler skipping the S3 path. The S3 integration test also goes red for offsets ignoring earlier chunks and for the priming not being skipped.
- `tsc` (producer, engine, aws-lambda), oxlint, oxfmt, `fallow audit` (new-only gate) and the comment checks pass.

On AWS: a 30-minute 1080p30 benchmark, on the same fixture as main's baseline with inputs pinned by sha256. Deployed with `--concurrency 300` and rendered with `--max-parallel-chunks 225` (225 chunks of 8 s). Measured on the same code before it was split into this stack (#5803, #5812, this PR). The split changed only file layout, a flag name and the in-chunk sample count check, which now uses ffprobe. I have not re-run AWS on the split branches.

| | Today (ffmpeg join) | Fragmented MP4 + S3 stitch | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Assemble, Step Functions state | 81.5 s | 1.8 s | **2.4 s** |
| Assemble, inside the function | download 2 GB, ffmpeg, upload 2 GB | 1.6 s | **2.2 s**: 0.06 s plan read, 2.16 s for 226 parts (3.3 MB downloaded, 2 MB header uploaded) |
| Chrome from a presigned URL, duration known | 1.8 s / 3.4 s | never within 60 s | **1.6 s / 3.1 s** |
| WebKit from a presigned URL, duration known | 5.5 s / 2.7 s | never within 60 s | **3.3 s / 5.5 s** |
| Seeks to 5, 900, 1799 s from the URL | all land | 5 s never lands | **all land** |
| Video / audio duration | 1800.000 / 1800.000 s | 1800.000 / 1800.021 s | **1800.000 / 1800.000 s** |

- The streaming rows come from one session: two rounds, all three layouts back to back, order rotated. "Today" is this run's output remuxed with `-movflags +faststart`, and "fragmented" is the same streams as fragmented MP4.
- Time to "ready to play through" (readyState 4) is left out on purpose. It also needs the link to outrun the video's 9.2 Mb/s, and on this 4-7 Mb/s link it swung from 2 s to over 60 s for the same file. On every round it moved together for this PR's file and today's layout.
- End to end: 289.5 s in Step Functions (plan 72.1 s, render map 215.0 s, assemble 2.4 s). Only the assemble is this change.
- Measured cost (Lambda REPORT lines plus Step Functions): $1.62. 227 invocations, all OK.
- Output:
  - 2.07 GB; `ffprobe -v error` silent. Boxes: `ftyp`, a 1.99 MB `moov` at the front, one `mdat`.
  - 54000 frames, and 84376 AAC packets (main's count) decoding to exactly 86,400,000 samples.
  - Loudness as on main, with no level jump at any chunk seam.
- Pictures at 5, 900 and 1799 s are byte-identical to an earlier run of the same fixture, and I looked at them, including the frames each player showed while streaming.
- Players:
  - A 10 s render from disk passes ffprobe, AVFoundation, Chrome and WebKit, with the same frame in each.
  - Streamed from its URL, the 30-minute file plays in AVFoundation with exact frames at 5, 900 and 1799 s.
- The stack, its buckets and its log group are torn down, and nothing is left.

## What I did not exercise

- Real Safari: safaridriver needs "Allow remote automation" on the test Mac, so the browser runs are Playwright **WebKit, not Safari**.
- An AWS run of the split branches themselves (see above).

title: perf(core): a preview loads each web font once, not once per scene
body:
## What changes

Studio's preview of a film with many scenes now loads each web font once. Before, every scene carried its own copy of the film's `@font-face` rules, and Chrome loads and keeps one face per rule, so a 17 MB font used across 154 scenes was held 154 times.

## Why it went wrong

The bundler already drops repeated `@font-face` rules (#4643), but it skips that for scene-parts builds, so each scene's style can be swapped on its own after an edit. Studio's preview and capture builds are scene-parts builds (`PREVIEW_BUNDLE_OPTIONS.sceneParts`), so every Studio preview kept one copy per scene. Renders are not scene-parts builds and were already deduplicated.

## How

- Scene-parts builds take every top-level `@font-face` out of the page's styles and put the last copy of each, in order, into one `<style data-hf-scene-fonts>` at the head start. It belongs to no scene; scene parts carry no `@font-face`. Other builds dedupe as before.
- The scene-parts manifest leaves that style out of the shared hash, so a scene edit that brings a font still swaps instead of reloading the film.
- A swap appends only the rules the page does not have yet, in a new fonts style after the last one. It never rewrites a loaded rule's style, which would load its font again.
- The attribute is written by the bundler and read by the runtime; nothing new to author.

## What I measured

A long, many-scene project (98 stylesheets; 4,092 `@font-face` rules, of which 4,030 are repeats; two large CJK variable fonts of 17 MB and 24.5 MB among 9 font files) served by `hyperframes preview` built from main and from this branch, each page opened in headless Chrome, 2 alternating rounds per side. Renderer resident memory, and the renderer's `malloc` from a Chrome memory-infra dump, 15 s after open:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| preview page, renderer resident | 5,166 / 4,780 MB | 410 / 394 MB |
| preview page, renderer `malloc` | 4,851 / 4,852 MB | 68 / 67 MB |
| preview page, after a seek to 4:30 | 5,182 / 4,807 MB | 462 / 422 MB |
| capture page (`?hf-capture=1`), renderer resident | 6,539 / 6,565 MB | 2,378 / 1,757 MB |

The capture page on main still loads every clip; #5787 fixes that part separately.

- `packages/core/src/compiler/htmlBundler.test.ts`: two scenes sharing a `@font-face` bundle with one rule, in the fonts style, and none in either scene's style.
- `packages/core/src/compiler/scenePartsManifest.test.ts`: adding a rule to the fonts style leaves the shared hash as it was.
- `packages/core/src/runtime/init.swapScenes.test.ts`: a swap still replaces the edited scene, keeps the loaded fonts style untouched, and adds only the new rule in a style after it.
- fails without the fix: with the five source files at main and the tests kept, all three fail (3 failed of 415). With the change, the four affected test files pass 3 runs in a row (415 tests), studio-server's preview route tests pass (114), and `tsc` passes in core.

## What I did NOT exercise

- `@font-face` nested in `@media` or `@supports`: left where it is, as the existing dedupe does.
- A swap that removes a font: the old rule stays loaded, unused, until the next full reload.

title: fix(engine): a chunk's first frame shows its own time, not the composition's opening frame
body:
## What the user sees

A distributed render (plan, then chunks, then assemble) could start any chunk after the first on the composition's **opening frame**: the frame at time 0, with the background video on its first frame and no overlays yet. It is one wrong frame per chunk boundary, so it shows as a flash at every seam. Whether a given chunk got it was down to timing, so two renders of the same plan gave different videos.

## Cause

On a BeginFrame capture session, the first display-producing `HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame` can return the frame Chrome composited during session init, not the seek the page has already applied. Logged just before that capture, the DOM was already correct (title opacity 1, native `<video>` hidden, injected frame visible and decoded), and Chrome answered `hasDamage: true` with a fresh screenshot. In some runs that screenshot was still the init frame. Every later frame of the session was on time (checked against the source video, frame by frame).

What triggers it is the chunk's BeginFrame liveness probe (`renderChunk` → `beginFrameSessionNeedsScreenshotFallback` → `probeBeginFrameLiveness`). It sends one more BeginFrame on the capture session after init and before the first seek. On main, on the host where it was stale 9 times in 10:

| chunk session (chunks 1 to 4, idle) | first frame stale |
|---|---|
| as shipped (probe on) | 10 of 10 |
| probe skipped | 0 of 12 |
| probe sent with `noDisplayUpdates: true` | 11 of 12 |
| locked warmup turned off (probe on) | 10 of 10 (ruled out) |

So any extra BeginFrame between init and the first seek is enough, whether or not it displays. The probe itself is needed: it is how a chunk detects a SwiftShader compositor stall. Local renders never probe their capture sessions this way, which is why they are not affected (next section).

## Local renders (`hyperframes render`): not affected

**Do local multi-worker renders flash too? No. 0 of 240 worker-start frames were stale on main, and 0 of 240 with this PR.** I rendered the same pinned fixture locally with `--workers 1`, with `--workers 4` (the default interleaved split: worker i draws frames i, i+4, ..., so the worker starts are frames 0 to 3), and with `--workers 4` plus `HF_CAPTURE_PARALLEL_STREAM=false` (the contiguous disk split: worker starts 0, 75, 150, 225). That was 5 runs of each idle and 5 under 16 CPU hogs, on two Linux hosts, plus 15 extra loaded `--workers 4` rounds alternating main and this PR. Every log reported `captureMode: beginframe` and the requested worker count. Worker-start frames were compared with the `--workers 1` render by per-frame PSNR (a stale one is about 21 to 25 dB).

| host | tree | `--workers 1` frame 0 | `--workers 4` interleaved starts | `--workers 4` contiguous starts | renders byte-identical to `--workers 1` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A (8 cores) | main | 0 of 10 stale | 0 of 100 | 0 of 40 | 45 of 45 |
| A | this PR | 0 of 10 | 0 of 100 | 0 of 40 | 44 of 45 |
| B (32 cores) | main | 0 of 10 | 0 of 40 | 0 of 40 | 30 of 30 |
| B | this PR | 0 of 10 | 0 of 40 | 0 of 40 | 30 of 30 |

Local output is byte-identical between main and this PR on both hosts, so the extra BeginFrame changes nothing there. One loaded `--workers 4` render with this PR differed at frame 5 only. That frame is worker 1's second frame, not a worker start, and showed the title one step behind the video. It did not recur in 15 alternating rounds (main 0 of 20 loaded `--workers 4` renders, this PR 1 of 20), so I cannot tell whether it is related.

## Fix

In `captureFrameSurface`, the first BeginFrame capture of a session first displays the seek once. It sends one visual BeginFrame with no screenshot at the capture tick minus half an interval. Ticks stay monotonic: the producer's liveness probe sits at base − 5 intervals and the init commit at base − 6. This covers chunk workers, parallel workers and retry pages, because each one is a fresh session. It adds one BeginFrame per session.

## Measured

A 10 s 1080p30 fixture with an H.264 background video, a GSAP title and AAC audio, split into 5 chunks. It was generated once and pinned by sha256, and every chunk of the same plan was rendered 10 times (5 idle, 5 under CPU hogs).

| | distinct outputs per chunk (0 to 4) | chunk first frames showing the opening frame |
|---|---|---|
| main, Linux host A (8 cores, 8 hogs) | 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 | 23 of 40 (18 of 20 idle, 5 of 20 loaded) |
| main, Linux host B (32 cores, 32 hogs) | 2, 2, 2, 1, 3 | 4 of 40 (0 idle, 4 of 20 loaded) |
| this PR, host A (8 hogs) | 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 | 0 of 40 |
| this PR, host B (16 hogs) | 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 | 0 of 40 |

Which way the race goes depends on the host: host A was usually stale when idle, host B only when loaded. On both hosts chunk 0 also flipped between Chrome's own paint of the native video and the injected extracted frame. With the fix it always shows the injected frame. A stale first frame measures 21 dB against the correct one; the rest of the chunk differs only by the encoder carrying that frame forward (about 50 dB).

Tests: the new `frameCapture-firstBeginFrame.test.ts` fails on main (both cases) and passes with the fix, 3 runs in a row. The engine's frameCapture and screenshotService suites pass (31 files, 333 tests). The full engine unit suite passes except 4 `ffprobe.test.ts` cases that read an LFS fixture which was not fetched in this checkout; they fail identically on main.

## Not exercised

- The producer Docker regression baselines. A render starting at frame 0 now shows the injected video frame on frame 0, not Chrome's native paint of the same frame. In this fixture that is a 42 dB difference, which should sit inside checkpoint tolerances, but I have not run them.
- macOS (screenshot or drawElement capture). Only the `beginframe` branch changed.
- Mid-session hard cuts. Only a session's first capture was seen to go stale; later frames were on time in every run.
- Why an extra BeginFrame before the first seek makes Chrome present the pre-seek frame. The table above pins the trigger, not Chrome's internal reason.

The plan step was deterministic apart from the plan folder path baked into `planHash`, which #5782 already fixes.

title: fix(core): font setup skips parsing stylesheets that cannot name a font
body:
## What

Font setup no longer runs a full CSS parse of a stylesheet that can't contain what it's looking for. Before compiling fonts, three scans each parsed every `<style>` block in full: one looking for custom properties, one for `font-family` declarations and one for Google Fonts `@import` rules. Each scan now skips a stylesheet whose text has no `--`, no `font-family` or no `@import`, respectively.

## Why

`deterministicFonts.test.ts` "handles a long incomplete font-face suffix" timed out under load. Its first case is a 1.2 MB stylesheet of `@font-face{{` repeated 100,000 times. The `@font-face` scanner it guards is linear and fast. Nearly all the time went to three full PostCSS parses of that stylesheet, none of which could find anything. That took 0.7 s on an idle 32-core Linux machine and 3.7 to 5.9 s with 48 CPU hogs, against vitest's 5 s default. The same three parses cost real time on any large stylesheet with no font rules.

The skip doesn't change what is found. An escaped name such as `font\-family` was already missed: PostCSS keeps the escape in `decl.prop`, so the exact-name checks never matched it.

## Test plan

- New test: a stylesheet with no `font-family`, custom property or `@import` never reaches `postcss.parse`. It fails on main ("called 3 times").
- Under load, 32 cores with 48 CPU hogs, `vitest run src/fonts/deterministicFonts.test.ts --maxWorkers=2`:
  - main's three files: 1 of 5 runs failed (timeout at 5,898 ms); the passing runs took 3.7 to 4.6 s on that case
  - this branch: 10 of 10 runs passed; the slowest case took 316 ms
- `src/fonts/` on Linux: 17 files, 257 tests passed. `tsc --noEmit` for core is clean.

title: perf(core): every graded clip draws through one WebGL context, not one per clip
body:
## What changes

Color grading now draws every graded clip through one WebGL context per page, instead of creating a context for each clip as it comes into view. Each clip still shows its pixels on its own canvas, now a 2D canvas the shared context's frame is copied to.

## Why it went wrong

Creating a WebGL context makes the page's main thread wait, synchronously, for the GPU process to set up a command buffer. Grading created one per graded clip the moment it became visible, kept at most 4 spare, and lost the rest, so a seek or playback across many graded clips kept creating contexts. On a busy or slow GPU process that wait has frozen the page for 30 s in the field: crash dumps taken when such a page was killed show its main thread inside `WebGLContextFactory` → `CommandBufferProxyImpl::Initialize`, waiting on the GPU process.

## How

- The runtime creates one WebGL context lazily, on a canvas outside the document, and every clip's program, textures and effect targets live in it.
- A clip draws into the shared canvas's bottom-left corner (grown, never shrunk, to the largest clip) and is copied to the clip's own 2D canvas in the same task, before the next clip draws.
- Retiring a spare clip renderer deletes its programs and textures only; the shared context is lost only when the runtime is destroyed. Its context-loss and restore events mark and rebuild every clip at once.
- Previews of a grading (`renderPreviews`) keep their own context, as before.
- `drawEntry` is split into `drawableFrame`, `syncSourceAppearance`, `placeCanvas` and `renderGradedFrame` with no change in behaviour, to stay under the complexity gate now that it is touched.

## What I measured

- `packages/core/src/runtime/colorGrading.test.ts`: six graded clips shown and hidden in pairs over a scripted seek run draw through one WebGL context, and every clip's pixels are copied from the shared canvas.
- fails without the fix: with `colorGrading.ts` at main and the test kept, the seek run creates 4 WebGL contexts instead of 1 (`expected 4 to be 1`). With the change, the seven test files that touch color grading pass 3 runs in a row (595 tests), and `tsc` passes in core.
- Seek times in a real app on Mac hardware, before and after: to follow in a comment (a headless Linux box without a GPU has no WebGL at all, so grading cannot run there).

## What I did NOT exercise

- `vfx.ts` (WebGL2, one context per effect host) is unchanged: a different owner and context type, left for its own change.

title: fix(core): font lookup on a Mac no longer waits 5 s on system_profiler
body:
## What

On macOS, system font lookup no longer runs `system_profiler SPFontsDataType`. A compile or render with `allowSystemFontCapture` on, and the first font list request in Studio, each blocked for 5 s on that call and got nothing back from it. Lookups now go straight to the font-folder scan that already answered every one of them.

## Why

Two problems with that call:

- **Slow.** It took 9.4 to 9.7 s on an Apple M5 Pro (macOS 26.5), three runs, and `-detailLevel mini` took 10.8 s. The locator kills it at 5 s, so every process waited out the full timeout. The call is synchronous, so the whole process waited.
- **Never matched.** Its output has `path` on each font file entry, not on the typefaces the parser read (`typeface.path`), so the index came back empty even when the call finished.

Measured on that Mac with `locateSystemFontVariants` for seven families (Times New Roman, Helvetica Neue, Georgia, Avenir Next, Menlo, SF Pro, one missing family):
- main: 5,085 ms
- this branch: 40 ms
- results identical for every family

`getSystemProfilerFamilies()`, which Studio's font list used, took 5,011 ms and returned 0 families.

`getSystemProfilerFamilies` is removed from `@hyperframes/core/fonts/system-locator`. Its only caller was Studio's font list route, which now lists the scanned folders alone, as it effectively did before. The two test timeouts raised to 15 s for this call are back to the default.

## Test plan

- New `systemFontLocator.darwin.test.ts`: with the platform reported as macOS, font lookups spawn no process. It fails on main (`execFileSync` called for `system_profiler`) and passes three runs in a row.
- `src/fonts/`: 18 files pass on Linux, three runs in a row, and on macOS (259 tests). On macOS, main's "still embeds a local file when the page has no Google link" timed out at 5 s on this call; it now passes.
- core and studio typecheck clean.

## Not covered

- Only one Mac and one macOS version (26.5). An older macOS whose output put `path` on typefaces, with a call that finished in under 5 s, would have resolved some families by their internal names. On such a machine, those families now go through the folder scan's file-name names.
- An Intel Mac. The second test Mac was offline.

title: perf(cli): check judges HEVC and ProRes frames from the original, not from preview copies
body:
## What

`hyperframes check` no longer waits for browser-playable copies of videos the browser cannot decode (HEVC, ProRes and similar). It judges the frames those videos show from stills of the original, extracted with FFmpeg the way `snapshot` and render already decode them. A frame whose still can't be made is reported as `media_frame_unchecked`, with the file, the time and the reason. It is never passed silently. The 120 s check deadline now covers everything `check` does, from lint onward.

## Why

On a first `check` after phone footage is added, `check` waited for a full-length, full-resolution H.264 copy of every such video before it started. That wait ran before the deadline's clock started, so nothing bounded it. On an 8 GB machine this took minutes. Turning copies off (`--no-proxy`) was fast but worse: the browser couldn't decode those videos, so their frames were never judged and `check` passed silently.

## Related work

Refs #5759 (a `check` that waited on project history). Making the preview's copies cheaper is separate work and is not changed here.

## How

- **No copies:** `runBrowserCheck` only scans which local videos the browser can't decode (codec probe, no transcode) and serves its page with copies off. `check` no longer starts copies. A CLI process that exits would kill a background transcode or be held open by one, and preview makes its own on demand.
- **Stills:** after every full seek, the page driver paints a still of each such video's original at that time over the `<video>`. This uses `createVideoStillInjector`, which is snapshot's per-frame block moved into one function that `snapshot` and `check` both call. Finding crops (`--snapshots`) do the same.
- **Deadline:** `runCheckPipeline` creates and starts the deadline first, and runs lint and HDR inspection inside it.
- **Removed:** the copy pre-resolve and its failed-copy echo filter. `check --proxy`/`--no-proxy` is still accepted from older scripts but now does nothing.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated (`checkBrowser.test.ts`, "videos the browser cannot decode"):
  - a project with an HEVC clip finishes `check` with the transcoder never called, on a page served with copies off;
  - the sampled frame is painted with the still of that clip's original, and only that clip's;
  - a still that can't be made becomes a `media_frame_unchecked` warning naming the file and time.
  - All three fail on main: the first times out waiting for the copy, the second never paints a still, the third reports nothing.
- [x] `check*`, `snapshot*` and static-server tests pass 3 runs in a row; `packages/cli` typecheck is clean.
- [x] Manual testing performed (numbers below)
- [ ] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

### Before and after

Linux, `check` limited to 8 GB of memory, no swap and 4 CPUs, with a cold copy cache before each run. Fixture projects are 52 s vertical compositions of four 13 s clips.

| Project | Published 0.8.168 | This branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4K HLG HEVC clips | 183.2 s (163.6 s of it making copies) | 24.1 s, 24.1 s |
| 1080p HEVC clips | 59 to 68 s earlier; 36.7 s on a rerun (23.5 s making copies) | 13.2 s, 12.7 s |
| 1080p H.264 clips only | 19.4 s | 12.3 s |

Every branch run returned `ok: true` with no `media_frame_unchecked`, and no copy cache was written. `check --snapshots` on the 4K HLG project saved frames that show the HEVC clips' own content at the right time: the clip's burned-in timecode reads 1.43 s at composition time 14.4 s, where that clip starts at 13 s. Before this change, `--no-proxy` on the same project ran 8.8 s and passed with those clips blank.

### Not verified

- macOS: the scan marks HEVC and ProRes on every platform, so stills are painted there too, but no run was made on a Mac.
- Real phone footage: only synthetic HEVC and HLG fixtures were used.
- HDR stills are FFmpeg's plain decode of the original. They are not tone-mapped the way an HDR render is, so colours in HDR clips are judged roughly, not exactly.
- `check` no longer warms the preview's copies. Preview still makes its own the first time it needs them.

title: perf(cloud): assemble chunk output with a single faststart index
body:
## Plan audio is encoded once — head `bd832cb4`, rebased on main `388011b2`

(`bd832cb4` adds only the `--` terminator to the new test's ffprobe argv, as the producer's ffprobe argv contract requires; the producer unit lane passes.)

When chunks carry their audio, the plan mixes the track at the frames' exact length (`totalFrames / fps`) in its one AAC encode. The separate fit step is gone: it probed the mix, then copied it or re-encoded the whole track to that length. What stays is the true-peak check: it keeps every delivered AAC at or below −1 dBTP (#3644), and the first encode does not guarantee that. It measures once and re-encodes only when the peak is over the ceiling. It now has its own stage timer, `audio-peak`.

- **Test** (`plan.test.ts`, "encodes the audio once, at the frames' exact length"): a 1.01 s composition at 30 fps is 31 frames, 49,600 samples, which is 48.4375 AAC frames. An ffmpeg shim counts AAC encodes: 1. The previous plan code does 2 (mix, then the pad re-encode), so the test fails on it. Mixing at the composition's length without the fit also fails it: 1,120 samples short. The edit list counts in ms, so the track shows 1.033 s; the previous code gave the same 1.033 s. Passes 3 runs in a row; `plan.test.ts` 57/57, `audioPadTrim.test.ts` 38/38, `chunkAudio.test.ts` 4/4.
- **Output:** on the 30-minute 1080p30 fixture, the plan audio decodes to the same 86,400,000 samples as before. The decoded difference is silent (RMS −inf). The packets are the same size; only the container bytes differ.
- **Direct plan invokes on Lambda, same stack, 30-minute fixture** (10,240 MB; each pair is one cold run then one warm run; two rounds in swapped order):

| | plan total (s) | audio mix (s) | fit, or `audio-peak` (s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 51.8, 48.8, 62.1, 56.3 | 20.5, 20.0, 19.4, 19.0 | 12.0, 10.6, 17.6, 16.3 (no timer) |
| after | 59.7, 54.9, 56.5, 53.6 | 18.5, 18.3, 19.4, 18.5 | 14.7, 14.7, 15.0, 15.1 |

  On this fixture the plan time does not change, within the run-to-run spread. Its 54,000 frames are exactly 1800 s, so the old fit already took its copy branch; there was no second encode to remove. Both versions spend the time in the true-peak scan. On the same file on a Linux box, the old fit takes 7.33 s (probe, copy, scan) and the new step 7.10 s (scan). The second encode this removes happens when the composition's length is not a whole number of frames, as in the test.
- `smoke.sh --plan-protocol both --chunk-counts 2,4` at `a732ba4a` exits 0: v1/v2 equivalence passes at 2 and 4 chunks, PSNR 37.11-37.12 dB. Everything is torn down.

## Rebase, CodeQL, v1 parity and package budget (at `7cadb443`)

- Rebased onto current main. The #5803 commit is already on main, so it is gone from this branch; the remaining commits apply unchanged (every file the PR touched is identical to the previous head).
- CodeQL flagged `js/insecure-temporary-file` on the read-only `open()` in the local stitcher. It now passes an explicit mode, as `parsers/src/assetResolution.ts` does; the file is never created there.
- **v1 plans now carry chunk audio too.** The Lambda smoke gate (`--plan-protocol both`) failed on the rebased branch: only v2 planned `chunksCarryAudio`, so v1 and v2 produced different chunks and a different video `time_base` (1/15360 vs 1/90000), with identical decoded frames. `plan()` now takes the same option and the v1 plan handler passes it, so both protocols render the same chunks; v1 stitches them locally, v2 inside S3. A handler test pins the option (it fails without it).
- **Package size budget, `@hyperframes/aws-lambda`: packed 63,198 → 66,677 (+3,479), unpacked 230,499 → 242,569 (+12,070).** Reason: S3-side MP4 assembly code. Measured with the same pnpm 10.17.1 pack the CI gate runs, this branch against main: `dist/handler.js` and `dist/index.js` each bundle the new S3 stitch code (+5,550 bytes apiece), and `dist/s3Stitch.d.ts` adds 970. Nothing else in the tarball changed, and it holds no source maps or tests from this PR. The budget rises by exactly that delta, so main's headroom is unchanged. If the budget-lowering PR lands first, this one rebases onto it.

### Live smoke on AWS at `7cadb443` (passes again at `a732ba4a`, above)

`examples/aws-lambda/scripts/smoke.sh --plan-protocol both --chunk-counts 2,4` in us-east-2 exits 0:

| protocol | chunks | wall | PSNR vs baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | 2 | 17.9 s | 37.12 dB |
| v1 | 4 | 12.1 s | 37.11 dB |
| v2 | 2 | 6.4 s | 37.12 dB |
| v2 | 4 | 6.4 s | 37.11 dB |

- `PASS: v1/v2 semantic equivalence` at 2 and 4 chunks. The v1 and v2 outputs are byte-identical.
- The 4-chunk v2 output: `ffprobe -v error` and a full decode print nothing. 60 of 60 frames, 2.000 s. Boxes are `ftyp`, `moov`, then `mdat` (faststart). Each chunk's first frame matches the in-process baseline (36.8 to 39.3 dB), so no chunk starts on a stale frame.
- Lambda cost about $0.01. The stacks and their buckets are deleted, and nothing is left.

## AAC tail and failed-output repair — current signed `e6a2f3ed67e989ee5f33ff4ed8b78ae43ba857ad`

A valid 51-frame/60-fps job can end with a one-frame chunk that owns no AAC packet. The stitcher now accepts that video-only contribution while retaining the plan audio exactly once; codec, video, timescale and unexpected-track mismatches still reject. Local output validates its header before opening a file, writes in a sibling work directory, and publishes only on success; failed or truncated copies clean up.

The failing-first real FFmpeg 7.0.2 case now matches the existing video-plus-plan-audio reference in decoded frames and PCM (51 video / 41 audio packets, 0.85 s). Local and FakeS3 results are byte-identical; the built Node consumer passes. Header/short-mdat cleanup and true-track-mismatch controls pass. Focused evidence repeated three times; producer distributed 257 + 8 tests and AWS Lambda 160 pass; normal signed commit hooks pass. No live S3/Lambda acceptance is claimed. Current hosted CI and independent approval remain required.

The full consolidated implementation, original reports and captures below remain part of this PR.


## Current signed successor `705169b0de4677edd34b6a5d47e74d8223c033e2`

Normal signed integration with main deeb8d43 preserves #5812/#5805/#5807 and the patch-identical #5803 squash. Four audio-plan conflicts retain the existing branch changes; the auto-merged duplicate plan-test block/import is removed. Final tree independently matches merge-tree using the established shared patch base.

Core/engine/producer builds pass; producer real ffmpeg/index cases5 three times, S3 assembly4, first-BeginFrame2, distributed249 plus Vitest8, AWS transport/handler/publisher/CDK56 and frame capture299 pass. Producer/engine/AWS/core/scripts typechecks and normal signed lint/format/type/fallow hooks pass. No live AWS or long segmented-AAC stitch acceptance claim. Fresh combined review and current-head hosted CI remain required.

## Consolidated scope — owner-authorized queue reduction

This survivor preserves #5812, #5805, #5807 as original commits; every original head is an ancestor of `ab43c32d3168391423f4bf1ace9628420e61a280`. Superseded PR branches stay intact.

Full preserved source union: local/S3 faststart assembly plus chunk-first-frame presentation. Normal signed lint/format/type/fallow hooks PASS; five producer audio/index tests and four S3 assembly tests pass. After rebuilding the newly needed core subpath, the frame-capture suite passes 2/2. The initial missing-build failure is retained in the task log. Full-target hostedCI and independent combined review remain required; no new live cloud benchmark/deployment claim.

All original reports and captures follow, attributed to their original heads. Their limits remain; fresh full-target CI and independent review are required before normal merge. No admin bypass, deployment, paid call or feature activation was performed by this consolidation.

## Original report — #5812 at a960f8a9

Stacked on #5803 (chunks carry their slice of the plan audio). #5805 builds on this and does the same thing inside S3.

## What changed

When a plan's mp4 chunks carry their audio (`chunksCarryAudio`), `assemble()` no longer runs an ffmpeg join. It writes a regular **faststart** MP4 from the chunks as they are: `ftyp`, one `moov` that indexes every sample, one 64-bit `mdat` holding each chunk's `mdat` payload unchanged and in order. Those are the same bytes S3 can copy into place (#5805).

- `readMp4Layout` reads a chunk's `ftyp` and `moov` through a ranged-read callback and locates its `mdat` payload without reading it, usually in two reads.
- `buildStitchedHeader` takes chunk 0's `moov` and merges every chunk's sample tables into it:
  - The tables: `stts`, `stss`, `stsc`, `stsz`, plus `co64` with each chunk offset moved to where its payload lands.
  - Durations are summed.
  - Chunk 0's audio edit list (the 1024-sample AAC priming skip) is kept for the whole track, so the audio shows exactly its fitted length. Video gets no edit list, which would round its length to the movie timescale.
  - The index is built once with a placeholder data offset and again with the real one; offsets are fixed 8-byte fields, so the size cannot change.
- Refusals:
  - Chunks with B-frames (`ctts`, or a video edit list that does not start at 0). Production chunks encode with `-bf 0`.
  - Chunks whose tracks or codecs differ from chunk 0.
  - Samples outside a chunk's `mdat`.
  - Only chunk 0's sample entry is kept: chunks repeat SPS/PPS in-band, and their entries differ only in per-file fields (x264 frame-number width, AAC bitrate fields).
- `writeStitchedMp4` writes the header, then streams each chunk's payload. `assemble()` uses it for such plans; `cfr` is refused there because it would re-encode.
- The plan audio no longer goes to the assembler for such plans, only to the chunks.
- No caller turns the option on yet (#5805 does). Every other path is unchanged.
- The repo had no MP4 box writer (searched `packages/` for `stsz`, `stco`, `co64` and `moov`). The installed mediabunny muxes in-memory samples and cannot index payloads stored elsewhere.

## What I measured

- `mp4Stitch.test.ts`: two synthetic chunks with known sample tables, stitched, then every sample read back through the new `moov`. Each sample's bytes sit at the indexed offset, and the keyframe flags, durations and audio edit list (120 ms after the priming) match. A chunk whose video starts at media time 512 is refused.
- `chunkAudio.test.ts` (from #5803), now through this path: real x264 + AAC chunks, three uneven ones with a 1-frame tail and a single one. `assemble()` gives the same framemd5, PCM and ffprobe stream entries (packets, durations, frame rates) as today's join of the video-only encodes with the plan audio.
- 3 runs in a row green. Each mutation turns a test red: offsets ignoring earlier chunks (both files), no B-frame guard, priming not skipped (both files).
- `planV2.test.ts`, `plan.test.ts`, `assemble.test.ts`: green.
- Producer, engine and aws-lambda `tsc`, oxlint, pinned oxfmt, `fallow audit` (new-only gate) and the comment checks (citations, ratchet) pass.

## What I did not exercise

- A real render through this local path alone. The AWS run in #5805 checks the same header against a 30-minute output.
- Renders over about 24 h at 48 kHz: version-0 duration fields overflow, and the stitcher refuses with a clear error instead of writing a version-1 box.
- The full producer unit suite has one failure, `audioPadTrim.integration` "true-peak ceiling". It fails the same way on main with the test box's ffmpeg 8.0.1.


## Original report — #5805 at 0a60dee4

Stacked on #5812 (the MP4 index builder), which is stacked on #5803 (chunks carry their audio). This is the AWS half: the final mp4 is assembled inside S3 as a regular faststart file, so browsers start it from a URL.

## What changed

On the AWS Lambda path, `format: "mp4"` renders (without `cfr`) now plan with `chunksCarryAudio`. Assemble builds a regular **faststart** MP4 inside S3: `ftyp`, one `moov` that indexes every sample, then one 64-bit `mdat`.

- `stitchMp4InS3` reads each chunk's `ftyp` and `moov` with two small ranged GETs and builds the header with #5812's `buildStitchedHeader`.
- One multipart upload writes the file:
  - Part 1 is the header plus just enough leading bytes of chunk 0 (downloaded) to reach S3's 5 MiB minimum.
  - Every other part is `UploadPartCopy` of one chunk's `mdat` byte range, so those bytes never pass through the function.
  - Part rule: every part but the last must be at least 5 MiB, and a copy reads one object. A range of at least 5 MiB is copied as it is. Anything smaller is downloaded into an uploaded part, which borrows the next range's head when the rest of that range can still be copied. Short renders take the same path, so there is no local fallback.
  - Any failure aborts the upload. The SAM template grants `s3:AbortMultipartUpload`, which `S3CrudPolicy` lacks; the snapshot test pins it.
- Audio layout: each chunk's audio packets sit inside that chunk's payload, interleaved with its video as ffmpeg muxes any MP4. A player streaming from the start reads audio and video from the same few MB.
- The lambda-local harness's disk-usage sampler no longer crashes when a scratch file disappears between listing and stat (hit while testing this).
- `chunksAreStitchedMp4`, `buildStitchedHeader`, `readMp4Layout` and `muxChunkWithAudio` are exported from `@hyperframes/producer/distributed` for this package.

## What I measured

Locally:
- `s3Stitch.test.ts`:
  - The part planner on exact sizes, and abort on a failed part.
  - 3 real x264 + AAC chunks through an S3 stand-in. It serves ranged reads, joins parts and rejects a non-last part under the minimum, which is set to 16 KiB so small chunks take every path that 5 MiB takes. Results: `ffprobe -v error` silent, boxes `ftyp, moov, mdat`, 91 frames and all audio packets. Frames, PCM and stream durations equal today's `assemble()`, and the local `assemble()` output is byte-identical to the S3 output.
- `handler.test.ts`: a plan whose chunks carry audio assembles through S3 and never calls the local join.
- 3 runs in a row green. Each mutation turns its test red: borrowing that leaves a short copy, no abort, the handler skipping the S3 path. The S3 integration test also goes red for offsets ignoring earlier chunks and for the priming not being skipped.
- `tsc` (producer, engine, aws-lambda), oxlint, oxfmt, `fallow audit` (new-only gate) and the comment checks pass.

On AWS: a 30-minute 1080p30 benchmark, on the same fixture as main's baseline with inputs pinned by sha256. Deployed with `--concurrency 300` and rendered with `--max-parallel-chunks 225` (225 chunks of 8 s). Measured on the same code before it was split into this stack (#5803, #5812, this PR). The split changed only file layout, a flag name and the in-chunk sample count check, which now uses ffprobe. I have not re-run AWS on the split branches.

| | Today (ffmpeg join) | Fragmented MP4 + S3 stitch | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Assemble, Step Functions state | 81.5 s | 1.8 s | **2.4 s** |
| Assemble, inside the function | download 2 GB, ffmpeg, upload 2 GB | 1.6 s | **2.2 s**: 0.06 s plan read, 2.16 s for 226 parts (3.3 MB downloaded, 2 MB header uploaded) |
| Chrome from a presigned URL, duration known | 1.8 s / 3.4 s | never within 60 s | **1.6 s / 3.1 s** |
| WebKit from a presigned URL, duration known | 5.5 s / 2.7 s | never within 60 s | **3.3 s / 5.5 s** |
| Seeks to 5, 900, 1799 s from the URL | all land | 5 s never lands | **all land** |
| Video / audio duration | 1800.000 / 1800.000 s | 1800.000 / 1800.021 s | **1800.000 / 1800.000 s** |

- The streaming rows come from one session: two rounds, all three layouts back to back, order rotated. "Today" is this run's output remuxed with `-movflags +faststart`, and "fragmented" is the same streams as fragmented MP4.
- Time to "ready to play through" (readyState 4) is left out on purpose. It also needs the link to outrun the video's 9.2 Mb/s, and on this 4-7 Mb/s link it swung from 2 s to over 60 s for the same file. On every round it moved together for this PR's file and today's layout.
- End to end: 289.5 s in Step Functions (plan 72.1 s, render map 215.0 s, assemble 2.4 s). Only the assemble is this change.
- Measured cost (Lambda REPORT lines plus Step Functions): $1.62. 227 invocations, all OK.
- Output:
  - 2.07 GB; `ffprobe -v error` silent. Boxes: `ftyp`, a 1.99 MB `moov` at the front, one `mdat`.
  - 54000 frames, and 84376 AAC packets (main's count) decoding to exactly 86,400,000 samples.
  - Loudness as on main, with no level jump at any chunk seam.
- Pictures at 5, 900 and 1799 s are byte-identical to an earlier run of the same fixture, and I looked at them, including the frames each player showed while streaming.
- Players:
  - A 10 s render from disk passes ffprobe, AVFoundation, Chrome and WebKit, with the same frame in each.
  - Streamed from its URL, the 30-minute file plays in AVFoundation with exact frames at 5, 900 and 1799 s.
- The stack, its buckets and its log group are torn down, and nothing is left.

## What I did not exercise

- Real Safari: safaridriver needs "Allow remote automation" on the test Mac, so the browser runs are Playwright **WebKit, not Safari**.
- An AWS run of the split branches themselves (see above).


## Original report — #5807 at 7d166358

## What the user sees

A distributed render (plan, then chunks, then assemble) could start any chunk after the first on the composition's **opening frame**: the frame at time 0, with the background video on its first frame and no overlays yet. It is one wrong frame per chunk boundary, so it shows as a flash at every seam. Whether a given chunk got it was down to timing, so two renders of the same plan gave different videos.

## Cause

On a BeginFrame capture session, the first display-producing `HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame` can return the frame Chrome composited during session init, not the seek the page has already applied. Logged just before that capture, the DOM was already correct (title opacity 1, native `<video>` hidden, injected frame visible and decoded), and Chrome answered `hasDamage: true` with a fresh screenshot. In some runs that screenshot was still the init frame. Every later frame of the session was on time (checked against the source video, frame by frame).

What triggers it is the chunk's BeginFrame liveness probe (`renderChunk` → `beginFrameSessionNeedsScreenshotFallback` → `probeBeginFrameLiveness`). It sends one more BeginFrame on the capture session after init and before the first seek. On main, on the host where it was stale 9 times in 10:

| chunk session (chunks 1 to 4, idle) | first frame stale |
|---|---|
| as shipped (probe on) | 10 of 10 |
| probe skipped | 0 of 12 |
| probe sent with `noDisplayUpdates: true` | 11 of 12 |
| locked warmup turned off (probe on) | 10 of 10 (ruled out) |

So any extra BeginFrame between init and the first seek is enough, whether or not it displays. The probe itself is needed: it is how a chunk detects a SwiftShader compositor stall. Local renders never probe their capture sessions this way, which is why they are not affected (next section).

## Local renders (`hyperframes render`): not affected

**Do local multi-worker renders flash too? No. 0 of 240 worker-start frames were stale on main, and 0 of 240 with this PR.** I rendered the same pinned fixture locally with `--workers 1`, with `--workers 4` (the default interleaved split: worker i draws frames i, i+4, ..., so the worker starts are frames 0 to 3), and with `--workers 4` plus `HF_CAPTURE_PARALLEL_STREAM=false` (the contiguous disk split: worker starts 0, 75, 150, 225). That was 5 runs of each idle and 5 under 16 CPU hogs, on two Linux hosts, plus 15 extra loaded `--workers 4` rounds alternating main and this PR. Every log reported `captureMode: beginframe` and the requested worker count. Worker-start frames were compared with the `--workers 1` render by per-frame PSNR (a stale one is about 21 to 25 dB).

| host | tree | `--workers 1` frame 0 | `--workers 4` interleaved starts | `--workers 4` contiguous starts | renders byte-identical to `--workers 1` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A (8 cores) | main | 0 of 10 stale | 0 of 100 | 0 of 40 | 45 of 45 |
| A | this PR | 0 of 10 | 0 of 100 | 0 of 40 | 44 of 45 |
| B (32 cores) | main | 0 of 10 | 0 of 40 | 0 of 40 | 30 of 30 |
| B | this PR | 0 of 10 | 0 of 40 | 0 of 40 | 30 of 30 |

Local output is byte-identical between main and this PR on both hosts, so the extra BeginFrame changes nothing there. One loaded `--workers 4` render with this PR differed at frame 5 only. That frame is worker 1's second frame, not a worker start, and showed the title one step behind the video. It did not recur in 15 alternating rounds (main 0 of 20 loaded `--workers 4` renders, this PR 1 of 20), so I cannot tell whether it is related.

## Fix

In `captureFrameSurface`, the first BeginFrame capture of a session first displays the seek once. It sends one visual BeginFrame with no screenshot at the capture tick minus half an interval. Ticks stay monotonic: the producer's liveness probe sits at base − 5 intervals and the init commit at base − 6. This covers chunk workers, parallel workers and retry pages, because each one is a fresh session. It adds one BeginFrame per session.

## Measured

A 10 s 1080p30 fixture with an H.264 background video, a GSAP title and AAC audio, split into 5 chunks. It was generated once and pinned by sha256, and every chunk of the same plan was rendered 10 times (5 idle, 5 under CPU hogs).

| | distinct outputs per chunk (0 to 4) | chunk first frames showing the opening frame |
|---|---|---|
| main, Linux host A (8 cores, 8 hogs) | 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 | 23 of 40 (18 of 20 idle, 5 of 20 loaded) |
| main, Linux host B (32 cores, 32 hogs) | 2, 2, 2, 1, 3 | 4 of 40 (0 idle, 4 of 20 loaded) |
| this PR, host A (8 hogs) | 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 | 0 of 40 |
| this PR, host B (16 hogs) | 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 | 0 of 40 |

Which way the race goes depends on the host: host A was usually stale when idle, host B only when loaded. On both hosts chunk 0 also flipped between Chrome's own paint of the native video and the injected extracted frame. With the fix it always shows the injected frame. A stale first frame measures 21 dB against the correct one; the rest of the chunk differs only by the encoder carrying that frame forward (about 50 dB).

Tests: the new `frameCapture-firstBeginFrame.test.ts` fails on main (both cases) and passes with the fix, 3 runs in a row. The engine's frameCapture and screenshotService suites pass (31 files, 333 tests). The full engine unit suite passes except 4 `ffprobe.test.ts` cases that read an LFS fixture which was not fetched in this checkout; they fail identically on main.

## Not exercised

- The producer Docker regression baselines. A render starting at frame 0 now shows the injected video frame on frame 0, not Chrome's native paint of the same frame. In this fixture that is a 42 dB difference, which should sit inside checkpoint tolerances, but I have not run them.
- macOS (screenshot or drawElement capture). Only the `beginframe` branch changed.
- Mid-session hard cuts. Only a session's first capture was seen to go stale; later frames were on time in every run.
- Why an extra BeginFrame before the first seek makes Chrome present the pre-seek frame. The table above pins the trigger, not Chrome's internal reason.

The plan step was deterministic apart from the plan folder path baked into `planHash`, which #5782 already fixes.

title: perf(aws-lambda): size distributed renders from account concurrency limits
body:
## Review fixes, head `088cf534` (rebased on main `b46ebede`)

One commit per review finding, each with a test that fails without it (the budget commit needs none):

| Finding | Commit | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 2. Redeploy removed an existing cap | `1f156cdc` | With `--concurrency` omitted, `deploy` no longer sends `ReservedConcurrency`, so SAM keeps the stack's current value on an update (UsePreviousValue); a new stack still gets the template's unreserved default. The state file records the deployed value, and `deploy` prints `Kept the stack's reserved concurrency of 8. Pass --concurrency=N to change it.` |
| 3. Progress crashed without `states:DescribeMapRun` | `7a894dac` | `getRenderProgress` catches only `AccessDeniedException` around the map-run read, returns the parent snapshot (status, plan and assemble progress) and a new `warnings` entry telling the caller to re-apply `lambda policies user`. `lambda progress` and `render --wait` print it. Any other error still throws. |
| 4. Upgrade rolled back on the documented deploy policy | `98110999` | `lambda policies role/user` now grant `lambda:DeleteFunctionConcurrency`; the required-actions test pins it and `states:DescribeMapRun`. |
| 5. Smoke gate exited 6 | `009f8609` | `_semantic-compare.sh` reads `Chunks[]` from the `RenderChunks`/`RenderChunksV2` `MapStateExited` output. The stack the script deploys has only the Distributed Map, so the inline-Map path is gone. |
| Note: `--chunk-size 30` capped at 16 | `5b10b05d` | With chunking pinned and no `--max-parallel-chunks`, the cap is now one wave across the worker concurrency, which is what the `--max-parallel-chunks` docs say; 16 stays when the concurrency is unknown. |
| 1. Size budget | `96bf7fba` | See below. |
| Follow-up: a way back to unreserved | `088cf534` | `deploy --concurrency=none` sends `ReservedConcurrency=-1`, so the state file records the stack as unreserved, and deploy prints `Removed the stack's reserved concurrency; each render now sizes itself to the account.` A positive N and an omitted flag behave as before. Any other value is now rejected; before, a non-number was silently ignored. |

### Upgrade note (also in the deploy docs)

Redeploying an existing stack without `--concurrency` keeps the reservation it already has, and `deploy` prints it. Stacks deployed by earlier CLI versions reserved 8 by default, so they stay at 8 until you pass `--concurrency=N`. Pass `--concurrency=none` to remove the reservation. New stacks reserve nothing and each render sizes itself to the account.

### Size budget

`@hyperframes/aws-lambda` measured with `pnpm@10.17.1 pack` after `bun run build`, rebased on main `70fbe32f` (which already raised the budget for S3-side MP4 assembly): this head packs to 67,763 / 244,685 bytes. The budget is the check's own 5% headroom over that: 71,152 / 256,920 (main's was 66,677 / 242,569). The growth is the Distributed Map progress reader, the account-concurrency lookup and the throttle handling.

### Live AWS at `cd699173` (same code as `5d4a603f`; that head only trims four comment lines)

us-east-2, every stack, bucket, log group and test IAM role deleted afterwards and checked empty.

- **(a) Upgrade with the documented policy.** main's CLI, no flags: reserved 8. Then this head's CLI, no `--concurrency`, run as an IAM role whose only policy is this head's `lambda policies role` output: `UPDATE_COMPLETE`, exit 0, the "Kept ... 8" line, parameter and function env still 8. Then, as the same role, a Path 2 redeploy with `ReservedConcurrency=-1` (the call that needs `DeleteFunctionConcurrency`): `UPDATE_COMPLETE`, 0 `UPDATE_FAILED` events, function unreserved, both Maps DISTRIBUTED/STANDARD.
- **(b) `render --wait` with the policy minus `states:DescribeMapRun`** (2-minute 1080p30 composition): printed `[RUNNING] 0%`, then the hint, then `3600/3600 frames` and `Render complete.`, exit 0. Execution SUCCEEDED; Map run 8/8 succeeded. Cost $0.07.
- **(c) `smoke.sh --plan-protocol both --chunk-counts 2,4`**: exit 0. PSNR 37.11-37.12 dB on all four renders; `PASS: v1/v2 semantic equivalence` at N=2 and N=4 with chunk hashes 2/2 and 4/4.

Unit tests, one file per command: `getRenderProgress` 20 pass, `handler` 21, CDK snapshot 18, `validateConfig` 38, producer `plan` 57, CLI `sam` 5, `policies` 16, `render` 5, `render-batch` 14, `state` 5; `semantic-compare.test.sh` passes. Each new test was turned red by reverting its fix.

**`--concurrency=none` at `088cf534`.** A fresh stack deployed with `--concurrency=8` (reserved 8). Then `--concurrency=none`, run as an IAM role whose only policy is this head's `lambda policies role` output: `UPDATE_COMPLETE`, exit 0, the "Removed" line, function unreserved, state file unreserved, 0 `UPDATE_FAILED` events. Torn down and checked empty.

Not done: no CDK deploy; no live run of the pinned-chunk-size cap (unit test only).

Current signed successor `98183d6548fd07a1babeee9b6da66452d2b61f1b` repairs a real published-module boundary: the new `@aws-sdk/client-lambda` stays external alongside the other declared AWS SDK dependencies. The exact built root import reproduced CI’s `Dynamic require of node:https` before the one-line fix, then root + SDK imports pass from isolated publish-config manifests using the actual built packages (no source substitutions or install). Targeted core/engine/producer/adapter builds and normal signed hooks pass. This is not a full clean installed packed-manifest suite or live AWS run. Fresh hosted build/edit gates and current-head independent review remain required.

## Current-main integration successor

Signed `e48fbde79a330a9c478a5cd085109f0a3c9154ab` preserves both original #5813 and #5762 heads and merges current main. The normal fallow gate exposed the policies command's existing large validation branches once touched by the new required action; validation/read/report helpers now preserve those results without suppressions or threshold changes. Policies16, producer plan56, progress18 and handler21 tests pass; all normal lint/format/type/fallow/sign hooks pass. Handler's ten real unpack cases exceeded its default five-second test command budget on this host; the bounded 15-second invocation passes21/21, with no test-source timeout change. No live AWS render or full workspace green claim. Multiple simultaneous unreserved renders still lack a shared fleet budget; this PR does not claim to fix that independently.

Current-head hosted CI and independent review remain required before normal merge. Previous reports and all their evidence/limits follow unchanged.

## Consolidated scope and review boundary

This PR now carries the complete Distributed Map and plan-owned account-concurrency change from #5762 plus its successor #5813. It targets `main`; review the **whole combined diff**, not only the last commit. #5762's exact head `730635d4` is an ancestor of this unchanged signed successor `54b74966` (one commit ahead, zero behind). The intermediate iterator-owned cap is replaced by the plan-owned cap here, so it is not shipped and then deleted in a second PR.

All original evidence and limits from both PRs are preserved below and remain attributed to their original heads. They do not establish a fresh current-main integration or a live account-sized render. New combined-target CI and independent review remain required before merge. Multiple concurrent unreserved renders still lack a shared account budget; the original limitation remains explicit. No AWS deployment, paid render or release was performed for this consolidation.

## Account-concurrency successor — original report

## What changes for the user

`hyperframes lambda deploy` no longer reserves 8 executions by default. Each render now runs as many chunks at once as it has, up to 90% of the account's unreserved Lambda concurrency. Before, a default 30-minute render failed: it planned 16 chunks against 8 slots, and chunks 9-16 ran out of throttle retries.

`--concurrency N` still wins. It reserves N for the function, and every render then runs at most N chunks at once, as before.

## How it works

- **The plan step picks the number.** It is the one place every caller goes through (CLI `render`, `render-batch`, the SDK, CDK adopters). The order is: the render config's `workerConcurrency` if set, else the function's reserved concurrency (passed in as `HYPERFRAMES_LAMBDA_RESERVED_CONCURRENCY`), else 90% of `UnreservedConcurrentExecutions` from `GetAccountSettings`.
- **Why 90%.** It leaves room for the account's other functions. At the default quota of 1000, that leaves 100 free, which is the floor AWS already keeps unreserved. Nothing is reserved, so an idle stack holds no capacity.
- **The planner and the Map now use the same number.** The plan sizes its chunks to it (one wave, 256 at most, as #5765 does today) and returns `MaxChunkConcurrency = min(concurrency, chunks)`. Both Maps read that value in place of the deploy-time constant from #5762, so the cap in the Map and the plan's assumption cannot drift apart.
- **When the account limit binds**, the existing plan-time warning from #5765 says the render runs in waves. It now also mentions a higher account quota as a fix next to `--concurrency`.
- **If `GetAccountSettings` fails** (access denied, throttled), the plan logs a WARN line naming the error and plans for 16 at once, the planner's default when it knows nothing.
- **IAM.** `lambda:GetAccountSettings` is added to the function role in both the SAM template and the CDK construct, with a parity test covering both. No caller policy changes, because the caller never makes this call.
- `@aws-sdk/client-lambda` is pinned to the `client-s3` version and kept external in the handler bundle, since the Node 22 runtime ships it.

## Tests

`handler.test.ts` has a mocked Lambda client and runs the real chunk-sizing rule on a 30-minute 1080p30 plan:
- (a) account has room: 204 chunks, all at once
- (b) small account: capped at 9, 21 chunks, with the waves warning
- (c) `GetAccountSettings` denied: falls back to 16 and logs a WARN
- (d) explicit concurrency wins, then reserved, and the account is never called

All four fail on the base handler. One mutation each turns its test red: drop the 90% share, use the chunk count as the Map cap, rethrow instead of falling back, drop the explicit-first check. The tests passed 3 runs in a row. The full `aws-lambda` suite passes (167) and `tsc` passes for `aws-lambda` and `cli`.

## Not exercised yet

- **The real AWS 30-minute run with no `--concurrency` flag** is pending a fresh AWS login. This body gets the measured chosen concurrency, peak Lambdas, wall time, cost and output checks when it runs.
- **`render-batch` is not fixed here.** Without a reserved concurrency, every render in a batch sizes itself to the whole account, and they can oversubscribe it together. The CLI docs now say to reserve one before a large batch. Splitting the account across a batch needs its own decision.


## Distributed Map — original #5762 report

## What changed

- **Chunk renders run in a Distributed Map** in both state machine definitions (`HyperframesRenderStack.ts` and `examples/aws-lambda/template.yaml`). The inline Map ran at most 40 chunks at once, so a 256-chunk render went in waves of 40. Each chunk is now a STANDARD child execution (EXPRESS children stop at 5 minutes; a chunk may run the Lambda's full 15). No tolerated failures: any failed chunk still fails the render, and the per-task retry rules inside each chunk are unchanged.
- **Fan-out is capped at the function's reserved concurrency** (`MaxConcurrencyPath` now reads a `MaxChunkConcurrency` value the `BuildChunkList` state sets from `reservedConcurrency` / `ReservedConcurrency`; 0 = no cap when unreserved). Before, the cap was the chunk count, so chunks past the reserved concurrency were throttled by Lambda (`TooManyRequestsException`), retried 4 times over about 30 s, and failed the render if the first wave took longer than that. Now they wait in the Map instead.
- **IAM**: the state machine role may start its own child executions and describe or stop them. CDK adds this itself for a `DistributedMap`; the SAM role gets the same statements, with ARNs built from `ProjectName` because `!Ref RenderStateMachine` inside its own role is a dependency cycle.
- **Progress costs at most 3 Step Functions calls per poll, whatever the chunk count**: chunk events now live in each child execution's history, not the parent's. Reading every child's history on every poll made `hyperframes lambda render --wait` crash with `Rate exceeded` at 225 chunks. `getRenderProgress` now makes `DescribeExecution` + `GetExecutionHistory` (parent) + one `DescribeMapRun` while the chunk Map runs. Frames come from the Map Run's item counts; once the Map exits, exact chunk frames and Lambda time come from the chunk results in the Map's output. A failed chunk's own history is read only when the counts show a failure (at most 5 children), so typed chunk errors such as `PLAN_HASH_MISMATCH` on `RenderChunkV2` still surface.
- **Chunk results carry `FramesEncoded` and `DurationMs`** (both definitions' `ResultSelector`), which is what lets the Map output replace the child histories. About 45 bytes per chunk in the state payload.
- **Progress polls back off on throttling**: the progress client retries `ThrottlingException` up to 8 times with the SDK's backoff instead of throwing after the default 3.
- **IAM for callers**: `hyperframes lambda policies` now lists `states:DescribeMapRun`. The stack roles do not need it; only the caller polling progress does.
- **What the progress numbers mean now** (while the chunk Map runs): frames are the succeeded share of total frames (exact once the Map exits); the running cost leaves out chunk Lambda time until the Map exits, then adds it exactly; `lambdasInvoked` counts started chunks, not retry attempts inside a chunk; `errors` lists a failed chunk's attempts, not transient failures inside chunks that later succeeded. Percent math, status and final totals are unchanged.
- SAM quotes any intrinsic it finds inside a `Definition`, so the SAM value goes through `States.StringToJson` to arrive as a number.
- **Throttles get their own retry**: `Lambda.TooManyRequestsException` now retries 10 times from 5 s, doubling up to 60 s, with full jitter (about 7 minutes in total), ahead of the 30 s catch-all, on all six Lambda tasks. With the cap a render should not throttle itself, but a second render on the same function can still take the reserved slots.
- **`CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` is terminal for Plan and PlanV2** in both definitions. #5765 produces that code at plan time, so retrying it cannot help.

Message for users when chunks exceed `--concurrency`: not in this PR. The planner-side lane owns the plan-time message; this PR only makes the state machine queue instead of fail. The CLI default of 8 is unchanged.

Sync between CDK and SAM: the existing snapshot test already compares the Lambda task payloads and terminal error lists of both. The new tests check Map mode, child type, label, concurrency path and IAM actions on both definitions. Nothing compares the full definitions; this PR does not add that.

## What I measured

- Progress fix: `getRenderProgress` 18 pass, exit 0, three runs in a row; snapshot 17 pass; policies 16 pass; `tsc --noEmit` exit 0. The four new tests (225 running chunks make exactly 3 calls; exact frames and cost from the Map output with 2 calls; a failed chunk's error surfaces from reading only failed children; a client built like the real one rides out 3 throttles) all fail on the previous head. One mutation each fails only its own test: always reading failed children, default SDK retries, dropping the failed-chunk errors, ignoring the Map output.
- Earlier: `bun test` (packages/aws-lambda): snapshot 17 pass, contract 6 pass, getRenderProgress 15 pass, exit 0, three runs in a row. `tsc --noEmit` exit 0. `fallow audit` pass, oxlint/oxfmt clean.
- RED on main's source with the new tests: snapshot 4 fail (resource count, Distributed Map mode, concurrency cap, IAM), getRenderProgress 1 fail (`framesRendered` 0, expected 150). The throttle-retry and terminal-code tests fail on the first commit's definitions (2 fail). Mutations: SAM-only `Mode: INLINE` fails only the Distributed Map test; dropping the child histories fails only the child-execution progress test.
- `sam validate --lint` (SAM CLI 1.169.0): valid. `sam` translate shows `MaxChunkConcurrency.$` becomes `States.StringToJson('${...}')` with an `Fn::Sub` over the `Fn::If`.

Real AWS, us-east-2, stack deployed with `hyperframes lambda deploy` from this branch. The render was a 2-minute 1080p30 composition (3600 frames, video plus audio) with `--max-parallel-chunks 60`:

| Reserved concurrency | Chunks | Peak child executions at once | Throttled tasks | Wall (submit to done) | Measured cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 60 | 60 (all started within 0.6 s) | 0 | 39 s | $0.147 |
| 8 (CLI default) | 60 | 8 (Map Run max concurrency 8) | 0 | 119 s | $0.117 |

- For comparison, the same composition on main earlier the same day split into 16 chunks at concurrency 8: 75 s, with 32 throttled task attempts. On main, a 30-minute render at concurrency 8 failed outright on `Lambda.TooManyRequestsException`.
- Both outputs are identical: same size and MD5, 3600 video packets, 120.0 s, audio present.
- `hyperframes lambda render --wait` progress advanced through the chunks (51%, 55%, ... 3600/3600 frames) with cost, read from the child executions.
- Stopping a render mid-Map aborted its 7 running children and left the other 52 unstarted, so the role's StopExecution grant works.
- Deployed definition checked: both Maps `DISTRIBUTED` / `STANDARD`, `MaxChunkConcurrency.$` resolved to `States.StringToJson('64')`, then `'8'` after the redeploy.
- The stack, both buckets and the log groups were deleted afterwards. Total spend about $0.28.

Real AWS, the progress fix, same region: fresh stack from this head (reserved concurrency 300), the same 2-minute composition with `--max-parallel-chunks 225` and `render --wait --wait-interval-ms 2000`, which is the interval that crashed:

| Run | `--wait` | SFN calls per poll (client-side counter) | Retries | Peak chunks at once | SFN wall | Measured cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | completed, exit 0 | 2 before and after the Map, 3 during it | 0 | 225 | 40.6 s | $0.364 |
| 2, with the previous poller beside it | completed, exit 0 | same, 3 at most | 0 | 225 | 29.8 s | $0.242 |

- Progress advanced on every poll during the Map: 10%, 39%, 66%, 84%, then 3600/3600 frames, then done. Outputs: 3600 video packets, 120.0 s audio.
- The previous poller, run on the same render as run 2: 93 then 228 calls per poll, then it died with `ThrottlingException: Rate exceeded` after 3 attempts on its third Map poll. The new `--wait` next to it never needed a retry.
- The CLI's own total ($0.328 / $0.240) reads the handlers' `DurationMs`, so it sits below the billed figure.
- Stack, buckets and log group deleted afterwards and checked empty. Spend for these two runs about $0.61.

## What I did NOT exercise

- The CDK construct was not deployed. It was synthesized and tested; the real runs used the SAM template, which is what `hyperframes lambda deploy` ships.
- No render above 225 chunks, and no 30-minute render on this branch.
- No chunk failure inside a child on real AWS. The failed-chunk error path is covered by the unit test only.
- The backoff was exercised by a unit test with a fake transport, not by a real throttle on the new poller (it never got throttled).
- The CDK construct was synthesized and snapshot-tested, not deployed, for the new `ResultSelector` fields too.

title: fix(cli): render starts in a sandbox that forbids lowering CPU priority
body:
## What

A render now starts in a sandbox that won't let a process lower its own CPU priority. The background lint step still asks for the lowest priority. When the system refuses, it prints one warning, "Lint runs at normal priority: …", and lints anyway.

## Why

Since 0.8.165 the render-setup worker calls `os.setPriority(PRIORITY_LOW)` before linting, so a lint never competes with a Studio boot. Inside an agent's sandbox that call throws `uv_os_setpriority returned EPERM`. The worker exited without a lint result, and the render died at start. Lower priority is a nicety, never a reason to fail the render.

That call is the only `setPriority` in the repo (`git grep -nE "setPriority|getPriority|renice"`).

## Test plan

- New case in `renderSetupWorker.priority.test.ts`: `setPriority` throws EPERM, and the worker still writes the lint result and warns once on stderr. Against main's worker it fails: the lint result is never written (0 calls). It passes three runs in a row on this branch. The existing low-priority case still passes.

## Not covered

I didn't reproduce a real EPERM inside an agent sandbox. The test throws the reported error from a mocked `setPriority`.

title: feat(render): add --audio-bitrate for AAC and Opus encodes
body:
## What
`hyperframes render` accepts `--audio-bitrate` (for example `128k` or `256k`) and threads it through the producer render config to every ffmpeg `-b:a` used for the AAC sidecar and the WebM Opus encode. Unset still emits `192k` for AAC and `128k` for Opus. MP4 and MOV still copy an AAC sidecar instead of re-encoding it at mux time.

## Why
Audio bitrate was hardcoded, so music-heavy renders could not raise it and size-capped or voice-only renders could not lower it.

## Related work
Fixes #5556

## How
- CLI validation matches `--video-bitrate`: trim the value and reject an empty string. It stays available with `--crf` and for MOV, because those constraints apply to the video encode.
- The optional `audioBitrate` is carried on the render request, the audio stage, duration pad/trim (including AAC true-peak correction), and the mux options.
- The mixer and pad/trim encode the AAC sidecar at the requested rate. The MP4/MOV mux copies that sidecar, so the bitrate is not applied by a second encode.
- WebM applies the same flag to the Opus encode. Docker forwards the flag.

## Test plan
- [x] Unit tests added/updated
- [x] Manual testing performed
- [x] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md

Unit tests cover flag parsing, docker forwarding, and the ffmpeg argument list for the default and overridden rates, including the AAC copy path omitting `-b:a`.

Manual check used the engine encode functions with ffmpeg 9.0.2, not a full `hyperframes render` (that path needs the studio/Chrome bootstrap):
- AAC sidecar at `--audio-bitrate 128k`: `ffprobe` stream `bit_rate` 128138 (1s) and 128048 (8s).
- MP4 mux with `audioCodec: "aac"` copied that stream (`bit_rate` 128138). No second encode.
- WebM Opus at `128k`: `ffprobe` reports stream `bit_rate=N/A`. Packet-derived rate on an 8s clip was 147437 bps, next to a direct `ffmpeg -c:a libopus -b:a 128k` encode of the same sine at 146472 bps.

Distributed render plans and the studio HTTP encoder options do not receive `audioBitrate`. Callers that leave it unset keep the previous rates.

title: fix(studio-server): history routes say why a project's history cannot open instead of a bare 500
body:
## What

Every Studio history route now answers with the reason when the project's history cannot open, instead of a bare 500 with no body.

## Why

`withHistory` opened the history (`historyOf`) before its `try`, and the blob route had no `try` at all. When the open throws (the history is owned by another process past the 5 s wait, the folder is gone or is now another project, a disk error), the error escaped to Hono and the client got `500 Internal Server Error` as plain text. Studio's claim then logs `HTTP 500` with nothing to go on, and the edit lands as an outside change instead of the person's entry, so we could neither see nor fix the real cause.

## Related work

None open on this file.

## How

- `withHistory` opens the history inside its `try`, so an open failure gets the same 409 with `{ error: <message> }` that an engine refusal already gets. No history at all stays a 404.
- The blob route goes through `withHistory` too; `withHistory` passes a `Response` from its task through untouched so the route can still send bytes.

Why 409 and not a new status: this file already answers refusals with 409, and Studio's client and host diagnostics key on the error text, which now arrives (for example `This project's history is open in another process (pid N).`).

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated: `history routes > say why when the project's history cannot open, on every route` opens a project's history, then has the routes open it again with no owner wait, so the real lock throws. It checks claim and blob both answer 409 with the lock's message.
- [x] `packages/studio-server`, `vitest run src/routes/history.test.ts`: exit 0, 28 passed, 3 runs in a row.
- [x] fails without the fix: with `origin/main`'s `history.ts` the new test fails (`SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'I', "Internal S"... is not valid JSON`, 1 failed, 27 passed). With only the blob route put back to main's version it fails the same way, so both halves are checked.
- [x] oxfmt, oxlint, studio-server `tsc --noEmit`, fallow audit, comment ratchet and citation checks: clean.
- [ ] Manual testing performed: not done. I did not reproduce the open failure in a running Studio or Desktop; the test drives the real lock through the real routes.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

What I did NOT exercise: hosts pick this up only with the next `@hyperframes/studio-server` release and their dependency bump. This change makes the reason visible; it does not stop the open from failing. Once reasons arrive, the most common one decides the next fix.


Size: 53 lines on purpose. This is a lone urgent fix for a live failure, merged on its own so the follow-up (forwarding history calls to the process that owns the history) can build on it.
