title: perf(cli): cloud render downloads the finished video over parallel connections
body:
## What

`hyperframes cloud render` gets the finished video back sooner:

- The download fetches the video over up to 8 parallel HTTP Range requests instead of one stream.
- The default `--poll-interval` drops from 10 s to 2 s, so a finished render is noticed within 2 s instead of up to 10 s.

## Why

Once the server finishes a render, the client was still losing time in two places: up to one full poll interval before it noticed, then a single-connection download of the result. Parallel ranged GETs against the presigned object URL are much faster than one stream for files of tens of MB.

## Related work

Refs #3944, which also touches `download.ts`. The bug it fixes (cleanup racing a write stream's pending open) cannot happen with this design: the staged file is opened with an awaited `fs/promises` `open` before any body is read, and it is closed before the staging directory is removed.

## How

- The first request asks for `Range: bytes=0-<8 MiB - 1>`.
  - `206` with `Content-Range: bytes 0-N/TOTAL`: the rest of the file is split into up to 7 more ranges, fetched at the same time, and each part is written at its offset into the staged file.
  - `200` (the server ignores Range): streamed exactly as before.
  - A file of 8 MiB or less comes back whole in that first response. An empty file (`416`) or a `206` with no total is fetched again without Range.
- Every part must return exactly its byte count, or the existing "Truncated download" error is raised. A sibling that answers `200` instead of `206` fails the download.
- One failed part aborts the others. The staged file is closed and removed, and an existing output is left untouched, keeping the guarantee from #3840. User cancellation still rejects with the caller's abort reason.
- No new dependency: stdlib `fetch`, `AbortSignal.any` and `fs/promises`.
- Poll default: `DEFAULT_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` goes to `2_000`. The help text, the CLI docs and the hyperframes-cli skill reference are updated (skills manifest regenerated).

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated. New `download.test.ts` cases run against a local `node:http` server:
  - one that honours Range (the bytes match, 8 requests);
  - small and empty files (one ranged request; the empty file falls back to a plain GET);
  - one that ignores Range (a single request, the bytes match);
  - one where a part dies mid-transfer (rejects, the previous output survives, no staged file is left).
  Each new case fails against the old `download.ts`, and the poll-default test fails against the old `poll.ts`.
- [x] Manual testing performed: real presigned S3 downloads, old vs new. The outputs were byte-identical (sha256) and the new path was consistently faster.
- [x] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: perf(producer): renders embed local fonts as-is instead of re-compressing them
body:
## What

Renders now embed a project's local `.ttf` / `.otf` fonts into the compiled HTML as-is, instead of re-compressing them to woff2 first.

## Why

woff2 compression is slow (seconds for a large font) and its cache lives on the local disk, so every fresh render machine pays it again for each local font. The compiled HTML is only a render-time artifact, so the smaller woff2 payload buys nothing there.

## Related work

None.

## How

- `fontToDataUri` (core) gains a `compress: false` option that returns `data:font/ttf` / `data:font/otf` with the original bytes, skipping compression and the cache. Its default is unchanged, so every other caller still gets woff2.
- The producer's local `@font-face` embed passes `compress: false`. woff2, ttc and the file-backed path for fonts over 5 MiB are untouched.
- Cost: the compiled HTML grows by roughly the raw-minus-woff2 size of each local font.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated: a core test (raw ttf/otf URIs, compressor never called, cache untouched) and a producer test (compiled HTML carries `data:font/ttf` / `data:font/otf` whose decoded bytes equal the files; the font cache dir stays empty). Both fail with the code change reverted.
- [x] Manual testing performed: rendered a fixture with a local TrueType `.ttf` and a CFF `.otf` (large text in each) to PNG frames with this branch and with `main`. Every frame is byte-identical (same sha256); a control render without the fonts differs, so the fonts are in effect. **No visible change.**
- [x] Cold-cache compile of that fixture: about 1.2 s on `main`, about 35 ms here (compiled HTML about 310 KB to 570 KB).
- [x] `htmlCompiler.test.ts` + `htmlCompiler.fontEmbed.test.ts` (148 pass), core `src/fonts/` (261 pass), core and producer typecheck clean.
- [ ] Documentation updated (if applicable): not applicable.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: feat(cli): lambda deploy works from the npm install, no repo checkout
body:
## What

`hyperframes lambda deploy` now works from the npm install alone, with no repo checkout.

- **Release workflow.** It builds the Lambda handler zip on the Linux x86_64 runner and attaches it (plus a `.sha256`) to the GitHub release for the tag. Before `npm publish` it writes `prebuilt/handler-zip.json` (asset URL + sha256 for this version) and `prebuilt/template.yaml` (the SAM template with `CodeUri: handler.zip`) into `@hyperframes/aws-lambda`.
- **CLI, outside a checkout.** `lambda deploy` reads the installed adapter's pin, downloads the zip into `~/.cache/hyperframes/lambda-handler/<version>-<sha256>/`, checks the sha256 (and refuses the zip on a mismatch), copies the packaged template next to it, and runs `sam deploy` from there. A cached copy is re-hashed and reused. `lambda destroy` no longer needs a checkout (`sam delete` reads the stack from CloudFormation).
- **CLI, inside a checkout or with `HYPERFRAMES_REPO_ROOT`.** Unchanged: it builds from source and deploys `examples/aws-lambda/template.yaml`.
- **Fallback.** With no checkout and no pinned zip (adapter missing, or an adapter release without one), deploy stops before doing anything. It prints one message that names the adapter install, the checkout alternative and the docs link. Before this, users hit two errors in a row: "install the adapter", then "could not find the repo root".

## Why

Today a user who installs the CLI and the adapter from npm still cannot deploy. Deploy builds the handler zip from monorepo source, and the template's `CodeUri` points into the monorepo. So "deploy from npm" needed a git clone and bun.

## Related work

Rebased on #5813 (merged). Refs #5772, which also touches `sam.ts`/`deploy.ts`/`template.yaml`. This PR keeps its edits to those files small: `sam.ts` takes the SAM directory instead of the repo root, and the template is untouched (the package's copy is rewritten at release time).

## How

- **Who owns the pin.** The adapter package owns "which zip goes with this version". `packages/aws-lambda/scripts/pin-handler-zip.ts` writes the pin, and `prebuiltHandler()` in `@hyperframes/aws-lambda/sdk` reads it. The CLI only downloads, verifies and stages. Older adapters have no `prebuiltHandler` export, so they fall through to the fallback message.
- **Release order.** The zip is built after `bun run build` and before `verify:packed-manifests`. The GitHub release is now created before `npm publish` (it used to come after), so the asset is on the release before any package that pins it is published.
- **Retries.** A retried run downloads the zip already attached to the release instead of building a new one. Zip builds are not byte-reproducible, so a rebuild would no longer match a pin that is already on npm. The upload has no `--clobber`, so a run never replaces an attached zip.
- **`build-zip.ts` no longer wipes the whole `dist/`.** It removes only its staging dir and zip. Otherwise zipping after `bun run build` would drop the package's own `dist/` from the publish. The pin script moves the zip out of the package, so nothing large gets packed.
- **Chrome source.** The prebuilt zip is built with sparticuz Chrome. `--chrome-source=chrome-headless-shell` outside a checkout is refused up front instead of deploying a mismatched stack.
- **Logs and errors.** A successful download logs the verified sha256. A refusal names the URL without its query string, so a presigned URL's signature never reaches the terminal or CI logs.
- **Download URL override.** `HYPERFRAMES_LAMBDA_HANDLER_URL` replaces the download URL. The pinned sha256 still decides whether the zip is used. The end-to-end check needs it because no release carries a zip yet. Mirrors can use it too.
- Job timeout raised from 10 to 20 minutes for the zip build and the ~130 MB upload.

## Package size

`@hyperframes/aws-lambda` ships `prebuilt/template.yaml` and `prebuilt/handler-zip.json` only at release time, so its size check runs on two packages: CI's (no `prebuilt/`) and the release's (`publish.yml` runs `verify:packed-manifests` after `pin-handler-zip`). After merging main, which shrank this package:

| State | Packed | Unpacked |
|---|---|---|
| CI (no `prebuilt/`, CI's own measurement) | 60,155 | 208,199 |
| Release (after `build:zip` + `pin-handler-zip`, Linux) | 67,355 | 241,634 |
| Budget | 70,000 | 244,000 |

One budget has to hold the release package (at or above its size) without leaving CI's package more than 15% under it (the check's ratchet). That window is 67,355-70,770 packed and 241,634-244,940 unpacked; the budget sits inside both. `verify:packed-manifests` passes in both states.

## Test plan

Ran on Linux x86_64 after a full root `bun run build`. Each new test was also run once with the code it covers broken, and went red.

- [x] `packages/aws-lambda/scripts/pin-handler-zip.test.ts`: 5 pass, 0 fail. Broken (template `CodeUri` rewrite): 1 fail.
- [x] `packages/cli/src/commands/lambda/prebuiltHandler.test.ts`: 6 passed. Broken (sha256 check skipped): the mismatch test fails.
- [x] `packages/cli/src/commands/lambda/deploy.test.ts`: 3 passed. Broken (no prebuilt staging): the fallback-message test fails.
- [x] `scripts/publish-workflow.test.mjs`: 6 pass, 0 fail. Broken (zip step no longer reports a reused asset): the retry test fails.
- [x] `sam.test.ts` 6 passed and `repoRoot.test.ts` 2 passed.
- [x] Typecheck of `cli` and `aws-lambda`, the comment checks, and `fallow audit` against main all pass.
- [x] Release steps run for real: `build:zip` then `pin-handler-zip.ts` produced a 129 MB zip, its `.sha256`, and the package's `prebuilt/` manifest and template.
- [x] Publish workflow dry run with `act` (0.2.89) in the `ubuntu-latest` runner image, on this head. It ran `publish.yml`'s steps verbatim from checkout through `verify:packed-manifests`, skipping only the two tag steps that need a real release event. Checkout, install, build, the handler zip step (the release download failed, so it built a fresh zip), and `verify:packed-manifests` with `prebuilt/` in place all passed. A final check step confirmed:
  - the `.sha256` file, `handler-zip.json` sha256, and byte count all match the zip;
  - `prebuilt/template.yaml` is the repo template with `CodeUri: handler.zip`;
  - the zip left `dist/` of the package, and the package build survived;
  - `npm pack` and `pnpm pack` tarballs both contain `prebuilt/handler-zip.json` (same sha256) and `prebuilt/template.yaml`, and no zip.
- [ ] Not run: the steps after `verify:packed-manifests` (create the release, attach the zip, npm publish). They write to GitHub and npm, so only their order, the attach condition, and the reuse-on-retry branch are covered, by the stubbed `gh`/`bun` test. The reuse branch (download an already attached zip) has never run against a real release.
- [x] End to end on real AWS from packed tarballs (`pnpm pack` of the adapter with its pinned `prebuilt/`, and the CLI packed as `hyperframes`), installed with `npm install` into an empty directory with no checkout above it and `HYPERFRAMES_REPO_ROOT` unset. The zip was served through `HYPERFRAMES_LAMBDA_HANDLER_URL` (a presigned S3 URL), since no release carries it yet.
  - Wrong bytes behind the URL: refused with the sha256 mismatch before SAM ran. No stack created, nothing cached.
  - First deploy: downloaded, verified, stack created.
  - Second deploy with no URL override: reused the verified cached zip, no download. SAM said "No changes to deploy".
  - One render of the 2 s distributed fixture: SUCCEEDED. ffprobe shows h264 640x360, 60 frames, 2.000 s, and a full decode is clean. Measured cost $0.0018.
  - `lambda destroy` from the same install deleted the stack. Afterwards no resource with the run's prefix was left.
- [ ] Not run: downloading from the real pinned release URL (needs the first release that carries the zip). The no-adapter fallback message only ran in unit tests.
- [x] Documentation updated: `docs/deploy/aws-lambda.mdx` prerequisites.

title: fix(cli): timeline delete --start/--end removes only that range
body:
## What a user sees

**Before:** `hyperframes timeline delete <clip> --start 2 --end 3` accepted both flags, never read them, and removed the whole clip. `--plan` showed an empty after-list. Every edit verb shared one flag set, so `split --start`, `delete --at`, `duplicate --overwrite` and the like were accepted and silently ignored. An `apply` plan edit like `{"verb": "delete", "ref": "#clip", "at": "2"}` was the same.

**After:**
- `timeline delete <clip> --start a --end b` removes only `[a, b)`. The part before `a` and the part after `b` stay, exactly as `split`, `split`, `delete` would leave them (it reuses `split`, so a video's tail keeps its media in-point and a sub-composition keeps its place). With one bound it cuts to the clip's edge; with neither it removes the clip as before. A range that reaches outside the clip, or is empty, is refused.
- Each verb accepts only the options it reads. A flag a verb does not use fails with `Unknown flag: --x` before anything is written, and an `apply` edit with a key its verb does not use is refused (`delete does not use at`). One table (`MUTATION_FIELDS`) is the single source for both the CLI flags and the plan keys.

| verb | options |
|---|---|
| move | `<time>`, `--overwrite`, `--snap` |
| trim | `--start`, `--end`, `--duration`, `--overwrite`, `--snap` |
| split | `<time>`, `--snap` |
| delete | `--start`, `--end`, `--snap` |
| set | `<field>=<value>`, `--volume`, `--rate`, `--track` |
| duplicate | `--at`, `--snap` |

All also take `--dir`, `--plan`, `--json`.

## Tests

`packages/cli/src/timeline/timeline.e2e.test.ts`: range delete on a video clip (plan and apply), out-of-clip range refusal, five verb/flag pairs refused without writing, and an apply key refusal. The range-delete and unused-flag tests fail on `main` (range delete returns an empty after-list there) and pass here. Timeline and flag-guard suites: 147 passed, 3 runs in a row.

title: perf(cli): check and inspect skip paint waits and screenshots nothing reads
body:
## Why

`hyperframes check` and `hyperframes inspect` are slow on CPU-only VMs. A per-phase profile on a CPU-only Linux box (software GL, no GPU) showed time spent on work no finding depends on:

- Each contrast sample took three full-frame PNGs: the one contrast measures, an "overview" one and, when contrast failed, an annotated one. The last two are only ever written out by `--snapshots`. That was half of contrast time (1.65 s of 3.17 s on `heygen-promo-preview-assets`).
- Every audit seek slept 120 ms to flush paint, including seeks that only read layout. Only a screenshot needs that. `inspect` never takes a screenshot, yet paid it on every seek.
- Every page open slept a fixed 1.5 s after the runtime was ready. The page is opened at DOMContentLoaded, so that sleep was what let late images and fetched assets land before the first screenshot, and it cost 1.5 s even when nothing was pending.
- The dense text-overlap pass (up to 240 box-only seeks) sent one seek and one read per sample. Between those calls the page went idle and the software renderer painted a frame nobody looks at: Chrome's main thread was busy 4.2 s during the grid on the CPU-only box vs 0.3 s on a GPU Mac, with equal script, style and layout time.

## What

- `collectContrast` takes the overview and annotated shots only when the pipeline asks for annotations, which it does only under `--snapshots`.
- `AUDIT_SEEK_OPTIONS` keeps the double-rAF and font waits but drops the sleep. The new `SCREENSHOT_SEEK_OPTIONS` adds it back for the seeks a screenshot follows: contrast samples (the pipeline tells `driver.seek`) and finding crops.
- The fixed 1.5 s settle after page open becomes `waitForLateSubresources`: wait for `document.readyState === "complete"`, then 100 ms of network idle, then every image decoded and fonts ready, capped at the same 1.5 s. It is never later than before, and a page with nothing pending moves on at once. This is shared by check, snapshot, compare and grade-compare.
- Screenshot seeks wait for every image to decode (`waitForImagesMs`, capped at the old 120 ms) instead of sleeping 120 ms.
- The contrast measurement screenshot is clipped to the union of the text boxes it samples (`captureBeyondViewport: false`, the same render path as the full shot), and `__contrastAuditFinish` reads the clipped image at that offset. A sample with no text to measure takes no screenshot unless `--snapshots` wants its frame.
- With the double-frame settle, the post-seek font check runs on the settle's second frame instead of waiting a third (`waitForCompositionFonts(page, ms, frames)`); the first frame's layout is what starts any pending font loads.
- An event that lands after the dense pass's page task, before the next seek, cannot be tied to one sample: its runtime finding gets `time` = the pass's first sample and `timeRange: [first, last]` instead of the last sample's time.
- New driver method `collectOverlapGrid(times)` runs the dense pass's seek, seek barrier, overlap audit and anchor lookup for every time inside one page task. It awaits only the runtime's seek barrier, so no frame is painted between samples. The seek cascade (`seekInPage`) and the anchor lookup (`anchorsInPage`) moved into named functions shared with the per-seek paths. The page logs a `console.debug` marker before each sample, so console and page errors raised during the grid keep the sample time they had before. The hold re-probes stay in Node, unchanged.

No sample counts, thresholds or flags change.

## Before / after

CPU-only Linux (software GL), the built CLI (`node bin/hyperframes.mjs check --json`), median of 3 runs, whole process. Each row adds one change on top of the row above.

| step | fast-capture-gsap | chat | heygen-promo-preview-assets |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | 4.68 s | 5.48 s | 11.16 s |
| skip unread screenshots, paint sleep only before screenshots | 3.97 s | 4.65 s | 9.43 s |
| dense overlap pass in one page task | 3.94 s | 4.59 s | 6.03 s |
| readiness wait instead of the fixed 1.5 s | 2.55 s | 3.08 s | 4.66 s |
| image-decode wait instead of the 120 ms paint sleep | 1.94 s | 2.44 s | 4.16 s |
| contrast screenshots only the text it measures | 1.80 s | 2.22 s | 3.85 s |
| font check shares the settle's second frame | **1.64 s (2.9x)** | **2.08 s (2.6x)** | **3.82 s (2.9x)** |

`inspect` (built): 2.67 → 1.47 s, 2.86 → 1.61 s, 2.96 → 1.94 s.

Findings: `check --json` output is identical to main on every run of every fixture at every step, once run-specific ports, ids, temp paths and the CLI version are normalised. The fixtures are the repo's producer test projects that pass lint (a lint error skips the browser pass).

## What check's time scales with on a VM

- Not core count: main took the same time pinned to 1, 2 or 4 cores (11.7 s on `heygen-promo-preview-assets`), because check drives one page serially. Memory is small: the largest process peaks at about 250 MB with the built CLI.
- Software rendering is what a CPU-only VM pays for: before this change, Chrome's main thread was busy 4.2 s during the sampling grid without a GPU vs 0.3 s with one, with equal script, style and layout time. What remains GPU-sensitive is rasterising heavy frames for the contrast pass.

## Tests

- `check.test.ts`: the grid seeks with `screenshot=true` only at contrast times.
- `checkBrowser.test.ts`: one contrast screenshot and no saved frames without `--snapshots`, two with it.
- `captureCompositionFrame.test.ts`: the audit seek has no sleep; the screenshot seek does.

- `checkBrowser.test.ts`: every dense sample's overlap audit runs inside the same page evaluate, and a console error raised at the 2.5 s sample is reported at 2.5 s. It fails if the grid goes back to one evaluate per sample, and if the marker handling is removed.

- `captureCompositionFrame.lateSubresources.browser.test.ts` (real headless Chromium): an image served 0.8 s and a fetched asset served 1.1 s after the page loads are both in when the page open returns. It fails without the readiness wait (the image is not loaded yet), and with the network-idle step removed (the fetch has not landed), and it passes on the old fixed sleep.

- `contrast-clip.browser.test.ts` (real headless Chromium): two text blocks over a two-tone backdrop give the same contrast entries from a clipped shot as from the full frame; it fails if the clipped image is read without the offset.
- `checkBrowser.test.ts`: the measurement shot is clipped to the text box; a sample with no text takes no screenshot; a runtime event that arrives after the grid gets the grid's `timeRange`.
- `captureCompositionFrame.test.ts`: a screenshot seek finishes without timers advancing (no fixed sleep); the double settle reads font status on its second frame and issues 3 page calls, not 4.

Each new test fails on the code it guards. The five affected test files (201 tests) passed 3 runs in a row.

title: fix(inspector): data-hf-id stamps alone do not make the live preview stale
body:
## What

Keep Desktop live inspection current after an ID-only HTML stamp, while preserving standalone Inspector reloads.

## Why

Desktop stamps `data-hf-id` into HTML on disk after its served preview already has those IDs. It deliberately does not reload for that write. A byte-sensitive live fingerprint therefore makes subsequent queries fail with `stale_preview` until an unrelated edit reloads the preview.

The standalone Inspector builds its own page from disk. It must reload after an ID stamp so an `hfId` query can find the newly stamped element. Ignoring IDs for that caller would reuse a page without them.

## How

- `sources.fingerprint` retains byte-sensitive hashing by default and accepts an internal `ignoreHfIds` option.
- The existing `live.ts` fingerprint export opts into ID normalization, as do its load and query checks through that wrapper. Its public call signature stays the same.
- `service.ts` keeps the default byte-sensitive fingerprint.
- Remove the two added comment lines that raised the file's comment share; the rationale is recorded here.

## Validation

- Targeted Vitest run: `sources.test.ts` and `serviceFingerprint.test.ts`, 7/7 pass.
- The live fingerprint remains unchanged for ID-only stamps and changes for a neighboring class edit; the default fingerprint changes on the stamp.
- The standalone test uses the actual Inspector session, bundler and HTTP server with a browser stand-in that fetches the served HTML. It first proves unchanged-page reuse, then proves the stamped ID appears after a reload. This test fails on the initial PR implementation because the reused HTML lacks the ID.
- Inspector typecheck, changed-file oxlint/oxfmt, comment citations and comment-share ratchet pass.
- No local browser, Electron/UI walk, model call or full CI/coverage run was performed for this follow-up. The original author reported a real live-browser test before this correction; the new standalone test proves session invalidation and served bytes, not browser execution.

## Related work

None. Found during a Desktop stress test.

title: perf(cli): check skips contrast screenshots it can compute from styles
body:
Follows #5868. Makes `hyperframes check` faster again on a CPU-only Linux VM, findings unchanged.

## What changes

- **Contrast reads a solid backdrop from styles.** When text sits on its own opaque fill, or on one opaque ancestor colour (including the page background) with nothing painted in between (no image, gradient, overlay, shadow, opacity, filter, blend, mask, rotation or rounded corner touching the text box), check computes its contrast from computed colours. The screenshot covers only the text it cannot prove; a sample where every text box is proven takes no screenshot.
- **Chrome starts while lint, hdr and bundling run.** Its launch arguments are guessed from the project's `index.html`. Once the project is bundled, check uses that browser only if the bundle needs exactly the same launch (viewport, WebGPU, GPU mode, server mode); otherwise it closes it and launches as before. A check that lint stops closes it too.
- **The browser shutdown tests stop their Chrome when a case fails.** Their cleanup killed only the helper process, and Chrome outlives a parent killed with SIGKILL, so every failed case left a browser and its profile running. It now also kills the browser that uses the case's profile and removes the profile.
- **The CLI keeps Node's compiled bytecode between runs** (`module.enableCompileCache()`, in the OS temp dir, about 5 MB). Check loads about 7.5 MB of JavaScript before it starts; a repeat run skips compiling it. The first run after an install or upgrade writes the cache and is about 0.2 s slower. `NODE_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1` turns it off, as for any Node program.

## Wall time

CPU-only VM (no GPU), built CLI (`node bin/hyperframes.mjs check <dir> --json`), median of 3 runs. Findings identical (normalised JSON) on every run.

| step | fast-capture-gsap | chat | heygen-promo-preview-assets |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | 4.68 s | 5.48 s | 11.16 s |
| #5868 | 1.64 s | 2.08 s | 3.82 s |
| solid backdrops from styles | 1.49 s | 2.01 s | 3.73 s |
| Chrome starts during lint | 1.48 s | 1.93 s | 3.49 s |
| compile cache (repeat runs) | 1.39 s | 1.84 s | 3.50 s |

The early Chrome only helps when lint, hdr and bundling take about as long as Chrome's launch (about 0.3 s here), so the smallest fixture gains nothing.

Contrast on `heygen-promo-preview-assets` stays about 1 s: its text sits on gradients, blurred glows, images and rounded pills, which only pixels can measure. One screenshot per text box was 2 to 4x slower than one shot over all of them, because each shot costs a full frame.

## Tests

- Real Chromium: a page with text on the canvas, on a panel, under an overlay, over an image, on a gradient, a rounded panel, a faded panel, with a text shadow and on a rotated panel. Only the first two are read from styles, and every reported contrast equals the pixel-sampled one.
- Unit: text on its own opaque fill is measured with no screenshot.
- Real Chromium: a browser started with the same launch is reused; one started for a different viewport is closed and replaced.
- Unit: the early browser is handed to the browser pass, and closed when lint stops the check.
- Process: with a browser that fails the two "ready" shutdown cases, the old cleanup left 16 Chrome processes and 4 profile dirs; the new one leaves none.

title: fix(core): the preview transport keeps ticking in a hidden tab
body:
Fixes cause 1 of #5710. Cause 2 (the unmute on a natural buffer end in `webAudioTransport.ts`) is not part of this PR.

## Problem

A hidden document runs no animation frames, but its media keeps playing. The transport ticked on `requestAnimationFrame` only, so `syncRuntimeMedia` stopped running while the tab was hidden. A clip was never paused at the end of its window and the next clip never started until the tab was shown again. Someone listening to a draft in another tab hears the raw source past each trim.

## Change

In `packages/core/src/runtime/init.ts`:

- `requestTransportTick` schedules the next tick on a 16 ms timer while `document.visibilityState === "hidden"`, and on `requestAnimationFrame` otherwise. `cancelTransportTick` cancels either.
- All four places that requested a frame (`scheduleNextTransportFrame`, `wakeTransport`, the initial tick) and the teardown cancel now go through these two helpers. `wakeTransport` checks for a pending tick of either kind.
- A `visibilitychange` listener moves a pending tick to the scheduler the new state calls for: a frame requested just before the tab hid would never fire. Teardown removes the listener.
- A paused, hidden transport still parks as before; the park timer is untouched.

Chromium does not throttle the timers of a page that is playing audio, so the hidden tick keeps time (per the report in #5710).

## Tests

Two tests in `packages/core/src/runtime/transportPark.test.ts`:

- **Hidden tab ends a clip**: plays a 1 s audio clip, hides the document, never steps an animation frame, and advances 100 timer ticks. The playhead passes 1 s and the clip's element is paused. Fails without the change.
- **Handoff on visibility change**: a pending frame is cancelled when the tab hides, the transport keeps playing on the timer, and a frame is requested again when the tab shows.

Both fail on `main` and pass here.

Ran locally:

- `bunx vitest run` in `packages/core`: 4510 pass, 1 fail. 7 suites fail with and without this change, because they cannot resolve unbuilt sibling packages (`@hyperframes/lint`, `@hyperframes/studio-server`).
- `bun run --filter @hyperframes/core test:hyperframe-runtime-ci`: passes.
- `tsc --noEmit`, oxlint, oxfmt, and the comment checks: clean.

Not covered by an automated test: real Chromium behaviour in a hidden tab. jsdom has no throttling, so the tests hold animation frames and drive the timer directly.

## Notes

- Open #5754 also edits `init.ts` and `transportPark.test.ts`; none of its changed lines touch the transport scheduling.
- Contribution for Stanford CS146S, claimed on the issue: https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes/issues/5710#issuecomment-6259007393

title: fix(cli): resume a cloud download part when its connection drops
body:
## What

`hyperframes cloud render` / `cloud get` downloads the output in parallel ranged parts. Until now one part losing its connection failed the whole download. Now:

- A ranged part whose connection drops re-requests only the bytes it is still missing (`bytes=<next>-<end>`), up to 3 retries with 0.25 / 0.5 / 1 s backoff. After that it fails with `Failed to download <url>: bytes <start>-<end> dropped 4 times` (the last error is the cause). The previous output is kept and no staged file is left behind, as before.
- A server that ignores Range (200, no `Content-Range`) still fails fast. Without ranges there is nothing to resume from, and retrying from zero would redownload the whole file.
- A user cancel or a sibling part's failure still stops everything at once: retries and backoff waits listen to the same abort signal.

## Why the test failed on Windows main

`splits a large file into parallel ranged requests` failed on the Windows lane with `TypeError: terminated`, caused by `SocketError: other side closed`, after 16.8 s. The socket info in the error shows one request written (205 bytes) and one complete response read (7,789,629 bytes = headers + the 7,789,435-byte last part). So the server closed a connection after sending everything, while the client was still writing that body to disk.

Inference (not reproduced on macOS or Linux): the Node test server's keep-alive idle timer (5 s by default) closed the socket. Windows completes a large loopback write at once, so the idle clock starts right away, while the test took 16.8 s under the parallel suite. On macOS and Linux the write only finishes as the reader drains, so the timer never wins.

Fix at the cause: the test server sets `keepAliveTimeout = 0`, so it never closes a socket during a test (`server.close()` still closes idle sockets at teardown). The client fix means a real server closing a connection early is now survived as well.

## Tests

- New: `resumes a range whose connection drops mid-body from the bytes it already has`. The server cuts the range covering one byte twice; the download completes byte-identical and the resume request starts at the cut byte.
- Changed: `keeps the previous output and leaves no staged file when one part keeps dropping`. The range always drops, the error says `dropped 4 times`, and the old output survives.
- Against main's `download.ts` both fail with the same `terminated` / `other side closed` as the Windows failure. With the fix, the download suite passes 17/17, 3 runs in a row (Linux).

title: feat(core): capture motion blur pose, discovery and compositor
body:
## What

Adds the three pure modules capture motion blur is built from, under `packages/core/src/runtime/captureMotionBlur/`:

- `pose.ts`: an element's box as a 2D affine in composition space (layout offsets plus every CSS transform up the ancestor chain), and the in-between poses a shutter sweeps through. It reads the individual `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` properties in CSS order (translate percentages against the border box), adds the offsetParent's border back and subtracts ancestor scroll, so the pose matches `getBoundingClientRect` for a box centered with `translate: -50% -50%`, a turned box or a box in a scrolled container.
- `discover.ts`: finds the elements that move fast enough for a smear to show (inline-style changes and CSS / WAAPI animations reaching 2 px per frame, outside any 3D context, outermost of nested candidates only). An element on an `offset-path`, or animated through `offset-distance`, is no mover: the pose has no offset-path term, so blurring it would only paint the element twice with no smear.
- `composite.ts`: the per-frame draw. It crops each mover from a capture of the scene and redraws it at every sample pose into a float buffer, additive at weight 1/n.

Nothing calls them yet, so this PR changes no behaviour.

## Why

Part 1 of 9 in the capture motion blur stack: #5875 → #5967 → #5968 → #5969 → #5970 → #5971 → #5990 → #5991 → #5992.

The whole stack delivers opt-in motion blur for compositions, drawn with Chrome's html-in-canvas (`drawElementImage`), in Studio preview and in renders. A composition turns it on with `data-motion-blur="on"` on its root; nothing blurs without that attribute. This first PR is the math and drawing with no wiring, so the later PRs can be read against modules that are already reviewed.

## Notes

- The modules are not reachable from any entry point until #5967.
- The pose composes individual transform properties, but the scan's skip of 3D `rotate` axes and z translates (`individualIs3d`, exported here) is wired into discovery in #5969.
- Not modelled by the pose, documented rather than fixed: an element under CSS `zoom`, a `position: fixed` element, and content inside `<foreignObject>`.
- Limits of these modules, all documented rather than fixed: image-space approximation (a mover's box contents move together; ink outside the box is not redrawn); trails are drawn over foreground elements above a mover; a transparent mover carries a halo of its background inside its box; a 2D flip through `scaleX = 0` blends as a rotation; sub-pixel `left` / `top` steps land in whole pixels (`offsetLeft` is rounded); a fast child inside a parent that moved earlier is not blurred (only the outermost candidate is kept); SVG elements are not scanned.

## Testing

Unit tests next to each module: affine multiply / invert / interpolate, the sweep taps and the individual `translate` / `rotate` / `scale` properties (each compared with its equivalent matrix transform, the `translate: 120px` and `180px` sweep included), a bordered offset parent and a scrolled container (`pose.test.ts`); mover discovery thresholds and nesting, and that an `offset-distance` animation or an `offset-path` element is no mover (`discover.test.ts`); the compositor's draw calls against a recording canvas fake (`composite.test.ts`). `bun run build`, `tsc --noEmit` in core and the core runtime tests pass. Comment ratchet against `origin/main` passes; no package size budget changes.

title: perf(engine): on a Mac, video frames for a render decode on the media engine
body:
## What changes for the user

On a Mac, a render that uses a long HEVC or H.264 clip spends less CPU in its setup step. Frame extraction now decodes on the Mac's media engine (VideoToolbox) instead of the CPU. The frames written are byte-identical.

## Why

Extraction decoded every source in software. On a 4K60 HEVC clip the decode alone is a large share of the CPU a render spends before the first frame. Per 20 s of 4K60 output at 30 fps, on an 8-core Linux box with one process capped at 4 cores:

| | decode only | whole extraction |
|---|---|---|
| SDR HEVC | 29 CPU-s | 62 CPU-s (decode 47%) |
| HLG HEVC, tone-mapped | 34 CPU-s | 145 CPU-s (decode 23%) |

So the most this can save is about half the extraction CPU for SDR and about a quarter for tone-mapped HDR. The tone-map itself (zscale) is unchanged. Mac timings follow in a comment.

## What this PR does

- On macOS, extraction adds `-hwaccel videotoolbox` when this ffmpeg lists `videotoolbox` under `-hwaccels`, and the source cannot carry alpha. Alpha-capable codecs keep their forced software decoder.
- `isFfmpegHwaccelAvailable` sits beside `isFfmpegFilterAvailable`. It is one cached probe per process, read from `ffmpeg -hwaccels` and kept apart from the `-filters` list.
- The HDR-passthrough path (VideoToolbox plus `format=nv12` when there is no zscale) is unchanged.

ffmpeg falls back to software for a stream VideoToolbox cannot decode. Checked with the ffmpeg Desktop ships (8.1.2, arm64): ProRes logs "Failed setup for format videotoolbox_vld" and still decodes every frame, exit 0.

## Same pixels

On a Mac, with the ffmpeg Desktop ships, a per-frame hash of software decode against VideoToolbox decode, each converted to the source's pixel format, is identical for:
- H.264 4:2:0 and 4:4:4
- HEVC 4:2:0 10-bit, 4:2:2 10-bit and 4:4:4
- VP9

The full extraction chain on the 4K60 clips writes byte-identical JPEGs, 60 of 60 for SDR and 60 of 60 for tone-mapped HLG.

## Tests

`videoFrameExtractor.mediaEngine.test.ts` runs real ffmpeg:
- macOS with VideoToolbox decodes on it.
- An ffmpeg without VideoToolbox decodes in software.
- VP9 keeps its software decoder.
- Off macOS it never asks for VideoToolbox.
- On a real Mac only: the frames match software decode byte for byte.

On the 8-core Linux box: exit 0, 4 passed, 1 skipped (the Mac-only case), 3 runs in a row.

Two mutations, each restored:
- Main's condition fails the media-engine test.
- Dropping the probe and alpha gates fails the software and alpha tests.

`psnrFilterAvailability.test.ts`: the hwaccel probe reads `-hwaccels`, and filter and hwaccel lists are probed separately (exit 0, 9 passed).

The whole existing extractor suite passes (4 files, exit 0), including the two tests that fake macOS. Typecheck ran on that box (exit 0); the local hook was skipped because a fresh worktree lacks the generated runtime files.

title: perf(producer): each distributed chunk downloads only its own slice of the plan audio
body:
## Merged with main after #5772

#5772 added a loop that sets download targets for files chunks read by URL; it still passed the old `chunksCarryAudio` flag this PR replaced with the `chunkAudio` mode. The merge passes `chunkAudio` there (`planV2.ts`); git flagged no conflict, the typecheck did. The size budget needs no change now: main's producer budget (768,210 B packed) covers this branch, which packs to 733,045 B.

## What changes for users

A distributed render whose mp4 chunks carry their own audio no longer makes every chunk download the whole mixed audio track. Each chunk downloads the track's index (its moov) and only the AAC packet bytes it encodes. On a 30-minute render that is about 0.5 MB per chunk instead of about 43 MB. The output is unchanged: every chunk carries the same audio packets as before, and the finished video's audio is the same.

## How

- A v2 plan whose chunks carry audio also writes `audio-chunks/`:
  - `frame.m4a`: the audio file without its mdat payload (ftyp, moov and the mdat header). It goes to every chunk.
  - `layout.json`: the file's size, where the payload sits, and where each chunk's packets start. It goes to every chunk.
  - `NNNN.bin`: chunk N's packet bytes, cut with the same `audioCutForChunk` the chunk uses. It goes to chunk N only.
- A chunk rebuilds a sparse copy of the whole file at the original offsets (bytes it does not own are holes) and runs the unchanged mux and cut on it. ffmpeg sees the same moov and the same packet bytes at the same offsets, so the chunk writes the same packets on every ffmpeg version.
- The whole `audio.m4a` still ships in the plan, so `HasAudio` is unchanged, but no role downloads it.
- A chunk whose plan has no `audio-chunks/` (a v1 plan, or one written before this change) reads the whole track as before.
- v1 plans are unchanged. Their chunks download the whole plan tarball, so slices there would only grow it.

### Why not cut each slice into its own m4a

That was the first version of this PR. Decoded audio stayed identical, but on ffmpeg 6.0 (the Lambda's ffmpeg-static) and 7.0.2, re-reading a stream-copied slice changes its last packet's duration (the slice's own edit list trims it). The stitch sums sample durations, so a 30-minute render's audio track came out about 2.2 s short of the video. ffmpeg 8.x does not show it, which is why it passed CI. The sparse rebuild does not depend on how any ffmpeg version writes or reads edit lists.

## Tests

- `chunkAudio.test.ts`: for three layouts (three uneven chunks, one chunk, and a 60 fps one-frame tail that owns no packets), a chunk muxed from a sliced plan has the same packets per stream (timestamps, durations, sizes and payload sha256) as one muxed from the whole file. Durations are 91 frames at 30 fps and 51 frames at 60 fps, which are not whole 1024-sample frames. Passes with ffmpeg 6.0, 7.0.2 and 8.1.1. The first version of this PR fails it on 6.0.
- `planV2.test.ts`: a sliced plan sends each chunk its own packet file plus the shared frame and layout, and nothing gets `audio.m4a`. A real `planV2WithPublisher` run (2.1 s tone, three chunks) writes and targets them.
- Each new assertion was broken once and went red: writing a chunk's bytes one byte late, a frame without its moov, sending packet files to every chunk, and turning the plan option off.

## Measured

Local v2 distributed render on a Linux dev box (8 cores, shared, ffmpeg 7.0.2): a 30-minute composition (1800.5 s at 30 fps, 54,015 frames, so not a whole number of AAC frames), 226 chunks of 240 frames. Each run goes through the producer's own plan, per-chunk materialization, `renderChunk` and assemble, with the same fixture, once on `main` and once on this branch. Chunks read from local disk, so the download time does not show here; the bytes are what a Lambda chunk fetches from S3.

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| plan audio bytes each chunk downloads (median) | 43,209,643 | 534,190 (339 KB moov frame + 3 KB layout + 192 KB packets) |
| all plan files each chunk downloads (median) | 73.1 MB | 30.5 MB |
| plan audio downloaded across the render | 9,765 MB | 120 MB |
| new plan step that writes the slices | none | 0.10 s |
| chunk materialize (median) | 134 ms | 58 ms |
| chunk encode + mux stage (median) | 665 ms | 359 ms |
| chunk wall time (median, shared box) | 5.94 s | 6.05 s |
| audio packets in all 226 chunks (timestamps, durations, sizes, payload sha256) | | identical: 84,400 of 84,400 |
| finished video's audio packets | | identical: 84,400 of 84,400 |
| decoded audio, 48 kHz, `pan=mono\|c0=FL` and stereo f32 hashes | | identical (86,424,576 samples per channel) |
| audio and video stream durations of the finished video | 1800.500 s / 1800.500 s | 1800.500 s / 1800.500 s |

- At the roughly 83 MB/s a render Lambda reads from S3, 43 MB is about 0.5 s of each chunk's start; 0.53 MB is a few milliseconds plus two more small GETs.
- Chunk wall time on the shared box is within its run-to-run noise; the box reads local files, so it cannot show the download saving.
- The remaining ~30 MB each chunk downloads is mostly a project `<audio>` source (`tone.m4a`, 29.6 MB) that chunks never play: capture does not wait on `<audio>` and the plan mixes the audio. That is a separate change to how compiled assets are targeted.
- 90 of 226 chunks have a few different video packets between the two runs. This PR does not touch capture or the video encode; two runs of `main` on this loaded box have differed the same way before. Not re-proven with a second `main` run here.
- Not measured on Lambda: no AWS session was available for this run.

title: chore: stop the fallow audit hook from piling up base snapshots
body:
## What

- Upgrades `fallow` from `^2.75.0` to `^3.34.1`.
- The pre-commit fallow hook now prunes audit snapshots unused for a day with fallow's own `audit-cache prune --max-age-days 1`, and still exits with the audit's status.
- Deletes `scripts/prune-fallow-audit-caches.mjs` and its test, which 3.x makes redundant, and lists both in `ALLOWED_DELETIONS` in `scripts/check-no-main-deletions.mjs` with the reason.
- Fixes the two findings 3.x reports on `main`: drops the unused `concurrently` devDependency and moves `yaml` (imported by `scripts/lint-skills.ts`) from devDependencies to dependencies.

## Why

`fallow audit --base` in 2.x writes a full git-worktree snapshot of the base into the temp folder for each checkout and each base commit (`fallow-audit-base-cache-<checkout hash>-<base sha>`), 0.4 to 0.9 GB apiece, and never removes it. On a machine with many worktrees, every new `origin/main` adds another full set, so the temp folder grows by several GB an hour. 3.x keeps one reusable snapshot per checkout and ships `audit-cache prune`, which also clears the snapshots of removed checkouts. That fixes the growth at its source, and the hand-written prune script can go.

## Related work

Refs #5751, which edits the same hook line. Whichever merges second rebases that one line.

## How

What 3.34.1 flags on `main` with no changes (repo-wide `fallow audit --gate all`):

- Inherited findings that fail the gate: `concurrently` unused devDependency, and `yaml` devDependency used in production. Both are fixed here, not baselined.
- Repo-wide report, 2.75 vs 3.34: package cycles 0 → 5, stale suppressions 6 → 35, health findings 130 → 180, duplicate clone groups 869 → 87 (3.x skips more generated and fixture files by default). None of these fail the default `new-only` gate, and this PR silences nothing: no new ignores, suppressions or config.

`fallow-type-aware@3.34.1` depends on `typescript@7.0.2`, so the lockfile adds the native `@typescript/typescript-*` platform packages. The root `typescript` stays at `^5.0.0`. The lockfile diff is limited to fallow, its platform packages and the two dependency moves.

## Test plan

- [x] `bun install --frozen-lockfile`: no changes.
- [x] `fallow audit --base origin/main --fail-on-issues` on this branch: passes under both `--gate new-only` and `--gate all`. Before the dependency fixes, `--gate all` reported the two inherited findings.
- [x] `lefthook run pre-commit --command fallow --force`: passes. With an unused export appended to a file in `packages/core`, the same hook exits 1 and names the export, so the prune that runs after the audit does not mask a failure.
- [x] Snapshot reuse: in a scratch repo, two audits against two different base commits leave one snapshot with 3.34 and two with 2.75.
- [x] `node scripts/check-no-main-deletions.mjs --base origin/main`: passes with the two entries; without them it exits 1 naming both files. Its test file passes 9/9.
- [ ] Unit tests added/updated (n/a: the only script test went with its script)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: fix(producer): graded video renders split into chunks that finish inside the worker limit
body:
## What changes for users

A distributed render of a composition with a color-graded `<video>` now gets chunks small enough to finish inside the worker time limit with default flags. Before, the planner priced every frame at a fixed cost per pixel (about 0.23 s for a 1080x1920 frame). A graded frame costs about 10 s on software GL, so a 45 s graded render was planned as 4 chunks of 270 frames, each needing about 2,800 s against a 900 s limit. Every chunk timed out and was retried until the execution gave up.

Compositions without color grading are planned exactly as before and pay nothing extra.

## How

- `resolveMaxParallelChunks` takes an optional measured seconds per frame and prices frames at the larger of it and the per-pixel estimate. Everything downstream (the one-wave width, the fit-the-limit split, the `CHUNK_EXCEEDS_WORKER_TIMEOUT` refusal) uses that price.
- The planner measures only when the composition has `data-color-grading` and the plan sizes chunks from the worker limit or concurrency (no explicit `chunkSize`, `targetChunkFrames` or `maxParallelChunks`).
- The measurement is the in-process renderer's own calibration (`measureCaptureCostFromSession`: 5 frames spread over the timeline, p95), run in a session set up like a chunk worker's: same capture options (`buildChunkCaptureOptions`, now shared with `renderChunk`), same software-GL engine config, and the same video frames injected. planV2 defers video extraction to chunks, so the planner extracts just the sampled frames first; without them a graded video has no frame to draw and would measure cheap.
- It runs beside the audio mix and pre-hash, so it adds wall time only when it is the slowest of the three.
- `chunkFrames.ts` is a move, not new logic: the chunk's frame and capture-option helpers left `renderChunk.ts` so the planner can use them without an import cycle (`renderChunk` imports `planV2`, which imports `plan`). `renderChunk.ts` re-exports what it exported before.

## Interaction with the chunk cap

With default flags the measured price flows into the fit-the-limit split, which may exceed the one-wave width (it warns and runs in waves, as today). An explicit `--chunk-size` still pins chunking and is still capped at one wave (16 when the worker concurrency is unknown); this PR does not change that.

## Measured

Devbox (Linux, software GL, same flags as a chunk worker, a shared and loaded box), planV2 with a 900 s worker limit and 8 workers, 1080x1920 at 24 fps. The graded and ungraded variants differ only by the `data-color-grading` attribute on the video. Chunks rendered one after another with `renderChunkV2`.

| variant | frames | measured cost per frame (plan) | plan time | chunks, per-pixel price (main) | chunks, this PR | predicted per chunk | measured per chunk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ungraded 5 s | 120 | not measured | 0.9 s | 1 x 120 | 1 x 120 | 87 s | 20.4 s |
| graded 5 s | 120 | 10.54 s (p95 of 5) | 73.6 s | 1 x 120 | 8 x 15 | 218 s | 160-178 s (8 chunks, all under the prediction) |
| ungraded 45 s (plan only) | 1,080 | not measured | 1.4 s | 4 x 270 | 4 x 270 | | |

- On main the graded 5 s render is one 120-frame chunk predicted at 87 s. The same 120 frames took 1,276 s in one local render on this box, so that chunk cannot finish inside 900 s.
- The measurement costs about 72 s of plan time on the graded render: browser start and the grading shader compile (~17 s), then 5 frames at ~10.5 s. Ungraded renders skip it, so their plan time does not change.
- For 45 s graded (1,080 frames) the same price gives 19 chunks of about 57 frames, about 660 s each, in 3 waves on 8 workers (from the sizing test; not rendered here).

## Tests

- `plan.test.ts`: a measured 10.5 s frame turns a 1,080-frame 1080x1920 plan whose chunks would each need far over 900 s into chunks that fit 75% of the limit, and a cheap measured frame keeps the per-pixel plan; `plan()` measures a graded fixture (mocked measurement) and splits it, and never measures the ungraded fixture. Both fail without the change (checked by removing the measured price from the sizing and by skipping the re-size in the planner).
- `renderChunk.test.ts`: the deferred-frame extraction tests now pass frame lists.

## Not in this PR

The grading shader itself is the cost: it compiles every effect into one program and software GL pays for the disabled ones. Compiling only the enabled effects is a separate change.

title: test(aws-lambda): handler tests never call real AWS
body:
## What

`packages/aws-lambda/src/handler.test.ts` no longer reaches real AWS.

When a render sets no `workerConcurrency`, plan reads the account's Lambda concurrency through `deps.lambda`, falling back to `new LambdaClient({})`. Most handler tests pass no `lambda`, so on a machine with AWS credentials they made a real `GetAccountSettings` call with whatever role the machine had. On a host with an instance role this slowed plan enough that `normalizes producer workflow codes to Step Functions error names` timed out at 5000 ms. CI passed only because it has no credentials, so the SDK fails fast.

## Change (tests only)

- Every `handler()` call in the file goes through one wrapper that injects a stub Lambda client which refuses, the same fallback (16 chunks at once) CI already exercised. Tests that pass their own `lambda` keep it.
- A file-level guard spies on `LambdaClient.prototype.send` and `S3Client.prototype.send`. Any send through a real client throws before it reaches the network, and `afterEach` fails the test, naming the commands sent.

No production code changes: the `deps.lambda` seam is right, the tests just did not use it.

## Proof

Linux host with an instance role, at the current main:

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| main, file as is | exit 1, 21 pass, 1 fail (`normalizes producer workflow codes...` timed out after 5000 ms) |
| main + guard only | exit 1, 16 pass, 6 fail; each failure lists the real sends, e.g. `+ "GetAccountSettingsCommand"` |
| guard + fix, 3 runs in a row | exit 0, 22 pass, 0 fail each time |



## Why a separate small PR
The handler tests on main reach real AWS when run with credentials, so they time out on any machine that has them. This fixes that test isolation on its own so the larger cloud render PRs can be reviewed without it.

perf(core): a color grade compiles only the effects it turns on
body:
Fixes #4881. Revives #4884 (closed as stale), rebased onto the shared WebGL context and canvas grading that landed since.

## What was wrong

Every `data-color-grading` element drew through one fragment shader with every effect compiled in. An effect set to 0 returns early, which is free on a GPU. Software GL (SwiftShader, which every distributed render chunk and `--no-browser-gpu` render use) pays for every effect on every pixel anyway, and pays again to compile the whole shader. So an adjust-only grade cost as much as one with ASCII, glitch, tape damage and crosshatch turned on.

## The fix

- Each optional stage of the main fragment shader sits behind `#ifdef HF_STAGE_*`. A guarded function falls back to returning its input.
- `FRAGMENT_SHADER_STAGES` is the one table that maps each define to the grade value that turns the stage on. It mirrors the shader's own `amount > 0` test.
- `useMainShader` compiles the variant for the grade's stages and caches it per context, least recently used first, sized to one Studio look-preview batch (32). Both draw sites (the live draw and look previews) bind the main program only through it.
- The variant is chosen on every draw from the grade as it is at that frame, including animated CSS custom properties. An effect that turns on mid-render compiles its variant on that frame and draws with it.
- The stage-free variant still compiles when the context is created, so a context that cannot run the shader still fails at creation.
- If a driver rejects a variant, that stage set draws through the all-stages variant (the previous shader) from then on, without recompiling every frame.

## Tests

- `packages/core/src/runtime/colorGrading.test.ts` (mocked WebGL, through the real runtime): an adjust-only grade compiles no stage; a grade compiles exactly its stages; each of the 25 stages is keyed to its own grade value; enabling everything defines exactly the stages the shader guards (pins the table against the GLSL both ways); variants are cached, reused and evicted least recently used first; the variant follows the animated grade; look previews compile their own stages; a rejected variant falls back to all stages and is not retried. 33 of these fail on main.
- `packages/cli/src/browser/colorGradingShaderStages.browser.test.ts` (real Chrome, SwiftShader, the flags distributed chunks use):
  - With every stage switched off and every stage's tuning values set, compiling each stage in draws the same pixels as compiling it out, for all 25 stages.
  - A stage that turns on mid-render through an animated property compiles and draws.
  - Compiling the whole shader takes tens of seconds on SwiftShader, so this test checks each stage on its own instead of against the whole shader.

## Measured

On a Linux x86_64 machine, `hyperframes render --no-browser-gpu --workers 1`, which launches Chrome with `--use-gl=angle --use-angle=swiftshader` as distributed chunks do. Synthetic fixture: a 2 s, 1080x1920, 24 fps generated test-pattern `<video>` (48 frames) with three grades. Before is this PR's base, after is this PR. Wall time includes browser launch and session setup.

| grade | before | after | per frame before | per frame after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (ungraded twin) | 52.6 s | 52.2 s | 1.10 s | 1.09 s |
| adjust only (contrast, saturation) | 474.8 s | 62.1 s | 9.9 s | 1.29 s |
| film look (deep-contrast preset, LUT at 0.3, bloom 0.35, grain, vignette) | 505.2 s | 95.3 s | 10.5 s | 1.99 s |

- Grading's own share per frame (graded minus ungraded): adjust only 8.8 s to 0.20 s, film look 9.4 s to 0.90 s.
- Output is unchanged: every frame of every render hashes the same before and after (`ffmpeg -f framemd5`, PSNR inf).
- Full-matrix check against the every-stage shader on SwiftShader (one-off, not committed, because compiling the whole shader takes tens of seconds per context): 96 looks through the preview path (no grade, each effect and detail value alone, wheels, curves, hue curves, secondaries, LUT, every effect at once, every preset) plus 4 live frames (adjust only, blur turned on mid-render by an animated property, vignette and halftone, compare split) drew byte-identical PNGs: 100 of 100. The every-stage side drew every non-empty stage set through the all-stages fallback (31 variants rejected, 4 all-stages compiles), so it is the previous shader.

title: fix(cli): non-English transcription reaches whisper, and whisper failures say why
body:
## What

- **Non-English transcription reaches whisper.** `transcribe --language fr` (any language other than English) now runs whisper when whisper is installed, with one note line: Parakeet picks its own language and has no `--language` option, so French or Spanish speech could come back in English. Without whisper installed, Parakeet runs as before. No language, or English, keeps Parakeet.
- **Whisper models are checked.** The twelve standard ggml models (tiny through large-v3-turbo) are pinned to a Hugging Face revision with their size and sha256, the way Parakeet's model files already are. A cached model of the wrong size is downloaded again, and a download that does not match its pin is discarded with a clear error instead of being kept. Other model names (quantized or custom) are used as downloaded, as before.
- **A whisper failure says why.** When whisper-cli fails or crashes (not a timeout or a cancel), the error names how it ended (exit code or signal), the whisper-cli version and where it came from, the model file's size and sha256 against its pin, and whisper-cli's last stderr lines with every path reduced to its file name.
- **`--dtw` is gone.** The transcript reader takes word times from each token's `offsets` and has never read `t_dtw`, the only field DTW fills. whisper.cpp 1.8+ also turns DTW off by itself whenever flash attention is on (the default). The flag did nothing for our output and could stop whisper-cli on its own (`unknown DTW preset` for a model whose name has no preset).

## Why

A user on 0.8.173 (macOS, Apple silicon, whisper from Homebrew) reported `transcribe -e whisper -m large-v3-turbo` crashing while whisper loaded the model, for French and Spanish, and Parakeet returning English for the same audio. The report carried one stack line and no stderr.

The crash did not reproduce: on Linux with a fresh model download (size and sha256 match Hugging Face), with whisper.cpp v1.9.5 built from source on an M4 Pro, and with Homebrew's own whisper.cpp 1.9.5 bottle against both ggml 0.27.0 and 0.26.0, French and Spanish transcribe correctly with the exact arguments the CLI passes. What is left is the user's machine: a damaged cached model (never checked before this change) or something in their whisper build. The model check covers the first, and the new error makes the next report show which.

## How

- `whisper/modelFile.ts`: `ModelFile`, `sha256File` and `verifies`, moved out of `sherpa.ts` so Parakeet and whisper share one check.
- `whisper/manager.ts`: `ensureModel` keeps a cached pinned model only at its pinned size, downloads into a temporary name, verifies against the pin, then renames into place. The download URL is pinned to the same revision.
- `api/transcribe.ts`: `pickRunner` takes the language decision, computed once in `needsWhisperForLanguage` (a non-English language Parakeet covers, whisper found, engine not `whisper`). The engine event carries the note; the command prints it as a `Note:` line.
- `whisper/transcribe.ts`: `diagnoseWhisperFailure` builds the error; `withoutPaths` strips paths. Timeouts and cancels keep their existing messages.

## Tests

- `manager.model.test.ts`: a cached pinned model of the wrong size is downloaded again; a download that fails its pin is discarded, leaving nothing; a pinned model of the right size and an unpinned model are used without downloading.
- `transcribe.metadata.test.ts`: a whisper-cli crash yields the full diagnosis, with no home path and no raw stderr property left for the command to repeat; whisper-cli is called without `--dtw`.
- `commands/transcribe.test.ts`: with whisper installed, `auto` and `parakeet` send `fr`/`es` to whisper and keep Parakeet for no language and `en-GB`; without whisper, `fr` stays on Parakeet; the note line is printed. The harness now fakes whether whisper is installed, so these tests no longer depend on the machine.
- Each new test fails with its source file reverted to main. CLI `src/whisper`, `commands/transcribe.test.ts` and `api.test.ts`: 3 runs in a row green; typecheck, oxlint, the comment ratchet and fallow clean.

title: perf(core): a heavy project's first preview page builds without repeated style and path scans
body:
## What

A heavy project with many composition variables gets its first preview page about 0.8 s sooner (2.3 s on a larger generated one). The bundler now finds the custom properties the authored stylesheets define in one pass, instead of compiling a regex and rescanning every authored `<style>` once per variable. The built page is byte-for-byte the same.

## Why

When the bundler writes each composition's variables as CSS, it skips a variable the project's own stylesheets already define (`authoredDefinesPredicate` in `htmlBundler.ts`). For each variable of each composition, it built `new RegExp("--<slug>\\s*:")` and ran it over all authored CSS joined together. On a heavy project that CSS is megabytes, and there are hundreds of variables across the mounted compositions, so the cost is variables times CSS size.

The preview's first build of a heavy project takes 7 to 7.7 s before the player gets its page. A profile of that build put 1.8 s in this predicate. The render compiler uses the same function (`emitRootCompositionVariableStyles`), so renders pay it too.

## Also in this PR

Two more costs of the same cold build, found in a profile of the real heavy project after the change above:

- **Each project path is checked once per build.** Every mount of a sub-composition rewrites its `url()`s and `src`s, and each rewrite asked `isSafePath`, which realpaths the path and every ancestor. The same few paths were checked once per mount. `resolveEntryPath` now remembers its answer for the build; a path cannot become safe or unsafe in the middle of one build. In the real profile this was 539 ms of `isSafePath` across two builds, and `rewriteCssAssetUrls` (727 ms) was most of what looked like style scoping (`scopeCssToComposition` itself is 120 ms).
- **The font text set walks the page in place.** `extractGoogleFontsText` spread the multi-MB page and its body text into arrays of single characters, then into a `Set`. It now walks both strings once with a `seen` set, in the same order, so the text it builds is the same string. On a 4 MB page: 258-309 ms -> 93-113 ms, same 84-character result, 3 rounds.

## Related work

None in this repo. An app that hosts the preview can cache an unchanged project's page on disk; this PR makes the first open and every open after an edit cheaper.

## How

- `namesBeforeAColon(css)` walks the CSS once. For every word (`[\w-]+`) followed by optional whitespace and `:`, it records each `--…` tail of that word. The predicate becomes a `Set` lookup.
- It answers exactly as the regex did, including its edges. A variable name is `--` plus `[a-z0-9-]`, so a match of `--<slug>\s*:` is always the `--…` tail of such a word. That covers `---x:` and selectors like `.btn--accent:hover`, which the regex also counted as defining `--accent`; this PR keeps that behaviour rather than changing it.
- The walk is linear: each word is matched once (global regex), and the colon check is a sticky regex at the word's end. No backtracking over long runs such as data URIs.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests: two new cases in `htmlBundler.test.ts`: a variable defined with space or a newline before its colon is not redefined; a variable whose name only begins a longer authored one (`--accent-dark`), or is only read through `var(--accent)`, is still emitted. Each fails under its own mutation (colon required right after the name; a longer name counted as a match), 1 failed / 185 passed each. The file passes 3 runs in a row, 186 tests.
- [x] Same answers as the regex: 1,000,000 (CSS, name) pairs from random CSS fragments (`--a`, `---a`, `.x--a`, `é`, whitespace, comments, `var(`), 0 mismatches.
- [x] Same page: a generated project shaped like the heavy one (40 sub-composition files mounted 160 times, 12 variables each, a 14.6 MB page) bundles to byte-identical HTML on main and on this branch (sha256 `9054f48d50eaad93…`, 14,750,448 bytes).
- [x] Before and after, that project with the preview's bundle options, on a 4-core Linux box, 4 builds each in one process:

| | Build 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 6995 ms | 6768 ms | 6716 ms | 6712 ms |
| this PR | 4652 ms | 4120 ms | 4552 ms | 4330 ms |

  In the CPU profile of one build, `hostScopedVariableRules` went from 2286 ms to under 60 ms (`namesBeforeAColon` 50 ms). `bundleProject` went from 5491 ms to 3344 ms.

- [x] On the real heavy project (a 3.9 MB page), on an Apple Silicon Mac, plain node, the app's own bundle, fonts and preview route, the released core vs the same core with this commit, 3 alternated rounds: the bundle went 1.96 / 1.88 / 1.89 s -> 1.11 / 1.04 / 1.16 s, and the first preview request (bundle, fonts, route) 3.27 / 3.24 / 3.15 s -> 2.44 / 2.36 / 2.70 s. The page is the same size, 3875 KB.
- [x] `htmlBundler.entryPaths.test.ts`: a sub-composition mounted three times with two `url()`s checks each path once and still rewrites both (`url(assets/logo.png)`, `url(compositions/texture.png)`). Without the memo it fails (4 repeated checks). Bundler tests pass 3 runs in a row (187); the generated project's page is still byte-identical to main, and builds in 3.8-4.3 s.
- [x] Font tests (`src/fonts`, 18 files, 259 tests) pass 3 runs in a row.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments".

title: fix(cli): snapshot --proxy exits once its frames are written, without waiting for copies
body:
## What

`hyperframes snapshot --proxy` now exits as soon as its frames are written. Before, it stayed running until every media copy its page server had started was finished: on ten one-minute 1080x1920 HEVC clips, 118 s instead of 19 s, plus 555 MB of copies nobody used.

## Why

The static page server pre-warms an H.264 copy of every browser-hostile clip when it serves the page, and serves `?hf-proxy=` requests by transcoding. Nothing stopped those copies when the server closed, so each spawned ffmpeg kept the CLI's process alive until it finished. A snapshot takes its frames from the original files, so once it is done the copies are pure cost.

## How

- `proxyTranscoder.ts`: each copy job gets an `abandoned` signal. When its last caller with a signal leaves, a queued copy is dropped (as before) and a started one now has its ffmpeg killed and its entry forgotten, so a new ask starts afresh and the kill is not remembered as a failure. A caller without a signal never leaves, so Studio's preview, `play`, publish and `check`, which pass none, always get their copy as before. This reverses one rule from #5340 ("a started copy is never stopped for a caller that leaves"): it now holds only while someone still waits for the copy.
- `mediaProxyPreview.ts`: `injectMediaCodecMapIntoHtml` takes an optional signal for its pre-warms.
- `staticProjectServer.ts`: the server owns one `AbortController`, passes its signal to every pre-warm and every `?hf-proxy=` request it serves, and aborts it in both `close` paths (listening and in-process).

## Before / after

Devbox (Linux, 4 CPUs), ten 60 s 1080x1920 HEVC clips, `media.autoProxy: true`, cold copy cache, one run each, both trees fully built:

| Command | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `snapshot --proxy --at 1,10,20` | 118.0 s, 555 MB of copies | 18.7 s, no copies |
| `check` | 143.5 s | 144.0 s |

`check` does not change: it resolves the copies it judges before it starts, so it waits for them by design. No ffmpeg was left running after any of the four runs.

## Tests

- `proxyTranscoder.test.ts`: the last caller leaving a started copy aborts its ffmpeg's signal, and the next ask spawns a fresh copy; a copy is kept while a caller without a signal still waits; with a real child process standing in for ffmpeg, leaving kills it (SIGKILL). The first and last fail on main; the old "a caller leaving a started copy does not stop it" test is replaced.
- `staticProjectServer.test.ts`: closing the server aborts the signal handed to its pre-warms and to a held `?hf-proxy=` request, and the held request answers. Fails on main.
- studio-server `proxyTranscoder` + `mediaProxyPreview` (47) and CLI `staticProjectServer`, `snapshot`, `snapshot.proxy`, `play` (122): 3 runs in a row green on the commit before this rebase onto main (no conflicts; the files this touches did not change upstream); typecheck, oxlint, the comment ratchet and fallow clean.

title: perf(cli): check splits its samples over a second Chrome when a core and memory are spare
body:
Follows #5871. `hyperframes check` is 8-10% faster on a 4-core CPU-only VM by splitting its per-sample work over a second Chrome when a core and memory are spare. Findings unchanged; one core or little free memory runs exactly as before.

## What changes

- **A second Chrome opens alongside the first** when the machine has a spare core and 250 MB free per Chrome: count = min(2, cores - 1, free memory / 250 MB), and 1 for a single `--at` sample. Free memory is the smaller of the host's free memory and `process.availableMemory()`, so a container's memory limit counts, not just the host's. One core, two cores or a low-memory box or container keep one Chrome.
- **The two pages share the sample list.** The first page starts at once; the second takes the next unclaimed sample as soon as it has settled, so a slow second launch never delays the first. Results are stored per sample and merged in sample order, so layout, motion, contrast and screenshots come out in the order one page seeking every sample produces. The dense overlap pass stays on the first page.
- **Runtime messages merge by sample time.** The second page's load-time messages are dropped (the first page reports the same load), its per-sample messages are merged by time into the first page's sample-loop messages, and a message both pages logged at the same time counts once.
- **The second Chrome only adds speed.** If it fails while sampling (renderer crash, OOM kill, closed target), the samples it took go back to the first page, which redoes them, and everything the second page logged is dropped, so the result is what one Chrome reports. A second Chrome that fails to open is ignored as before.
- **The first page never waits for a second Chrome that is still opening.** Once the first page has taken every sample, an open still in flight is cancelled and that Chrome closed, so short grids (`--at a,b`, short compositions) do not pay for a second Chrome start. The same happens when the first page fails, so its error surfaces at once.
- Both Chromes are owned by the existing launch registry and the check deadline, so a stopped or timed-out check closes both. The `contrastMs` timing field sums both pages' contrast work, so with two Chromes it can exceed the wall time.

No switch to force one Chrome: with the fallback above, a second Chrome that misbehaves costs speed, not findings.

Why separate Chromes and not two pages in one: all pages of one Chrome render screenshots through its single GPU process, so splitting samples over two pages left the contrast-heavy fixture 0.1-0.17 s slower once the second page was opened. Separate Chromes each bring their own GPU process. A third Chrome was no faster than two on 4 cores.

## Wall time

4-vCPU CPU-only VM (no GPU), built CLI (`node bin/hyperframes.mjs check <dir> --json`), before and after alternated run by run, median of runs 2-8.

| fixture | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| fast-capture-gsap | 1.45 s | 1.32 s (-9%) |
| chat | 1.96 s | 1.76 s (-10%) |
| heygen-promo-preview-assets | 3.40 s | 3.14 s (-8%) |

A second pass at a different time: -2% / -11% / -15%. The box is shared, so single passes move a few percent.

At the current head (after the fallback below), on a busier box (load 5-10), 6 interleaved runs, median of runs 2-6: 1.59 -> 1.46 s (-9%), 2.54 -> 2.11 s (-17%), 4.06 -> 3.44 s (-15%); findings identical to main on all 18 runs.

## Memory

Peak of the whole process tree (Node and every Chrome process, proportional set size), 2 runs each.

| fixture | 4 cores, before | 4 cores, after | 1 core, before / after (one Chrome) |
|---|---|---|---|
| fast-capture-gsap | 405 MB | 509 MB | 402 MB / 409 MB |
| chat | 506 MB | 630 MB | 489 MB / 488 MB |
| heygen-promo-preview-assets | 754 MB | 913 MB | 727 MB / 726 MB |

Pinned to one core, check keeps one Chrome, and its wall time and peak memory match before; the heaviest fixture peaks well inside a 2 GB VM.

## Findings

`check --json` findings are identical before and after on all 24 runs of the three fixtures. The model is that a frame is a function of its time, which the snapshot crops already rely on: a page script whose console output depends on the order of seeks can report a message at a different sample time than one page would.

A second Chrome killed mid-check: `kill -9` of the second Chrome during a `heygen-promo-preview-assets` check, 3 runs. Before the fallback, every run lost the whole browser pass (`check_runtime_failure: Attempted to use detached Frame`, browser checks skipped); with it, all 3 runs report findings identical to one Chrome, and no Chrome is left running.

## Tests

- Unit: a grid split over a helper page returns exactly what one page seeking every sample returns, and the two pages never seek the same time.
- Unit: the browser pass with two Chromes reports the same runtime messages as with one, with one load-time message.
- Unit: the Chrome count follows cores, free memory and a single `--at`; the message merge orders by time and drops the helper's load and same-time repeats.
- Unit: a helper page that crashes mid-grid has its samples redone by the first page and the result equals the serial one, with no unhandled rejection; the browser pass with a crashing second Chrome reports what one Chrome reports (its crash message dropped).
- Unit: a helper page still mid-sample when the first page runs out of samples is waited for; a second Chrome that never finishes opening is cancelled and the check reports what one Chrome reports.
- Unit: a container memory limit below 500 MB keeps one Chrome on a host with plenty free.
- Each of these fails when its rule is broken (merge in worker order, append the helper's messages, drop the core cap, keep the helper's load messages, let a helper error escape, skip the requeue, keep a crashed helper's samples or messages, read host memory only, never cancel the open, skip the time sort, skip waiting for a helper mid-sample).

title: test(engine): browser tests kill a Chrome whose close hangs instead of timing out
body:
`frameCapture-videoMetadataHints.browser.test.ts` failed once on a Windows runner with "Hook timed out in 10000ms" in its `afterAll`: `browser.close()` did not finish within vitest's 10 s hook limit. The test's own assertions had passed. The engine's production code already bounds a hung close (`closeBrowserAfterFailedProbe` closes, then kills the process and disconnects), but the test fixtures called `browser.close()` with no limit.

## What changes

- `__fixtures__/loopback.ts` gains `closeTestChrome(browser)` next to `launchTestChrome`: it waits up to 5 s for `close()`, then SIGKILLs Chrome's process and disconnects. A test teardown now ends in at most about 5 s, inside the hook limit.

## Tests
