title: fix(player): an embed without a height shows its film, and heavy films are measured in Safari
body:
## What this fixes

**An embed that sets no height on `<hyperframes-player>` showed nothing.** The `width` and `height` attributes set the composition size, not the element's box, and the player had no height of its own, so `<hyperframes-player src="...">` was 0 px tall. That is the primary snippet in the player README and in the package docs. The player now carries its composition's aspect ratio in an in-flow sizer inside its shadow root:

- no height set: the player is as wide as its container and as tall as the film's shape (800 px wide, a 1920x1080 film: 800x450);
- a height set by the embed still wins (`height: 300px` stays 800x300, `flex: 1` in a 600 px column stays 600 tall);
- a width-only embed gets the matching height (400 px wide: 400x225).

Why a sizer and not `aspect-ratio` on the element: with `aspect-ratio` and only a height set, a block takes its width from the ratio, so a `height: 100vh` embed would shrink sideways. The test page measures that case on a plain block: 533 px wide instead of 800 in Chrome. The sizer only adds height when the embed gave none.

`tests/browser/player-box.ts` checks all five embeds in Chrome and runs in the player-perf load shard. It fails on main (`plain: player box is 800x0`) and passes with the fix, 3 runs in a row. The Safari workflow loads the same page in Safari and Chrome before the films.

## What this adds

A heavy-film playback bench that runs in real Safari and in Chrome on the same macOS runner. Nothing in CI ran WebKit before this.

- Seven heavy fixture films under `packages/player/tests/perf/fixtures/heavy-*`: 16 simultaneous 1080p layers, three concurrent 4K decodes (HEVC and H.264), transparent overlays as VP9 alpha WebM and as HEVC alpha MOV, filters with blend modes, backdrop blur and a WebGL shader, a two-minute timeline with about 4,000 tweens, and four sub-compositions under three audio tracks. The existing `10-video-grid` and `gsap-heavy` films run too.
- The media is generated by ffmpeg on the runner (`browsers/make-media.sh`), not committed. HEVC with alpha only encodes through VideoToolbox, so it needs macOS.
- `browsers/bench-page.js` measures inside the page, so both browsers are scored by the same code: frame intervals during 8 s at 1x, per-frame main-thread work split into the composition's script and the rest, decoder drops and presented frames, what the runtime does to each media element while playing, and seek-to-paint latency.
- `fixtures/_control` plays the same media natively, without the player.
- `browsers/run.ts` drives Safari through safaridriver and Chrome through chromedriver over plain WebDriver HTTP, with no new dependency.
- `.github/workflows/player-safari.yml` runs on PRs touching the player or runtime, nightly, and on demand. It reports to the job summary and an artifact; the job fails only when the player-box check fails or a film can't run.
- The perf host page now sets only the player's width, so the bench exercises the fix, and it fails the run if the player box is empty.
- The runtime's per-tick media sync writes `volume` and `muted` only when the element's live value differs, the same guard it already used for `preload` and `playbackRate`. No performance claim.

## What I measured, with the player on screen

Safari 26.6 and Chrome 155 on a GitHub macOS runner, 2 runs per film:

- **Video decoding keeps up in Safari.** Decoder drops are 0 to 5 per film on every film; the 16x1080p film presents 29.5 fps in its second run.
- **Safari's main thread misses the 8 ms bar on GSAP-heavy films.** `gsap-heavy`: p95 work 12 ms, 230 of about 480 frames over 8 ms (Chrome: p95 3 to 6 ms). The two-minute timeline: p95 work about 230 ms per frame and 397 dropped frames in 8 s, while the composition's own script is only 18 to 20 ms of it, so Safari spends the rest on style, layout and paint (Chrome: p95 27 to 32 ms). That is the next root cause to chase.

## Retractions

- **Every earlier "the player makes Safari drop video frames" number was a harness artifact.** The perf host page never sized the player, so it measured a 0 px player. Safari counts frames of a video it never shows as dropped; Chrome does not. Screen recordings showed the player black in both browsers while a bare iframe of the same film was visible. With the player on screen those drops are gone. The bug was real for embedders, which is the fix above.
- "A per-frame transform on an ancestor makes Safari drop video frames", "per-frame volume/mute writes cost Chrome 31% decoder drops" and "Safari freezes the 16x1080p film" did not hold either (details in the earlier revisions of this description).

## What I did NOT exercise

- An enforced frame bar. The runner is a VM: Safari's native presented rate swings 22 to 29 fps between runs, and Chrome's rAF cadence there is unstable (idle median 17 to 30 ms), so Chrome's dropped-frame column is runner noise. Zero dropped frames and no frame over 8 ms would flake here, so the film numbers are reported, not gated.
- The catalog wrapper page's player sizing; I did not open it.
- Audio plays muted (the perf host page mutes the player).

## Before

The embed test page at main, in Chrome, each case labelled. The no-height and width-only players are 0 px tall, so only their outline shows. The gray box is not a player: it is a plain div with `aspect-ratio` and only a height, showing why the fix does not use `aspect-ratio` on the element.

![Before: unsized players collapse to 0 px](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6c4e9539-0961-4ef0-9b2e-837c86971e17)

## After

The same page with this change. The no-height and width-only players show the film at its shape; the height-only, both-set and flex-fill embeds are unchanged in size and picture.

![After: unsized players take the film's shape](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c6c37778-c727-4e20-ab71-122ee81e6623)

Embeds that set a height keep it. A Safari frame from the runner follows in a comment once the workflow at this head finishes.

title: ci(docs): catch docs that drift from the CLI
body:
## What

Two CI checks so the docs can't quietly drift from the code, plus the stale facts they found.

1. **CLI references** (`docs.yml`, job `cli-references`): every `hyperframes <command> --flag` shown in `docs/**/*.mdx` must exist in the real CLI. The source of truth is the CLI's own command modules (`scripts/cli-command-tree.ts`: 88 commands, 668 flags), not `--help` text. Unknown commands or flags fail with a "did you mean"; deprecated or hidden ones warn. Quoted CLI output can opt out with `{/* cli-references: ignore */}`.
2. **Docs impact** (`docs-impact.yml`): a PR that changes CLI commands, flags or public package exports must touch `docs/`, or carry the `docs-not-needed` label, or a `docs-impact: none` line in the PR body.
3. **Docs fixes found by the audit:** Linux install steps lead with the .deb (what the download page hands Linux browsers by default; file names checked against the live release feed), the command finder lists `models` and `clean`, and the update-notice example shows current versions.

## Why

The docs had drifted in small ways nobody noticed (Linux install, missing commands). Agents read these pages too, so a stale command becomes a failed run.

## How

- Check 1 scans fenced blocks (joining `\` continuations), inline code and `<InstallCommand>` props; handles `npx`/`bunx`/env prefixes, placeholders (`<x>`, `...`, `$X`) and anything after `--`; flag spelling follows `reject-unknown-flags.ts`.
- Check 2 compares merge base with HEAD. The CLI side builds the base tree in a temp worktree only when `packages/cli/src` changed; exports are read from git with the TypeScript parser (no build). Measured on the last 149 main commits: 6 changed exports, 1 touched docs.

title: fix(producer): disk-space error suggests --workers 1 only when one worker would stream
body:
## What

When a render fails its disk-space check, the error now names why that render stores frames on disk and offers only the change that takes it off disk:

- Multi-worker render that would stream on one worker (mp4, mov, webm): free disk, or re-run this render with `--workers 1`. The message also says one worker is slower, so the default worker count stays right for renders that fit on disk.
- `png-sequence` or `gif` output: these store every frame at any worker count, so `--workers 1` is no longer offered; free disk or render to mp4.
- Streaming switched off (`PRODUCER_ENABLE_STREAMING_ENCODE=false`) or the opt-in duration cap: the message names the switch and does not offer `--workers 1`, because one worker would still store its frames.
- Already one worker: free disk.

The CLI reference's "Long renders and the capture path" section says the same.

## Why

The old message ended "Re-run with --workers 1, use --low-memory-mode, or free up disk space" for every render. That was wrong in two ways:

1. For some renders it was false. A `png-sequence` or `gif` render, a render with streaming switched off, or a render already on one worker stores every frame at one worker too, so the suggested retry fails the same way.
2. Where it was true, it read as general advice. Agents that hit it once kept passing `--workers 1` on later renders in the same session, including renders that fit on disk, and those ran on one worker for no reason.

Whether a one-worker run would stream is already decided by `explainStreamingEncodeGate`; the message now asks it instead of repeating a hand-written list of routes.

## Related work

Refs #5334, which proposes falling back to one-worker streaming automatically when headroom is short. That is a behavior change; this PR only changes the error text and does not overlap its files.

## How

- `diskCaptureRemedy(cfg, outputFormat, durationSeconds, workerCount)` in `captureStage.ts` asks `explainStreamingEncodeGate` whether a one-worker run of the same render would stream and returns the reason and remedy. `--workers 1` appears only when the render uses more than one worker and the gate says one worker streams.
- `runCaptureStage` computes it once and passes it to both shortfall checks (the estimate before capture and the measured projection after ten frames).
- No behavior change: worker counts, defaults and routing are untouched; only the error text differs.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated: `captureStage.test.ts` covers each case (multi-worker mp4 offers `--workers 1`; one worker, png-sequence, gif, streaming off and the duration cap do not), and the measured-shortfall tests check the text reaches the thrown error on both the sequential and the parallel branch. 20/20 pass, 3 runs in a row (Linux).
- [x] Break checks (Linux): forcing the message to always offer `--workers 1` fails 2 tests; forcing it to never offer it fails the other 2.
- [x] Producer typecheck, oxlint, oxfmt and fallow audit clean on the changed files (Linux).
- [ ] Manual testing performed: no render was run to trigger the error; the change is error text only.
- [x] Documentation updated: `docs/packages/cli.mdx`.
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments".

title: perf(cli): commands start sooner by compiling registry schemas on first use
body:
## What changes for users

`hyperframes check` (and any command that reads project config) reaches its first real step about 50 ms sooner.

The project config module imports the registry, and the registry's validation module compiled two JSON schemas with Ajv at import time. Every such command paid that compile at startup, even when it never validated a registry item. The schemas now compile on the first validation call and are reused after that. Validation results are unchanged.

## Numbers

`check` on `fast-capture-gsap`, built CLI through `bin/hyperframes.mjs` (compile cache on), CPU-only Linux VM, 12 interleaved runs per side:

| | time to check's first step (min / median) | wall (min / median) |
|---|---|---|
| main | 254 / 279 ms | 1438 / 1482 ms |
| this PR | 217 / 225 ms | 1391 / 1462 ms |

A CPU profile of `check` on a GitHub `ubuntu-latest` runner attributes ~88 ms of the ~263 ms before check's first step to these two compiles.

## Tests

`validation.startup.test.ts` counts Ajv compiles: none when the module is imported, two on the first validation, none after. On main's eager version it fails (`expected 2 to be +0`). Registry suite: 263 passed, 3 runs in a row.

title: perf(producer): local renders check the audio peak in parallel segments, as cloud plans do
body:
## What

`measureTruePeakDbfs` now decides on its own whether to scan in parallel segments: it reads the file's length and sample rate and, for 48 kHz audio long enough to split, runs the segmented scan that distributed plans already use. Every caller gets it, including local `hyperframes render`, which until now scanned the whole mix in one single-threaded pass on every peak check. The value is the same digit as the single pass, so the rendered file is byte-identical.

## Why

A local render with audio measures the mix's true peak at least once in the assemble step, and again after each loudness correction. Only the distributed plan passed the segment information, so local renders of long films ran the slow single pass up to four times. Moving the choice into the function means a future caller cannot miss it.

## Related work

Refs #5925 (the segmented scan, used only by the distributed plan until now).

## How

Callers of `measureTruePeakDbfs` on main, and what each does now:

- `padOrTrimAudioToVideoFrameCount` (local render, from `stages/assembleStage.ts`): was one pass; now segmented for 48 kHz audio long enough to split.
- `constrainAacTruePeak` (distributed plan, from `distributed/plan.ts`): already segmented. It no longer probes the sample rate itself or passes `segments`; the function's own probe replaces that probe one for one. Segments are now cut from the probed file length instead of the target length; the count can only differ when the two sit on opposite sides of a segment boundary, and the peak is the same either way.
- The two `audioTruePeak` test files.

`scanTruePeak` is not exported. Files that are not 48 kHz, or whose length is unknown, keep the single pass. The `segments` option is removed.

Cost: one audio probe per measurement, also on short files that stay on the single pass. On a 17 s fixture the assemble step measured 735 ms before and 694 ms after (within noise).

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated: a new fake-ffmpeg test enters through `padOrTrimAudioToVideoFrameCount` and fails on the single-pass path (`expected [ 'ebur128=peak=true' ] to deeply equal [ …(3) ]` with the production files reverted to main), passes with the change. Fake-ffmpeg tests 5/5 and real-ffmpeg tests 4/4, 3 runs each; `audioPadTrim.test.ts` 38 pass; integration 2/2 (Linux).
- [x] Manual testing performed (Linux, released CLI build vs this branch, one run each):

  | fixture | sha256 (first 16), before = after | assemble before | assemble after |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 142 s portrait, video + audio | 1173ac25935a137c | 16.5 s | 15.0 s |
  | 17 s 1080p, video + audio (single pass by length) | 3f34a6fe520e960a | 0.74 s | 0.69 s |

  The four peak measurements on the 142 s film took 2.51 s before and 1.40 s after. Most of that film's assemble time is the loudness-correction re-encodes, which this PR does not touch.
- [x] Full `bun run producer:test:unit` 3 runs in a row, 61/61 files, including the ffprobe argv contract test (Linux).
- [x] Typecheck, oxlint, oxfmt and fallow clean on the changed files (Linux).

title: perf(cli): a repeat check starts with the CLI and Chrome already up
body:
## What changes for users

A repeat `hyperframes check` from an agent (output not a terminal, same environment, outside CI) is served by a check process that already has the CLI loaded and Chrome running, so it skips Node start-up, module loading and Chrome launch. Findings are the same as a cold check.

## How the warm check works

- After a check exits, the client starts one detached **warm check process**. It loads check's modules, launches the Chrome the next check of the same project would launch, and waits on a local endpoint.
- **Endpoint and trust.** The endpoint lives in a per-user private directory: `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/hyperframes-warm`, else `~/.cache/hyperframes/warm`, or `LOCALAPPDATA\hyperframes\warm` on Windows. It must be a real directory owned by the user, with no group or other permission bits; a random token sits next to it in a `0600` file. Anything else means the check runs cold. On Windows the pipe name is an HMAC of the token. Before any request, the two sides prove the token to each other over fresh nonces. The client sends only its nonce until the server has proved itself, and gives up after 2 s.
- **One check per process.** The request carries the arguments, the working directory and an HMAC digest of the environment, never the environment itself. The warm process serves only a client whose environment digest matches its own (ignoring `_`, `PWD`, `OLDPWD`). It runs the CLI **once**, exactly as a cold process would (its own telemetry, exit handling and `.env` loading), streams stdout and stderr back, returns the exit code, then exits. No state carries between checks.
- It is used only when stdout and stderr are not terminals and `CI` is unset. A client it cannot serve runs cold. That covers a wrong proof (the warm process keeps waiting), a second client while one is being served, and a different environment (the warm process exits and leaves the endpoint for the new one). Frames over 64 MB are refused.
- It exits after 5 idle minutes, on SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP relayed from its client, or when its client disconnects mid-check.
- **Chrome is owned over the DevTools pipe only, with no debugging port** (now for every CLI launch, not just the warm one). A pipe-owned Chrome exits when its parent dies, including on `kill -9`; with a port it does not. Before this change, a cold `check` killed with `kill -9` on macOS or Linux left Chrome running.

- **Windows:** the OS does not end a process's children with it. Over the pipe the browser and most of its children still exit when the CLI dies, but a renderer stuck in page script survives. On Windows only, each launch starts a small detached watchdog. When the CLI closes Chrome cleanly, the watchdog exits without touching anything. When the CLI dies, Chrome had to be force-killed, or Chrome died on its own, it stops the leftovers. A process is matched only when all of these hold: it is the browser process or a direct child of it (recorded parent PID), its executable is this launch's exact Chrome path, and it was created after this launch started. Nothing is matched by name. The residual risk: if our browser dies and another Chrome from the same install reuses its PID, that newer launch's children pass every check.

Orphan proof: a check whose page busy-loops is killed with `kill -9` / `TerminateProcess`, and the exact Chrome PIDs that were alive are checked 5 s later (`chromeOrphans.process.test.ts`, GitHub runners):

| | Linux | macOS | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| before this PR (debugging port) | 10 of 10 survive | 10 of 10 survive | 2 of 10 survive (the busy renderers) |
| this PR, cold check | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| this PR, warm process killed | 0 | 0 | not measured PID-exact (same launch code and watchdog) |
| Windows watchdog left after 30 s | | | 0 |

On Windows the test fails with the watchdog removed, and also with its start-time guard pushed into the future. On Linux and macOS it fails when Chrome is launched with a debugging port instead of the pipe. The warm process tests also cover `kill -9` of the warm process, `kill -9` of the client mid-check, and the idle exit, each taking its Chrome with it.

A separate probe (Puppeteer `pipe: true`, parent `kill -9`'d, 3 trials per OS) found Chrome exiting 3/3 on Linux, macOS and Windows; launched with `--remote-debugging-port` it survived 3/3 on macOS and Linux.

## Numbers

`check --json` wall time through the real bin on GitHub runners, median of 3 per fixture, with a ready warm process vs `CI=1` (cold):

| fixture | Linux cold | Linux warm | macOS cold | macOS warm | Windows cold | Windows warm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fast-capture-gsap | 1143 | 784 (-31%) | 2585 | 2423 (-6%) | 3202 | 1874 (-41%) |
| chat | 1815 | 1570 (-13%) | 3744 | 3741 (0%) | 4536 | 2802 (-38%) |
| decision-tree | 1642 | 1341 (-18%) | 4467 | 4250 (-5%) | 3851 | 2510 (-35%) |
| product-promo | 2056 | 1707 (-17%) | 7594 | 7060 (-7%) | 5446 | 3393 (-38%) |
| heygen-promo-preview-assets | 4168 | 3755 (-10%) | 10520 | 9864 (-6%) | 8671 | 6588 (-24%) |
| kinetic-type | 4079 | 4024 (-1%) | 7051 | 6689 (-5%) | 7825 | 6511 (-17%) |

All times are in ms. Findings: warm and cold reports are the same on every fixture and OS, apart from the per-run report id and server port, and one sub-pixel bbox value (0.02-0.03 px) in one warm run on Linux and one on Windows. Cold runs show the same jitter: in 10 cold and 10 warm checks of decision-tree on a Linux VM, one cold run had the other value and all warm runs matched. An idle warm process with its Chrome holds about 345 MB on macOS and 475 MB on Linux.

## Also in this PR

- **Windows: a busy warm process no longer stalls the next check.** The warm process stopped listening as soon as it accepted a client. On Windows the pipe name stays alive through the served connection, so a second `check` started meanwhile saw a busy pipe and waited 30 s for a free instance before running cold (measured on windows-latest: 30,008 ms then `ETIMEDOUT`; 0-1 ms with the server still listening). That pushed the "second client runs cold" test past its 60 s budget on loaded runners while the first client's busy-loop Chrome kept spinning, which starved the tests beside it and ran the Windows test lane out of time. The warm process now keeps listening while it serves (it already declines anyone else) and stops when the served check finishes. On windows-latest the test drops from 38-43 s to about 5 s and `warmCheck.process.test.ts` from 82-84 s to 57-62 s.
- **Windows root build:** `packages/inspector/build.mjs` built paths with `new URL(...).pathname`, which is `/D:/a/...` on Windows and opened `D:\D:\a\...`, so `bun run build` failed on Windows. It now uses `fileURLToPath`, as does `producer`'s plan-parity harness, whose "run directly" check never matched on Windows. `scripts/file-url-paths.test.mjs` fails on any package code that turns `import.meta.url` into a path with `.pathname`.

## Tests

- `warmCheck.process.test.ts` (macOS, Linux, Windows):
  - a served check prints what a cold check prints, then the warm process and its Chrome exit;
  - `kill -9` of the warm process takes its Chrome, and `kill -9` of the client mid-check stops the warm process and its Chrome;
  - idle exit takes its Chrome;
  - a request-less connection is survived and the next client is served;
  - a different environment is declined; while a check is being served, a new connection is answered and declined at once, and a second client runs cold;
  - a wrong proof is declined and a genuine client is then served;
  - an impostor holding the endpoint, forging a proof or staying silent, receives only the client's nonce.
- `warmCheckProtocol.test.ts`: a 0777 directory, a symlinked directory, a 0644 token and a symlinked token each mean no endpoint; also the environment digest, framing and the frame cap.
- `warmCheckClient.test.ts`: every frame is delivered, including stdout after stderr (the client used to drop everything after its first write).
- Mutation checks: each case fails under a matching mutant: pipe removed, client trusts any server, server trusts any client, directory checks removed, handshake timeout removed, frame cap removed, `||=` write restored.
- `chromeOrphans.process.test.ts` (macOS, Linux, Windows): a `kill -9` of the CLI mid busy-loop leaves no Chrome process 5 s later and no watchdog 30 s later; a check that finishes leaves neither. The finishing case reads the Chrome tree and the watchdog that the check records when its first page opens: on Windows each process listing is a PowerShell call of about a second, so polling from outside could miss a short-lived Chrome entirely and fail the test's own precondition.
- `scripts/check-cli-process-ownership.mjs` now treats the warm process and its client as process roots, alongside `cli.ts`.

title: fix(producer): renders the fast capture refuses keep their parallel workers
body:
## What

A render whose fast capture (drawElement) the engine refuses at session start (a CSS effect such as `filter`, an at-risk timeline, a software rasterizer, ...) is no longer pinned to 1 worker by the single-worker inversion, or to 3 by the parallel router. It now renders on the worker count the resolver picks, like any other screenshot render.

## Why

The inversion and the router decide the worker count before capture, on the bet that drawElement will run. The engine's init-time gates that can refuse drawElement only run inside a capture session. The orchestrator already skipped both routes when the browser probe session had hit a gate (`probeDeGated`), but that probe is conditional (`probeRequiresBrowser`): a composition with a static duration and no runtime media skips it. For those renders nothing had checked the gates, so a refused comp was still pinned, then fell back to screenshot capture on 1 worker. A large share of inverted Mac renders end exactly like that, slower than multi-worker screenshot capture on the same machine.

## Related work

Refs #5650 (a static compile-time WebGL gate). This PR uses the engine's own init-time answer, so it covers every gate the engine applies.

## How

- `renderOrchestrator.ts`: when either route is eligible and no probe session exists, open the capture session early and initialize it (the same `createCaptureSession` + `initializeSession` the probe stage uses, with the capture options and frames dir). If the engine refused drawElement, both routes and the short-band attribution answer what they already answer for a gated probe: not eligible. Calibration then runs and the resolver picks the count. If drawElement was accepted, the same session is handed to capture, so the inverted path opens no extra browser. If the gate check itself fails, it logs and routes as before; the capture stage owns retrying or failing its own session.
- `isProbeDeGated` is the single definition of "a session ran the gates and one refused", shared by both predicates and the new check.
- `perfSummary.ts`: the render's `drawElement.gateReason` now includes the probe's gate. Parallel screenshot workers run with drawElement clamped off and report no gate of their own, so without this a gated render on N workers read as having no gate. `workerInversion` / `parallelRouter` read `none` for a gated render, which is what happened.

Known cost: a router-eligible render that drawElement accepts now opens one browser session before capture that the 3-worker capture closes unused (the parallel path opens its own sessions). An inversion-eligible accepted render reuses it.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated
- [x] Manual testing performed
- [ ] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

`renderOrchestrator.deGateProbe.test.ts` enters through `executeRenderJob` with a composition the probe stage skips and the engine session mocked to refuse drawElement (`css_effect:filter`). With the fix reverted it fails with `expected 1 to be 4` (inversion) and `expected 3 to be 4` (router); a third case checks an accepted comp still inverts and capture reuses the gate-check session. `perfSummary.test.ts` covers the carried gate reason. Both pass 3 runs in a row. The full producer unit lane (`bun run producer:test:unit`) passed 3 times; typecheck, oxlint, the format check and fallow audit pass.

Before/after ran on Linux, with drawElement requested through the producer config (not `PRODUCER_EXPERIMENTAL_FAST_CAPTURE`, which turns the inversion and router off), standing in for a Mac: there the engine refuses drawElement with `swiftshader` at session init, the same code path as a CSS-effect refusal on a Mac. Fixture `overlay-montage-prod` (1271 frames), router off, interleaved runs on a shared host:

| run | load at start | workers | capture | gate | inversion | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main 1 | 8.9 | 1 | beginframe | swiftshader | inverted | 131.4 s |
| branch 1 | 6.7 | 3 | beginframe | swiftshader | none | 86.5 s |
| main 2 | 7.6 | 1 | beginframe | swiftshader | inverted | 127.1 s |
| branch 2 | 7.3 | 3 | beginframe | swiftshader | none | 112.1 s |
| main 3 | 14.3 | 1 | beginframe | swiftshader | inverted | 142.2 s |
| branch 3 | 9.7 | 3 | beginframe | swiftshader | none | 105.0 s |
| control: main, inversion off | 12.5 | 3 | beginframe | (none reported) | none | 87.9 s |

Median 131.4 s on main, 105.0 s on this branch. On Linux the engine's non-drawElement capture is beginframe; on a Mac it is screenshot.

Output: the 1-worker and 3-worker renders are not byte-identical (PSNR average 60.8 dB, minimum 49.7 dB over 1271 frames). The 3-worker path on main is itself not byte-stable run to run on this fixture (two outputs, 61.4 dB apart), and the control row (main with the inversion turned off) produces the same bytes as every branch run (sha256 `bf223650ebf2265a…`): this branch picks a path main already ships, it does not render anything new.

Not run: a Mac render (no Mac available for this run), and the router case on a host where the resolver picks a count other than 3 (on the test host it picks 3, so before and after matched there; the unit test covers it).

## Session handoff (not in this PR)

The engine's parallel coordinator creates every worker session itself (`executeWorkerTask`: per-worker frames dir, browser pool off, a fresh frame-injector hook, per-phase deadlines, a worker-0 GPU check before init), so handing it an already initialized session needs a new engine API through parallel capture, its adaptive retry and the streaming path. The early session also differs from a fresh worker: it initialized with drawElement on and no frame injector, while a refused render's parallel workers run with drawElement clamped off and accepted router workers each verify drawElement with their injector attached. Remaining cost: one browser start for a render that reaches this check and then captures in parallel (included in the timings above); the single-worker inversion path already reuses the session.

title: test: queue runs on slow windows runners stop failing four timing tests
body:
The Windows `engine-cli` lane fails PRs in the merge queue on tests that race a slow runner. Two PRs were removed from the queue this morning (merge-group runs 39390349029 and 39392152547, same base). Over the last 20 hours of Windows runs, 8 reds came from four tests. Each one passes in 1 to 5 s on a healthy runner and fails only when the runner is 5 to 10x slower (on the same job, the download test took 9.5 s instead of its usual 1 s).

| Test | Reds in 20 h | Why it raced the clock | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| capture: late subresources | 4 | Raced the capture's fixed 1.5 s wait for late images and fetches. A starved runner had not even loaded the page's 300 ms image by then. | The wait becomes the `lateSubresourceTimeoutMs` option (default unchanged, 1.5 s). The test lifts it and checks only that the capture waits. |
| engine: export stall | 2 | A real 5 s ffmpeg run against a real 2 s "no new frame" stop. A starved runner left more than 2 s without a frame. | Split into two tests that never race. A fake-clock runFfmpeg test checks that new frames keep a run alive past three stall windows and that a repeated frame count does not. A real-ffmpeg test checks that extraction asks for stall-only stopping (no deadline) and that its real ffmpeg arguments report frames while they run. |
| engine: download cancellation | 1 | Two bugs in the test. (1) It cancelled the first download before its request was sent, so the second download took the never-ending fake response meant for the first one and survived only by retrying after its own time limit. (2) That limit ran on the real clock: the harness freezes `Date` with fake timers to hold every 1000 ms limit, but `vi.waitFor` advances fake timers by 50 ms, so the limit became 950 ms and was not held. | The harness freezes `Date` with `vi.setSystemTime` (no fake timers, so `vi.waitFor` leaves it alone). The test cancels only after the first request is in flight. |
| cli: keepalive process | 1 | Its 5 s limit mostly measured a cold `node --import tsx` start (1.4 to 2.7 s on healthy Windows runs). The behaviour under test takes 250 ms. | The limit is sized for startup (30 s). A process that never exits still fails it. |

The harness fix in (3) also speeds up three deadline tests in the same file that were quietly waiting the real 950 ms on every run (about 970 ms each on Windows, now about 65 ms).

### Proof

Each check below was run locally, one file at a time.

- Download file: 85/85 pass, 3 runs in a row. Cancellation test 1,000 ms before, about 55 ms now.
  - If both callers share one request (scope dropped from the in-flight key), both cancellation tests fail.
  - If the time limit no longer aborts the request, all three deadline tests fail.
- runFfmpeg stall test: passes.
  - Fails without `markActivity` on a new frame.
  - Fails if a repeated frame count counts as progress.
- Extraction test: passes 3/3, about 1.5 s.
  - With the old hard deadline (`timeout` instead of `stallTimeout`), it fails with `expected { timeout: 2000 } to match { stallTimeout: 2000 }`.
  - With `-nostats`, it fails on the "reports frames while running" check.
- Late subresources: passes 3/3.
  - With the assets made slower than 1.5 s (the slow-runner case): the old test fails with `{ complete: false, width: 0 }`, the same failure CI shows. The new test passes.
  - Without the network-idle wait, the new test fails (the fetched asset is missing).
- Keepalive: passes 3/3 (1.45 s, mostly startup).
- Checks: oxfmt, oxlint, typecheck, fallow, comment citations and comment ratchet all exit 0.

Not covered here: the other Windows reds in the window (`warmCheck.process`, `browserFallback`) came from open PRs that change those files, not from main.

title: perf(producer): multi-worker mp4 renders start encoding while frames are still being captured
body:
## What

On a multi-worker mp4 render that captures frames to disk, the encoder now starts with capture instead of after it. It is fed frame 0, 1, 2... strictly in order as each frame file lands, with the same encoder arguments as the after-capture encode, so the output is byte-identical and less encode is left once capture ends.

## Why

On this path capture and encode ran one after the other: the encoder only started once every worker had finished, so a render's wall clock was roughly capture plus encode. The streaming path already overlaps them, but the multi-worker streaming mode stays off by default for screenshot capture, so a large share of multi-worker renders took the serial path.

## Related work

Refs the default-off multi-worker streaming path (`HF_CAPTURE_PARALLEL_STREAM`), which this does not change.

## How

- The parallel coordinator reports, per captured frame, the file it just finished writing (`ParallelProgress.landedFrame`). The write is synchronous and completes before the report, so a reported frame is never partial.
- `encodeWhileCapturing` (encode stage) spawns the existing streaming encoder at capture start and feeds frames in index order: it waits for frame N to be reported, reads it from the worker's dir, or from the merged frames dir if the post-batch merge has already renamed it (rename is atomic, so the frame is in one place or the other). Once capture succeeds it reads any remaining frames from the merged dir and closes the encoder.
- The overlapped run uses the same options builder as the after-capture encode (`videoEncoderOptions`, now shared). For software libx264 from JPEG frames, image2pipe and the image-sequence input decode the same JPEG bytes into the same frames, so the bitstream is identical.
- Safety:
  - A capture failure (worker death, missing frames, cancel) goes through the existing catch, which aborts the encoder and waits for it to exit before rethrowing, so it cannot hang.
  - Adaptive retries keep the frames they already have, so the in-order reader just waits for the retried frames.
  - It is off under drawElement capture, where a failed self-check wipes every frame and recaptures.
  - It runs only when a core is spare for the encoder: the render must use fewer capture workers than the CPU count worker sizing sees (the same `cpuCount` `computeWorkerSizing` reports). With every core capturing, the encoder only slows capture down, so the render keeps today's serial encode.
  - If the overlapped encode fails for any reason, the frames are encoded after capture exactly as before, with a warning, so a failure costs time but never the render.
- Scope: software h264 mp4, SDR, JPEG frames, no chunked encode, no GPU encode. PNG sequence, GIF, WebM/MOV, HDR, layered composite, chunked encode and HLS keep today's behaviour.
- Frame assignment stays contiguous per worker, so the in-order reader keeps pace with worker 0 and overlaps about 1/N of the frames on long films (more on short ones, where workers finish unevenly). I tried round-robin assignment: it overlaps almost all of the encode but changes the captured pixels (the output sha differs from main's, consistently across runs), so it is out of scope here.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated: `encodeWhileCapturing.test.ts` (integration lane, real ffmpeg, preset medium crf 16). Frames land out of order across two workers' dirs and must be encoded in index order, byte-identical to `runEncodeStage` on the same frames; frames already moved by the merge, or never reported, are still read; `abort` stops an encoder that is waiting on frames. Each test failed with the change broken: with the sources at main, `encodeWhileCapturing is not a function`; when feeding only after capture, the overlap test times out (`condition not reached`); with one encoder argument changed (crf 17), `expected '29745d05…' to be '135a554a…'`. A gate test (4 workers with 8 cores runs the overlap; 4 workers with 4 cores and 1 worker do not) fails with `expected true to be false` once the spare-core check is removed. It passed 3 runs in a row.
- [x] Producer unit suite passed 3 times in a row with 0 failures (Linux), plus engine and producer typecheck, oxlint, oxfmt and fallow.
- [x] Manual testing performed: rendered four fixtures on a shared 4-CPU Linux box, forcing the screenshot capture, 4-worker disk path, main and this branch alternating, 3 runs each, each run starting at load 16 or below:

| film | main wall (median) | branch wall (median) | encode left after capture, main / branch | frames encoded during capture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| style-1-prod, 17 s 1080p, video + audio | 70.7 s | 62.9 s | 11.2 / 3.5 s | ~60% |
| 42 s portrait, video | 124.2 s | 104.1 s | 23.2 / 13.1 s | ~37% |
| 142 s portrait, video | 427.1 s | 402.3 s | 89.1 / 61.7 s | ~26% |

With the spare-core gate:
- 8 s 1080p film with no core spare (8 workers, the CPU count worker sizing sees): this branch takes today's serial path (no overlap logged) and produces the same sha. Main 17.6 / 17.7 / 20.9 s (median 17.7), branch 17.0 / 18.7 / 22.9 s (median 18.7). It is the same code path; the gap is run-to-run noise, since the box's load rose through the set. Before the gate, at 4 workers with a 4-CPU budget, this film was 1.3 s slower at the median (18.1 to 19.4 s): the encoder competed with capture because no core was spare.
- 17 s film at 2 workers (cores spare): main 54.1 / 46.7 / 44.1 s (median 46.7), branch 50.8 / 39.9 / 41.0 s (median 41.0).
- Earlier ungated runs at 2 workers: 8 s film 27.9 s to 23.4 s.

The CPU count worker sizing reads is the machine's core count. It does not see a container CPU quota: the Linux box above caps each job at 4 CPUs through a cgroup quota, and sizing still sees 8. So on a quota-limited container the gate uses the same core count sizing does.

Byte identity: the 8 s and 142 s films produce the same output sha on main and on this branch in every run. The two other video fixtures are not byte-stable run to run even on main (capture varies), so for all four I also ran today's encode on the very frames each overlapped render used. The video-only output matched in every case (8 s `1af06eca`, 17 s `f7142e7b`, 42 s `60d81447`, 142 s `7afb62fb`), and the final mp4 shas for the 17 s film on this branch fall in the same set main produces.

Not run: macOS and Windows renders (no reachable machine), HLS, and the drawElement disk path (excluded by design).

- [ ] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments"

title: fix(cli): check says it is making video copies instead of going silent for minutes
body:
## What changes for the user

`hyperframes check` on a project whose videos Chrome cannot decode (HEVC or HDR footage, typical of phone clips) now says what it is doing during the one-time transcode, instead of printing nothing for minutes:

```
[hyperframes] Making browser-playable copies of 12 videos Chrome cannot decode. Only the first check of these files waits for this; later checks reuse the copies.
[hyperframes] browser-playable copies: 1/12
...
[hyperframes] browser-playable copies: 12/12
[hyperframes] media proxy pre-resolve: 12/12 ready, 0 failed (98581ms)
```

Once the copies are cached, a later check prints only the existing summary line.

## Why

A field report: `npx hyperframes check` on a 174 s project with 12 videos in 14 nested sub-compositions printed nothing after font setup for more than 6 minutes, and the user gave up. Reproduced with a generated project of the same shape:

| 12 clips, 1080p, 14.5 s each | check, first run | check, copies cached |
|---|---|---|
| h264 | 7-8 s | |
| HEVC | 48-53 s | |
| HEVC HLG (10-bit HDR) | 97-107 s, of which 93-98 s is making the copies | 5-9 s |

These timings are from an 8-core Linux box. One 30 s 4K HEVC clip alone takes 32 s to copy there. The copies are full-size and full-length, two at a time, so a dozen phone clips on a laptop take several minutes. This step runs before the check's deadline clock starts and had no output until it finished, so it looked like a hang.

## How

- `resolveProxies` (studio-server) takes an optional callback that runs as each copy settles. Publish is unchanged.
- `preResolveHostileMediaProxies` uses the existing `getProxyCachePath` to count the copies that are not cached yet. When some are missing, it announces them and counts each one as it settles. All lines go to stderr, so `check --json` stdout stays pure JSON.

Not in this PR: making the copies faster (smaller copies sized to the composition, or hardware encoding on macOS). Those change the copies preview and publish share, so they need their own decision.

## Verification

- Unit tests: the start line and the count appear only when some copies are missing, and a fully cached run prints only the summary. `resolveProxies` calls the callback once per source. Each test fails when its behaviour is removed: always announcing, never counting, never calling the callback.
- Ran the built CLI on the generated HLG project, from an empty cache and then cached; the output above is from that run.
- `checkBrowser` tests passed 3 runs in a row. Typecheck, lint, format and fallow are green.

title: perf(core): reuse fonts, asset paths and scene parses across a page build
body:
> **Now targets `main`.** It was stacked on #5893, which merged as 0d51eb0de on 2026-10-21; main is merged in at 41ee6f658 (see "Merged main after #5893"). ## What A heavy project's page builds faster, and the built page stays byte-for-byte the same. Three changes, one commit each: 1. **Google Fonts:** with a warm font cache, a build no longer asks fonts.googleapis.com again. An offline build with a warm cache now makes no network request. 2. **Inlined assets:** a build resolves (realpaths) and reads each inlined asset once, not once per `url()` per mount. The preview's `onRead` tracker also hears about each path once per build. 3. **Scenes mounted many times:** a scene file is read, hf-id stamped, parsed and CSS-scoped once per build. Only the scope selector, ids and variables are done per mount. ## Why The Desktop perf handoff ranks these as the next server-side page-build costs after #5893, measured on the real heavy project: - inlining sub-compositions: about 1.2 s, of which CSS scoping is 0.84 s; - per-asset `realpath` checks: about 0.73 s; - Google Fonts fetched again on every build, although a cache is written. Root causes: 1. **Fonts.** The woff2 files were cached on disk. The CSS lookup that names them (`fetchGoogleFontCss`) was cached only in a per-process `Map`. Every new process therefore asked the network before it could reach the woff2 cache. Offline, the lookup failed and the warm woff2 cache was never read, so the fonts went unresolved. This was a check-order problem: the disk cache sat behind a lookup that was never on disk. Keys and TTL were not involved. 2. **Asset paths.** #5893 memoized `resolveEntryPath`. The inlining pass (`maybeInlineRelativeAssetUrl`, used for render, snapshot and every build with `inlineAssets` on) still called `resolveWithinProject`, and so `isSafePath`, for every `url()`, `src` and `srcset` of every mount. Each call realpaths the path and its ancestors. It then statted, read and base64-encoded the same file again. In the preview build (`inlineAssets: false`) the remaining per-mount cost was `onRead`: the studio's `recordPreviewRead` realpaths and readlinks every path it is given, and the bundler gave it the same sibling paths on every mount. 3. **Scenes.** For every mount, `inlineSubCompositions` called `resolveHtml`, which read the file and ran `ensureHfIds` (a parse and a serialize). It then parsed the file four times: twice in `checkSubCompositionUsability` and twice to mount it. Finally it ran postcss over each `

"NEW" : "HOT", stat: m * 3, caption: `Caption ${m}`, tone: ["calm", "bold", "warm"][m % 3], }; hosts.push( `
`, ); } writeFileSync( join(out, "index.html"), `
${hosts.join("\n")}
`, ); console.log(JSON.stringify({ out, scenes: SCENES, mounts: MOUNTS, rules: RULES, elements: ELEMENTS })); ``` Each build runs in a fresh `node` process (`env -u NODE_ENV`), so in-memory caches start empty, as they do on a new app launch. The font cache on disk is warm. Google Fonts is a local zero-latency mock, so font time here does not include network time; the network requests avoided are counted instead. Preview mode uses `PREVIEW_BUNDLE_OPTIONS` + `stampHfIds` + an `onRead` that calls studio-server's real `recordPreviewRead`. Render mode uses the default options (`inlineAssets` on, runtime inlined). Variants run in rotated order every round (base, 1, 2, 3; then 1, 2, 3, base; …). Each variant is the dist built at its commit, so per-item deltas are cumulative steps. **Not measured here:** the real 1.3 GB project, any Mac, the Desktop app, and network time for the font lookups. On the real project the per-item costs above come from the handoff's profiles, not from this PR. macOS `realpath` and `readlink` are much slower than on this Linux pod, so item 2's share may differ there. ## Not changed These are the next costs in the profile of the generated project; none is touched here: - `autoHealMissingCompositionIds`: about 1.3 to 1.6 s, mostly `getElementById` and linkedom `id` reads; - `parsesAsScript`: about 0.5 s; - `enforceCompositionPixelSizing`: about 0.4 s; - `namespaceCollidingSvgIds`: about 0.45 s; - the font step (`injectDeterministicFontFaces`): about 2.5 s of CPU on a 15 MB page, mostly parsing and scanning the whole page. ## Test plan - [x] Unit tests added: - `deterministicFonts-cssDiskCache.test.ts`: a warm cache in a new process makes no fetch and gives the same page; a faceless or 503 lookup is asked again. Fails on base. - `inlineSubCompositions.reuse.test.ts`: 3 mounts parse the file twice in total (file + body), not 12 as on base; each mount gets its own scope, variables and rewritten asset paths; `ensureHfIds` runs once for 4 mounts (4 on base). - `compositionScoping.scoper.test.ts`: the fuzz and mutation checks above, and postcss parses a sheet once for 4 mounts. - `pageBuild.golden.test.ts`: the byte-identity goldens. - [x] `packages/core`: 219 files, 4779 tests pass. `packages/producer` unit and `packages/studio-server` pass. title: fix(engine): a sharp sound in a film's first moments no longer grows louder with each audio pass
body:
**Changes the audio bytes of every render with sound; merge waits on a product sign-off.**

## What

Every AAC encode now starts in a stretch of digital silence that is dropped afterwards. A sharp sound in a film's first moments no longer gets louder each time the audio is encoded again.

## Why

A film whose soundtrack opens on a very quiet noise floor and then hits a sharp sound came out with that sound much louder than authored. Each extra encode made it louder again. On the `dogs-captions` fixture, the onset at 78 ms has a sample peak of 0.25 in the mix:

- 0.43 after the mixer's encode
- 0.72 after the assemble pad encode
- 1.02 after one true-peak correction

The -1 dBTP loop then turned the whole film down 4.2 dB over three correction passes to hold that one onset under the ceiling.

**Root cause.** The built-in ffmpeg AAC encoder starts every stream with its rate control cold. When the first frame is quiet but not silent (here a -70 dBFS floor that still costs about 3200 bits), lambda stays around 120-230. The first loud block then switches the right channel to eight short windows. Its first window group codes band 0, where the low-frequency energy is, three scalefactor steps too coarse (sf 182, codebook 1, while the bands above sit at 156/145/142). A coefficient near 0.6 of a step rounds up to a whole step: 2^(3/4) = x1.69 = +4.5 dB.

A re-encode sees an input exactly 2^(3/4) louder, moves its scalefactor by exactly 3, and the same rounding repeats. That is why the growth is the same 4.5 dB per generation:

| generation | right-channel peak |
|---|---|
| source | 0.2513 |
| 1 | 0.4256 |
| 2 | 0.7185 |
| 3 | 1.2125 |
| 4 | 1.4437 |

The left channel stays at its level.

If the stream starts in digital silence instead, that first frame costs about 160 bits. The rate loop raises lambda to its cap, and the same block is coded at sf 140 with the escape codebook; nothing rounds up. I traced this with an instrumented ffmpeg 7.0.2 encoder that reproduces the numbers above exactly.

What it is not, and what does not matter:
- **Not timing.** Not priming, an offset or a doubled trim: alignment lag is 0 everywhere, and the error is confined to one output frame.
- **Not a tool or the decoder.** Not M/S, intensity stereo, noise substitution or TNS: each one off, and all four off together, still inflate. Both ffmpeg AAC decoders agree, so it is in the stream.
- **Not level.** The same source at -6 dB inflates by the same x1.69.
- **Only the cold start.** Any pre-roll before the first sample removes it: 1 to 47 frames or 10 s of silence, or 1 s / 10 s of the film's own audio. Constant-quality encoding (`-q:a`) never shows it.
- **Not one build.** It reproduces identically with ffmpeg 8.0.1; `ffmpeg-static` 5.3.0 bundles the same 7.0.2 encoder.

**Where our code starts a stream cold**, line numbers at the base of this PR:
1. `packages/engine/src/services/aacEncode.ts:48`: `Math.max(0, cut - PRE_ROLL_FRAMES)`. Every parallel segment got a 10 s pre-roll except the first, which started at t=0.
2. `packages/engine/src/services/aacEncode.ts:63-64`: audio under two minutes was one encode from t=0 with no pre-roll.
3. `packages/engine/src/services/audioMixer.ts:1612` and `:831`: short films without a master chain encoded AAC straight out of the mix graph, from t=0.
4. `packages/producer/src/services/render/audioPadTrim.ts:181-200` and `:208-232`: the pad and trim encodes re-encode the mixed AAC from t=0.
5. `packages/producer/src/services/render/audioPadTrim.ts:126-148`, called at `:501`: every true-peak correction re-encodes the pad output from t=0.

## Related work

Refs #5788 (parallel segment encode, which introduced the per-segment pre-roll this extends to the first segment) and #5942 (rebased on it; its segmented true-peak check is unchanged here).

## How

- **`aacEncode.ts` is now the one place an AAC stream starts.**
  - The first segment also starts `PRE_ROLL_FRAMES` early. The part before t=0 is digital silence (`adelay=...S:all=1`), and the existing packet slice that already drops other segments' pre-roll drops it.
  - The single-encoder shortcut is gone, so short audio takes the same ADTS + remux path long audio already used. The container is unchanged: same 1024-sample priming edit list, same packet count, same exact duration.
  - New options: `filter`, applied before the segment trim, and `segments`, to keep one encoder.
  - Output is pinned to 48 kHz, which the frame math already assumed.
  - `encodeAac` is exported from the engine.
- **`audioMixer.ts`:** every non-empty mix goes through the float sum and `encodeAac`. This removes the direct-to-AAC branch and its `floatWav` flag.
- **`audioPadTrim.ts`:**
  - Pad, trim and correction call `encodeAac` with their filter, on one encoder as before. The copy step keeps its argv runner.
  - The correction filter ends in `apad,atrim=0:T` instead of `-t T`, so its length stays exact.
  - The test-only `buildPadTrimAudioArgs` is deleted.

I tried an edit-list pre-roll (shift the timestamps, let the container skip the silence) and rejected it: output `-t` then cuts one frame off the end.

**Temporary disk use.** Short films (under two minutes, no master chain) now write the float mix WAV before encoding, about 384 KB per second of film (~23 MB per minute). Films of two minutes or more, and any film with a master chain, already wrote it. Peaks sampled every 0.2 s during real renders:

| render | peak mix work directory | peak mix WAV | left after the render |
|---|---|---|---|
| `style-9-prod` (16.1 s), before | 4 MB | none | nothing |
| `style-9-prod`, after | 10 MB | 5 MB | nothing |
| `dogs-captions` (144.4 s), after | 78 MB | 52 MB | nothing |
| `style-9-prod`, after, AAC encode forced to fail | 4 MB | n/a | nothing |

The work directory is removed in the `finally` around the mix and in `bail()`. With the forced failure the render fails as before and leaves nothing behind. No repo fixture has a root effects chain, so `master-fx.wav` was not exercised by a real run; it is written to the same work directory.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated
- [x] Manual testing performed
- [ ] Documentation updated (if applicable)
- [x] Comments follow CONTRIBUTING.md "Comments": they say why, not what, and a bug fix says what the code must do and how to reproduce the bug

**New test** in `aacEncode.test.ts`, "keeps a sharp onset at its level when the audio opens quietly, encode after encode". It builds 36 deterministic half-second signals: a -70 dBFS noise floor from the first sample, then a two-tone onset. Each goes through `encodeAac` twice, and the worst peak growth over the first 100 ms must stay under 1 dB.

| | ffmpeg 7.0.2 | ffmpeg 8.0.1 |
|---|---|---|
| this fix reverted | fails: 3 of 36 signals over 1 dB (`expected 2.7295612067400246 to be less than 1`) | fails: 3 of 36 over 1 dB (`expected 3.2549254843678943 to be less than 1`) |
| with this fix | passes, worst signal +0.10 dB, 3 runs in a row | passes, worst signal +0.10 dB |

Whether a signal triggers depends on the encoder build's arithmetic, so the test uses 36 signals; a future encoder could stop triggering on all of them.

**`dogs-captions` -1 dBTP loop.** The mixer encode of the fixture's float mix, then the assemble pad and true-peak loop, 3 runs each. The before run's audio is byte-identical to a real render's.

| | AAC encode passes (corrections) | correction gains | final true peak | loudness (source -17.9 LUFS) | onset sample peak (source 0.2513) | assemble audio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 6 (3) | -0.8, -2.5, -4.2 dB | -2.8 dBTP | -22.2 LUFS (-4.3 LU) | 0.7204 | 15.7-16.6 s |
| after | 4 (1) | -0.9 dB | -1.4 dBTP | -18.9 LUFS (-1.0 LU) | 0.2266 (the source minus the 0.9 dB correction) | 7.9-8.9 s |

Encode passes count the mixer's two parallel segments separately in both rows. A real `dogs-captions` render after the change measures -1.4 dBTP and -18.9 LUFS. The remaining -0.9 dB correction comes from ordinary generation overshoot later in the film (55.8, 82.8, 83.3 s), not from the onset; the before run has a similar set of frames.

**Outside the onset**, with each run's applied gain undone:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| codec error vs source, 200 ms to end | -25.2 dB | -24.9 dB |
| codec error vs source, first 100 ms | +4.0 dB | -39.5 dB |
| per-frame peak ratio vs source, median / 99th percentile | 0.997 / 1.087 | 0.997 / 1.081 |
| short-term loudness, before vs after | max 0.10 LU apart, mean 0.01 LU, over 142 s | |

The output is not bit-identical outside the onset: before and after differ by codec noise (-24.3 dB). Changing an encode's first frames changes the encoder's state for the whole stream; both are equally far from the source.

**Checks:**
- `bun run producer:test:unit`: 3 runs, all green.
- Engine `aacEncode`, `audioMixer` (all five mixer test files) and producer `audioPadTrim` unit and integration tests: green.
- `tsc` for engine and producer, `oxlint`, `oxfmt` 0.41.0, and `fallow audit --base origin/main`: clean.

**Listening pair** (first 12 s of `dogs-captions`' final audio): the two videos at the bottom of this description, first **before**, then **after**.

**Not measured:** the distributed render path (its plan-time true-peak correction now uses the same encoder), HLS output, the ffmpeg builds bundled on macOS and Windows, other fixtures' loops, whole-render wall time, and listening.

title: fix(cli): check no longer calls films moved by SVG masks, strokes or canvas static
body:
## What was wrong

`hyperframes check` warned `sweep_static: Nothing on screen moved under seek` on films that visibly move, and failed `keepsMoving` assertions with `motion_frozen`, when the motion is:

- an SVG `<mask>` or `<clipPath>` whose shape grows (a circle-radius reveal),
- a `stroke-dashoffset` line reveal,
- thin strokes drawn on a 2D canvas (a line chart drawing on),
- a WebGL canvas.

Snapshots at the same times showed the reveal growing, so an agent was told a moving film was static and went off to "fix" something that wasn't broken.

## Root cause

Both verdicts compare fingerprints from `motion-signature.browser.js` across seeks. The sweep uses the full signature and keepsMoving uses the quantized liveness. Both are built from a fixed list of DOM channels on each rendered element: box, opacity, clip-path string, a few paint properties, text, and an 8x8 downsample of media. Some paint never reaches any of those channels:

- Mask, clipPath and gradient children have no box (`checkVisibility()` is false), so they are skipped. Meanwhile the masked element's computed `mask` / `clip-path` stays the constant `url(#m)`.
- `stroke-dashoffset` and `mask-size` are not channels, and they don't move the bbox.
- The canvas channel draws the canvas into 8x8 with bilinear filtering, which reads only a few source pixels per cell, so thin strokes fall between them.
- A WebGL canvas without `preserveDrawingBuffer` reads back blank.

Measured in Chromium 152 with the exact injected scripts, each of these leaves both fingerprints unchanged while the screenshot changes.

## The fix

Every one of those paint paths ends up in the composited frame. So when the DOM fingerprints say "still", the rendered frames get the last word.

- **Comparison.** Frames are compared by `framesDiffer` in `motion-signature.browser.js`, still the single owner of "what counts as motion". It decodes the screenshots in the page, the same way the contrast pass does, so no image library is needed. A frame counts as moved only when at least 16 pixels change by more than 24/255 on some channel. Antialiasing or dither noise therefore cannot make a still film pass, while a 5x5 dot, a growing 1px line or a mask reveal all count.
- **`sweep_static`.** Before reporting, check re-seeks the layout samples and compares each frame with the first. A difference counts only if the first sample time, re-seeked, still renders its first frame; paint driven by the wall clock (an unregistered rAF loop) is not motion under seek. Any counted difference means no finding. If none differs, the original verdict stands, including the `error` for a stuck animation.
- **`keepsMoving`.** For each span the liveness calls frozen, check captures the frame every half `maxStaticSec`. Each capture is compared with the last one that differed, and spans split where the frames change. A span stays `motion_frozen` only if its frames really hold.
  - With `withinSelector`, the capture hides every box outside the scope's subtree, so only the paint the scope's liveness signs is compared; a still title over a moving background stays frozen.
  - A span marks only frames that still hold its signature, so the cut that ends one span never takes a sample from the next.
  - A scope that matched nothing is left alone, so it stays `motion_selector_missing`.

The DOM fingerprints stay as the fast path. A film whose fingerprint already moves never captures a frame (both paths pin this in tests). Only a film that would otherwise be flagged pays: one capture per layout sample for the sweep, and one per half `maxStaticSec` inside frozen spans for keepsMoving.

## What I measured

Tests (macOS, Chromium 152 headless shell):
- New `checkSweep.chromium.test.ts` drives the real `runAuditGrid` with the real page driver:
  - mask radius reveal, stroke-dashoffset reveal, a 1px canvas line and a WebGL fade: no `sweep_static`, and no `motion_frozen` under `keepsMoving`, both unscoped and scoped;
  - a still title: still `sweep_static` without a spec, and still `motion_frozen` for 0–6 s with one;
  - a still `#title` over a moving background: still `motion_frozen` within `#title`;
  - a canvas animated from `performance.now()` in a rAF loop: still `sweep_static`;
  - the still title's frames read as unchanged across 10 seeks;
  - one changed pixel reads as noise and a 5x5 square as motion.
- New pipeline cases in `check.test.ts`:
  - a stuck, still or audio-only signature with differing frames is not flagged;
  - keepsMoving scopes with changing frames are not frozen, with captures bounded to one per half `maxStaticSec`;
  - a span whose frames change once is split into both halves, asserted on `runAuditGrid` directly;
  - two frozen spans touching at a cut both stay frozen;
  - a scope that matched nothing stays `motion_selector_missing` next to a frozen one;
  - frames that change with the wall clock keep `sweep_static`;
  - neither path captures when the DOM already moved.
- Mutations, each turning only its own tests red:
  - sweep frame check off: 7 red;
  - keepsMoving frame check off: 7 red;
  - any changed pixel counts: the noise pin goes red;
  - frames always differ: the still-film pins go red.
- `check.test.ts`, `checkBrowser.test.ts`, `motionAudit.test.ts`, `checkSweep.chromium.test.ts`, `motion-signature.browser{,.chromium}.test.ts`, `motion-sample.browser.test.ts`: 266 passed, 0 skipped, three runs in a row.

Built CLI, main vs this branch, verdicts:

| Film | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| mask radius reveal | `sweep_static` warning | none |
| stroke-dashoffset reveal | `sweep_static` warning | none |
| 2px canvas line chart | `sweep_static` warning | none |
| WebGL fade | `sweep_static` warning | none |
| same four films with `keepsMoving` | `motion_frozen` error | none |
| still title (control) | `sweep_static` warning | `sweep_static` warning |
| still title with `keepsMoving` | `motion_frozen` error | `motion_frozen` error |
| 12 producer fixtures | none | none |

Wall time on a quiet machine (median of 3 alternating runs): the seven existing fixtures that reach the browser took 12.94 s on main and 13.06 s on this branch. They run no new code, so that is noise. A film headed for a still or frozen verdict pays for its frame captures: about +0.5 s on a 6 s still title.

## What I did NOT exercise

- Windows. The Chromium suites are opt-in there, as for the existing ones; the noise threshold, not per-platform bit-exactness, is what keeps a still film still.
- keepsMoving `withinSelector` is clipped to the scope element's own box. Paint a descendant throws outside that box is not compared.

title: test(studio): real-Chrome tests recover from a stuck Chrome launch or close
body:
## What

Studio's two real-Chrome tests no longer hang when Chrome gets stuck starting or closing on a Windows runner.

- `launchTestChrome` gives each launch 20 s. A launch that used up those 20 s is killed by Puppeteer and tried once more, whatever error it ends with: on Windows Puppeteer reports a stuck launch as "The browser is already running" rather than a timeout, because Chrome has already written its profile lockfile. Before, the launch had no limit, so a stuck launch used up the whole 60 s test budget.
- New `closeTestChrome` gives `browser.close()` 5 s, then kills Chrome and disconnects. Before, close waited for Chrome to exit, with no limit.
- `gsapValueAtPlayhead.browser.test.ts` and `gsapUndoRestore.browser.test.ts` use both helpers. Their assertions are unchanged.

## Why

A merge-queue run of the Windows studio-2 lane failed with one test, `gsapValueAtPlayhead.browser.test.ts`, timing out at 60 s. The PR in that run changes no studio file. Its two unbounded steps were the Chrome launch (`timeout: 0`) and `browser.close()`. Puppeteer's close sends `Browser.close` and then waits for the process to exit, with no limit.

Engine's browser tests hit the same close hang on Windows runners, and #5898 fixed it the same way (`closeTestChrome` in `packages/engine/src/services/__fixtures__/loopback.ts`). This PR gives studio the same close. The launch limit is new: studio launched with `timeout: 0`, so a launch that never finished could only end at the 60 s test timeout.

Measured on windows-latest before this change: the test alone passed 40/40, 160 launch/show/close cycles never stalled (launch at most 3.4 s, close at most 3.2 s), and six full studio-2 shards passed. So the stall is rare and only shows up under a full shard's load. The 20 s per launch is about 6x the slowest launch measured.

## Other Windows browser-test reds: different causes, not folded in

- Engine `videoFrameTransport.browser.test.ts` (a main push): its `beforeEach` (`newPage`, `goto`, frame setup) hit the 10 s hook limit. Launch and close were not involved; that run already had #5898's close.
- CLI `captureCompositionFrame.lateSubresources.browser.test.ts` (two runs): no hang. It finished in 6.5 s with a wrong value: the frame came back while a late image was still incomplete (`complete: false, width: 0`). That is a readiness race, followed up separately.

## Why a studio copy of the close helper

The CLI's `closeManagedBrowser` can't be used here: the CLI depends on studio, so importing it would create a cycle. Engine's `closeTestChrome` is an unexported test fixture, and studio doesn't depend on engine. One shared helper would need a shared test-utils package, which is out of scope for this PR. So the 15-line close is copied here.

## Tests

- `packages/studio/tests/chromeTestUtils.test.ts` (new, fake browser and fake launch, fake clock, no real timers):
  - a close that never settles gets the Chrome killed and disconnected
  - a close that finishes is left alone
  - a launch that times out is tried once more, and each try is bounded at 20 s
  - a launch that fails with Windows' "already running" error after the full 20 s is tried once more
  - any other launch error is thrown without a retry
- Mutations, each turning exactly its own test red: drop the kill, drop the retry, set the launch back to `timeout: 0`, retry only on `TimeoutError`.
- The new file plus both real-Chrome files: 3 runs in a row, 17/17 passed each, no Chrome left running.
- Windows proof on windows-latest (throwaway probe, not part of this PR). Real Chrome, real Puppeteer 25.11.0. Launches cut short at 300, 600 and 1000 ms all failed with `Error: The browser is already running for ...`, not `TimeoutError`. On ubuntu-latest every one was a `TimeoutError`. The probe then gave the helper a first launch that failed with that real Windows error, held to the full 20 s:
  - this PR's helper retried: 2 calls, a working Chrome after 20.5 s
  - the previous head's helper gave up: 1 call, failed at 20.0 s
- oxlint, oxfmt, studio `tsc --noEmit` clean.
